div.p: ON RELIGION. Our ancestors willed that the fixed and solemn ceremonies should be expounded by the knowledge of the pontiffs, the authorities for conducting affairs well by the observation of the augurs, the predictions of Apollo by the books of the seers, the averting of portents by the Etruscan discipline. By ancient institution, too, attention is given to divine matters: when something is to be commended to the gods, by prayer; when something is to be sought, by a vow; when a vow is to be discharged, by thanksgiving; when an inquiry is to be made by entrails or lots, by consulting them; when a solemn rite is to be performed, by sacrifice, by which also the warnings of prodigies and lightning-strokes are dealt with. So great, moreover, was the zeal of the ancients not only for preserving but even for enlarging religion, that, at a time when the state was most flourishing and most wealthy, by a decree of the senate the sons of ten leading men were handed over to the several peoples of Etruria, one to each, in order to acquire the discipline of the sacred rites; and for Ceres, whom they had established the custom of worshipping in the Greek manner, they sought a priestess from Velia, named Calliphana, by name, although that town had not yet received the citizenship, lest the goddess should lack a priestess skilled in her ancient rites. And although they had in the city a most beautiful temple of hers, when in the disturbance of Gracchus they were warned by the Sibylline books to placate the most ancient Ceres, they sent the Ten Men to Henna to propitiate her, since they believed her rites had sprung from there. Likewise our generals, when masters of their victories, having undertaken vows, often went to Pessinus to discharge them to the Mother of the gods.

ON ANCIENT INSTITUTIONS. Among the ancients nothing was done, neither in public nor even in private, without an auspice first being taken. From this custom auspices are even now interposed at weddings, who, although they have ceased to seek auspices, yet by the very name retain the traces of the old usage.

ON NATURAL DISPOSITION. Aemilius Lepidus, while still a boy, advanced into the battle-line, slew an enemy, and saved a fellow-citizen. The witness of so memorable a deed is the statue, wearing the boy's locket and girt with the bordered toga, set up on the Capitol by decree of the senate: for the senate thought it unjust that he should be deemed not yet ripe for honour who was already ripe for virtue. Lepidus therefore outran the maturity of his years by the swiftness of his brave deed, and carried back from the battle a twofold praise, when his years scarcely allowed him to be even a spectator of it: for hostile arms, drawn swords, the flying of weapons, the din of approaching cavalry, and the onset of clashing armies strike no small terror even into young men; yet amid these the boyhood of the Aemilian house had the strength to earn a crown and to seize spoils.

And, to begin from the cradles of the highest honour, Publius Valerius, who by his reverence for the people's majesty gained the name of Publicola, when, the kings having been driven out, he saw the whole force of their power and all its insignia transferred to himself under the title of the consulship, by moderation reduced the invidious eminence of the magistracy to a tolerable condition by emptying the fasces of their axes and lowering them before the people in the assembly. He also diminished their number by half, of his own accord taking Spurius Lucretius as colleague, to whom, because he was older, he ordered the fasces to be carried first. He also passed a law in the centuriate assembly that no magistrate should be willing to scourge or put to death a Roman citizen against the right of appeal. Thus, that the condition of the state might be more free, he gradually demolished his own power. And what of the fact that he pulled down his own house, because, set in a higher place, it seemed to have the appearance of a citadel—did he not come off as much higher in glory as he was lower in his dwelling?

The leader of Roman chastity was Lucretia, whose manly spirit, by the malign error of fortune, was allotted a woman's body. Forced to suffer outrage by violence from Sextus Tarquinius, son of King Superbus, when in most weighty words she had bewailed her injury in the assembly of her kinsmen, she slew herself with a blade which she had brought concealed under her dress, and by so spirited a death furnished to the Roman people the cause of exchanging consular government for royal.

Let us see, then, by how many steps of benefits fortune, with kindness never failing, led Q. Metellus from the first day of his birth to the very end of his appointed span, up to the highest pinnacle of a blessed life. It willed that he should be born in the city that is foremost in the world; it gave him most noble parents; it added the rarest gifts of mind and bodily strength, so that he might be equal to his labours; it provided him with a wife conspicuous for chastity and fruitfulness; it bestowed on him the distinction of the consulship, the power of a commander, and the splendid display of a most magnificent triumph; it brought it about that at one and the same time he saw three sons of consular rank, one of them also censorian and triumphal, and a fourth of praetorian rank, and that he gave three daughters in marriage and took their offspring to his bosom. So many births, so many cradles, so many manly togas, so many wedding torches, the highest abundance of honours, of commands, of every kind of congratulation; and meanwhile no funeral, no groan, no cause for sorrow. Contemplate the heavens, and yet you will scarcely find there such a state of things, since indeed we see that grief and pain are assigned even to the breasts of the gods by the greatest poets. A fitting end took up this course of his life: for when Metellus had passed through the span of an extreme old age and died by a gentle kind of death, expiring amid the kisses and embraces of his dearest pledges, his sons and sons-in-law carried him through the city on their own shoulders and laid him upon the pyre.

C. Sergius Orata was the first to set up hanging baths. This extravagance, begun from slight beginnings, advanced almost to whole seas of suspended hot water. The same man, of course, lest he should have his gluttony subject to the judgment of Neptune, devised private seas for himself, by intercepting the waves with estuaries and shutting up separate shoals of various fish behind moles, so that no storm fell so savage that Orata's table did not abound in a variety of dishes. With spacious and lofty buildings too he pressed upon the shore of the Lucrine lake, deserted up to that time, in order to enjoy a fresher use of shellfish; and there, while he plunged himself too greedily into the public water, he came to trial with Considius the tax-farmer. In which L. Crassus, pleading the case against him, said that his friend Considius was mistaken in thinking that Orata, removed from the lake, would lack oysters: for, if he were not allowed to seek them from there, he would find them on his roof-tiles.

Metellus, the chief pontiff, would not allow the consul Postumius, who was also flamen of Mars, when he was setting out for Africa to wage war, to leave the city, lest he depart from the sacred duties, and he imposed a fine upon him; and the highest authority yielded to religion, because it did not seem that Postumius could safely commit himself to the contest of Mars while the ceremonies of Mars were deserted.

The women dined sitting beside the men who reclined. This custom passed from the intercourse of men to the divine: for at the feast of Jupiter, he himself was invited to dinner upon a couch, but Juno and Minerva upon chairs. This kind of strictness our own age preserves more diligently on the Capitol than in its own houses, doubtless because it matters more that the discipline of goddesses should be maintained than that of women.

This spirit was not lacking even to the boyhood of Marcus Cato: for when he was being brought up in the house of his uncle Marcus Drusus, and the Latins had come to him as tribune of the plebs to obtain the citizenship, and he was asked by Quintus Poppedius, the leader of Latium and a guest of Drusus, to help the allies before his uncle, with a steadfast countenance he answered that he would not do it. Then, interrupted again and again, he persisted in his resolve. Thereupon Poppedius lifted him to a high part of the house and threatened to throw him down from there unless he yielded to his entreaties: but not even by this could he be moved from his purpose. And so this saying was wrung from the man: 'Let us congratulate ourselves, Latins and allies, that he is so small; for with him as a senator we could not even have hoped for the citizenship.' Thus with a tender spirit Cato grasped the gravity of the whole senate-house, and by his perseverance repulsed the Latins, who were eager to lay hold of the rights of our citizenship. The same Cato, when he had come in his boy's toga to pay his respects to Sulla, and had seen the heads of the proscribed brought into the hall, moved by the atrocity of the thing, asked his tutor, named Sarpedon, why no one could be found to kill so cruel a tyrant: and when the tutor answered that it was not the will but the means that men lacked, since his safety was guarded by a great escort of soldiers, the boy begged him to give him a sword, declaring that he would very easily kill him, since he was accustomed to sit upon Sulla's couch. The tutor both recognized Cato's spirit and shuddered at his design, and ever afterwards always brought him to Sulla searched for weapons. Nothing is more admirable than this: a boy, in the very workshop of cruelty, did not fear the victor who was at that very time butchering consuls, towns, legions, and the greater part of the equestrian order. Had you set Marius himself in that place, he would have thought more swiftly of his own flight than of Sulla's death.

It is hard to leave Publicola, but I am glad to come to Furius Camillus, whose passage from great disgrace to the highest command was so moderate that, when the citizens, the city being captured by the Gauls, sought his help while he was an exile at Ardea, he would not go to Veii to receive the army before he had learned that everything concerning his dictatorship had been transacted by solemn law. Glorious was the Veientine triumph of Camillus, distinguished his Gallic victory, but far more admirable that delay: for it is much, much more laborious to conquer oneself than the enemy, neither in adversity fleeing by over-hasty haste, nor in prosperity grasping it with unrestrained joy.

And to come from the senators as a whole to individuals: Lucius Cornelius the consul, in the First Punic War, when he had captured the town of Olbia, in fighting for which Hanno, the Carthaginian general, had most bravely fallen, carried out his body from his own tent with a splendid funeral and did not hesitate to celebrate the obsequies of an enemy himself, believing that that victory alone, both among gods and among men, would carry the least odium which had carried the most humanity.

And whereas she did not endure an outrage inflicted, Verginius, a man of plebeian birth but of patrician spirit, that his house might not be defiled by disgrace, did not spare his own blood: for, when Appius Claudius the decemvir, relying on the powers of his office, was too persistently seeking the violation of his maiden daughter, he led the girl into the forum and killed her, choosing to be the slayer of a chaste girl rather than the father of a corrupted one.

This good fortune is famous; that other is more obscure, yet set above a divine splendour: for when Gyges, puffed up in spirit by the kingdom of Lydia, abounding in arms and riches, had come to consult Pythian Apollo whether any mortal was happier than himself, the god, sending forth his voice from the hidden recess of the shrine, preferred to him Aglaüs of Psophis. He was the poorest of the Arcadians, but already advanced in years, who had never passed beyond the boundaries of his little field, content with the produce of his tiny farm. Yet Apollo, with the keenness of his oracle, had truly grasped the very end of a blessed life, not merely sketched it. Therefore to Gyges, vaunting insolently of the glitter of his fortune, he replied that he approved more highly the cottage that laughs in security than the palace gloomy with cares and anxieties, and a few clods of earth free from fear than the richest fields of Lydia filled with dread, and one yoke of oxen or two, easily tended, than armies and arms and cavalry burdensome with their devouring expense, and a little granary holding only what is necessary, which no one too greatly covets, than treasures exposed to the plots and desires of all. Thus Gyges, while he longed to have the god as a supporter of his vain opinion, learned where solid and genuine happiness lay.

2.pr. THINGS WISELY SAID OR DONE Now I shall set forth that kind of happiness which lies wholly in the disposition of the mind, and is not sought by prayers, but, born in breasts endowed with wisdom, shines out in prudent words and deeds.

To this man, surely, Aesopus the tragic actor ought rather to have given his son in adoption than to have left him heir of his goods—a youth of a luxury not only abandoned but even frenzied. It is agreed that he was wont to set out little birds, commendable for their song, bought at enormous prices, in place of fig-peckers, and to sprinkle his drinks with pearls of great value dissolved in vinegar, desiring to throw away as quickly as possible his most ample patrimony as though it were some bitter burden. Those who followed the sect of these two, the one an old man, the other a young one, stretched out their hands further: for no vice ends where it begins. Thence fish dragged from the shores of the ocean, thence chests of money poured into kitchens, and the pleasure of eating and drinking found at the cost of estates.

Praiseworthy was the religious compliance of the twelve fasces, more praiseworthy the obedience of the four-and-twenty in a like matter: for when Tiberius Gracchus had sent a letter from his province to the college of augurs, in which he indicated that, while reading the books pertaining to the sacred rites of the people, he had noticed that at the consular elections which he himself had held the tabernacle had been taken with a fault; and when this had been reported by the augurs to the senate, by its order C. Figulus returned to Rome from Gaul and Scipio Nasica from Corsica, and they abdicated the consulship.

Women who had been content with a single marriage were honoured with the crown of chastity: for they judged that mind in particular to be uncorrupted, of a matron of sincere fidelity, which knew not how to leave the bed of its laid-aside virginity, believing that the experience of many marriages was, as it were, a sign of a certain lawful intemperance.

Gaius Cassius struck with his fist Sulla's son Faustus, his schoolmate, who was praising his father's proscription in the school and threatening that he himself, when his age allowed, would do the same. A hand worthy not to defile itself with public parricide!

1e.1. And, to take something also from the Greeks: that famous Alcibiades—whether his virtues or his vices were the more ruinous to his country I cannot tell, for by the former he deceived his fellow-citizens, by the latter he crushed them—when as a boy he had come to his uncle Pericles and had seen him sitting alone and sad, asked why he wore such confusion on his face. And when Pericles said that by command of the state he had built the Propylaea of Minerva, which are the gates of the citadel, and that, having spent an enormous sum of money on that work, he could not find how to render account of his administration, and was therefore troubled, the boy said: 'Then look rather for a way not to render account.' And so a man most eminent and most prudent, failing in his own counsel, made use of a boy's, and brought it about that the Athenians, entangled in a war with their neighbours, should have no leisure for demanding accounts. But let Athens see for itself whether to lament or to glory in Alcibiades, since to this day it wavers in doubtful judgement of mind between execration and admiration of the man.

2.pr. ON COURAGE. Now that we have disclosed the beginnings and first advances of virtue, we shall pursue the deed itself, whose most weighty force and most effective sinews consist in courage. Nor does it escape me, Romulus, founder of our city, that in this kind of praise the first place ought to be assigned to you. But suffer yourself, I beseech you, to be outrun by a single example, to which you yourself also owe some honour, since by his benefit it came about that so glorious a work of yours, Rome, did not fall to ruin.

Equal to Furius in moderation was Marcius Rutilus Censorinus: for, having been created censor a second time, he summoned the people to an assembly and rebuked them in the gravest speech he could, because they had twice conferred upon him that power whose duration their ancestors, because it seemed too great, had judged should be shortened. Each acted rightly, both Censorinus and the people: the one taught them to entrust honours with moderation, the other entrusted them to a moderate man.

What shall I say of Quintius Crispinus, whose gentleness the most powerful passions, anger and the love of glory, could not shake? He had both received Badius the Campanian most kindly into his hospitality at his own home and, when he was seized by ill health, had restored him with most attentive care. By that man, after that wicked revolt of the Campanians, he was challenged to combat in the battle line; and although he was somewhat superior both in bodily strength and in courage of spirit, he chose to admonish the ingrate rather than to conquer him; for "What are you doing," he said, "madman, or whither does perverse desire carry you sideways? Is it too little for you to rage in public impiety, unless you have also slipped into private impiety? You alone, of course, find Quintius pleasing among the Romans, the one Roman against whom you would wickedly wield your arms—Quintius, to whose household you owe both the requital of honour and your own safety! But the bond of friendship and the gods of hospitality—pledges sacred to our blood, cheap in your breast—forbid me to engage you in hostile contest. Indeed, even if in the clash of armies I had recognized you, fortuitously laid low by the thrust of my shield-boss, I should have recalled the blade already pressed to your throat. Let it therefore be your crime to have wished to kill your host; you shall not be my host slain. Accordingly, seek some other right hand by which to die, since mine has learned to save you." The heavenly power gave to each the due end, since indeed in that battle Badius was cut down, while Quintius came off renowned for a distinguished fight.

Nor was Pontius Aufidianus, a Roman knight, endowed with any other strength of spirit, who, after he learned that his daughter's virginity had been betrayed by her tutor to Fannius Saturninus, not content with afflicting the wicked slave with punishment, killed the girl herself as well. Thus, that he might not celebrate her shameful marriage, he led her bitter funeral.

To our city, moreover, the end of the second Punic war and the conquest of Philip, king of Macedonia, gave the confidence for a more licentious life. At which time the matrons dared to besiege the house of the Bruti, who were prepared to interpose their veto to the abrogation of the Oppian law, which the women desired to be repealed, because it permitted them neither to use a garment of varied colour, nor to have more than half an ounce of gold, nor to ride in a yoked vehicle within a mile of the city, except for the sake of a sacrifice. And indeed they obtained that a right preserved for twenty continuous years should be abolished: for the men of that age did not foresee to what kind of adornment the persistent zeal of that unaccustomed gathering tended, or how far the audacity victorious over the laws would pour itself out. But if they could have foreseen the apparatus of the female mind, to which every day something more sumptuously novel is added, they would have resisted luxury rushing in at its very entrance. But why do I speak further about women, whom both the weakness of their mind and the denial of more serious occupations urge to confer all their zeal upon a more careful adornment of themselves, when I see that the men of former times, both of name and of outstanding spirit, slipped into this byway unknown to ancient self-restraint? And let this be clear from their own quarrel.

On a similar principle, P. Cloelius Siculus, M. Cornelius Cethegus, and C. Claudius were ordered, and even compelled, to give up the office of flamen because the entrails had been brought forward with too little care.

No divorce between wife and husband occurred from the founding of the city to the hundred and fiftieth year. The first, however, was Sp. Carvilius, who dismissed his wife on the ground of barrenness. He, although he seemed moved by a tolerable reason, yet was not free of blame, because they judged that not even the desire for children ought to have been preferred to conjugal fidelity.

Come, what a consul was Lucius Quintius Cincinnatus! When the conscript fathers wished to continue him in his office, not only on account of his outstanding deeds, but also because the people were attempting to create the same tribunes for the next year—neither of which could lawfully be done—the senate dispelled both, at once by checking the eagerness of the people and by compelling the tribunes to follow the example of his own modesty; and he alone was the cause that the most ample order and the people were safe from the reproach of an unlawful deed.

Come now, how famous and how memorable an example ought the clemency of Marcus Marcellus to be held! When Syracuse had been captured by him, he took his stand on its citadel, so as to behold from on high the fortune of a city once most opulent, then afflicted. But gazing upon its mournful downfall, he could not restrain his weeping. If anyone, ignorant of the man, had looked upon him, he would have believed it to be another's victory. And so, city of Syracuse, in your greatest disaster you had something of congratulation mingled with it, because, if it was not permitted to you to stand unharmed, you fell gently beneath so mild a victor.

What a severe guardian of chastity did Publius Maenius show himself to be! For he punished a freedman, very dear to him, because he had learned that he had given a kiss to his daughter, now of marriageable age—although especially he could seem to have slipped not from lust but from error. But he judged it of great importance that the discipline of chastity be implanted in the still tender senses of the girl by the bitterness of the punishment, and by so grim an example he taught her to carry not only her virginity unblemished but even her kisses pure to her husband.

Cn. Domitius, in an altercation that had arisen, reproached his colleague L. Crassus, because he had pillars of Hymettian marble in the portico of his house. Crassus at once asked him at how much he himself valued his own house, and when he answered "six million sesterces," said, "By how much, then, do you think it would be worth less, if I should cut down ten little trees from it?" "Even by three million sesterces," said Domitius. Then Crassus said, "Which of us, then, is the more given to luxury, I, who bought ten pillars for a hundred thousand sesterces, or you, who reckon the shade of ten little trees at the sum of three million sesterces?" A speech forgetful of Pyrrhus, unmindful of Hannibal, and now yawning in the abundance of overseas pay! And yet how much more cramped than the buildings and groves of succeeding ages, which they brought in; and they preferred to leave to posterity a refinement begun by themselves rather than to retain the self-restraint received from their ancestors.

But when, while Q. Sulpicius was sacrificing, his cap slipped from his head, this lost him the same priesthood; and the squeaking of a shrew-mouse, heard by Fabius Maximus and C. Flaminius, gave cause for laying down, the one his dictatorship, the other his mastership of the horse.

But that matronly honour might be the safer under the protection of modesty, they did not permit one who was summoning a matron to law to touch her body, so that her robe might be left inviolate by the touch of another's hand. The use of wine was once unknown to Roman women, lest, of course, they should slip into some disgrace, since the nearest step from Father Liber to intemperance is wont to lead to unlawful love. But that their chastity might not be gloomy and harsh, but tempered by an honourable kind of affability—for with their husbands indulging them they used abundant gold and much purple—in order to make their beauty more becoming, they reddened their hair with ash with the greatest diligence: for then no eyes of those lying in wait for others' marriages were feared, but both to see chastely and to be looked upon was guarded by mutual modesty.

But Fabius Maximus, when he perceived that the consulship had been held five times by himself, and again and again by his father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and ancestors, at the elections in which his son was being created consul with the highest agreement, dealt with the people as steadfastly as he could, that they should at last give the Fabian house a respite from this honour—not that he distrusted his son's virtues, for he was illustrious, but lest the highest command should be continued in a single family. What is more effective or more powerful than this moderation, which overcame even fatherly affection, which is held the most potent?

But Quintus Metellus, waging the Celtiberian war in Spain, when he was besieging the city of Centobriga and now, with the engine brought up, seemed about to throw down that part of the wall which alone could be torn away, preferred humanity to a victory near at hand: for when the people of Centobriga had set the sons of Rhoetogenes—who had gone over to Metellus—before the blows of the engine, so that the boys should not be destroyed by a cruel kind of death in the sight of their father, although Rhoetogenes himself declared that there was no hindrance to prevent him from carrying through the storming even at the cost of the destruction of his own blood, Metellus withdrew from the siege. By this so clement a deed, although he did not capture the walls of one city, he nevertheless captured the hearts of all the Celtiberian cities and brought it about that he had need of not many sieges to reduce them under the dominion of the Roman people.

But Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus, after the honours which he had borne most splendidly had been crowned by the gravity of the censorship, exacted punishment from a son of doubtful chastity, and, having punished him, paid the penalty by a voluntary withdrawal, avoiding the sight of his fatherland.

For what did Metellus Pius, the leading man of his times, mean then, when in Spain he allowed his arrivals to be received by his hosts with altars and incense? When he gazed with glad mind upon walls covered with tapestries of Attalus? When he allowed the most elaborately prepared games to be interposed among huge banquets? When he celebrated feasts in a palm-embroidered robe, and received golden crowns let down from the ceilings as though upon a heavenly head? And where these things? Not in Greece nor in Asia, by whose luxury severity itself could be corrupted, but in a rough and warlike province, especially when the most keen enemy Sertorius was blinding the eyes of the Roman armies with Lusitanian weapons: so far had his father's Numidian camp slipped from his memory. It is clear, then, by how swift a passage luxury flowed in: for he whose youth saw the ancient morals, his old age began the new.

To these must be added that a Vestal Virgin was judged by P. Licinius, the chief pontiff, to deserve admonition with the lash, because on a certain night she had been too careless a guardian of the eternal fire.

But whenever some quarrel had arisen between husband and wife, they would come to the chapel of the goddess Viriplaca, which is on the Palatine, and there, having spoken in turn what they wished, with the strife of their minds laid aside, they would return in concord. The goddess is said to have obtained this name from the appeasing of husbands; she is indeed to be venerated, and perhaps to be worshipped with special and choice sacrifices, inasmuch as she is the guardian of daily and domestic peace, in an equal yoke of affection rendering, by her very title, the honour owed by women to the majesty of husbands.

The grateful mind of our ancestors was not lacking to render rewards to the elder Africanus, since indeed they tried to adorn his greatest merits with equal honours. They wished to set up statues to him in the comitium, on the rostra, in the senate-house, and finally in the very chapel of Jupiter Best and Greatest; they wished to place his image, clad in triumphal dress, upon the couches of the Capitol; they wished to grant him a continuous consulship through all the years of his life and a perpetual dictatorship: by suffering none of these to be given him either by plebiscite or decreed by senatorial decree, he bore himself in refusing honours almost as greatly as he had borne himself in earning them. With the same strength of mind he protected the cause of Hannibal in the senate, when his own fellow-citizens, sending envoys, accused him as one stirring up seditions among them. He added too that the conscript fathers ought not to interfere in the affairs of the Carthaginian commonwealth, and with the deepest moderation consulted the safety of the one and the dignity of the other, content to have treated each as an enemy only as far as victory.

The humanity of the later Africanus too was displayed splendidly and widely: for when Carthage had been stormed, he sent letters around the cities of Sicily, that they should recover through envoys the ornaments of their temples that had been carried off by the Carthaginians and take care that they be restored to their former places. A benefit equally welcome to gods and to men!

I should say that this man of censorian rank had proved too savage, did I not behold Publius Atilius Philiscus, compelled in his boyhood by his master to make profit of his body, afterwards so severe a father: for he killed his own daughter because she had stained herself with the charge of debauchery. How holy, then, ought we to think chastity to have been in our state, in which we observe that even peddlers of lust turned out such severe avengers of it?

A like change appeared in the house of the Curiones, since indeed our forum beheld both the most grave severity of the father and the sixty million sesterces of debt of the son, contracted by the infamous injury of noble youths. And so at the same time and in the same household dwelt different ages, the one most frugal, the other most worthless.

But the divine power of Vesta preserved a pupil of the chief Virgin Aemilia, when the fire had gone out, safe from all blame: for when, as she prayed, she had placed upon the hearth a piece of fine linen, the best she had, the fire suddenly blazed up.

Such was the modesty between spouses: what, does it not appear consistent among the other ties of kinship? For, that I may signify its greatest force by the smallest indication, for a long time neither did a father bathe with his grown son, nor a father-in-law with his son-in-law. It is therefore manifest that as much reverence was paid to blood and affinity as to the immortal gods themselves, since amid those so sacred bonds it was believed no more lawful to strip oneself than in some consecrated place.

But Marcus Marcellus, who first taught that both Hannibal could be conquered and Syracuse captured, when in his consulship the Sicilians had come into the city to complain about him, neither held a meeting of the senate on that matter, because his colleague Valerius Laevinus happened to be absent—lest on that account the Sicilians should be more timid in complaining—and, when Laevinus returned, of his own accord brought forward the question of admitting them, and patiently endured those complaining against him. He also compelled those whom Laevinus had ordered to withdraw to remain, that they might be present at his own defence, and then, both parties having pleaded, he followed them as they left the senate-house, that the senate might more freely give its opinions. And when their complaints were rejected, he kindly received them as suppliants begging to be taken into his patronage. Besides this, having drawn Sicily by lot as his province, he yielded it to his colleague. The praise of Marcellus cannot be varied as often as he himself used new degrees of moderation towards the allies.

Equal to this deed is the humanity of the same man. When his quaestor was selling captives set up at the spear, a boy of outstanding beauty and gentlemanly appearance was sent to him. When he had ascertained about him that he was a Numidian, left an orphan by his father, brought up in the household of his uncle Masinissa, and that, without his uncle's knowledge, he had entered prematurely upon warfare against the Romans, Africanus judged that pardon should be granted for his error and that the reverence owed to the friendship of a king most faithful to the Roman people should be shown. And so, having presented the boy with a ring and a golden brooch and a broad-striped tunic and a Spanish cloak and an adorned horse, he sent him to Masinissa with horsemen to escort him, reckoning these to be the greatest fruits of victory—to restore their ornaments to the gods, his own blood to men.

There follows an example of an excellent name and a memorable deed. Marcus Claudius Marcellus, curule aedile, named a day for Gaius Scantinius Capitolinus, tribune of the plebs, before the people, because he had solicited his son for debauchery; and when Scantinius asserted that he could not be compelled to appear, because he held a sacrosanct power, and on that account implored the aid of the tribunes, the whole college of tribunes declared that it would not intercede to prevent the inquiry into chastity from being carried through. And so Scantinius, cited as defendant, was condemned on the single witness who had been tempted. It is agreed that the young man, brought forward to the rostra, with his face fixed on the ground persistently kept silent, and by his modest silence availed very much for his own vengeance.

But the trial of P. Clodius—with how great luxury and lust it abounded! In which, so that the defendant, evidently guilty of the crime of unchastity, might be acquitted, the nights of matrons and of noble young men, bought at a great sum, were paid out to the judges in the place of a wage. In which outrage, so foul and so manifold, you would not know whom first to detest, him who devised that kind of corruption, or those who allowed their chastity to become the surety of perjury, or those who exchanged their religion for debauchery.

It is no wonder, therefore, if for the increase and protection of this empire the persistent indulgence of the gods has ever kept watch, an empire in which the smallest matters of religion are seen to be weighed with such scrupulous care; for our state must be reckoned never to have turned its eyes away from the most exact observance of the ceremonies. In this state, when M. Marcellus, holding his fifth consulship, wished to consecrate, in fulfilment of vows undertaken, a temple to Honour and Virtue, first at Clastidium and afterwards at the capture of Syracuse, he was prevented by the college of pontiffs, who denied that one shrine could rightly be dedicated to two gods: for, they said, if any prodigy should occur in it, it could not be told to which of the two the rite ought to be performed, and it was not customary to sacrifice to two gods at once except to gods of a fixed pair. By this admonition of the pontiffs it was brought about that Marcellus set up the images of Honour and Virtue in separate buildings; and neither did the authority of that most eminent man prove an obstacle to the college of pontiffs, nor the additional expense to Marcellus, to prevent religion from being restored to its own proper course and observance.

Our ancestors also instituted a solemn banquet and called it the Caristia, to which no one was admitted except kinsmen and relations by marriage, so that, if any quarrel had arisen among persons closely related, it might be removed amid the sacred rites of the table and the cheerfulness of minds, with promoters of concord brought in.

How admirable too Tiberius Gracchus showed himself! For as tribune of the plebs, when he waged avowed enmity with the Scipios, Africanus and Asiaticus, and Asiaticus could not give security for the money adjudged against him and therefore had been ordered by the consul to be led into the public prison, and had appealed to the college of tribunes, when none was willing to interpose his veto, Gracchus withdrew from his colleagues and composed a decree. Nor did anyone doubt that in writing it he would use words steeped in anger against Asiaticus. But he first swore that he had not been reconciled with the Scipios, then read out this decree: that, since Lucius Cornelius Scipio on the day of his triumph had cast into prison the enemy leaders led before his chariot, it seemed unworthy and alien to the majesty of the commonwealth that he himself should be led to the same place: therefore he would not allow it to be done. Gladly then did the Roman people learn that their opinion had been deceived by Gracchus, and they pursued his moderation with due praise.

The memory of Lucius Paulus too must be grasped in this kind of praise. When he heard that Perseus, in a brief moment of time made a captive out of a king, was being brought to him, he went to meet him adorned with the insignia of Roman command, and when Perseus tried to fall at his knees he raised him with his right hand and exhorted him to hope in the Greek tongue. Having brought him into his tent, he ordered him to sit next at his own side in the council, and did not judge him unworthy of the honour of his table. Let the battle-line be set before our gaze in which Perseus was overthrown, and the sequence of these things which I have related; men will be in doubt by which spectacle they are more delighted: for if it is noble to cast down an enemy, no less praiseworthy nevertheless is it to know how to pity the unfortunate.

Metellus Celer too proved a keen punisher of a debauched mind, by naming a day before the people for Gnaeus Sergius Silo, on account of money promised to a mother of a household, and by condemning him on this one charge: for then not a deed, but the intention, was brought to trial, and it harmed him more to have wished to sin than it profited him not to have sinned.

Equally disgraceful was that banquet which Gemellus, a tribune's constable of free blood but, by his office, disfigured into a servile condition, prepared for the consul Metellus Scipio and the tribunes of the plebs, to the great shame of the state: for, having set up a brothel in his own house, he prostituted there Munia and Flavia, both renowned, the one for her father, the other for her husband, and the noble boy Saturninus—bodies of shameful submission, to be the mockery of drunken lust! Feasts for a consul and tribunes not to be celebrated, but to be punished!

L. Furius Bibaculus is overshadowed by so many and so illustrious consulships, and scarcely finds a place for an example after Marcellus, yet he must not be defrauded of the praise of a pious and religious spirit. As praetor he carried the sacred shields, the ancilia, by order of his father, who was master of the college of the Salii, with six lictors going before him, although by virtue of the privilege of his office he had exemption from this duty: for our state has always held that all things must be placed after religion, even in those matters in which it wished the honour of supreme majesty to be conspicuous. Wherefore they did not hesitate to make their commands serve the sacred rites, judging that they would have the governance of human affairs in their power if they had served the divine power well and steadfastly.

Youth rendered to old age such heaped-up and circumspect honour, as though the elders were the common fathers of the young men. Wherefore on the day of a senate the young men would escort to the senate-house some one of the conscript fathers, either a kinsman or a friend of their father, and, fixed before the doors, would wait until they should discharge also the duty of escorting him back. By this voluntary station they strengthened both their bodies and their minds for sustaining public duties without flagging, and were themselves teachers, by the modest rehearsal of toil, of the virtues that were soon to come to light. When invited to dinner, they diligently asked who would be present at that banquet, lest they should anticipate the arrival of their elders by reclining first; and when the table was removed, they suffered the elders to rise and depart before them. From which it appears how sparing and how modest a manner of speech they were accustomed to use at the time of dinner too, when these were present.

Gaius Claudius Nero too must be numbered among the rest as an example of remarkable moderation. He had been a sharer in the glory of Livius Salinator in crushing Hasdrubal. Yet he chose to follow Salinator triumphing on horseback rather than to use the triumph which the senate had equally decreed to him, because the action had been done in Salinator's province. And so he triumphed without a chariot—the more gloriously indeed, because the other's victory alone was praised, but this man's moderation also.

This humanity of Lucius Paulus reminds me not to be silent about the clemency of Gnaeus Pompeius. He did not suffer Tigranes, king of Armenia—who both had on his own account waged great wars with the Roman people and had protected with his own forces Mithridates, that most bitter enemy of our city, when driven out of Pontus—to lie too long as a suppliant in his sight, but, having restored him with kindly words, ordered him to set back upon his head the diadem which he had cast off, and, having imposed certain conditions, restored him to his former state of fortune, judging it equally fine both to conquer kings and to make them.

This was the gravity of the assembly; the following, of the senate. Titus Veturius, the son of that Veturius who in his consulship had been surrendered to the Samnites on account of a treaty disgracefully struck, when, on account of the ruin of his house and a grievous debt, he had been compelled, a mere youth, to give himself as a bondsman to Publius Plotius, and was afflicted by him with servile beatings because he had refused to suffer debauchery, laid a complaint before the consuls. Informed of this matter by them, the senate ordered Plotius to be led to prison: for it willed that chastity, in whatever station it was placed, should be safe to Roman blood.

But chiefly criminal was the lust of Catiline: for, seized by a mad love of Aurelia Orestilla, when he saw one obstacle preventing them from being joined in marriage, he made away by poison with his own son, whom he had as his only one and now of pubescent age, and at once kindled the marital torch from his pyre, and discharged his childlessness to his new wife in the place of a gift. Then, conducting himself as a citizen with the same spirit with which he had conducted himself as a father, he paid the penalty equally to the shade of his son and to his country, wickedly assailed.

1e.1. But Campanian luxury was exceedingly useful to our state: for, embracing with its enticements Hannibal, unconquered in arms, it handed him over to be conquered by the Roman soldier. It called forth that most vigilant leader, it called forth that most keen army, to sleep and pleasures, with lavish feasts, abundant wine, the fragrance of unguents, and a too-wanton use of love. And then at last was Punic ferocity broken and bruised, when the Seplasia and Alba began to be its camp. What, then, is fouler than these vices, what even more ruinous, by which virtue is worn away, victories grow languid, glory lulled to sleep is turned into infamy, and the strength of mind and body alike is overpowered, so that you would not know whether it should be held more pernicious to be captured by enemies or by them?

1e.2. These same vices entangled the city of the Volsinians too in grave and shameful disasters. It was opulent, it was ordered in morals and laws, it was held the capital of Etruria: but after it had slipped into luxury, it fell into the depth of injuries and baseness, so that it subjected itself to the most insolent domination of slaves. These, at first very few daring to enter the senatorial order, soon seized the whole state, ordered wills to be written at their own pleasure, forbade the banquets and gatherings of freeborn men, married the daughters of their masters. Finally they sanctioned by law that their debaucheries should go unpunished among widows and married women alike, and that no maiden should marry a freeborn man whose chastity someone of their own number had not first tasted.

1e.3. Come now, Xerxes, rejoicing in luxury through the remarkable display of his royal wealth to such a degree that by an edict he set forth a reward for whoever should find a new kind of pleasure—how great a ruin of a most ample empire did he escape, while he was captivated by excessive delights!

1e.4. Antiochus too, king of Syria, was an example of no greater self-restraint. His army, imitating his blind and senseless luxury, had for the greater part golden nails fastened to its sandals, and procured silver vessels for kitchen use, and set up tents adorned with woven figures—a desirable plunder to a greedy enemy rather than any hindrance to one energetic for conquering.

1e.5. For king Ptolemy lived as an appendage of his own vices, and was therefore called Physcon. What was more worthless than his worthlessness? He forced his elder sister, married to their common brother, to marry himself. Then afterwards, having ravished her daughter by force, he dismissed the mother herself, to make an empty place for marriage with the girl.

1e.6. In keeping with its kings, therefore, was the people of the Egyptian nation, who, having gone out of the walls of their city under the leadership of Archelaus against A. Gabinius, when they were ordered to surround their camp with a palisade and ditch, all cried out that this work should be contracted out to be done at public expense. Wherefore minds so enervated by delights could not sustain the spirit of our army.

1e.7. But more effeminate still was the multitude of the Cyprians, who endured with an even mind to have their queens mount their chariots upon the bodies of women constructed, as it were, into steps, so that they might set the print of their feet more softly: for it would have been better for men, if only they were men, to lack life than to comply with so dainty a command.

2.pr. ON CRUELTY This is the partnership of vices: of the wanton countenance and the eyes clinging to ever-new desire, and of the mind flowing in dainty adornment and flitting through the various motions of enticements. But the bearing of cruelty is grim, its appearance savage, its breath violent, its voice terrible, all things full of threats and bloody commands. To grant it silence is to add increase: for what limit will it set for itself, if it has not been recalled even by the reins of reproach? In short, since to be feared lies with it, to hate lies with us.

This judgement of the mind was at work in the breasts of private citizens too: for when the city had been captured by the Gauls, and the flamen of Quirinus and the Vestal Virgins were carrying the sacred objects with the burden divided between them, and when L. Albanius, conveying his wife and children in a cart, had caught sight of them as they crossed the Sublician bridge and began to climb the slope that leads to the Janiculum, being closer to public religion than to private affection, he ordered his own people to get down from the cart, and, placing the Virgins and the sacred objects upon it, abandoned the journey he had begun and conveyed them to the town of Caere, where they were received with the utmost veneration. The grateful memory of this even to our own day bears witness to that hospitable kindness: for from there came the institution that sacred rites are called "ceremonies," because the people of Caere honoured them devoutly even when the condition of the state was broken, just as they would in its flourishing. That rustic and rather mean cart of theirs, opportunely capacious, might either equal or surpass the glory of any most resplendent triumphal chariot.

The elders at banquets used to sing, to the flutes, the outstanding deeds of their forefathers comprised in song, so that they might make the youth more eager to imitate them. What is more splendid, what indeed more useful than this contest? The young rendered to the old their due honour, and the age that had finished its course attended with the fuel of its ardour those entering on the active life. What Athens, what school, what foreign studies should I prefer to this domestic discipline? Thence arose the Camilli, the Scipios, the Fabricii, the Marcelli, the Fabii; and—that I may not be too long by running through, all together, the several luminaries of our empire—thence, I say, that most illustrious part of heaven, the divine Caesars, shone forth.

Not even the later Africanus suffers us to keep silent about him. He, as censor, when he was closing the lustrum, and in the sacrifice of the suovetaurilia the clerk recited before him from the public records the solemn formula of prayer in which the immortal gods were asked to make the affairs of the Roman people better and greater, said: 'They are good and great enough: therefore I pray that they may keep them forever unharmed,' and at once ordered the formula in the public records to be amended in this manner. This modesty of vows the censors thereafter used in closing the lustra: for he prudently perceived that increase had then to be sought for the Roman empire when triumphs were sought within the seventh milestone, but that for one possessing the greater part of the whole world it was greedy to desire anything beyond, while he was abundantly fortunate if he lost nothing of what he held. Nor did any other moderation of his in the censorship appear before the tribunal. Reviewing the centuries of the knights, when he noticed that Gaius Licinius Sacerdos, being summoned, had come forward, he said that he knew the man had committed deliberate perjury: therefore, if anyone wished to accuse him, he would use his own testimony. But, no one coming forward for that business, he said: 'Lead your horse across, Sacerdos, and gain by way of profit the censor's mark, lest I be seen to have acted in your case the parts of accuser, witness, and judge.'

How splendid an example of humanity bestowed, how pitiable an example of humanity denied did the same Gnaeus Pompeius prove! For he who had covered the brows of Tigranes with the royal emblem—his own head, stripped of three triumphal crowns, in his own kind of world had nowhere a place of burial, but, cut off from his body, was carried, deprived of a pyre, as the abominable gift of Egyptian treachery, pitiable even to the victor himself: for as soon as Caesar beheld it, forgetting the enemy he put on the face of a father-in-law and rendered to Pompeius both his own tears and those of his daughter, and took care that the head be cremated with very many and most precious perfumes. But if so mild a spirit had not existed in the divine prince, he who a little before had been held the pillar of the Roman empire—so does fortune turn the affairs of mortals—would have lain unburied. When Caesar heard of Cato's death too, he said that he both envied Cato that glory and that Cato had envied him his own, and he preserved Cato's patrimony intact for his children. And, by Hercules, the safety of Cato would have been no small part of Caesar's divine works.

And what wonder is it if the whole body of senators decreed this? Gaius Pescennius, a triumvir for capital cases, loaded with public chains Gaius Cornelius, who had served out his campaigns in the bravest soldiering and had four times been honoured by his commanders, in the name of valour, with the office of chief centurion, because he had had commerce of debauchery with a freeborn youth. When the tribunes were appealed to by him, and although he denied nothing about the debauchery but said he was prepared to make a wager that that young man had openly and publicly made profit of his body, they were unwilling to interpose their intercession. And so Cornelius was compelled to die in prison: for the tribunes of the plebs did not think it fitting for our commonwealth to bargain with brave men, so as to buy domestic indulgences with foreign dangers.

At the same crisis of the state C. Fabius Dorsuo gave a memorable example of religion preserved: for when the Gauls were besieging the Capitol, lest the regular sacrifice of the Fabian clan should be interrupted, girded in the Gabine fashion, carrying the sacred objects in his hands and on his shoulders, he passed through the midst of the enemy's outposts to the Quirinal hill. There, having performed everything in the customary solemn manner, he returned to the Capitol, with almost divine veneration, a victor over the victorious arms as if conqueror himself.

This temperance of spirit was noted also in Quintus Scaevola, a most eminent man: for, brought forward as a witness against a defendant, when he had answered what seemed greatly likely to harm the safety of the man in peril, as he departed he added that he ought so to be believed only if others also affirmed the same, since for anyone to fall by the testimony of one man would be of the worst example. Thus he rendered both the faith due to his oath and wholesome counsel to the common good.

The spirit of Marcus Antonius too was not lacking in the understanding of such humanity: for he handed over the body of Marcus Brutus to his own freedman for burial, and, that it might be cremated more honourably, ordered his own general's cloak to be cast upon it, esteeming the fallen enemy with his hatred laid aside; and when he learned that the cloak had been intercepted by the freedman, stirred by anger he at once punished him, having first used this preface: "What? Did you not know whose man's burial I had entrusted to you?" The fields of Philippi gladly beheld his brave and dutiful victory, but not even those words of most noble indignation did they hear unwillingly.

1e.1. Led by the commemoration of a Roman example into Macedonia, I am compelled to make proclamation of the character of Alexander, who, as his warlike valour earned him boundless glory, so his clemency earned him a special love. He, while with tireless course he traversed all nations, being once caught by a snowy storm in a certain place, himself sitting in a lofty seat near the fire, noticed a Macedonian soldier, now worn out with age, stupefied by the excessive cold; and, making his estimate not of fortune but of the age of each of them, he came down and with those hands with which he had crushed the wealth of Darius set the body, doubled up with cold, in his own seat: that would be salutary to the soldier which among the Persians had been a capital offence—to have occupied the royal throne. What wonder, then, is it if under such a leader men counted it pleasant to serve so many years, to whom the safety of a common soldier was dearer than his own eminence? The same man, yielding not to any human being but to nature and fortune, although he was slipping away through the violence of disease, nevertheless raised himself on his elbow and stretched out his right hand to all who wished to touch it. And who would not have longed to kiss that hand, which, already overwhelmed by fate, was equal—more alive in humanity than in breath—to the embrace of a most mighty army?

1e.2. A humanity not of so robust a stock, but yet itself also to be honoured with remembrance, will be told of Pisistratus, the tyrant of the Athenians. When a certain young man, inflamed with love for his maiden daughter, had kissed her, having met her by chance in public, and his wife was urging him to exact capital punishment from the young man, he replied: "If we kill those who love us, what shall we do to those by whom we are hated?" A saying least worthy to have it added that it flowed from the mouth of a tyrant. In this manner he bore his daughter's injury; his own much more praiseworthily. Torn at, throughout a dinner, with endless abuse by his friend Thrasippus, he so restrained both his temper and his voice from anger that you would have thought a servant was being abused by a tyrant. As Thrasippus was leaving, too, fearing that out of fear he would withdraw too soon from the banquet, he began to detain him with familiar invitation. Thrasippus, carried away by the impulse of his roused drunkenness, spattered his face with spittle, and yet could not inflame him to vengeance for himself. He even drew back his own sons, who were eager to come to the aid of their father's violated dignity. And on the next day, when Thrasippus wished to exact punishment from himself by a voluntary death, Pisistratus came to him and, having given his pledge that he would remain in the same degree of friendship, called him back from his purpose. If he had done nothing else worthy of the honour of remembrance, yet by these deeds he would abundantly have commended himself to posterity.

1e.3. Equally gentle was the spirit of King Pyrrhus. He had heard that at a certain banquet of the Tarentines too little honourable talk had been held about him; he summoned those who had been present and inquired whether they had said the things that had reached his ears. Then one of them said: "Unless the wine had failed us, the things which were reported to you would have been play and jest compared with what we were going to say about you." So witty an excuse of their drunkenness and so frank a confession of the truth turned the king's anger into laughter. By this clemency and moderation he achieved that the Tarentines, when sober, gave him thanks, and, when drunk, prayed for his welfare. From the same height of humanity, when the envoys of the Romans were seeking his camp to ransom captives, he sent Lyco the Molossian to meet them, that they might come more safely; and that they might be received more honourably, he himself, in royal attire, ran out beyond the gate to greet them, not corrupted by the success of his fortunes into laying aside regard for courtesy toward those who at that very time were most at odds with him in arms.

1e.4. He reaped the due fruit of so gentle a nature at the very last moment of his fate: for when, under dire auspices, he had invaded the city of the Argives, and Alcyoneus, the son of King Antigonus, had brought to his father—for Antigonus was present as a defender to his hard-pressed men—Pyrrhus's severed head, rejoicing as though he had brought some most fortunate work of victory, Antigonus rebuked the young man because, forgetful of the sudden fall of so great a man and of human chances, he exulted with unrestrained joy; and, lifting the head from the ground, he covered it with the broad-brimmed hat with which, after the custom of the Macedonians, he kept his own head veiled, and took care that, restored to the body of Pyrrhus, it be cremated most honourably. He even ordered Pyrrhus's son Helenus, dragged to him as a captive, to bear both the dress and the spirit of a king, and gave Pyrrhus's bones, enclosed in a golden urn, to be carried to his fatherland of Epirus, to his brother Alexander.

1e.5. The Campanians, however, when our army, with its consuls, had been sent under the yoke by the Samnites at the Caudine Forks, and was entering their city not only unarmed but even stripped, received it with reverence just as if it were a victor bearing the spoils of the enemy before it, and at once, by most kindly furnishing to the consuls the insignia of honour, to the soldiers clothing, arms, horses, provisions, they changed both the destitution and the disgrace of the Roman disaster. Had they used this same spirit on behalf of our empire against Hannibal too, they would not have furnished material for raging to the savage axes.

1e.6. Mention having been made of our bitterest enemy, I shall end the topic which is in hand with the works of his gentleness, which he showed toward the Roman name: for Hannibal did not suffer the body of Aemilius Paulus, slaughtered at Cannae, after it had been sought out, to lie unburied, so far as lay in his own power. Hannibal consigned Tiberius Gracchus, surrounded by an ambush of the Lucanians, with the highest honour of burial, and handed over his bones to our soldiers to be carried to his fatherland. Hannibal carried out with a lawful funeral Marcus Marcellus, slain in the Bruttian territory while he was reconnoitring the enterprises of the Carthaginians more eagerly than prudently, and, having presented him with a Punic cloak and a golden crown, placed him on the pyre. Therefore the sweetness of humanity penetrates even into the savage natures of barbarians, and softens the grim and ferocious eyes of enemies and bends the spirits most insolent in victory. Nor is it for it an arduous and difficult thing, amid opposing arms, amid swords drawn at close quarters, to find a peaceful path. It conquers anger, prostrates hatred, and mingles the enemy's blood with the enemy's tears. This drew forth even that admirable utterance of Hannibal, when he was determining the arrangements for the funerals of the Roman generals. Indeed, Paulus and Gracchus and Marcellus brought him somewhat more glory buried than overthrown, since indeed he deceived them by Punic cunning and honoured them by Roman gentleness. You too, brave and dutiful shades, were allotted obsequies not to be regretted: for as it is more to be wished to fall in one's fatherland, so it is more glorious to fall for one's fatherland, and you recovered by your valour the dignity of the final rite which had been lost through misfortune.

2.pr. ON GRATITUDE It has pleased me to set before the eyes both grateful expressions of mind and ungrateful deeds, so that to vice and to virtue their just reward of estimation might accrue from the very comparison. But since by their opposite character they have distinguished themselves, let them be separated also by our pen, and let those things hold the prior place which earn praise rather than those which earn reproach.

An equally foul end follows the punishment of the lustful centurion, that of Marcus Laetorius Mergus, a military tribune. Cominius, tribune of the plebs, named a day before the people for him, because he had solicited his orderly for debauchery. Nor could Laetorius bear the consciousness of that deed, but punished himself, before the time of trial, first by flight, then even by death. He had fulfilled the measure of nature, yet, though he had met his fate, by the verdict of the whole plebs he was condemned on the charge of unchastity. The military standards, the consecrated eagles, and the most certain guardian of the Roman empire, the severe discipline of the camp, pursued him even to the shades below, since he was trying to prove the corrupter of that purity of which he ought to have been the master.

Great care for preserving religion was also taken among our ancestors in the consulship of P. Cornelius and Baebius Tamphilus. For when, in the field of L. Petilius the scribe, beneath the Janiculum, the cultivators were turning the earth rather deeply and two stone chests were found, in one of which an inscription indicated that the body of Numa Pompilius had lain, while in the other were stored away seven books in Latin concerning the law of the pontiffs and as many in Greek concerning the discipline of wisdom, they took care that the Latin books should be preserved with great diligence; but the Greek ones, because they were thought in some part to pertain to the dissolution of religion, Q. Petilius, the city praetor, by authority of the senate, had burned by the sacrificial attendants in a fire kindled in the sight of the people: for the men of old did not wish anything to be preserved in this state by which the minds of men might be drawn away from the worship of the gods.

I feel what citizens, and what deeds and sayings of theirs, and with how . . . a compass of speech I am embracing. But since . . . many things must be said briefly, surrounded by an infinite number of persons and things excelling in renown, to furnish both . . . the plan of our purpose too has taken upon itself not to praise everything, but to recall. Wherefore, with kind indulgence, the two Metelli, Macedonicus and Numidicus, the greatest ornaments of their country, will suffer themselves to be told in brief. Most keenly had Metellus Macedonicus disagreed with Scipio Africanus, and their conflict, sprung from a rivalry of virtue, had advanced to grave and attested enmities; but yet, when he heard the death of Scipio cried aloud, he burst forth into the open and, with mournful countenance and confused voice, said: 'Run, run together, citizens! The walls of our city are overthrown: for unlawful violence has been brought upon Scipio Africanus, resting within his own household gods.' O commonwealth, at once wretched in the death of Africanus and happy in so humane and so civil a lamentation of Macedonicus! For at the same time he recognized both how great a leader he had lost and what kind of one he still had. The same man advised his sons to put their shoulders under Scipio's funeral bier, and to this honour of the obsequies he added that utterance, that it would not be that afterwards this office could be rendered by them to a greater man. Where are those so many quarrels in the senate-house? Where so many altercations before the rostra? Where the all-but-togaed battles of the greatest citizens and leaders? All those things, assuredly, his moderation, to be pursued with special veneration, blotted out.

This moved Gaius Marius, then commander, when he pronounced that Gaius Lusius, his sister's son, a military tribune, had been lawfully killed by Gaius Plotius, a soldier of the ranks, because he had dared to solicit him for debauchery.

King Tarquinius, moreover, ordered M. Atilius the duumvir, because he had given to Petronius Sabinus, having been bribed, a book containing the secret of the rites of the civil sacred ceremonies, which had been entrusted to his keeping, to be sewn up in a sack and thrown into the sea; and that kind of punishment was long afterwards prescribed by law for parricides, and most justly so, since the violation of parents and of the gods must be expiated by an equal penalty.

But Metellus Numidicus, driven from his country by a popular faction, withdrew into Asia. In which, when by chance a letter was handed to him as he was watching games at Tralles, in which it was written that his return into the city had been granted him with the greatest agreement of the senate and people, he did not leave the theatre before the spectacle was performed, nor in any part revealed his joy to those sitting nearest, but contained his utmost gladness within himself. It is agreed that the same man wore the same countenance both as an exile and when restored. So much, by the benefit of moderation, did he always keep a middle course between prosperity and adversity with firmness of spirit.

But, to run briefly over those too who, in avenging chastity, used their own grief in place of the public law: Sempronius Musca scourged with whips Gaius Gellius, caught in adultery; Gaius Memmius likewise pounded with hams Lucius Octavius, similarly caught; Carbo Attienus by Vibienus, and likewise Pontius by Publius Cerennius, when caught, were castrated; and the man who had caught Gnaeus Furius Brocchus exposed him to be debauched by his household slaves. To these it was no crime to have indulged their own anger.

1e.1. And to attach foreign examples to domestic ones: a Greek woman named Hippo, when she had been captured by an enemy fleet, threw herself into the sea, that by death she might preserve her chastity. Her body, washed up on the Erythraean shore, the earth nearest the waves covered, consigned to burial, with a mound that conceals it to this day; but the glory of her holiness, handed over to eternal memory, Greece by celebrating with the highest praises makes daily more flourishing.

1e.2. This is a more vehement, that a more deliberate example of chastity. When the army and forces of the Gallo-Greeks had been partly destroyed, partly captured, by the consul Gnaeus Manlius on Mount Olympus, the wife of the chieftain Orgiago, of marvellous beauty, was compelled to suffer outrage by the centurion to whom she had been handed over for safekeeping; and when it came to that place to which the centurion, having sent a messenger, had ordered the woman's kinsmen to bring the price by which they might ransom her, while the centurion was weighing out the gold, his mind and eyes intent on its weight, she ordered the Gallo-Greeks in the tongue of her own nation to kill him. Then, holding in her hands the head, cut off, of the slain man, she came to her husband and, casting it before his feet, set forth the order of her injury and of her revenge. What else than that her body had come into the power of the enemy could anyone say of this woman? For neither could her spirit be conquered nor her chastity captured.

1e.3. But the wives of the Teutons begged Marius, the victor, that they might be sent by him as a gift to the Vestal virgins, affirming that they would be, equally with them, free from the embrace of a man; and when this was not granted, on the next night they took away their breath with nooses. Better did the gods that they did not give this spirit to the women's husbands in the battle line: for had they been willing to imitate the courage of their women, they would have rendered the trophies of the Teutonic victory uncertain.

2.pr. FREELY SAID OR DONE But liberty, a thing of vehement spirit attested alike by sayings and by deeds, as I have not invited, so, coming of its own accord, I have not shut out. Placed between virtue and vice, if it has tempered itself in a salutary measure it earns praise; if it has poured itself out where it ought not, it earns reproach. And it is thus more pleasing to the ears of the crowd than approvable to the mind of the wisest man, inasmuch as it is more often safe by another's pardon than by its own foresight. But since it is our purpose to follow through the parts of human life, let it be related by our good faith with its own estimation.

But in matters that pertain to the guardianship of religion, I am not sure whether M. Atilius Regulus surpassed all men, who, from a most glorious victor reduced by the treachery of Hasdrubal and of Xanthippus, the Spartan general, to the wretched fortune of a captive, and sent to the senate and people of Rome as an envoy, that he, a single old man, might be exchanged for several young Carthaginians, gave advice to the contrary and returned to Carthage, not, indeed, ignorant to what cruel men, and to men justly hostile to him, he was returning, but because he had sworn to them that, if their captives were not given back, he would return to them. The immortal gods could surely have softened that savage cruelty; but, that the glory of Atilius might be the brighter, they suffered the Carthaginians to follow their own character, since in the third Punic war, by the destruction of their city, they were to pay the just penalties for having so cruelly tormented a most religious spirit.

So many families having been enumerated in a single kind of praise, the later Cato denies that the Porcian name, as though void of this glory, ought to be passed over in silence, relying on no small token of the highest moderation. He had brought into the city the Cyprian money with the greatest diligence and integrity. On account of this service the senate was ordering a motion to be introduced, that at the praetorian elections his candidacy should be considered out of the regular order. But he himself did not allow this to be done, declaring it unjust that something should be decreed to him that was granted to no one else, and, lest anything be made new in his own person, he judged it better to try the rashness of the Campus than to use the benefit of the senate-house.

How much more venerable toward the gods was the senate of our state! which, after the disaster at Cannae, decreed that matrons should not extend their mourning beyond the thirtieth day, so that the rites of Ceres might be performed by them, since, with nearly the greater part of the Roman manhood lying on that accursed and dreadful soil, no household was free of grief. And so mothers and daughters and wives and sisters of the recently slain were compelled to wipe away their tears, lay aside the tokens of their grief, put on white garments, and offer incense at the altars. By this firmness in maintaining religion a great blush was brought upon the gods of heaven for raging any further against that nation which could not be deterred from their worship even by the bitterness of its injuries.

As I am now attempting to pass to foreign examples, Marcus Bibulus, a man of the highest dignity and one who had held the highest offices, lays his hand upon me. He, when he was tarrying in the province of Syria, learned that his two sons of excellent disposition had been killed by the soldiers of Gabinius in Egypt. Their slayers Queen Cleopatra sent to him in chains, that he might exact vengeance for the most grievous loss by his own decision. But he, when this benefit was offered him—than which none greater could be granted to one in grief—compelled his grief to yield to moderation, and ordered the butchers of his own blood to be led back, untouched, on the spot to Cleopatra, saying that the power of this vengeance ought to belong not to himself, but to the senate.

1e.1. Archytas of Tarentum, while at Metapontum he plunged himself deeply into the precepts of Pythagoras, having with great labour and over a long time grasped the solid work of learning, after he returned to his country and began to revisit his lands, perceived that they had been spoiled and ruined by the negligence of his bailiff, and, gazing upon the ill-deserving man, said: 'I should have taken punishment of you, were I not angry with you': for he preferred to let him go unpunished rather than, on account of anger, to punish more grievously than was just.

1e.2. Too liberal was the moderation of Archytas, more tempered that of Plato: for when he had blazed up too vehemently against the fault of a slave, fearing lest he himself might not be able to discern the measure of punishment, he entrusted the arbitration of the chastisement to his friend Speusippus, thinking it would be disgraceful to himself if he allowed it that the fault of the slave and the punishment of Plato should deserve an equal censure. Wherefore I marvel the less that he was so steadfastly moderate towards his pupil Xenocrates. He had heard that Xenocrates had spoken many impious things about him: without any hesitation he rejected the accusation. The informer pressed him with a steady countenance, asking why he was not believed: Plato added that it was not credible that one whom he so greatly loved should not in turn be loved by him. At last, when the malice of the one sowing enmities had taken refuge in an oath, that he might not dispute about his perjury, he affirmed that Xenocrates would never have said those things, unless he had judged it expedient for himself to say them. You would think that his spirit had passed its life's station not in a mortal body, but in a heavenly citadel, and indeed armed, repelling from itself by an unconquered fight the assaults of human vices, and keeping all the numbers of virtue shut within the bosom of its own loftiness.

1e.3. By no means equal to Plato in the recommendation of letters was the Syracusan Dio, but, as concerns the displaying of moderation, of a more vehement trial. Driven from his country by the tyrant Dionysius, he had sought Megara, where, when he wished to meet Theodorus, the chief man of that city, at his house, and was not admitted, having been long and much detained before the doors, he said to his companion: 'This must be borne patiently: for perhaps we too, when we were in the grade of our dignity, did something of the sort.' By this tranquillity of mind he rendered the condition of his exile more placid to himself.

1e.4. Thrasybulus too must be laid hold of in this place, who led back into their country the Athenian people, compelled by the savagery of the Thirty Tyrants to leave their homes and wretchedly passing a scattered and wandering life, strengthened in spirit and in arms alike. He then made a victory remarkable for the restoration of liberty somewhat more glorious by the praise of moderation: for he interposed a plebiscite that no mention should be made of past matters. This oblivion, which the Athenians call amnesty, recalled the shaken and falling condition of the state to its former state.

1e.5. Of no less admiration is the following. Stasippus of Tegea, when his friends urged him to remove or thrust aside, by any means whatever, a rival grievous in the administration of the commonwealth, but otherwise an upright and accomplished man, said that he would not do it, lest, in the place which a good citizen held in the guardianship of his country, a bad and wicked one should seize it, and he preferred that he himself should be vehemently pressed by his adversary rather than that his country should lack an excellent advocate.

1e.6. The breast of Pittacus too was equipped with moderation. He, having gained the tyranny conferred by his fellow-citizens, only reminded Alcaeus the poet—who had used against him most obstinately both the bitterness of hatred and the powers of his genius—of what he could do in crushing him.

1e.7. The mention of this man prompts me to relate the moderation of the seven sages. Someone had bought a cast from fishermen drawing a net in the Milesian region. Then, a golden Delphic table of great weight having been drawn up, a controversy arose, they affirming that they had sold the catch of fish, he saying that he had bought the chance of the haul. This case, on account of the novelty of the thing and the magnitude of the money, having been brought before the whole people of that state, it was resolved to consult Delphic Apollo as to whom the table ought to be adjudged.
