The god answered that it should be given to him who surpassed the rest in wisdom, in these words: 'Who first of all in wisdom? To him I assign the tripod.' Then the Milesians by common consent gave the table to Thales. He yielded it to Bias, Bias to Pittacus, he at once to another, and so on through the whole circle of the seven sages it came at last to Solon, who transferred both the title of the highest prudence and the prize to Apollo himself.

1e.8. And, that we may render testimony of moderation to Theopompus too, king of the Spartans, when he had first instituted that ephors should be created at Lacedaemon, set thus against the royal power to come—just as at Rome the tribunes of the plebs are set against the consular authority—and his wife had told him that he had done this so as to leave his sons a lesser power, he said: 'I shall leave it, but a more lasting one.' Excellently indeed: for that power alone is safe which sets a measure upon its own strength. Therefore Theopompus, by binding the kingdom with lawful bonds, the further he drew it back from license, the nearer he brought it to the goodwill of his citizens.

1e.9. But Antiochus, when by Lucius Scipio the boundaries of his empire had been pushed back beyond Mount Taurus, having lost the province of Asia and the neighbouring nations, undissemblingly bore thanks to the Roman people, because, freed from too great an administration, he now enjoyed moderate bounds of his kingdom. And indeed nothing is so glorious or so magnificent that it does not require to be tempered by moderation.

2.pr. ON THOSE WHO, OUT OF ENMITY, WERE JOINED IN FRIENDSHIP OR KINSHIP. Since this matter has been illustrated by many and distinguished authors, let us pass over to the distinguished bending of the human soul from hatred to favour, and let us indeed pursue it with a glad pen: for if a calm sea after a rough one, and a clear sky after a cloudy one, are felt with cheerful aspect, if war changed into peace brings the greatest joy, so the bitterness of offences laid aside is to be celebrated with a bright narrative.

It was believed that the consul Varro fought so unsuccessfully against the Carthaginians at Cannae because of the wrath of Juno, since, when as aedile he was holding the circus games, he had placed, on the chariot of Jupiter Best and Greatest, a boy-actor of remarkable beauty to hold the trappings. This deed, recalled to memory some years later, was expiated by sacrifices.

Hercules too is recorded to have exacted both a grave and a manifest penalty for his religion being withdrawn from him: for when the Potitii had transferred the rite of his sacred ceremonies, which they had held as if by inheritance, assigned by him as a gift to their clan, at the prompting of Appius the censor to the lowly ministry of public slaves, all of them, who were more than thirty in number, men of full age, perished within a year, and the name of the Potitii, divided into twelve families, all but became extinct, while Appius himself lost his sight.

A keen avenger of his own divine power was Apollo also, who, when Carthage had been overcome by the Romans and he was stripped of his golden robe, brought it about that the sacrilegious hands were found cut off amid the fragments of his statue.

No less effective an avenger of contempt for religion was his son too, Aesculapius, who, when a grove consecrated to his temple had for the most part been cut down by Turullius, a prefect of Antony, to build ships for him, . . . in the very midst of that wicked ministry, when the party of Antony had been defeated and Turullius had been marked out for death by the command of Caesar, by the manifest powers of his divine will dragged him to the very place which he had violated, and brought it about that there above all he was killed by Caesar's soldiers, so that by the same death he both paid the penalty for the trees already cut down and secured immunity from a like injury for those still standing, and multiplied for the gods the veneration which he had always enjoyed in the highest degree among his worshippers.

Q. Fulvius Flaccus, moreover, did not go unpunished, because in his censorship he transferred marble tiles from the temple of Juno Lacinia to the temple of Equestrian Fortune which he was building at Rome: for it is said that after this deed his mind was no longer sound. Indeed he expired in the deepest sickness of soul, when he had heard that, of his two sons serving in Illyricum, the one had died and the other was gravely afflicted. Moved by his misfortune, the senate took care that the tiles should be carried back to Locri, and by the most circumspect sanctity of a decree undid the impious work of the censor;

just as, by Hercules, it avenged with a just punishment the wicked greed of Pleminius, the legate of Scipio, in plundering the treasury of Proserpina: for when it had ordered him to be dragged in chains to Rome, [he,] before pleading his cause, was consumed in prison by a most foul kind of disease, and the goddess, by the order of the same senate, and indeed by doubling the sum, recovered her money.

1e.1. As to the crime of Pleminius, it was well avenged by the conscript fathers; but as to the violent profanation by King Pyrrhus, she defended herself powerfully and effectively: for when the Locrians had been compelled to give him a great sum of money out of her treasury, as he was sailing loaded with his impious plunder, by the force of a sudden storm he was dashed, with his whole fleet, upon the shores neighbouring the goddess; and there the money, found unharmed, was restored to the keeping of the most holy treasury.

1e.2. But King Masinissa did not act in a like manner. For when his admiral had put in at Melita and had likewise carried off from the temple of Juno ivory tusks of extraordinary size and brought them to him as a gift, as soon as he learned whence they had been conveyed, he had them carried back to Melita in a quinquereme and placed in the temple of Juno, engraved with letters of his nation indicating that the king had received them in ignorance and had gladly restored them to the goddess. A deed befitting the character of Masinissa rather than Punic blood!

1e.3. And yet what need is there to weigh character by nation? A man born in the midst of barbarism undid another's sacrilege; a man born at Syracuse, Dionysius, took it for a kind of pleasure to follow up so many of his own sacrileges, as many as we shall now relate, with jesting remarks. For when he had plundered the temple of Proserpina at Locri, as he was being carried over the deep with a favouring wind for his fleet, he said to his friends with a laugh: "Do you see what good sailing is granted to sacrilegious men by the immortal gods themselves?" Having stripped also from Olympian Jupiter a golden mantle of great weight, with which the tyrant Gelo had adorned him from the spoils of the Carthaginians, and having thrown over him a woollen cloak, he said that the golden mantle was heavy in summer and cold in winter, while the woollen one was more suited to both seasons of the year. The same man ordered the golden beard to be taken away from Aesculapius at Epidaurus, declaring that it was not fitting that his father Apollo should be seen beardless and he himself bearded. The same man took away silver and golden tables from the shrines, and because there was written upon them, in the manner of Greece, that they belonged to the good gods, he declared that he was making use of their goodness. The same man would carry off the golden Victories and bowls and crowns which were held out by the outstretched hands of the statues, saying that he was accepting them, not taking them away, and that it would be utterly foolish to argue that, from those of whom we pray for blessings, we should be unwilling to take what they hold out to us. This man, although he did not pay the penalties he owed, yet by the disgrace of his son made satisfaction in death for the punishments he had escaped in life: for with slow step the divine wrath proceeds to its vengeance, and compensates for the tardiness of the punishment by its severity.

1e.4. That he might not fall into this, Timasitheus, leader of the people of Lipara, provided by a counsel useful to himself in a way different from that useful to his whole country, by his example: for when a golden bowl of great weight, which the Romans had dedicated to Pythian Apollo by the title of a tithe, had been intercepted in the strait by his fellow-citizens who were practising piracy, and the people were being urged to divide it, when he learned . . .

4e.2. To King Deiotarus, who did almost everything by auspice, the sight of an eagle proved salutary; for, having seen it, he kept himself from using a certain dwelling, which on the following night was levelled with the ground by collapse.

So greatly, moreover, were they held by love of their country, that for many generations no senator divulged the secret counsels of the conscript fathers. Q. Fabius Maximus alone, and he himself through imprudence, told what had been done in secret in the senate-house concerning the declaring of the third Punic war to P. Crassus, who was returning home as he himself was seeking the country, on the road, remembering that he had been made quaestor three years before, but not knowing that he had not yet been enrolled by the censors in the senatorial order—the one way by which entry into the senate-house was given even to those who had already held magistracies. But although the error of Fabius was honest, yet he was vehemently rebuked by the consuls: for they never wished silence, the best and safest bond of conducting affairs, to be weakened. Therefore, when Eumenes, king of Asia, most devoted to our city, had announced to the senate that war was being prepared by Perseus against the Roman people, it could not be known what either he had said or the fathers had answered until it was learned that Perseus had been captured. Faithful and deep was the breast of the state, fortified by the senate-house and the wholesomeness of silence and entrenched on every side, whose threshold those entering put off their private affection and put on the public. And so you would believe that not merely one man, but no one, had heard what had been committed to the ears of so many.

When the Etruscans were bursting into the city across the Sublician bridge, Horatius Cocles seized its farther end and, with tireless fight, held back the whole column of the enemy until the bridge could be broken down behind his back; and when he saw his country freed from the threatening danger, he cast himself, armed, into the Tiber. The immortal gods, admiring his courage, granted him to come through unharmed: for, neither dashed by the height of the fall, nor weighed down by the burden of his arms, nor driven about by any whirling eddy, nor even wounded by the weapons that were hurled from every side, he had a safe issue of his swimming. Thus one man turned upon himself the eyes of so many citizens and so many enemies—the citizens dumbstruck with admiration, the enemy hesitating between joy and fear—and one man drew apart two armies locked in the fiercest fight, repelling the one, defending the other. In short, one man brought as much protection to our city by his shield as the Tiber brought by its bed. Wherefore the Etruscans, as they departed, could say: 'We conquered the Romans, but were conquered by Horatius.'

Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, twice consul and pontifex maximus, and with a gravity of life equal to the splendour of his honours, waged long and vehement enmities with Fulvius Flaccus, a man of the same eminence. These, as soon as they were declared censors together, he laid aside in the Campus, thinking that those ought not to be at variance through private enmities who were publicly joined in the highest power. This judgement of his spirit both the present age approved and the ancient writers of annals have handed down to us to be praised,

And to begin from public acts: when Marcius was attempting to . . . his fatherland, and, with a huge army of Volscians brought up to the gates of the city, was threatening death and darkness to the Roman empire, his mother Veturia and his wife Volumnia did not suffer him by their prayers to carry out the abominable work. In their honour the senate adorned the order of matrons with most kindly decrees: for it ordained that men should yield the path to women, confessing that there had been more salvation for the commonwealth in the matron's gown than in arms, and to the ancient distinction of earrings it added the new distinction of the headband. It also permitted them to use purple raiment and golden trimmings. Besides this, it took care that a temple and an altar to Womanly Fortune should be built in that place where Coriolanus had been prevailed upon, testifying its mindful spirit of the benefit by exquisite cultivation of religion. This same spirit it showed also in the time of the Second Punic War: for when Capua was being besieged by Fulvius, and two Campanian women had refused to dismiss from their souls their goodwill toward the Romans—Vestia Oppia, a mother of a household, and Cluvia Facula, a courtesan, of whom the one daily sacrificed for the safety of our army, the other did not cease to supply sustenance to captured Roman soldiers—when that city was overwhelmed the senate restored to these women both their liberty and their goods, and declared that, if they should seek any further reward, it would gladly give it. That, amid so great rejoicing, the senators had leisure to return gratitude to two most humble women is remarkable, and still more that they returned it so promptly.

When Privernum had been captured and those who had incited that town to rebel had been killed, the senate, inflamed with indignation, was debating what should be done about the rest of the people of Privernum too. By a doubtful chance, therefore, their safety wavered, exposed at the same time both to victors and to the angry. But, when they perceived that their only help remained in entreaty, they could not forget their freeborn and Italian blood: for their chief man, asked in the senate-house what punishment they deserved, answered, "What they deserve who judge themselves worthy of liberty." By his words he had taken up arms and had inflamed the exasperated minds of the senators. But Plautius the consul, favouring the cause of the people of Privernum, offered a path of retreat from his spirited saying and asked what kind of peace the Romans would have with them if impunity were granted. But he, with a most steadfast countenance, said, "If you give a good one, a lasting peace; if a bad one, not a long-lasting one." By this utterance it was brought about that to the conquered not only pardon but even the right and benefit of our citizenship was given.

We have heard that Appius Claudius was often accustomed to say that business was better entrusted to the Roman people than leisure: not because he was ignorant how pleasant the state of tranquillity is, but because he observed that powerful empires are roused by the activity of affairs to the pursuit of virtue, and dissolve into idleness through too much repose. And indeed business, a thing forbidding in name, kept the character of our state in its proper condition, while repose, of soothing title, has stained it with very many vices.

Claudius Centumalus, ordered by the augurs to lower the height of his house, which he had on the Caelian Hill, because it obstructed them as they took the augury from the citadel, sold it to Calpurnius Lanarius and did not disclose what had been commanded by the college of augurs. Calpurnius, forced by them to demolish the house, brought M. Porcius Cato, the father of the famous Cato, as arbiter with Claudius, under the formula "whatever it was right for him to give or do in good faith." Cato, when he had been instructed that Claudius had deliberately suppressed the priests' injunction, at once condemned him in favour of Calpurnius—with the greatest equity indeed, because a seller in good faith ought neither to raise the hope of advantages nor to obscure the knowledge of disadvantages.

L. Sulla, whom no one can sufficiently worthily either praise or blame, because, while he sought victories, he displayed a Scipio to the Roman people, and while he exercised them, a Hannibal—for, having admirably defended the authority of the nobility, he cruelly flooded the whole city and all the parts of Italy with rivers of civil blood—ordered four legions of the opposing party, which had followed his pledge, to be cut down in the public villa which was in the Campus Martius, while they in vain implored the pity of his deceitful right hand. Their pitiable cries the ears of the trembling city received; the Tiber, impatient of so great a burden, was forced to carry their bodies, mangled by the sword, on its bloodied waters. Five thousand men of Praeneste, called out beyond the walls of the town with hope of safety given through P. Cethegus, when they had thrown down their arms and stretched their bodies on the ground, he had killed and at once scattered through the fields. Four thousand seven hundred slain by the edict of his dire proscription he entered in the public records, so that, of course, the memory of so glorious a deed should not fade away. Nor content to rage against those who had disagreed with him in arms, he added to the number of the proscribed even citizens of quiet mind, sought out by a name-caller on account of the greatness of their money. Against women too he drew his swords, as though too little glutted by the slaughter of men. This too is a token of his insatiable ferocity: he wished the severed heads of the wretched men, all but retaining their countenance and breath, to be brought into his sight, so that he might devour them with his eyes, since with his mouth it was wicked. How cruelly, moreover, did he conduct himself toward the praetor M. Marius! Whom, dragged through the mouths of the crowd to the tomb of the Lutatian house, he did not deprive of life before he had torn out his unhappy eyes and broken each part of his body. I seem scarcely to be telling things like the truth: but he even slew on the spot M. Plaetorius, because he had fallen lifeless at his torture—a novel punisher of pity, with whom to look upon crime with reluctant mind was to commit crime. But did he at least spare the shades of the dead? Not at all: for the ashes of C. Marius, whose quaestor, though afterwards his enemy, he had once been, he dug up and scattered in the channel of the Anio. Lo, by what deeds he thought the name of fortunate should be claimed!

How greatly, moreover, the magistrates of old bore themselves in maintaining their own majesty and that of the Roman people may be recognized from this, that among the other tokens of preserving their gravity they also guarded this with great persistence, never to give answers to Greeks except in Latin. Indeed they compelled even those very men, after shaking off the volubility of tongue in which they are most powerful, to speak through an interpreter, and that not only in our city but even in Greece and Asia, doubtless so that the honour of the Latin voice might be spread more venerably through all nations. Nor were they lacking in zeal for learning, but they judged that in no matter ought the Greek cloak to be set under the toga, deeming it unworthy that the weight and authority of empire should be surrendered to the allurements and sweetness of letters.

Cloelia makes me forgetful of my plan, having dared an exploit almost at the same time, and certainly against the same enemy and in the same Tiber: for, given among the other maidens as a hostage to Porsenna, by night she passed the enemy's guard, mounted a horse, and by a swift crossing of the river freed herself not only from the siege but her country also from fear, a girl bearing before men the lamp of courage.

as they also did not wish the illustrious counsel of Livius Salinator in ending feuds to be unknown to posterity: for he, although, burning with hatred of Nero, he had gone into exile, chiefly afflicted by his testimony, yet, after the citizens recalled Nero thence and gave him as colleague in the consulship, commanded himself to forget both his own genius, which was most keen, and the injury, which he had received in its gravest form, lest, if with a disagreeing spirit he should be willing to share the command, by showing himself an obstinate enemy he should prove a bad consul. And indeed this inclination of mind to a more tranquil disposition, at a harsh and difficult crisis of the times, brought the greatest safety to the city and to Italy, because, striving with an equal onset of valour, they crushed the terrible Punic forces.

What too is more grateful than that Roman youth, which, in the consulship of Nautius and Minucius, of its own accord offered its names to the military oath, in order to bring protection to the Tusculans, whose territory the Aequi had occupied, because a few months before they had most steadfastly and most bravely defended the dominion of the Roman people? Therefore—a thing new to hear—lest a will grateful to the fatherland should seem to have grown idle, the army enrolled itself.

Thus the man of Privernum dared to speak in the senate; but Lucius Philippus the consul did not hesitate to exercise liberty against that same order: for, reproaching its sluggishness before the rostra, he said that he had need of another senate, and was so far from repenting of the saying that he even ordered a hand to be laid on Lucius Crassus, a man of the highest dignity and eloquence, who was taking it grievously in the senate-house. He, the lictor thrown off, said, "You are not consul to me, Philippus, because neither am I senator to you."

Scipio Africanus used to say that it was disgraceful in warfare to say "I had not thought it would happen," meaning, of course, that what is carried out by the sword ought to be conducted only after the plan has been explored and thoroughly sifted. With the highest reason: for the error committed to the violence of Mars cannot be corrected. The same man denied that one ought to engage with the enemy in any way other than either when an opportunity offered or when necessity arose. Equally prudently: for to let slip the chance of conducting an affair successfully is the greatest madness, and to refrain from battle once driven into a position where one must fight brings about the ruin of a pestilent cowardice; and of those who do such things, the one does not know how to use the kindness of fortune, the other how to resist its injury.

I have recalled a trial famous in its own time; but I shall report none that has even been blotted out by silence. C. Visellius Varro, seized by a grave illness, allowed three hundred thousand sesterces to be entered as owed by him to Otacilia Laterensis, with whom he had had a commerce of lust, with this design: that, if he died, she might demand that sum from his heirs—which he wished to be a kind of legacy, colouring a lustful liberality under the name of a debt. Then he escaped from that storm, contrary to the prayers of Otacilia. Offended that she had not, by his death, brought her hope of plunder to ripeness, she suddenly, from a compliant mistress, began to act the stripped-for-action money-lender, demanding the coins which she had caught at with as shameless a front as with an empty stipulation. In this matter C. Aquilius, a man of great authority and excelling in the knowledge of the civil law, having been brought in as judge, with the leading men of the state called to his counsel, by his prudence and conscientiousness repelled the woman. And if by the same formula Varro could both have been condemned and acquitted by his adversary, I do not doubt that he too would gladly have chastised his shameful and forbidden error: as it was, he himself checked the calumny of the private action, and left the crime of adultery to be punished by a public inquiry.

Yet C. Marius lightens the odium of this cruelty: for he too, by an excessive desire of persecuting his enemies, wickedly drew his anger, by butchering with ignoble savagery the most noble body of C. Caesar, a consular and censorian, and indeed at the tomb of a most seditious and abject man: for this alone was wanting to the evils of the then most wretched state, that Caesar should fall as an expiation for Varius. His victories were almost not worth so much, for, forgetful of them, he earned more guilt at home than praise in warfare. The same man for some time held the severed head of M. Antonius with joyful hands amid his feasts, with the utmost insolence of mind and words, and allowed the sacred rites of his table to be contaminated by the blood of a most distinguished citizen and orator; and he even received into his bosom P. Annius, who had brought it, spattered with the traces of the fresh slaughter.

Wherefore you are not to be condemned on the charge of rustic harshness, C. Marius, because you were unwilling that your old age, crowned with a twin laurel, illustrious with Numidian and German trophies, should, though conqueror of a conquered nation, be made more polished by eloquence—lest, I suppose, by the exercise of a foreign talent you should come forth a late deserter from the rites of your fathers. Who, then, threw open the door to this custom, by which now the ears of the senate-house are deafened with Greek pleadings? As I think, Molo the rhetorician, who sharpened the studies of M. Cicero: for it is established that he, before all foreigners, was heard in the senate without an interpreter. This honour he took not undeservedly, since he had assisted the highest force of Roman eloquence. Of conspicuous good fortune is the municipality of Arpinum, whether you wish to look upon the most glorious contemner of letters or the most abundant fountain of them.

I return now to Romulus, who, when challenged to single combat by Acron, king of the Caeninenses—although he believed himself superior both in number and in courage of soldiers, and it would have been safer to go down into battle with his whole army than alone—chose by preference to seize the omen of victory with his own right hand. Nor did fortune fail his undertaking: for, Acron being slain and the enemy routed, he carried off the spoils won from him to Jupiter Feretrius. So much for this; for valour consecrated by public religion needs no private praise.

There is also a famous example in the elder Africanus and Tiberius Gracchus of enmities laid aside, since indeed, from whose table's sacred rite they had come parted by hatred, from it they departed joined both in friendship and in kinship: for Scipio, not content to have shared concord with Gracchus at the feast of Jupiter on the Capitol on the authority of the senate, also at once there betrothed his daughter Cornelia to him.

A great example of a grateful people shone forth in the case of Quintus Fabius Maximus: for when, after the commonwealth had been administered salutarily through five consulships, he had died, the people vied in contributing money, by which a larger and more splendid funeral procession might be conducted for him. Let someone make light of the rewards of virtue, when he observes that brave men are buried more fortunately than cowards live.

What? Did liberty leave the people safe from its assault? Nay, it both assailed them likewise and found them equally patient. Gnaeus Carbo, tribune of the plebs, the most turbulent champion of the lately buried Gracchan sedition and likewise the most burning torch of the rising civil evils, led Publius Africanus—who was coming from the ruins of Numantia with the highest brilliance of glory—from almost the very gate to the rostra, and asked him what he thought about the death of Tiberius Gracchus, whose sister he had in marriage, so that by the authority of a most illustrious man he might add much increase to the conflagration now begun, because he did not doubt that, on account of so close a connection by marriage, he would speak something piteously for the memory of his slain kinsman. But Africanus answered that he seemed to have been lawfully slain. When at this saying the assembly, kindled by tribunician fury, had violently cried out against him, "Let those be silent," he said, "to whom Italy is a stepmother." Then, a murmur arising, "You will not bring it about," he said, "that I should fear unbound those whom I brought in chains." The whole people, rebuked a second time and insultingly by one man—how great is the honour of virtue!—was silent. His own recent Numantine victory, and his father's Macedonian one, and the ancestral spoils of conquered Carthage, and the chained necks of two kings, Syphax and Perseus, before the triumphal chariots, then closed the mouths of the whole forum. Nor was the silence given to fear, but because, by the benefit of the Aemilian and Cornelian clans, many fears of the city and of Italy had been ended, the Roman plebs was not free against the liberty of Scipio.

Weighty too, and indeed profound, was the opinion of Q. Metellus in the senate, who, when Carthage had been conquered, declared that he did not know whether that victory had brought more good or more harm to the state, since, just as he had been of service by restoring peace, so by removing Hannibal he had done some harm: for it was by Hannibal's crossing into Italy that the now sleeping valour of the Roman people had been roused, and one ought to fear lest, freed from a keen rival, it should slip back into the same slumber. Therefore he set on an even balance the burning of houses, the laying waste of fields, the draining of the treasury, and the blunting of the sinews of our ancient strength.

With much more spirit, and as was worthy of a military temper, did C. Marius conduct himself in a like kind of trial: for when C. Titinius of Minturnae was trying to despoil of her dowry his wife Fannia, whom he had deliberately married unchaste, after divorcing her on that charge, Marius, taken as judge between them, with the inquiry held in his presence, led Titinius aside and advised him to desist from his undertaking and restore the dowry to the woman. When he had done this several times in vain, forced by him to pronounce sentence, he condemned the woman of unchastity to one sesterce, and Titinius to the sum of the whole dowry, declaring beforehand that he had followed this manner of judging because it was clear to him that Titinius, plotting against the patrimony of Fannia, had sought marriage with an unchaste woman. And this Fannia is the one who afterwards, when Marius had been judged a public enemy by the senate, and smeared with the mud of the marsh from which he had been dragged, and was now being led into her house at Minturnae to be guarded, helped him with whatever aid she could—mindful that, because she had been judged unchaste, it should be set down to her own character, and that, because she had kept her dowry, to his conscientiousness.

Damasippus had no praise to corrupt, and so his memory is censured by a more licentious accusation. By his order the heads of the leading men of the state were mingled with the heads of victims, and the headless body of Carbo Arvina was fastened to a gibbet and carried about. So far either the praetorship of a most disgraceful man availed much, or the majesty of the state nothing.

With the greatest diligence, moreover, our ancestors retained this custom, that no one should interpose himself between the consul and the nearest lictor, although he might be walking together with him for the sake of duty. A son alone, and he a boy, had the right of walking before his father the consul. This custom was so persistently retained that Q. Fabius Maximus, five times consul, a man both long since of the highest authority and then of extreme old age, when invited by his son the consul to walk between him and the lictor, lest he should be crushed by the crowd of the enemy Samnites, to whose parley they were going down, was unwilling to do it. The same man, sent by the senate as a legate to his son the consul at Suessa Pometia, after he noticed that he had come forward, for the sake of his office, outside the walls of the town, indignant that of the twelve lictors no one had bidden him dismount from his horse, full of anger persisted in sitting. When his son perceived this, he ordered the nearest lictor to attend upon him. Obeying this voice at once, Fabius said, "Not, my son, have I despised your supreme authority, but I wished to test whether you knew how to act the consul: nor am I ignorant what is owed to the reverence of a father, but I judge public institutions to be of more weight than private affection."

Next after Romulus, Cornelius Cossus consecrated spoils to the same god, when, as master of the horse, he had met the leader of the Fidenates in battle and slain him. Great was Romulus as the beginner of this kind of inaugurated glory; but much also was gained by Cossus, in that he had the strength to imitate Romulus.

But humanity of this kind appeared remarkable also in Marcus Cicero: for with the greatest zeal he defended Aulus Gabinius, a defendant on a charge of extortion, who had driven him from the city in his consulship; and the same man protected, in two public trials, Publius Vatinius, always hostile to his dignity—doing this without any reproach of fickleness, and indeed with some praise, because it is somewhat more glorious that injuries should be overcome by benefits than that they should be requited by the obstinacy of mutual hatred.

To Fabius, moreover, even while he was alive, gratitude was returned with the highest glory. When he was dictator, his master of horse Minucius, by a plebiscite—a thing which had never before been done—was made his equal, and, the army being divided, had clashed separately in Samnium with Hannibal. There, having rashly entered upon a contest that was going to have a destructive end, he was preserved by the aid of Fabius, and both himself called him father and wished him to be hailed as patron by his own legions, and, having laid aside the yoke of equal command, subjected the mastership of the horse, as was fitting, to the dictatorship, and corrected the error of the imprudent crowd by this token of a grateful mind:

Wherefore we ought to wonder the less that the most ample authority of Gnaeus Pompeius so often struggled with liberty, and not without great praise, since with calm brow he bore being the sport of the license of men of every kind. Gnaeus Piso, when he was prosecuting Manilius Crispus as defendant, and saw that, though evidently guilty, he was being snatched away by the favour of Pompey, carried away by youthful impulse and zeal for the accusation, hurled many and grave charges against the most powerful defender. Then, asked by him why he did not accuse him too, "Give sureties to the commonwealth," he said, "that you will not, if you are accused, stir up a civil war, and I will send the judges into council about you before about the life of Manilius." Thus in one and the same trial he sustained two defendants, Manilius by accusation, Pompey by liberty, and the one of them he pursued by law, the other by declaration—the only means by which he could.

How wise was that deed of the consular L. Fimbria! Appointed judge for M. Lutatius Pinthias, a distinguished Roman knight, in a matter of a wager which the latter had made with his adversary on the ground that he was a good man, he never would conclude that trial by his pronouncement, lest either, if he gave judgment against him, he should rob an approved man of his reputation, or he should swear that a man was good when that matter was bound up with countless praises.

Much talk flowed even from that trial in which a certain man was condemned of theft who, on a horse the use of which had been lent to him as far as Aricia, had ridden up the further slope of that town. What else can we praise here than the scrupulousness of that age, in which such tiny departures from modesty were punished?

3.pr. WHAT WOMEN PLEADED CAUSES BEFORE MAGISTRATES FOR THEMSELVES OR FOR OTHERS Not even those women must be passed over in silence whom the condition of their nature and the modesty of the matron's robe could not restrain from keeping silent in the forum and the courts.

Munatius Flaccus too, a keener than more commendable defender of the Pompeian name, when he was being besieged by the commander Caesar, shut up within the walls of Ategua in Spain, exercised his maddened cruelty in the most savage kind of frenzy: for all the citizens of that town whom he had perceived to be more devoted to Caesar, he slew and hurled from the walls. The women too, the names of their husbands who were in the opposing camp being called out, so that they might behold the slaughter of their consorts, and the children placed upon their mothers' laps, he butchered. Some infants he ordered to be dashed to the ground in the sight of their parents, others to be thrown up and caught on spears. These things, intolerable even to hear, were administered at a Roman's command by Lusitanian hands—by the protection of which people Flaccus, walled about, was resisting with crazed obstinacy the divine resources of Caesar.

2e.1. We shall now pass over to those things in which, though there is equal grief, yet there is no blush of our state. The Carthaginians, having cut off the eyelids of Atilius Regulus and shut him in a machine in which sharpened goads stood out on every side, killed him by sleeplessness and the continuous strain of pain alike—a kind of torment scarcely worthy of him who suffered it, most worthy of those who devised it. Using the same cruelty, they laid our soldiers, reduced into their power in a certain sea-fight, beneath their ships, so that, crushed by their keels and weight, they might glut a barbarian ferocity by an unaccustomed manner of death, intending to violate the very sea by fleets polluted with so foul a crime.

2e.2. Their leader Hannibal, whose virtue consisted for the greater part of savagery, made a bridge of Roman bodies over the river Vergellus and led his army across, so that the land might experience the wicked passage of the Carthaginian land-forces as equally as Neptune did that of the naval ones. The same man would leave our captives, worn out by burdens and the march, with the front part of their feet cut off. But those whom he had led into his camp, joining pairs, generally of brothers and kinsmen, he forced to fight it out with the sword, nor was he glutted with blood before he had reduced them all to a single victor. With just hatred, then, but a tardy punishment nevertheless, the senate drove him, become a suppliant of king Prusias, to a voluntary death.

2e.3. As much, by Hercules, as it drove king Mithridates, who by a single letter destroyed eighty thousand Roman citizens scattered through the cities of Asia for the sake of trade, and sprinkled the hospitable gods of so great a province with unjust, but not unavenged, blood, since indeed it forced his spirit, struggling against the poison, at last to succumb with the greatest torment, and at the same time gave expiations for those crosses by which, on the advice of the eunuch Gaurus, lustful in his compliance, criminal in his command, he had afflicted his friends.

2e.4. Of Zisemis, son of Diogyris, king of Thrace, although the ferocity of the people itself makes his cruelty less to be wondered at, yet the rage of his savagery makes it to be related: for him it was no crime either to cut living men in half through the middle, or to force parents to feed on the bodies of their children.

2e.5. Again Ptolemy Physcon emerges, a little before the most foul example of lustful madness, the same to be reported among the chief tokens of cruelty: for what is more savage than this deed? His own son named Memphites, whom he had had by Cleopatra, the same his sister and wife, a boy of free-born form and best hope, he ordered to be killed in his sight, and at once sent the head and feet, cut off, covered with a cloak in a casket, as a birthday gift to the mother—just as though he himself were exempt from the disaster which he was inflicting on her, and not the more unhappy because, in their common bereavement, he had rendered Cleopatra pitiable to all, himself hateful. So much, with blind frenzy, does every cruelty boil up at its highest, when it has found a defence from itself: for when he observed with how great hatred his country held him, he sought a remedy for his fear in crime, and, in order to reign more safely with the plebs butchered, surrounded a gymnasium crowded with youth with arms and fire, and slew all who were in it, partly with the sword, partly with the flame.

2e.6. Ochus, moreover, who afterwards was called Darius, bound by the most holy oath of the Persians not to kill any one of the conspiracy which had with him crushed the seven Magi, either by poison or by sword or by any violence or by want of food, devised a crueller manner of death, by which he might destroy those hateful to him without breaking the bond of his religious obligation: for he filled with ashes a place fenced in with high walls, and, placing over it a projecting beam, he would set on it those received kindly with food and drink, from which, lulled to sleep by slumber, they would fall into that treacherous heap.

2e.7. More open and more foul was the cruelty of the other Ochus, surnamed Artaxerxes, who buried alive up to the head his sister Atossa, who was at once his mother-in-law, and his uncle, with more than a hundred sons and grandsons, set in an empty space, he transfixed with javelins, provoked by no injury, but because he saw that in these the greatest praise of uprightness and bravery among the Persians consisted.

2e.8. Roused by a like kind of rivalry, the city of the Athenians, by a decree unworthy of its glory, cut off the thumbs of the youth of Aegina, so that that people, powerful in fleets, might not be able to come down with them into a contest of naval strength. I do not recognize Athens borrowing a remedy for its fear from cruelty.

2e.9. Savage too was that inventor of the bronze bull, in which men shut up, with fires placed beneath, were forced, by a long and hidden torment, to give forth their bellowing breath, so that their wailings, uttered with the human sound of the voice, could not implore the pity of the tyrant Phalaris. And because he wished pity to be wanting to the wretched, he, shut up first in the most foul work of his own art, deservedly inaugurated it.

2e.10. Nor indeed were the Etruscans too little ferocious in devising a punishment, who allowed the bodies of the living, bound and tied face to face with corpses, so that each part of the limbs was fitted to its corresponding part, to rot away together—bitter torturers of life and death alike.

2e.11. Just as those barbarians, who, they say, after the entrails and viscera of slaughtered cattle have been taken out, insert men into them, so that only their heads project, and, that they may last longer for punishment, prolong the unhappy breath with food and drink, until, putrefying within, they are torn by the creatures which are wont to be born in decaying bodies. Let us complain now with the nature of things, because it willed that we should be subject to many and harsh discomforts of ill health, and let us bear it ill that the condition of heavenly strength was denied to the human state, when mortality itself, at the impulse of cruelty, has devised so many torments for itself.

3.pr. ON ANGER OR HATRED Anger too and hatred raise great waves in human breasts, the former swifter in its onset, the latter more persistent in its desire of harming, each a passion full of consternation and never violent without torment to itself, because, when it wishes to inflict pain, it suffers, anxious with bitter solicitude lest vengeance should not come to pass. But the surest images of their characteristics are those which the gods themselves willed to be seen in famous persons, either by some saying or by a too-vehement deed.

Having related the praises of Q. Fabius, there offer themselves men of wonderful steadfastness, who, sent as legates by the senate to Tarentum to demand redress, when they had received there the gravest insults—one even being befouled with urine—being brought into the theatre, as is the custom of Greece, carried out their embassy in the words in which they had received it. Of what they had suffered they did not complain, lest they should speak anything beyond what had been commanded; and the regard for ancient custom implanted in their breasts could not be shaken loose by the grief which is felt most gravely from an insult. Truly, Tarentine state, you sought the end of enjoying the wealth in which you had long abounded to the point of envy: for while, puffed up by the splendour of your present fortune, you fastidiously valued the support of rugged virtue, propped on itself alone, you rushed, blind and senseless, upon the most powerful point of our empire.

Nor ought we to separate from these examples the memory of Marcus Marcellus, in whom there was such vigour of spirit that, at the Po, with a few horsemen he attacked the king of the Gauls, surrounded by a vast army; and having at once cut him down, he stripped him of his arms and dedicated them to Jupiter Feretrius.

But Cicero's deed seemed so worthy of approval that not even his bitterest enemy, Publius Pulcher, hesitated to imitate it. He, accused on a charge of incest by the three Lentuli, protected one of them, a defendant on a charge of bribery, with his patronage, and brought himself, looking upon the judges and the praetor and the temple of Vesta, to act as a friend to Lentulus, amid which the other, desiring to overwhelm his safety with a foul charge, had pleaded with a hostile voice.

as creditably, by Hercules, as did Quintus Terentius Culleo, born of a praetorian family and, among the few of the senatorial order, distinguished, who, by the best of examples, followed the chariot of the elder Africanus as he triumphed, wearing the cap of liberty on his head, because he had been a captive of the Carthaginians and had been recovered by him: for to the author of his liberty, as to a patron, he rendered, with the Roman people looking on, a deserved acknowledgment of the benefit received.

What then? Liberty without Cato? No more than Cato without liberty: for when, as a judge, he had taken his seat over a guilty and infamous senator as defendant, and tablets had been produced containing the commendation of Gnaeus Pompeius for him—tablets that beyond doubt would be effective for the culprit—he removed them from the inquiry by reciting the law by which it was provided that senators should not be allowed to use such aid. To this deed the person removes wonder: for what in another would seem audacity, in Cato is recognized as confidence.

This wisdom was displayed in civil affairs, that other in military service. The consul Papirius Cursor, when, besieging Aquilonia, he wished to join battle, and the keeper of the sacred chickens reported to him a most excellent omen though the birds were not feeding favourably, being made aware of his deceit, believed indeed that a good omen had been given to himself and his army, and went into the fight; but he placed the liar before the very battle line, so that the gods might have someone by whose death they could expiate whatever anger they had conceived. And it was directed, whether by chance or even by the providence of the heavenly power, that the first weapon hurled from the opposite side struck the chicken-keeper himself in the breast and laid him low, lifeless. When the consul learned this, with confident spirit he both attacked Aquilonia and took it. So quickly did he perceive how the wrong done to the commander ought to be avenged, how the violated religious duty ought to be expiated, by what means the victory could be grasped. He played the part of a stern man, a religious consul, an energetic commander, sweeping up by one impulse of his mind the measure of fear, the kind of punishment, and the path of hope.

But that I may pass from manners ruined by luxury to the most severe institutions of our forefathers, formerly the senate kept its assiduous station in that place which even today is called the Senaculum: nor did it wait to be summoned by an edict, but, called thence, came straightway into the senate-house, esteeming him a citizen of doubtful praise who discharged the duties owed to the state not of his own accord but at command, because whatever is compelled by authority is credited rather to him who exacts it than to him who renders it.

The same kind both of valour and of combat was used by Titus Manlius Torquatus, Valerius Corvinus, and Scipio Aemilianus. These too slew the enemy's leaders, who had even challenged them; but because they had done the deed under another's auspices, they did not lay up the spoils to be consecrated to Jupiter Feretrius. The same Scipio Aemilianus, when he was serving in Spain under the command of Lucullus and the powerful town of Intercatia was being besieged, was the first to scale its walls. And there was no one in that army who, whether by nobility, or by natural disposition of spirit, or by future deeds, deserved more that his safety should be spared and considered. But in those days each of the noblest young men bore the most toil and danger for the enlargement and protection of his country, thinking it disgraceful to himself to be surpassed in valour by those whom he excelled in rank. And therefore Aemilianus demanded for himself this service of war, which others were avoiding on account of its difficulty.

But Caninius Gallus acted admirably as both defendant and accuser, both by leading into matrimony the daughter of Gaius Antonius, whom he had condemned, and by holding Marcus Colonius, by whom he had been condemned, as the manager of his affairs.

But the chariot of Flamininus, triumphing over King Philip, was attended not by one, but by two thousand citizens of Rome wearing the cap of liberty, whom he had recovered—men intercepted in the Punic wars and in slavery in Greece—and by his own care had collected and restored to their former rank. A twofold glory of that commander, by whom at once both the conquered enemy and the preserved citizens furnished a spectacle to the fatherland. The safety of those men too was doubly welcome to all, both because so many and because so grateful had recovered their longed-for state of liberty.

Gnaeus Lentulus Marcellinus the consul, when in an assembly he was complaining about the excessive power of Pompey the Great, and the whole people had assented to him with a clear voice, said, "Cry out, cry out, Quirites, while it is permitted: for soon it will not be permitted you to do so with impunity." The power of that eminent citizen was then assailed, on this side by an odious complaint, on that by a pitiable lamentation.

Now I shall pass on to the acts of the senate. When it was sending the consuls Claudius Nero and Livius Salinator against Hannibal, and saw that they, though equal in virtues, were yet most bitterly at variance with each other in their enmities, it reconciled them with the greatest zeal, lest because of their private dissensions they should administer the state too unprofitably; for unless concord is present in the command of the consuls, a greater desire arises of obstructing another's work than of producing one's own. But where an obstinate hatred also intervenes, each sets out as a surer enemy of the other than both are of the opposing camp. The same men, when on account of a censorship conducted too harshly they were brought to trial before the rostra by Cn. Baebius, tribune of the plebs, the senate freed from pleading their cause by its own decree, restoring to that office free from all fear of judgment a man who ought to demand an account, not render one. Equal was that wisdom of the senate. Ti. Gracchus, tribune of the plebs, who had dared to promulgate an agrarian law, it punished with death. The same senate decreed admirably that, in accordance with his law, land should be distributed to the people man by man through three commissioners, since indeed it thereby removed at one and the same time both the author and the cause of a most serious sedition. How prudently then it conducted itself in the matter of king Masinissa! For when it had made use of his most ready and most faithful service against the Carthaginians, and perceived that he was too greedy in enlarging his kingdom, it ordered a law to be passed which would grant to Masinissa a liberty released from the authority of the Roman people. By doing this it both retained the goodwill of one who had deserved excellently of it, and also drove from its own doors the savagery of Mauretania and Numidia and the other peoples of that region, never resting in a faithful peace.

2e.1. Time would fail one relating our domestic examples, since our empire has achieved its growth and its protection not so much by the strength of bodies as by the vigour of minds. Let Roman prudence therefore, for the greater part, be laid up in silent admiration, and let entrance be given to examples of this kind from foreign peoples. Socrates, the earthly oracle, as it were, of human wisdom, thought that nothing more ought to be asked of the immortal gods than that they should grant good things, because they alone knew what was useful for each man, whereas we for the most part desired in our prayers that which it would have been better not to obtain. For indeed, mind of mortals wrapped in the thickest darkness, over how wide a field of error you scatter your blind petitions! You crave riches, which have been the ruin of many; you covet honours, which have brought down a good many; you turn kingdoms over in your mind, whose ends are often seen to be pitiable; you lay hands on splendid marriages; but these, just as sometimes they bring distinction, so sometimes they utterly overthrow households. Cease, therefore, foolish soul, to gape after the future causes of your own evils as though they were the happiest of things, and commit yourself wholly to the judgment of the heavenly powers, since those who are wont to bestow good things readily can also choose them most fittingly. The same Socrates used to say that they reached glory by an easy and short road who took care that, whatever they wished to seem, that they should also be. By this saying he plainly advised that men should drink in virtue itself rather than pursue its shadow. The same man, being consulted by a certain young man whether he should take a wife or abstain altogether from marriage, replied that whichever of the two he did, he would repent of it. "On the one side," he said, "loneliness, childlessness, the dying-out of your line, an alien heir will await you; on the other, perpetual anxiety, a continuous web of complaints, the reproach of the dowry, the heavy frown of in-laws, a mother-in-law's chattering tongue, a lier-in-wait for another's marriage, the uncertain outcome of children." He did not allow the young man, amid a series of hard things, to make a choice as though of joyful material. The same man, when the criminal madness of the Athenians had passed a grim sentence upon his life, and with brave spirit and steadfast countenance he had received the cup of poison from the executioner's hand, the goblet now brought to his lips, while his wife Xanthippe amid weeping and lamentation cried out that he was perishing innocent, said, "What then? Did you think it better for me to die guilty?" That immense wisdom, which could not forget itself even in the very departure from life!

2e.2. Come, how prudently did Solon judge that no one ought to be called happy while he still lived, because right up to the last day of our fate we are subject to a doubtful fortune. The funeral pyre, then, completes the title of human happiness, for it sets itself against the onset of evils. The same man, when he saw one of his friends grieving heavily, led him up onto the citadel and urged him to cast his eyes around over all the parts of the buildings lying below. When he observed that this had been done, "Now think to yourself," he said, "how many griefs both have been beneath these roofs of old, and are passing today, and will dwell in them in ages to come; and cease to bewail the misfortunes of mortals as though they were your own." By this consolation he showed that cities are pitiable enclosures of human calamities. The same man used to say that, if all men had brought together their evils into one place, it would come to pass that they would prefer to carry their own home again rather than bear off their share from the common heap of miseries. From this he concluded that we ought not to judge the things we suffer by chance to be of an exceptional and unbearable bitterness.

2e.3. Bias, moreover, when enemies had invaded his native city of Priene, and all whom only the savagery of war had allowed to depart unharmed were fleeing laden with the weight of precious things, being asked why he carried off nothing of his own goods with him, said, "But I carry all my goods with me": for he bore them in his breast, not on his shoulders, things to be seen not with the eyes but appraised by the mind. These, shut up in the dwelling-place of the mind, can be shaken loose by the hands neither of mortals nor of gods, and as they are at hand to those who remain, so they do not desert those who flee.
2e.4. Concise too in Plato's words, but prevailing in sense, is that opinion of his who declared that the world would at last be happy when either the wise had begun to reign or kings to be wise.

2e.5. There was also that king of subtle judgment, who, they say, when the diadem had been handed to him, before he placed it on his head, held it back and considered it long, and said, "O cloth more noble than happy! which, if anyone knew thoroughly with how many anxieties and dangers and miseries it is stuffed, he would not be willing even to pick it up as it lay on the ground."

2e.6. How praiseworthy was the answer of Xenocrates! When he was present in the deepest silence at the slanderous conversation of certain men, and one of them asked why he alone held his tongue in check, he said, "Because I have sometimes repented of having spoken, of having kept silent never."

2e.7. Of a deeper prudence too is the precept of Aristophanes, who in a comedy brought on Pericles, sent back from the dead, prophesying . . . that one ought not to rear a lion in the city, but, if it had been reared, it was fitting to comply with it: for he advises that young men of especially high birth and excited temperament should be reined in, but that, once they had been fed with too much favour and lavish indulgence, they should not be hindered from obtaining power, because it is foolish and useless to belittle those strengths which one has oneself fostered.

2e.8. Wonderfully too spoke Thales: for being asked whether the deeds of men escaped the gods, he said, "Not even their thoughts," so that we should wish to have not only our hands but also our minds pure, since we believe that the heavenly power is present at our secret thoughts.

2e.9. Nor indeed is what follows any less wise. A father, consulting Themistocles about his only daughter, asked whether he should give her in marriage to a poor but accomplished man, or to a rich but little approved one. He said to him, "I prefer a man in want of money to money in want of a man." By this saying he advised the foolish man to choose for a son-in-law a man rather than riches for the man.

2e.10. Come, how commendable was the letter of Philip, in which he thus rebuked Alexander for having tried to draw to himself the goodwill of certain Macedonians by largesse: "What reasoning, my son, led you into so empty a hope as to think that those men would be faithful to you whom you had driven to love of you by money?" That came from affection in the father, from experience in Philip, who was for the greater part a trader of Greece rather than a conqueror of it.

2e.11. Aristotle, moreover, when he was sending his pupil Callisthenes to Alexander, advised him to speak with him either as seldom or as agreeably as possible, so that, of course, he might either be safer through silence in the king's hearing or more acceptable through his speech. But Callisthenes, while he rebuked Alexander for rejoicing in the Persian form of salutation, a Macedonian as he was, and kindly persisted in recalling him, against his will, to Macedonian customs, was ordered to be deprived of breath, and felt a late repentance for the wholesome counsel he had neglected. The same Aristotle used to declare that one ought to speak of oneself in neither direction, since to praise oneself is the mark of a vain man, to blame oneself of a foolish one. His too is that most useful precept, that we should consider pleasures as they depart. By showing them thus indeed he diminished them: for he sets them before our minds when they are weary and full of repentance, so that they may be sought again less eagerly.

2e.12. And not without prudence did Anaxagoras, when someone asked him who, then, was happy, say, "No one of those whom you consider fortunate, but you will find that man in the number of those whom you believe to be made up of the wretched. He will not be one abounding in riches and honours, but the faithful and persistent cultivator either of a small farm or of an unambitious learning, happier in his retirement than in his outward show."
2e.13. Wise too was the saying of Demades: for when the Athenians were unwilling to decree divine honours to Alexander, he said, "Take care lest, while you guard the heaven, you lose the earth."

2e.14. How subtly, moreover, did Anacharsis compare laws to the webs of spiders! For as those webs hold back the weaker creatures but let the stronger pass through, so by these laws the lowly and the poor are bound fast, but the rich and the powerful are not held.

2e.15. Nothing too was wiser than the deed of Agesilaus, since indeed, when he had learned by night of a conspiracy that had arisen against the state of the Lacedaemonians, he at once abrogated the laws of Lycurgus, which forbade punishment to be inflicted on the uncondemned; but when the guilty had been seized and put to death, he immediately restored them, and provided at the same time for both things: that the wholesome punishment should be neither unjust nor lawfully hindered. And so, in order that the laws might always be able to exist, they for a while did not exist.

2e.16. But I do not know whether the counsel of Hanno was not of the most outstanding prudence: for when Mago was announcing to the senate of the Carthaginians the outcome of the battle of Cannae, and, as proof of so great a success, was pouring out golden rings filling the measure of three pecks, which had been stripped from our slaughtered citizens, Hanno asked whether any of the allies, after so great a disaster, had revolted from the Romans; and when he heard that no one had gone over to Hannibal, he urged that envoys should at once be sent to Rome, through whom terms of peace might be discussed. And if his opinion had prevailed, Carthage would neither have been defeated in the second Punic war nor destroyed in the third.

2e.17. Not even the Samnites paid small penalties for a like error, in that they had neglected the wholesome counsel of Herennius Pontius. He, surpassing the rest in authority and prudence, being consulted by the army and by its leader his own son as to what ought to be done about the Roman legions shut up at the Caudine Forks, replied that they should be sent away unharmed. Being asked on the next day about the same matter, he said they ought to be destroyed, so that either the gratitude of the enemy might be earned by the greatest benefit, or their strength broken by a most grievous loss. But the improvident rashness of the victors, while it scorned both sides of expediency, by sending them under the yoke kindled them to its own destruction.

2e.18. To many and great examples of wisdom I shall add a very small one. The Cretans, when they wish to use a most bitter curse against those whom they vehemently hate, pray that they may take delight in a bad habit, and by this modest kind of vow they find a most effective outcome of vengeance: for to desire something uselessly and to dwell on it persistently—that neighbouring sweetness is near to ruin.

3.pr. THINGS CRAFTILY SAID OR DONE There is another kind of deeds and sayings which has slipped by a slight deviation from wisdom into the name of craftiness, and which, unless it has taken on strength from deceit, does not find the end of its purpose, and seeks praise by a hidden path rather than by an open road.

This too must be recalled to memory, that it was not permitted to the tribunes of the plebs to enter the senate-house, but, with benches placed before the doors, they examined the decrees of the fathers with the most attentive care, so that, if they disapproved any of them, they would not suffer them to be ratified. And so to old decrees of the senate the letter C used to be subscribed, and by this mark it was signified that the tribunes too had given their assent. They, although they kept watch on behalf of the interests of the plebs and were occupied in restraining commands, yet allowed themselves to be furnished with silver vessels and golden rings provided at public expense, so that by the use of such things the authority of the magistrates might be more adorned.

Antiquity offers a great example of courage amid these things. The Romans, driven back by the army of the Gauls, when they were betaking themselves to the Capitol and the citadel, and all could not lodge upon these hills, took the necessary decision of leaving the aged men behind in the level part of the city, so that the youth might the more easily guard the remnants of the empire. But not even at that time, so wretched and so mournful, did our city forget its valour: for the men who had held the highest offices, with doors flung open, seated themselves in their curule chairs with the insignia of the magistracies they had held and of the priesthoods they had obtained, so that they themselves might in their downfall retain the splendour and ornaments of their past life, and might give to the people an example for bearing their misfortunes more bravely . . . The sight of them was at first venerable to the enemy, who were moved both by the novelty of the thing and by the magnificence of their dress and by the very kind of their boldness. But who would doubt that the Gauls and victors would soon turn that admiration into laughter and into every kind of insult? Marcus Atilius therefore did not wait for this ripening of the affront, but struck with his staff a violent blow on the head of a Gaul who was stroking his beard, and to him, who in his pain rushed to kill him, he the more eagerly offered his body. Thus valour knows not how to be taken captive, is ignorant of the disgrace of submission, holds it sadder than any fate to yield to fortune, and devises new and splendid kinds of death—if indeed anyone perishes who is extinguished in such a way.

But of Caelius Rufus, as his life was tainted, so the mercy which he showed to Quintus Pompeius is to be approved. When this man had been laid low by Caelius in a public trial, and his mother Cornelia would not give back the estates entrusted to her, and Pompeius had implored his help by letter, Caelius most persistently stood by him in his absence: he even read out in court a letter of his, the token of his utmost necessity, by which he overthrew the impious avarice of Cornelia. A deed which, on account of its surpassing humanity, is not to be repudiated even with Caelius as its author.

3.pr. ON ABSTINENCE AND SELF-CONTROL. With great care and special zeal it must be related how greatly the onset, like to the frenzy of lust and avarice, has been removed by counsel and reason from the breasts of illustrious men, because that household, that state, that kingdom alone will easily stand in an everlasting grade where the desire of love and of money claims for itself the least strength: for wherever those most certain plagues of the human race have penetrated, injustice rules, infamy blazes, violence dwells, wars are begotten. With propitious tongues, then, let us commemorate characters opposed to these so dire vices.

But Metellus, who through his persistent love toward his exiled father gained a name as renowned by his tears as others by their victories—called Pius—did not hesitate, as consul, to entreat the people on behalf of Quintus Calidius, a candidate for the praetorship, because, as tribune of the plebs, he had carried the law by which his father was restored to the citizenship. He even constantly declared him the patron of his house and family. Nor by this did he detract anything from the pre-eminence which beyond doubt he held, because it was not with a humble but with a grateful mind that he submitted his eminent dignity to the great merit of a man far his inferior.

To Pompey, who had a white bandage tied around his leg, Favonius said, "It makes no difference on what part of the body the diadem is," reproaching him with royal powers by the jeer of a scrap of cloth. But he, his countenance changed neither way, guarded against both: lest he should seem either with cheerful brow gladly to acknowledge his power, or with a sad one now to profess it. And by that forbearance he gave access against himself even to men of lower rank and fortune: of whose number it will be enough to have related two.

As their majesty was enlarged, so their abstinence was most tightly bound: for the entrails of the victims sacrificed by them, carried to the quaestors of the treasury, were sold; and in the sacrifices of the Roman people there was, along with the worship of the immortal gods, also the self-restraint of men, our commanders learning at those altars how holy hands they ought to keep. And so much was attributed to self-restraint that the debts of many were paid off by the senate, because they had administered their provinces with integrity: for those by whose service they saw that the public authority had maintained its splendour abroad, they thought it unworthy and disgraceful to themselves that the dignity of these should collapse at home.

There must now be rendered to the Roman youth the title of glory that is their due, which, when Gaius Sempronius Atratinus as consul was fighting with too little success against the Volsci at Verrugo, that our line, already wavering, might not be driven back, dismounted from their horses, formed itself into companies, and burst into the army of the enemy. When these were dislodged, the youth seized the nearest hillock and brought it about that the whole onset of the Volsci, turned upon themselves, gave to our legions a saving respite for the strengthening of their spirits. And so, when the enemy were already thinking of setting up trophies, the battle being broken off by nightfall, they departed uncertain whether they retired as victors or as vanquished.

For the impulse of Gaius Marius's grateful mind was not only outstanding but even overwhelming: for he gave the citizenship, against the terms of a treaty, in the very battle line, to two cohorts of Camertines who were sustaining the onset of the Cimbri with marvellous valour. And indeed he both truly and admirably excused this deed by saying that amid the clash of arms he had not been able to hear the words of the civil law. And truly that was then a time in which it was more fitting to defend the laws than to listen to them.

Helvius Mancia of Formiae, a freedman's son, of extreme old age, was accusing Lucius Libo before the censors. In this contest, when Pompey the Great, reproaching him with his lowliness and his age, had said that he had been sent back from the dead to accuse, "You do not lie, Pompey," he said: "for I come from the dead, I come as accuser against Lucius Libo. But while I lingered there, I saw, bloodied, Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus weeping that, born of the highest family, of a most upright life, most loving of his fatherland, in the very flower of his youth he had been killed by your order. I saw, conspicuous for equal renown, Marcus Brutus mangled by the sword, complaining that this had befallen him first by your treachery, then even by your cruelty. I saw Gnaeus Carbo, the keenest defender of your boyhood and of your father's goods, in his third consulship bound with chains which you had ordered to be cast upon him, protesting that, against all right and wrong, when he was in the highest command, he had been slaughtered by you, a Roman knight. I saw, in the same plight and outcry, the praetorian Perpenna cursing your savagery, and all these with one voice indignant that, uncondemned, they had perished under you, a young executioner." Over the most vast wounds of the civil wars, now closed by old scars, it was permitted, with impunity, to a man of a country town, redolent of his father's slavery, of unbridled rashness, of intolerable spirit, to reopen them. And so at the same time it was both most brave and most safe to revile Gnaeus Pompeius. But the somewhat lower lot of the person who follows does not permit us to pursue this with longer complaint.

The youth of the equestrian order, moreover, every year twice graced the city with a spectacle of themselves, under great authors: for the custom of the Lupercalia was begun by Romulus and Remus then, when, exulting with gladness because their grandfather Numitor, king of the Albans, had permitted them to found a city in that place where they had been reared, beneath the Palatine mount, at the exhortation of Faustulus their foster-father, whom Evander the Arcadian had consecrated, having made a sacrifice and slain goats, and being carried away by the cheerfulness of the feast and the more generous wine, the band of shepherds being divided, girded with the skins of the slaughtered victims, they attacked, in jest, those who met them. The memory of this merriment is repeated in the annual round of the festival. But the knights, robed in the trabea, Q. Fabius established should ride past on the Ides of July. The same man, as censor with P. Decius, for the sake of ending the sedition which the elections, reduced to the power of every meanest man, had kindled, distributed the whole forensic crowd into four tribes only and called them urban. By this so wholesome deed, a man otherwise excelling in warlike works was surnamed Maximus.

That strenuous man too was the flower of the equestrian order, by whose wondrous valour Fabius Maximus Rullianus, master of the horse in the war that was being waged against the Samnites, was cleared of the charge of having joined battle ill: for, when Papirius Cursor was setting out for the city to take the auspices afresh and Fabius had been set over the camp and forbidden to lead the army into the line, he nevertheless joined hands with the enemy, but as unluckily as rashly; for beyond doubt he was being overcome. But that young man of excellent disposition, the bridles of the horses stripped off, drove them, fiercely spurred, against the Samnites facing him, and by the stubborn presence of his spirit restored to his country the victory wrested from the enemy's hands and, with it, the hope of a great citizen.

Lucius Sulla follows everywhere in the footsteps of Gaius Marius in the rivalry of praise: for as dictator he both bared his head and rose from his curule chair and dismounted from his horse for Pompey, though a private citizen, and proclaimed in the assembly that he did this gladly, mindful that by him, when he was eighteen years old, his own party had been aided with his father's army. Many distinctions came to Pompey, but I know not whether anything more admirable befell him than this, that he compelled Sulla to forget himself by the magnitude of his benefit.

Diphilus the tragic actor, when at the Apollinarian Games, in the course of the action, he had come to that verse in which this sentiment is contained, "By our misery he is great," with his hands directed at Pompey the Great pronounced it, and, recalled several times by the people, without any hesitation persistently played him by his gesture as guilty of excessive and intolerable power. He used the same impudence in this part too: "The time will come when you shall grievously groan for that valour."

Of what strength then were those soldiers who, with the violent stroke of their oars driving the Punic fleet to flight, swimming over the slippery surface of the sea as though over the firmness of plains, dragged it back to shore on foot?

Let there be, even amid the highest splendour, some place for grateful lowliness. When Marcus Cornutus the praetor was contracting, by order of the senate, for the funeral of Hirtius and Pansa, those who at that time conducted the business of undertaking promised both the use of their resources and their own ministry free of charge, because these men had fallen fighting for the commonwealth; and by persistent demand they wrung it out that the equipment of the obsequies should be assigned to be furnished by them for a single sesterce. Their praise the addition of the law-given condition increases rather than diminishes, since indeed they scorned profit, though living for nothing else than profit. With the leave of their own ashes, the kings of foreign nations will suffer themselves to be brought in after this so despised troop—kings who either ought not to have been touched upon, or ought to have been placed in the very last part of domestic examples. But that the memory of an honourable deed, performed even by these lowest of men, should not perish, let them hold a separate place, so as to seem neither added to these nor preferred to those.

2e.1. Darius, while still of private fortune, delighted by the cloak of Syloson of Samos, by a rather curious contemplation of it brought it about that it was given to him of free will—and indeed by one who desired it. How grateful an estimate of that gift was lodged in his mind he showed when he had gained the kingdom: for he handed over the whole city and island of the Samians to Syloson to enjoy. For the price of the thing was not reckoned, but the occasion of generosity was honoured, and it was looked to more from whom the gift proceeded than to whom it came.

2e.2. King Mithridates too appeared magnificently grateful, since, on behalf of Leonicus, the most ardent defender of his safety, who had been taken by the Rhodians in a naval battle, he exchanged all his captive enemies, judging it better to be cheated by his most hateful foes than not to return gratitude to one who had deserved well.

2e.3. Generous was the Roman people in the magnitude of its gift, in that it gave Asia to King Attalus as a present. But Attalus too was grateful in the equity of his will, in that he bequeathed that same Asia to the Roman people. And so neither the munificence of the one nor the mind of the other, so mindful of the benefit, can be praised in as many words as there are most ample states either given in friendship or restored in piety.

2e.4.
