But I know not whether especially the breast of King Masinissa was filled with the pledges of a grateful mind: for, having been enlarged more liberally than his kingdom by the benefit of Scipio and at his persuasion, he carried the memory of that illustrious gift to the very end of his life—endowed even with a long old age by the immortal gods—with the most constant faith, so that not only Africa but all nations knew that he survived a greater friend to the Cornelian family and to the city of Rome than to his very self. He, when he was hard pressed by a grievous war with the Carthaginians and scarcely sufficed for the protection of his own empire, nevertheless handed over to Scipio Aemilianus, because he was the grandson of Africanus, a good and great part of his Numidian army, which he might lead into Spain to Lucullus the consul, by whom he had been sent to seek auxiliaries, and, with most ready mind, preferred regard for an old benefit to a present danger. He, when, his age now failing, he was sinking on his couch, leaving the great resources of his kingdom to a number of four-and-fifty sons, besought by letter Manius Manilius, who as proconsul held Africa, to send to him Scipio Aemilianus, then serving under him, thinking his death would be the more fortunate if he laid his last breath and his last instructions in the embrace of his right hand. He, as Scipio's arrival was outrun by his fate, had given these instructions to his wife and children: that they should know one people on earth, the Roman, and one house among the Roman people, that of Scipio; that they should reserve everything intact for Aemilianus; that they should hold him the arbiter of dividing the kingdom; and that what he had determined they should hold immutable and sacred, just as if it had been provided for by a will. By so many and such various deeds, in an unwearied series of devotion, Masinissa extended himself to his hundredth year. By these and similar examples the beneficence of the human race is nourished and increased: these are its torches, these its goads, by which it burns with the desire of helping and of deserving well. And truly the most ample and most splendid riches are these: to be able to be rated widely by benefits happily bestowed. Since we have established the religious worship of these, we shall now relate the neglect of them, by way of branding it, that it may be the more pleasing.

The spirit of Marcus Castricius too was inflamed with liberty. He, when he was holding a magistracy at Placentia, and Gnaeus Carbo the consul ordered a decree to be made by which hostages should be given to him by the people of Placentia, neither obeyed his supreme command nor yielded to his greatest forces; and even, when Carbo said that he had many swords, replied, "And I have years." So many legions were astonished, beholding so robust a remnant of old age. The anger too of Carbo, because it had very little material for raging—being about to take away but a little span of life—collapsed upon itself.

Of the same time and renown was that soldier who, at the battle of Cannae—where Hannibal crushed the strength of the Romans more than he broke their spirit—when he had hands useless from wounds for holding his arms, embraced the neck of a Numidian who was trying to despoil him and, gnawing away his nose and ears, made it hideous, and breathed his last amid bites full of vengeance. Set aside the unjust issue of the fight: how much braver was the slain than the slayer! For the Carthaginian, even in victory, became a comfort to a dying man, while the Roman, at the very end of life, became the avenger of himself.

Now there is the demand, full of rashness, of Servius Galba, who endured to interrupt the deified Julius, as, his victories accomplished, he was administering justice in the forum, in this manner: "Gaius Julius Caesar, for Gnaeus Pompeius the Great, once your son-in-law, in his third consulship I went surety for money, on which account I am now sued. What am I to do? Am I to pay?" By openly and plainly reproaching him with the sale of Pompey's goods, he had deserved to be removed from the tribunal. But that breast, milder than mildness itself, ordered Pompey's debt to be paid from its own treasury.

So remarkable in adversity is this manly spirit of a common soldier; that of a commander I am now about to relate: for Publius Crassus, waging war in Asia against Aristonicus, was caught between Elaea and Smyrna by the Thracians, of whom he kept a great number in his guard; and, that he might not come into Aristonicus' power, he escaped disgrace by a chosen manner of death: for the rod, which he had used for guiding his horse, he drove into the eye of one of the barbarians. He, inflamed by the force of pain, pierced Crassus' side with a dagger; and while he avenged himself, he freed the Roman commander from the shame of lost majesty. Crassus showed Fortune how unworthy a man she had wished to afflict with so grievous an insult, since he prudently and bravely broke the wretched snares she had cast upon his liberty, and restored himself, when he had been already granted to Aristonicus, to his own dignity.

Come now, Cascellius, a man famous for his knowledge of the civil law—how dangerously stubborn! For by no one's favour or authority could he be compelled to draw up a formula concerning any of those things which the triumvirs had granted, placing by this judgment of his mind all their benefits outside the whole order of the laws. The same man, when he spoke rather freely about the times of Caesar, and his friends warned him not to do so, answered that two things which seem most bitter to men furnished him great license—old age and childlessness.

2e.1. A woman of foreign blood inserts herself among such great men, who, undeservedly condemned by King Philip when drunk, cried out that she appealed against the verdict; and when he asked to whom she appealed, "To Philip," she said, "but sober." She shook off the drowsiness from the yawning man and by her presence of mind compelled the drunkard to come to his senses, and, the case being more diligently examined, forced him to deliver a juster verdict. Thus she wrung out the equity which she had not been able to obtain, having borrowed protection rather from liberty than from her innocence.

2e.2. Now that liberty was not only brave but even witty. A certain woman of extreme old age, at Syracuse, when all were seeking with their prayers the death of the tyrant Dionysius on account of the excessive harshness of his character and his intolerable burdens, she alone daily in the morning prayed the gods that he might be unharmed and might survive her. When he learned this, marvelling at goodwill not owed to him, he summoned her and asked why she did this and on account of what merit of his. Then she said, "The reason of my purpose is sure: for as a girl, when we had a grievous tyrant, I desired to be rid of him. When he was killed, one somewhat more foul occupied the citadel. I judged it of great importance that his domination too should be ended. As the third, we began to have you, a more troublesome ruler than your predecessors. And so, lest, if you are taken away, a worse one should succeed into your place, I devote my own life for your safety." So witty an audacity Dionysius blushed to punish.

2e.3. Between these women and Theodorus of Cyrene there could be as it were a marriage of spirited courage, equal in virtue, unlike in fortune: for he, to King Lysimachus, who was threatening him with death, said, "Indeed a magnificent thing has befallen you, because you have attained the power of a Spanish fly." And when, kindled by this saying, Lysimachus had ordered him to be fastened to a cross, "Let this be terrible to your courtiers," he said: "to me, indeed, it makes no difference whether I rot on the ground or aloft."

3.pr. ON SEVERITY The breast must arm itself with hardness while the deeds of grim and stern severity are narrated, so that, every milder thought set aside, it may have leisure for things harsh to hear: for thus drawn and inexorable punishments and various kinds of penalties will run forth into the midst—useful safeguards indeed of the laws, but by no means to be placed in the calm and quiet number of pages.

3.1a. Marcus Manlius was hurled down from that very place from which he had driven the Gauls, because he had wickedly attempted to crush the liberty he had bravely defended. The preface to this just vengeance was, doubtless, this: "Manlius you were to me, when you were driving the Senones headlong; after you began to imitate them, you became one of the Senones." Upon his punishment a mark of eternal memory was set: for on his account it was resolved to ordain by law that no patrician should dwell in the citadel or the Capitol, because he had had his house in that place where we now see the temple of Moneta.

3.1b. An equal indignation of the state burst out against Spurius Cassius, whom the suspicion of coveted domination harmed more than three magnificent consulships and two most splendid triumphs profited: for the senate and Roman people, not content with afflicting him with capital punishment, threw down his house, that he might be punished also by the ruin of his household gods; and on the site they built the temple of Tellus. And so what had before been the dwelling of an uncontrolled man is now a monument of religious severity.

3.1c. The fatherland punished with a like end Spurius Maelius, who dared the same thing. The site of his house, indeed, that the justice of the punishment might reach posterity more notable, took the name Aequimelium. How great a hatred, therefore, against the enemies of liberty the ancients had implanted in their minds they testified by the ruins of the walls and roofs in which such men had lived. And so too the household gods of Marcus Flaccus and Lucius Saturninus, most seditious citizens, when their bodies had been slaughtered, were torn out from their deepest foundations. But the Flaccian site, after it had long remained almost empty, was adorned by Quintus Catulus with the Cimbric spoils.

3.1d. There flourished in our state the highest nobility and the most ample promise of Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus. But because they had attempted to overturn the constitution of the state, their corpses lay unburied, and the last honour of the human condition was wanting to the sons of Gracchus and the grandsons of Africanus. Nay, even their intimates, that no one might wish to be a friend to the enemies of the commonwealth, were hurled down from the Rock.

The same purpose of mind was used by Scipio Metellus: for, having unsuccessfully defended in Africa the party of Gnaeus Pompey, his father-in-law, and making for Spain by sea, when he perceived that the ship in which he was carried had been captured by the enemy, he ran his sword through his breast; and then, fallen prostrate on the stern, when the Caesarian soldiers asked where the commander was, he answered, 'The commander is well,' and had strength to utter only so much as was enough to attest the fortitude of his spirit for everlasting praise.

Of your most glorious end too, Cato, Utica is the monument, in which from your bravest wounds more glory than blood flowed forth: since, by most steadfastly falling upon your sword, you gave to mankind a great lesson how much more to be preferred is dignity without life to the wise than life without dignity.

His daughter was of no womanish spirit. For when she had learned, on that night which was followed by the day of the foulest deed, of the plan which her husband Brutus had formed for killing Caesar, after Brutus had gone out of the bedroom she asked for a barber's knife as though to cut her nails, and, letting it fall as if by chance, wounded herself. Then, recalled to the bedroom by the cries of her maidservants, Brutus began to chide her for having forestalled the barber's office. But Porcia said to him privately: 'This deed of mine is not rash, but in such a state of ours it is the surest proof of my love towards you: for I wished to try, if your plan should turn out less than you wished, with how calm a spirit I should kill myself with the sword.'

More fortunate in his offspring was the elder Cato, from whom the beginnings of the Porcian family flowed. When in battle he was being fiercely attacked by an enemy . . . his sword slipped from its sheath and fell. When he noticed that it was lost, lying beneath a throng of fighters and surrounded on every side by the feet of the enemy, with such steadfast spirit he brought it back into his power that he seemed not to snatch it up under the pressure of danger, but to take it up free from fear. Astonished at this sight, the enemy came to him the next day as suppliants, seeking peace.

The courage of the toga too must be inserted among military deeds, since it earns the same praise whether displayed in the forum or in the camp. When Tiberius Gracchus, in his tribunate, having seized the favour of the people by most lavish largesses, held the commonwealth oppressed, and openly kept declaring that, the senate being destroyed, everything ought to be done through the plebs, the conscript fathers, called together into the temple of Public Faith, were deliberating with the consul Mucius Scaevola what should be done in such a storm; and when all were of the opinion that the consul should defend the commonwealth by arms, Scaevola denied that he would do anything by force. Then Scipio Nasica said: 'Since the consul, while he follows the order of law, is bringing it about that the Roman empire shall fall together with all its laws, I myself as a private citizen offer myself as a leader to your will.' And then, wrapping his left hand in the lowest part of his toga and raising his right, he cried aloud: 'Let those who wish the commonwealth to be safe follow me.' And by that voice, the hesitation of good citizens being shaken off, he compelled Gracchus, with his wicked faction, to pay the penalties he deserved.

Likewise, when the tribune of the plebs Saturninus and the praetor Glaucia and Equitius the tribune-elect of the plebs had stirred up the greatest commotions of sedition in our city, and no one set himself against the aroused people, first Marcus Aemilius Scaurus exhorted Gaius Marius, then holding his sixth consulship, to defend liberty and the laws by force, and at once ordered arms to be brought to himself. When these were brought, he clad his body, worn out with extreme old age and almost dissolved, and, leaning upon a spear, took his stand before the doors of the senate-house, and with the last small remnants of his breath brought it about that the commonwealth did not perish: for the presence of his spirit impelled the senate and the equestrian order to exact vengeance.

But, as we have just shown the bright glory of arms and of the toga, so let us now also display the bright glory of the stars, the divine Julius, the surest likeness of true valour. When he saw his line giving way before the countless multitude and fierce onset of the Nervii, he snatched a shield from a soldier who was fighting too timidly, and, covered by it, began to fight most fiercely. By this deed he spread courage through the whole army and by the divine ardour of his spirit restored the tottering fortune of war. The same man, in another battle, seized by the throat the standard-bearer of the Martian legion, who had already turned to take flight, and dragged him in the opposite direction, and, stretching his right hand towards the enemy, said: 'Where are you going? There are the men with whom we fight.' And with his hands indeed he set right a single soldier, but by exhortation so keen the panic of all the legions, and taught them, who were ready to be conquered, to conquer.

But, to follow out the deed of human valour: when Hannibal was besieging Capua, in which there was a Roman army, Vibius Accaus, prefect of a Paelignian cohort, threw the standard across the Punic rampart, cursing himself and his comrades-in-arms if the enemy should gain possession of the standard, and was the first to make the charge to recover it, the cohort following behind. When Valerius Flaccus, tribune of the third legion, saw this, turning to his men he said: 'We have come hither, as I see, as spectators of another's valour; but far be that disgrace from our blood, that we Romans should be willing to yield in glory to Latins. I at least, choosing either a glorious death or a happy issue of my boldness, am ready to charge forward even alone.' When these words were heard, the centurion Pedanius, holding in his right hand the standard he had torn loose, said: 'This shall presently be within the enemy's rampart with me: therefore let those follow who do not wish it to be taken,' and with him he burst into the camp of the Carthaginians and drew the whole legion along with him. Thus the brave rashness of three men did not allow Hannibal, a little before in his own hope master of Capua, to be master even of his own camp.

To their valour Quintus Occius yields in nothing, who on account of his courage was surnamed Achilles: for, not to recount his other exploits, yet abundantly from two deeds, which I am about to relate, will it be known how great a warrior he was. Having gone to Spain as lieutenant to the consul Quintus Metellus and waging the Celtiberian war under him, when he learned that he was challenged to single combat by a young man of that nation—and it happened that a table was set for him for the sake of lunching—he left it and secretly ordered his arms to be carried outside the rampart and his horse to be led out, that he might not be hindered by Metellus, and, pursuing that Celtiberian who was riding around most insolently, he slew him, and, stripping off the spoils from his body, carried them back into camp exulting with joy. The same man compelled Pyrresus, who excelled all the Celtiberians in nobility and valour, to yield to him, when he had been called out by him to a contest of combat. Nor did the young man of most ardent breast blush to hand over to him his sword and his cloak in the sight of both armies. Indeed he even asked that they should be joined to each other by the bond of hospitality, when peace should be restored between the Romans and the Celtiberians.

Nor can we pass over Acilius, who, when as a soldier of the tenth legion he fought a sea-battle for the party of Gaius Caesar, his right hand having been cut off, which he had flung upon a ship of the Massilians, seized the stern with his left, nor ceased to fight before he had captured it and sunk it in the deep. This deed lies before us with too little fitting renown. Yet the Athenian Cynaegirus, who used a like persistence in pursuing the enemy, wordy Greece, in the song of its own praises, has driven into the memory of all ages by the heralding of literature.

The naval glory of Acilius was followed, with terrestrial praise, by Marcus Caesius Scaeva, a centurion of the same commander: for, when he was fighting in defence of the fort over which he was set, and Iustuleius, prefect of Gnaeus Pompey, was striving with the utmost zeal and a great number of soldiers to capture him, he slew all who had come nearer, and, fighting without any backward step, fell over the huge heap which he himself had made. When his head, shoulder, and thigh were wounded, his eye torn out, his shield was seen pierced with a hundred and twenty blows. Such was the discipline in the camp of the divine Julius that nourished soldiers of whom the one, his right hand lost, the other, his eye lost, clung to the enemy—the one a victor after this loss, the other not vanquished even by this loss. But your unconquerable spirit, Scaeva, in which part of the realm of nature I should pursue with admiration I know not, since by your surpassing valour you have left it doubtful whether you displayed the braver fight among the waves or sent forth the braver voice on land: for in that war, in which Gaius Caesar, not content to enclose his own work within the shores of Ocean, laid heavenly hands upon the island of Britain, when you had been carried on a raft with four comrades to a rock near the island, which vast forces of the enemy held, after the tide by its ebbing had easily reduced to a ford for crossing the space by which the rock and the island were divided, and a vast multitude of barbarians was flowing up, while the rest withdrew on the raft to the shore, you alone, keeping your post unmoved, with weapons rushing upon you from every side and the enemy from every quarter striving with keen zeal to attack you, drove against the enemy's bodies with one right hand javelins enough for the day's battle of five soldiers. At the last, your sword drawn, beating off each boldest man now by the thrust of your boss, now by the stroke of your point, you were, to Roman eyes on this side, to British eyes on that, a spectacle incredible, had you not been seen. Then, after anger and shame compelled you, wearied, to attempt everything, your thigh pierced by a dart and your face bruised by the weight of a stone, your helmet now shattered by blows and your shield consumed by many holes, you trusted yourself to the deep and, laden with two coats of mail, swam out among the waves which you had stained with the enemy's blood; and when you had seen your commander, your arms not lost but well expended, though you deserved praise, you sought pardon for having returned without your shield—great in battle, but greater in your memory of military discipline. And so by the best appraiser of valour both your deeds and also your words were honoured with the rank of centurion.

But as concerns the surpassing courage of fighters, the mention of Lucius Siccius Dentatus may fitly close all Roman examples, whose deeds and the honours of his deeds might be judged to exceed the bounds of truth beyond belief, had not sure authorities, among whom Marcus Varro, willed them to be attested in their records. They report that he went down into the battle-line a hundred and twenty times, using such strength of spirit and body that he seemed always to have drawn to himself the greater part of the victory: that he carried off thirty-six spoils from the enemy, among whose number eight were those of men with whom, in the sight of both armies, he had fought upon challenge; that he rescued from the midst of death and saved fourteen citizens; that he received forty-five wounds in his breast, his back free of scars; that he followed nine triumphal chariots of commanders, turning the eyes of the whole city upon himself by the numerous procession of his gifts: for there were borne before him eight golden crowns, fourteen civic crowns, three mural crowns, one siege crown, eighty-three necklaces, a hundred and sixty bracelets, eighteen spears, twenty-five medallions—rewards enough even for a legion, let alone a single soldier.

2e.1. That blood too, from many bodies into one, was mingled with great wonder at Cales. When in that town Fulvius Flaccus was avenging the Campanian treachery by inflicting capital punishment upon the chief men of the state before his tribunal, and, on receiving a letter from the senate, was being compelled to set an end to their punishment, Titus Iubellius Taurea, a Campanian, of his own accord offered himself to him and said in as clear a voice as he could: 'Since, Fulvius, you are held by so great a desire of drinking our blood, why do you delay to draw the bloody axe upon me, that you may be able to boast that a man somewhat braver than yourself has been slain at your command?' Then, when Fulvius declared that he would gladly have done it, were he not hindered by the will of the senate, Taurea said: 'But look upon me, to whom the conscript fathers have prescribed nothing, performing a deed pleasing indeed to your eyes, but greater to your spirit,' and at once, having killed his wife and children, he fell upon his sword. What a man must we think him to have been, who by the slaughter of his own and of himself wished to attest that he chose to brand Fulvius' cruelty rather than to use the senate's mercy?

2e.2. Come, how great was the ardour of Darius' spirit! who, when he was freeing the Persians from the foul and cruel tyranny of the Magi, and was pressing one of them, thrown down in an obscure place, with the weight of his body, to his partner in the glorious deed, who hesitated to strike a blow at the Magus, lest in aiming at him he should wound Darius himself, said: 'You have no reason to use your sword more timidly out of regard for me: you may drive it through both of us, provided this man perishes as quickly as possible.'

2e.3. Here Leonidas, the noble Spartan, comes to mind, than whose purpose, deed, and end nothing is braver: for with three hundred citizens, set against all Asia at Thermopylae, he reduced to the utmost despair that grievous Xerxes, terrible both to sea and to land, who, not content to be terrible to men, threatened fetters even to Neptune and darkness to heaven, by the stubbornness of his valour. But, despoiled by the treachery and crime of the inhabitants of that region of the advantage of the place, by which he was most aided, he chose to die fighting rather than to desert the post assigned him by his country; and with so eager a spirit he exhorted his men to that battle, in which they were to perish, that he said: 'So breakfast, comrades, as men who are to dine among the dead.' Death had been proclaimed: the Lacedaemonians, just as though victory had been promised, obeyed the command undismayed.

2e.4. The fight and equally the death of Othryades, glorious . . . is seen wider in the praise of Thyrea than in the ground itself by its extent. He, with letters written in his own blood, carried back the victory wrested from the enemy almost after his own death into the bosom of his country with the bloody inscription of a trophy.

2e.5. A pitiable fall follows the most excellent harvests of Spartan valour. Epaminondas, the greatest good fortune of Thebes and likewise the first disaster of Lacedaemon, when by successful battles at Leuctra and Mantinea he had crushed the ancient glory of that city and its public valour, unconquered to that time, pierced by a spear, failing in blood and breath, asked those who tried to revive him first whether his shield was safe, then whether the enemy had been utterly routed. When he had learned these things to the satisfaction of his mind, he said: 'It is not the end, comrades, of my life, but a better and . . . beginning has come: for now your Epaminondas is born, because he dies thus. I see Thebes made the head of Greece by my leadership and auspices, and the brave and high-spirited city of Sparta lies cast down by our arms: Greece is freed from bitter domination. Childless too, yet not without children I die, since I leave behind two wondrous daughters, Leuctra and Mantinea.' He then ordered the spear to be drawn from his body and expired with that countenance with which, had the immortal gods suffered him to enjoy his victories, he would have entered his country's walls unhurt.

2e.6. Nor was there small steadfastness of mind even in Theramenes the Athenian, compelled to die in public custody, in which, by command of the Thirty Tyrants, he drank without hesitation the cup of poison held out to him, and what was left of it he jokingly dashed to the ground, forcing it to give a clear sound, and, smiling at the public slave who had handed it to him, said: 'I drink to Critias' health: see then that you carry this cup straightway to him.' Now this was the cruellest of the Thirty Tyrants. Truly it is to free oneself from punishment, to endure punishment so easily. And so Theramenes, dying just as though upon his own couch at home, departed from life, punished by his enemies' judgement, ended by his own.

2e.7. But Theramenes drew his manliness from letters and learning, whereas to Rhoetogenes the Numantine the ferocity of his own nation, as it were a mistress, stood forth to make him grasp a like valour: for, when the affairs of the Numantines were ruined and broken, since he surpassed all his fellow-citizens in nobility, wealth, and honours, he set fire to his own quarter, the fairest in that city, having gathered kindling from every side, and at once placed a drawn sword in the midst and ordered men to fight against one another in pairs, so that the vanquished, his neck cut, should be thrown upon the burning roofs. When by so brave a law of death he had destroyed them all, at the last he plunged himself into the flames.

2e.8. But, to relate the destruction of a city equally hostile to the Roman people, when Carthage was taken, the wife of Hasdrubal, reproaching him with impiety because he had been content to obtain life for himself alone from Scipio, dragging their common children, who did not refuse death, with her right and left hand, cast herself into the conflagration of her burning country.

2e.9. To this example of a woman's courage I shall add the equally brave fate of two girls. When, by the destructive sedition of Syracuse, the whole stock of King Gelon was drained away by most evident disasters and reduced to a single daughter, the maiden Harmonia, and attacks were made upon her in rivalry by her enemies, her nurse exposed to the hostile swords a girl of like age, adorned in royal dress; and she, that she might not be slaughtered even by the sword, proclaimed of what condition she was. Harmonia, marvelling at her spirit, could not endure to survive so great a loyalty, and, recalling the slayers and declaring who she was, turned them to her own slaughter. Thus to the one a hidden falsehood, to the other the open truth, was the end of life.

3.pr. ON ENDURANCE. By the distinguished deeds of men and women alike, courage has presented itself to the eyes of mankind, and has urged endurance to come forth into the midst—endurance established, to be sure, on no weaker roots, nor less abounding in noble spirit, but so joined to courage by likeness that it may seem to be either with it or born of it.

Praiseworthy too is the modesty of the people, who, by offering themselves unwearied to the toils and dangers of military service, took care that it should not be necessary for the commanders to enrol under the oath the head-counted poor, whose excessive poverty was suspect, and therefore they did not entrust to these the public arms. But this custom, formed by long usage, C. Marius broke by enrolling the head-counted as soldiers, a citizen otherwise magnificent, but, from the consciousness of his own newness, not at all favourable to antiquity, and mindful that, if the military standards persisted in spurning lowliness, he could be called by a malicious interpreter of virtues a "head-counted commander." And so he judged that fastidious kind of levy ought to be obliterated in the Roman armies, lest the contagion of such a mark should penetrate even to the bruising of his own glory.

For what is more in keeping with the deeds I have related above than the deed of Mucius? When he bore it ill that our city was being pressed by Porsenna, king of the Etruscans, in a grievous and long war, he secretly entered his camp girt with a sword and tried to kill him as he was sacrificing before the altars. But, overpowered in the very effort of his purpose, at once dutiful and brave, he neither concealed the cause of his coming nor . . . showed with wondrous endurance how greatly he despised tortures: for, hating, I believe, his right hand, because it had not been able to serve him in the slaying of the king, he suffered it, thrust into the fire, to be burned. Surely the immortal gods looked upon no worship brought to their altars with more attentive eyes. Porsenna himself, too, forgetful of his own danger, he compelled to turn his vengeance into admiration: for he said: 'Return to your own, Mucius, and tell them that, when you sought my life, your own life was granted you by me.' Not flattering this clemency, Mucius, sadder at Porsenna's safety than gladder at his own, restored himself to his city with the surname of Scaevola for everlasting glory.

In his twenty-fourth year, Scipio, when in Spain, Carthage being overthrown, he had taken the auspices for capturing greater Carthage, and had brought into his power many hostages whom the Carthaginians had held shut up in that city, a maiden among them of surpassing beauty and of grown age—he being a young man, unmarried, and victor—after he learned that she had been born in an illustrious place among the Celtiberians and was betrothed to Indibilis, the noblest of that nation, having summoned her parents and her betrothed, handed her over inviolate. The gold too, which had been brought for the ransom of the girl, he added to the sum of her dowry. By this self-control and munificence Indibilis, being put under obligation, repaid the gratitude due to his merits by attaching the spirits of the Celtiberians to the Romans.

ON THE UNGRATEFUL The senate mangled in the senate-house the parent of our city, placed by him on the highest step of dignity, and did not count it a crime to take away life from one who had implanted an eternal breath in the Roman empire. A rude indeed and savage age, which not even the highest piety of posterity can disguise, foully stained as it is with the blood of its founder.

3.2a. This error of an ungratefully fallen mind a fitting repentance of our state follows. The most joyous increase and the most certain safeguard of Roman strength, Furius Camillus, could not preserve his own safety in the city whose safety he himself had established, whose good fortune he had increased: for, by Lucius Apuleius the tribune of the plebs, he was made a defendant as though an embezzler of the Veientine plunder, and by harsh and, if I may so say, iron verdicts was sent into exile—and indeed at that time when, robbed of his son, a young man of the best disposition, he ought to have been relieved by consolations rather than burdened with calamities. But the fatherland, forgetful of so great a man's greatest services, joined to the obsequies of the son the condemnation of the father. "But," it says, "the tribune of the plebs complained that fifteen thousand asses were missing from the treasury": for at so much was the penalty fixed. A sum unworthy on account of which the Roman people should lack such a leader!

3.2b. While the former complaint was still quivering, another arises in succession. The elder Africanus rendered the commonwealth, not only bruised and broken by the arms of the Punic War but already almost bloodless and dying, mistress of Carthage. His most illustrious services they repaid with wrongs: his fellow citizens made him a dweller of an ignoble village and a neighbour of a deserted marsh. And the bitterness of his voluntary exile he did not carry to the shades below in silence, ordering it to be inscribed on his tomb: "Ungrateful fatherland, you do not even have my bones." What is more unworthy than that necessity, or juster than that complaint, or more moderate than that revenge? It denied him its ashes, whom it had not suffered to crumble into ash. Therefore the city of Rome felt this one vengeance of an ungrateful mind from Scipio—a greater one, by Hercules, than the violence of Coriolanus: for the latter assailed his fatherland with fear, the former with shame. And of this he could not even bear to complain—such was the steadfastness of his true piety—except after his death.

3.2c. To one who had suffered such things, I believe, the things which befell his brother could be a consolation. For King Antiochus conquered, and Asia added to the dominion of the Roman people, and a most splendid triumph, furnished the cause for him to be made a defendant for embezzlement and ordered to be led to prison.

3.2d. In no way inferior in virtue, the younger Africanus, though less than his grandsire, was not even happier in his end: for, two cities, Numantia and Carthage, which were menacing the Roman empire, having been driven from the nature of things, he found at home the robber of his breath, and did not find in the forum the avenger of his death.

3.2e. Who is ignorant that Scipio Nasica earned in the toga as much praise as either Africanus in arms—he who did not suffer the commonwealth, seized by the throat by the destructive band of Tiberius Gracchus, to be strangled? But he too, on account of the most unjust estimation of his virtues among the citizens, withdrew to Pergamum under the title of an embassy, and passed what remained of his life there without any longing for an ungrateful fatherland.

3.2f. I am still engaged with the same name, nor have I yet exhausted the complaints of the Cornelian clan: for Publius Lentulus, a most illustrious citizen and most devoted to the commonwealth, when on the Aventine he had routed by a dutiful and brave fight the wicked attempts and the battle-line of Gaius Gracchus, having received great wounds, bore this reward of that battle in which he had retained the laws, peace, and liberty in their proper state—that he should not die in our city: since indeed, driven by envy and detraction, having obtained a free embassy from the senate and held an assembly in which he prayed to the immortal gods that he might never return to an ungrateful people, he set out for Sicily and, by perseveringly remaining there, made himself master of his prayer. Five Cornelii, then, one after another, are just so many most notorious examples of an ungrateful fatherland.

3.2g. And of these the withdrawals were indeed voluntary: but Ahala, when as master of horse he had killed Spurius Maelius, who was aiming at kingship, paid the penalty for the liberty of the citizens that he had guarded by his own exile.

In the reign of Servius Tullius, a cow of remarkable size and outstanding form was born to a certain head of a household in the Sabine country. The most reliable authorities of the oracles replied that it had been produced by the immortal gods for this purpose: that whoever should sacrifice it to Diana on the Aventine, his country should obtain the empire of the whole world. Glad at this, the owner drove the cow to Rome with the greatest haste and set it before the altar of Diana on the Aventine, intending by his sacrifice to give the Sabines the rule of the human race. The priest of the temple, informed of this matter, brought a scruple of religion upon his guest, that he should not slay the victim before he had washed himself in the water of the nearby river; and while the man made for the channel of the Tiber, the priest himself sacrificed the cow, and by a pious theft of the sacrifice restored to our city the lordship over so many states and so many peoples.

Maesia of Sentinum, as a defendant, pleaded her own cause, with the praetor L. Titius convening the court, before a very great concourse of the people, and, having carried out all the modes and measures of a defence not only diligently but even bravely, was acquitted both at the first hearing and by almost all the votes. Because under the appearance of a woman she bore a manly spirit, they called her Androgyne.

When Livius Salinator, about to wage war against Hasdrubal, was leaving the city, and Fabius Maximus advised him not to come down into the battle line before he had learned the strength and spirit of the enemy, he replied that he would not let slip the first opportunity of fighting; and being asked by the same man why he wished to join battle so hastily, he said, "That as quickly as possible I may take either glory from conquered enemies or joy from prostrated citizens." Anger and virtue then divided his speech between them, the one mindful of his unjust condemnation, the other intent on the glory of a triumph. But I do not know whether it belonged to the same man to say this and so to conquer.

The practice of handling arms was imparted to the soldiers by the consul P. Rutilius, colleague of Cn. Mallius: for he, following the example of no commander before him, summoning trainers of gladiators from the school of C. Aurelius Scaurus, instilled into the legions a subtler method of avoiding and dealing blows, and mingled valour with skill and again skill with valour, so that the one might become braver by the impulse of the other, and the other more cautious by the knowledge of the one.

The valour of Pompeius too is worthy of praise, who, while he was discharging the office of an embassy, was intercepted by King Gentius, and when ordered to betray the counsels of the senate, offered his finger, applied to a burning lamp, to be consumed, and by that endurance at once struck the king with despair of learning anything from him by tortures, and bred in him a great desire of seeking the friendship of the Roman people. And, that I may not be compelled, by searching out more examples of this kind at home, too often to proceed to the abominable memory of civil wars, content with two Roman examples, which, while they contain the commendation of most illustrious families, yet contain no public grief, I shall subjoin foreign ones.

3e.1. By the ancient custom of Macedonia, boys of the noblest birth were at hand to King Alexander as he sacrificed. One of these, having seized a censer, stood before him. Upon his arm a burning coal fell. Although he was so burned by it that the smell of his scorched body reached the nostrils of the bystanders, yet he both suppressed his pain in silence and held his arm motionless, lest by shaking the censer he should hinder Alexander's sacrifice, or by uttering a groan should mar it with ill omen. The king, the more delighted by the boy's endurance, wished to take the surer proof of his perseverance: for he sacrificed on purpose the longer, nor by this did he repel him from his resolve. Had Darius fixed his eyes upon this marvel, he would have known that the soldiers of that race could not be conquered, when he had observed their tender age endowed with so great strength. There is also that vehement and steadfast warfare of the spirit, powerful in letters, the priestess of the venerable mysteries of learning—philosophy. When she is received into the breast, every base and useless passion being driven away, she strengthens it wholly with the bulwark of solid virtue, and makes it more powerful than fear and than pain.

3e.2. I shall begin with Zeno of Elea. He, being of the greatest prudence in examining the nature of things and most ready in rousing the spirits of young men to vigour, published the faith of his teachings by the example of his own valour: for, having left his country, in which he could enjoy secure liberty, he sought Agrigentum, overwhelmed by a wretched servitude, relying with such confidence on his own genius and character that he hoped that even from a tyrant, and from Phalaris, the savagery of a maddened mind could be torn away by him. When afterwards he perceived that with him the habit of domination prevailed more than the wholesomeness of counsel, he inflamed the noblest young men of that state with the desire of freeing their country. When an information of this matter had leaked out to the tyrant, calling the people together into the forum he began to torture him with various kinds of torment, asking again and again whom he had as partners in his plan. But Zeno neither named any of them, and rendered each man nearest and most faithful suspect to the tyrant, and, rebuking the Agrigentines for their cowardice and timidity, brought it about that, suddenly roused by an impulse of mind, they laid Phalaris low with stones. Thus the voice of one old man, set upon the rack—no suppliant voice, no wretched wailing, but a brave exhortation—changed the spirit and the fortune of a whole city.

3e.3. A philosopher of the same name, when he was being tortured by the tyrant Nearchus, against whose life he had entered into a plan, both for punishment and for the sake of disclosing his accomplices, conqueror of pain but desirous of vengeance, said that there was something which it would be very much to the tyrant's advantage to hear in private; and, the rack being loosened, when he perceived him exposed to his treachery, he seized his ear with a bite and did not let go before both he himself was deprived of life and the other of part of his body.

3e.4. An emulator of such endurance was Anaxarchus, who, when he was being tortured by Nicocreon, tyrant of the Cyprians, and could by no force be restrained from torturing the tyrant in turn with the lashes of most bitter revilings, at last, to him who threatened the cutting-off of his tongue, said: 'You will have no power, effeminate youth, over this part too of my body,' and at once spat the tongue, bitten off and chewed, into his face, open with rage. That tongue had held the ears of many, and chiefly of King Alexander, astonished with admiration of it, while it set forth most prudently and most eloquently the condition of the earth, the nature of the sea, the motions of the stars, and finally the nature of the whole world. Yet it almost perished more gloriously than it had flourished, because by so brave an end it confirmed the illustrious practice of its profession, and not only abandoned Anaxarchus' life but rendered his death more glorious.

3e.5. In Theodotus too, a man of the greatest weight, the tyrant Hieronymus wearied the hands of his torturers in vain: for Theodotus broke the lashes, slackened the cords, undid the rack, and put out the hot plates, before the tyrant could bring it about that he should disclose the accomplices of the tyrannicide. Nay more, by sullying with a false accusation the bodyguard, in whom the whole sum of the tyranny turned as if on a certain hinge, he tore from his side a faithful guardian, and by the benefit of his endurance not only concealed what was secret, but also avenged his own tortures. By them Hieronymus, while he eagerly mangled an enemy, rashly destroyed a friend.

3e.6. Among the Indians, indeed, the practice of endurance is believed to be so obstinately pursued that there are those who pass their whole life naked, now hardening their bodies in the icy chill of Mount Caucasus, now exposing them to flames without any groan. And by this no small glory is acquired through contempt of pain, and the title of wisdom is given.

3e.7. These things arose from deep and learned breasts; yet that which follows, no less admirable, a slavish spirit conceived. A barbarian slave, bearing grievously that Hasdrubal had killed his master, suddenly attacked and slew him; and when, having been seized, he was tortured in every way, he nevertheless kept on his face, most steadfastly, the joy which he had taken from his revenge. Not by a fastidious approach, then, is virtue won: she suffers lively spirits, once roused, to penetrate to her, nor offers a draught of herself either bountiful or grudging with any distinction of persons; but, set out equally for all, she weighs what desire rather than what dignity you have brought, and in the seizing of her goods she leaves to you yourself the weighing of the burden, so that as much as you have had the spirit to undergo, so much you carry away with you. Whence it comes about both that men born in a humble station rise to the highest dignity, and that the offspring of the noblest images, fallen back into some disgrace, turn the light received from their ancestors into darkness. These things will be made plainer by their own examples; and I shall begin first with those whose change for a better state offers a splendid material for the telling.

But as Spain is the witness of this man's abstinence, so Epirus, Achaea, the Cyclades islands, the maritime part of Asia, and the province of Cyprus are witnesses of Marcus Cato's. Whence, when he undertook the office of conveying the money, he had a spirit as averse from all love as from gain, though engaged in the greatest material for both kinds of intemperance: for he had royal riches within his own power, and the most fertile cities of so much of Greece, full of delights, were the necessary stopping-places of his whole voyage. And this Munatius Rufus, the faithful companion of his Cyprian expedition, signifies in his writings. His testimony I do not embrace: for that praise rests upon its own proper proof, since from the same womb of nature both self-control and Cato were born.

Publius Mucius the tribune of the plebs believed the same thing permitted to himself which he believed permitted to the senate and Roman people, who burned alive all his colleagues who under the lead of Spurius Cassius had so acted that, the magistrates not being replaced, the common liberty was called into doubt. There is surely nothing more confident than this severity: for one tribune dared to inflict on nine colleagues that punishment which nine tribunes would have shuddered to exact from one colleague.

In this class of acuteness Junius Brutus must be reckoned among the first: for when he observed that all the flower of the nobility was being plucked out by the king Tarquinius, his uncle, and that among the rest his own brother too had been killed, because he was of a more vigorous wit, he pretended that he was of a dull mind, and by this deceit concealed his very great virtues. Setting out also for Delphi with the sons of Tarquinius, whom the king had sent to honour Pythian Apollo with gifts and sacrifices, he brought gold to the god under the name of an offering, secretly enclosed in a hollowed-out staff, because he feared that it might not be safe for him to venerate the heavenly power with open liberality. Then, when their father's commissions had been carried out, the young men consulted Apollo as to which of them seemed likely to reign at Rome. He replied that the supreme power of our city would lie with him who should first give his mother a kiss. Then Brutus, as though he had slipped by chance, deliberately threw himself down and, thinking the earth to be the common mother of all, kissed it. That kiss so craftily pressed upon Tellus granted liberty to the city, and to Brutus the first place in the annals.

C. Afrania, moreover, the wife of the senator Licinius Bucco, prompt to contract lawsuits, always spoke for herself before the praetor, not because she was lacking in advocates, but because she abounded in shamelessness. And so, by constantly exercising the tribunals with barkings unaccustomed in the forum, she became the most notorious example of feminine calumny, so much so that as a reproach for the depraved characters of women the name of C. Afrania is cast in their teeth. She prolonged her breath to the second consulship of C. Caesar and P. Servilius: for of such a monster it is rather the time at which it was extinguished than that at which it arose that should be handed down to memory.

A man of ardent spirit and accustomed to warlike deeds the goads of anger drove to this; but C. Figulus, a most gentle man, most renowned for the peaceful study of the civil law, they rendered unmindful of his prudence and moderation: for, kindled by grief at the defeat of his consulship—the more so because he remembered that it had been given twice to his father—when on the day after the elections many had come to him to consult, he dismissed them all, declaring beforehand, "Do you know how to consult us, but not how to make us consul?" A thing gravely and deservedly said, but yet somewhat better not said: for who can be wisely angry at the Roman people?

The use of light-armed troops was first discovered in that war in which the commander Fulvius Flaccus besieged Capua: for when our cavalry, because they were fewer in number, could not resist the cavalry of the Campanians in their frequent sallies, Q. Navius, a centurion, established that chosen men of nimble body from among the infantry, armed with seven short and curved spears each and protected by a small shield, should join the riders by a swift leap and again slip away by a quick movement, so that, placed beneath the cavalry battle, the infantry might the more easily assail with their weapons both the men and the horses of the enemy; and that novelty of fighting crippled the unique resource of Campanian treachery, and therefore honour was paid to its author Navius by the general.

Drusus Germanicus too—the surpassing glory of the Claudian family and a rare ornament of his country, and, what is above all, answering wonderfully, by the greatness of his deeds for the measure of his age, to his stepfather and brother, the two Augusti, the divine eyes of the commonwealth—it is agreed kept the practice of love shut within love of his wife. Antonia too, a woman who surpassed by her praises the manly renown of her family, repaid her husband's love with excellent fidelity, who, after his death, flourishing in beauty and age, held the companionship of her mother-in-law in place of a marriage; and in the same bed the vigour of one youth was extinguished, the experience of the other's widowhood grew old. Let this chamber set the highest crown upon such proofs.

But as the mind of the senate and people, stirred up after the manner of a sudden storm, is to be pursued with gentle complaint, so the ungrateful deeds of individuals are to be reviled with freer indignation, because, masters of their own counsel, when it was permitted to weigh each side by reason, they preferred crime to piety: for with what cloudburst, with what storm of words does the impious head of Sextilius deserve to be overwhelmed, who did not shrink to tear Gaius Caesar—by whom both zealously and even successfully he had been defended as a defendant on a most grievous charge—from the rites of his treacherous table and the altars of his abominable household gods, when Caesar, a fugitive at the time of the Cinnan proscription, was compelled to implore his protection on the Tarquinian estate by the condition of his disaster and to claim it by the right of the benefit, and to hand him over to the savage victor to be slaughtered? Suppose his accuser, turned by public fortune into the name of a suppliant, had begged with so lamentable an entreaty, clasping his knees: still he would seem cruelly repulsed, because misery makes pleasing even those whom injury makes hateful. But Sextilius set, with his own hands, not his accuser but his patron before the most savage violence of his enemy—a man unworthy of life if through fear of death, most worthy of death if through hope of reward.

Thus far severity is the guardian and avenger of liberty; but for the sake of dignity also and of discipline it is equally grave: for the senate surrendered Marcus Claudius to the Corsicans, because he had made a shameful peace with them. When he was not accepted by the enemy, it ordered him to be put to death in the public prison—in how many ways, the majesty of the empire once injured, is anger a persistent avenger! It rescinded his act, took away his liberty, extinguished his breath, defiled his body with the insult of prison and the detestable mark of the Gemonian Stairs. And this man indeed had deserved the senate's animadversion; but Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Hispallus's son experienced it before he could deserve it: for, when the province of Spain had fallen to him by lot, it decreed that he should not go there, adding the reason that he did not know how to act rightly. And so Cornelius, on account of the dishonourable conduct of his life, without any provincial administration, was all but condemned under the law of extortion. Not even in the case of Gaius Vettienus, who had cut off the fingers of his left hand that he might not serve in the Italian War, did the severity of the senate slacken: for, his goods confiscated, it decreed that he himself should be punished with perpetual chains and brought it about that the breath which he had been unwilling honourably to pour out in the battle line he should disgracefully waste away in chains.

The elder Scipio too embraced the protection of cunning: for when, making for Africa from Sicily, he wished to fill up the number of three hundred horsemen from the bravest Roman foot-soldiers, and could not so suddenly equip them, since the shortness of time forbade it, he achieved his end by the shrewdness of a plan: for of those young men, the noblest and richest, whom he had with him throughout all Sicily but unarmed, he ordered three hundred to make ready as quickly as possible splendid arms and chosen horses, as though he were going to carry them off at once with him to the assault of Carthage. When they, with troubled minds, had obeyed the order, prompt indeed but in view of the long and dangerous war, Scipio proclaimed that he would remit that expedition for them, if they would consent to hand over their arms and horses to his soldiers. The unwarlike and timid youth snatched at the condition and eagerly yielded their equipment to our men. Thus the cunning of the general provided that . . . by what was demanded at once, the fear of military service, first welcome and then removed, should become the greatest benefit.

Hortensia, moreover, the daughter of Q. Hortensius, when the order of matrons had been burdened with a heavy tax by the triumvirs, and none of the men dared to lend them his patronage, pleaded the cause of the women before the triumvirs both steadfastly and successfully: for, her father's eloquence being reproduced, she obtained that the greater part of the money imposed should be remitted to them. Q. Hortensius then lived again in his female offspring and breathed in the words of his daughter; and if his male descendants had been willing to follow her force, so great an inheritance of Hortensian eloquence would not have been cut off by a single woman's pleading.
4.pr. ON INTERROGATIONS UNDER TORTURE And, that we may carry through all the modes of trials, let us report interrogations under torture which were either not believed or rashly trusted.

And so not even those are to be approved—although their deed was protected by the splendour of their nobility—who, because Cn. Flavius, once of the most humble lot, had attained the praetorship, offended, threw away the golden rings from themselves and the trappings stripped from their horses, attesting the impotence of their grief by all but professed mourning.

Next let us be free for these too, whose spirit was never free at any moment . . . of laying aside money. Gnaeus Marcius, a young man of patrician stock, the famous offspring of King Ancus, to whom the captured Volscian town of Corioli added a surname, when, having performed deeds of conspicuous courage, he was praised by the consul Postumius Cominius in a careful speech before the soldiers and was being given all the military gifts, and a hundred iugera of land, and the choice of ten captives and as many adorned horses, a herd of a hundred oxen, and as much silver as he could carry, wished to accept nothing of these except the safety of a single captive who was his guest-friend, and a horse to use in battle. By this so circumspect moderation of spirit you would not know whether he chose his rewards or rejected them with the greater praise.

But to pass to another act of an ungrateful mind consonant with this: Marcus Cicero defended Gaius Popilius Laenas of the Picene region, at the request of Marcus Caelius, with no less care than eloquence, and, when his cause was very doubtful and wavering, sent him home safe to his household gods. This Popilius afterwards, neither in deed nor in word injured by Cicero, of his own accord asked Marcus Antonius that he might be sent to pursue and slay that proscribed man; and, having obtained the role of that detestable service, exulting with joy he ran to Caieta and ordered the man—I pass over that he was of the highest dignity, but certainly one distinguished by the office of saving help . . . to be venerated by him privately—to offer his throat, and at once, in supreme and untroubled leisure, cut off the head of Roman eloquence and the most illustrious right hand of peace, and returned to the city, brisk with that burden as though with rich spoils: for it did not occur to one carrying so wicked a load that he bore that head which had once pleaded on behalf of his own. Too weak are letters to brand this monster, since one who could lament such a fall of Cicero worthily enough—another Cicero—does not exist.

Imitating this deed, Manius Curius the consul, when he had been compelled suddenly to proclaim a levy and not one of the young men had answered, all the tribes being thrown into the lot, ordered the first name to be drawn from the urn out of the Pollia, which had come out first, to be cited, and, when that man did not answer, set the young man's goods up at the spear. When this was announced to him, he ran to the consul's tribunal and appealed to the college of tribunes. Then Manius Curius, having said by way of preface that the commonwealth had no need of that citizen who did not know how to obey, sold both his goods and himself.

What follows must be related. Q. Fabius Labeo, appointed by the senate as arbiter for fixing the boundaries between the people of Nola and of Naples, when he had come to the place itself, advised both parties separately to lay aside their greed and prefer to draw back rather than to advance in the dispute. And when each party, moved by the man's authority, had done this, a certain amount of empty land was left in the middle. Then, when the boundaries had been fixed as they themselves had marked them out, he adjudged whatever was left of the soil to the Roman people. But although the men of Nola and of Naples, circumvented, could complain of nothing—since the verdict had been given according to their own demonstration—nevertheless by a dishonest kind of trickery a new revenue accrued to our state. They say that the same man, when by a treaty struck with king Antiochus, whom he had overcome in war, he ought to receive half the number of his ships, cut them all in two through the middle, so as to deprive him of his whole fleet.

Such are the movements of anger of individuals or of a few against the whole people; those of a multitude toward leading men and its generals are of this kind. When Manlius Torquatus was bringing into the city a most ample and most glorious victory over the Latins and Campanians, and all the elders, exulting with joy, came to meet him, none of the younger men advanced to meet him, because he had struck with the axe his young son who had fought most bravely against his command. They pitied a man of their own age punished too harshly: nor do I defend their deed, but I point out the force of anger, which was able to divide both the ages and the feelings of a single state.

But Manius Curius, the most exact rule of Roman frugality and likewise the most perfect specimen of courage, presented himself to the Samnite envoys to be gazed upon, seated on a rustic stool by his hearth and dining from a wooden bowl—what kind of feast the equipment indicates: for he despised the riches of the Samnites, while the Samnites marvelled at his poverty: for when they had brought to him a great weight of gold sent by the state, and he was invited with kind words to be willing to use it, he relaxed his countenance with a laugh and at once said: 'Ministers of a superfluous, not to say silly, embassy, tell the Samnites that Manius Curius prefers to rule over the rich rather than to become rich himself, and take back that gift, precious indeed, yet devised for the harm of men, and remember that I can neither be conquered in battle nor corrupted with money.' The same man, when he had driven King Pyrrhus out of Italy, touched nothing at all of the royal booty with which he had enriched the army and the city. And when seven iugera of land apiece were decreed by the senate to the people, and to himself fifty, he did not exceed the measure of the popular assignment, thinking him an unfit citizen for the commonwealth who was not content with that which was granted to the rest.

In what manner I am now to touch upon you, Pompey the Great, I know not: for I both behold the greatness of your fortune, which once had occupied all lands and all seas with its splendour, and I remember that its ruin is greater than ought to be attempted by my hand. But nevertheless, even though we too be silent, the death of Gnaeus Carbo—by whom, when a very young man, you were protected as you contended in the forum about your father's goods, and who was slain by your order—will hover before the minds of men not without some reproach, because by so ungrateful a deed you indulged the power of Lucius Sulla more than your own sense of shame.

3e.1. And that foreign cities may not insult us when we have confessed our faults: the Carthaginians resolved to remove from their sight Hannibal—who, on behalf of their safety and victory, had slaughtered so many of our generals and so many of our armies as, if he had killed so many common soldiers of the enemy, would have been a matter of great glory.

3e.2. Lacedaemon bore no man either greater or more useful than Lycurgus, since indeed Pythian Apollo is reported to have answered him, when he sought an oracle, that he knew not whether to enrol him in the number of men or of gods. Yet neither the utmost purity of his life, nor his most constant love toward his fatherland, nor the laws salutarily devised could avail him so that he should not experience hostile citizens: for he was often pelted with stones, at one time driven from the forum, even deprived of an eye, and at last expelled from the very fatherland. What would other cities do, when even that one which claims for itself an outstanding praise of steadfastness and moderation and gravity proved so ungrateful toward one who had deserved so well?

3e.3. Take Theseus away from the Athenians, and there will be no Athens, or not so famous an Athens, since indeed he gathered into one city his citizens, scattered in villages, and imposed upon a people living separately and after the rustic manner the form and image of a most ample state. The same man, when scarcely yet arrived at the age of youth, repelled the cruel commands of that most powerful king Minos; the same man tamed the unbridled insolence of Thebes; the same man brought aid to the children of Hercules, and crushed by the courage of his spirit and the strength of his right hand whatever of monster or of crime there was anywhere. Yet, when he had been removed from the Athenians, Scyros, an island smaller than Delos, received his bones when dead. And further, Solon, who brought to the Athenians laws so excellent and so useful that, if they had been willing to use them perpetually, they would have had everlasting empire; who recovered Salamis, like a hostile citadel from close at hand threatening their safety; who first saw the tyranny of Pisistratus arising and alone dared openly and repeatedly to declare that it ought to be crushed by arms—he passed his old age a fugitive in Cyprus, nor did it fall to his lot to be buried in the fatherland of which he had deserved so well. Well would the Athenians have dealt with Miltiades, if, after the three hundred thousand Persians were conquered at Marathon, they had sent him straight into exile and not compelled him to die in prison and in chains. But, I suppose, they thought they had raged abundantly thus far against one who had deserved so well. Nay, not even his body did they suffer, when they had forced it to expire thus, to be consigned to burial before his son Cimon delivered himself to be bound with the same chains. This paternal inheritance—chains and prison—the son of the greatest general, himself destined to be the greatest general of his age, could boast that he alone had inherited. Aristides too, by whom the justice of all Greece is reckoned, and who was an outstanding example of self-restraint as well, was ordered to depart his fatherland. Happy Athens, which after his exile could find anyone either a good man or a citizen loving his country, when with him at that time holiness itself migrated! Themistocles, the most celebrated example of those who have experienced an ungrateful fatherland—when he had rendered it unharmed, famous, opulent, the chief of Greece—felt it so far hostile that he was compelled to flee to the unmerited mercy of Xerxes, whom a little before he had destroyed. Phocion indeed, most amply furnished with those gifts which are judged most powerful to produce the love of men—clemency and generosity—was all but set upon the rack by the Athenians. Certainly after his death he found no little clod of the Attic region to be cast upon his bones, being ordered to be thrown beyond those borders within which the best of citizens had lived. What, then, is wanting to prevent it from being judged a public madness, by the highest consensus to punish the greatest virtues as though the gravest offences and to repay benefits with injuries? This, as everywhere, so especially at Athens, ought to seem intolerable—in which city an action against the ungrateful was established, and rightly, because the commerce of giving and receiving a benefit, without which the life of men scarcely . . . is taken away by whoever neglects to return equal gratitude to one who has deserved well. How great a reproach, then, do those deserve who, when they had the most equitable laws but the most iniquitous dispositions, preferred to use their own characters rather than the laws? But if by any providence of the gods it could be brought about that those most excellent men, whose misfortunes I have just related, holding to the law that avenges the ungrateful, should drag their fatherland into court before another state, would they not have rendered an ingenious and garrulous people mute and tongueless by this demand? "Your discordant hearths and the divided cottages of your villages were made the pillar of Greece: Marathon shines with Persian trophies; Salamis and Artemisium count the shipwrecks of Xerxes; the walls drained by mighty hands rise up in fairer works. The authors of these things—where did they live? Where do they lie? Answer! Indeed you compelled Theseus to be buried on a tiny rock, and Miltiades to die in prison, and Cimon to put on his father's chains, and Themistocles the conqueror to clasp the knees of his conquered enemy, and Solon together with Aristides and Phocion to flee your household gods, ungrateful one—while meanwhile, our ashes being foully and pitiably scattered, you honour, decorated with the honour of an altar, more sacred than the sanctuaries, between the very Areopagus, that venerable dwelling of divine and human contention, and the lofty citadel of guardian Minerva, the remains of Oedipus, polluted by the murder of his father and the marriage of his mother. So much more pleasing to you are others' evils than your own goods. Read, then, the law which holds you bound by an oath, and, because you were unwilling to render the due rewards to those who deserved well, pay the just expiations to those you have injured." Their mute shades are silent, bound by the necessity of fate; but Athens, forgetful of benefits, with a tongue loosed for licentious speech, is not silent in answering reproach.

4.pr. But let us pass over the ungrateful and rather speak of the dutiful: for it is somewhat better to give one's leisure to a pleasing than to a hateful subject. Come, then, into our hands, prosperous prayers of parents, offspring propagated under happy auspices, you who bring it about that it is both a joy to have begotten and a pleasure to beget.

Equally tenacious of his purpose was Lucius Domitius: for when as praetor he was governing Sicily and a boar of remarkable size had been brought to him, he ordered the shepherd, by whose hand it had been killed, to be brought to him, and, having asked who had dispatched that beast, after he learned that he had used a hunting spear, he crucified him, because he himself, in order to drive out the brigandage by which the province was being laid waste, had proclaimed that no one should have a weapon. Someone might say that this should be placed on the borderline between severity and savagery—for by argument it can be bent either way—but the reason of public command does not allow a praetor to be thought too harsh.

For we must forgive the gibe of M. Antonius, who used to say that he had written out no speech for this reason: that if anything done in an earlier trial should be likely to harm the man he was afterwards going to defend, he might be able to affirm that it had not been said by him; for he had a tolerable excuse for a scarcely decent deed: for on behalf of those whose lives were in peril he was prepared not only to use his own eloquence, but even to abuse his own sense of shame.

And the same was able to do so much that it held immovable the whole cavalry of the Roman people, sent by the consul Fabius to pursue the forces of the enemy when it was both safe and easy to destroy them, mindful of an agrarian law obstructed by him. It even made the army hostile to the leader Appius, whose father, while he strove for the eminence of the senate, had most keenly attacked the advantages of the plebs, and forced it by a voluntary flight to turn its back to the enemy, lest it should win a triumph for its commander. How often a victor over victory! It rendered its congratulation, in the case of Torquatus, to be scorned; in the case of Fabius, its most beautiful part to be omitted; in the case of Appius, the whole of it to be set after flight.

The same was the feeling of Fabricius Luscinus, greater than the whole state of his times in honours and authority, equal in property to every poorest man, who sent back into Samnium ten pounds of bronze and five pounds of silver and ten slaves sent to him by the Samnites, all of whom he held in his patronage—by the benefit of his self-control most rich without money, abundantly attended without the service of a household, because not the possessing of much but the desiring of little made him wealthy. Therefore his house, just as it was empty of the bronze and silver and slaves of the Samnites, so was filled with the glory won from them. Consonant with the rejected gifts were the prayers of Fabricius: for, setting out as envoy to Pyrrhus, when he heard, in his presence, the Thessalian Cineas relating that there was a certain man at Athens, famous for wisdom, who persuaded that men should be willing to do nothing else than for the sake of pleasure, he received that utterance as a portent, and at once prayed Pyrrhus and the Samnites to embrace that wisdom. Though Athens may glory in her learning, yet a prudent man would prefer the execration of Fabricius to the precepts of Epicurus. Which the outcome too declared: for the city that gave most to pleasure lost the greatest empire, the one that delighted in toil seized it, and the former could not protect its liberty, the latter could even bestow it.

Thus severity exercised itself in punishing men, but it acted no more sluggishly even in afflicting women with punishment. Horatius, victor first in the battle of the three Curiatii, then by the terms of the fight of all the Albans, when, returning home from that most illustrious battle line, he had seen his maiden sister weeping for the death of Curiatius her betrothed more lavishly than that age ought, killed her with the sword by which he had managed his fatherland's affairs well, judging insufficiently chaste the tears which were given to a too-precipitate love. Indicted on this charge before the people, his father defended him. Thus the girl's somewhat too inclined disposition toward the memory of her future husband had both a fierce avenger in her brother and a father so rigid an approver of the vengeance.

Sertorius, having experienced the indulgence of nature equal to the strength of his body and the wisdom of his mind, forced by the Sullan proscription to become leader of the Lusitanians, when he could not bend them by a speech from their wish to engage with the Romans in a full battle line, led them by a crafty plan to his own opinion: for he set up in their sight two horses, one most strong, the other most feeble, and then ordered the tail of the strong one to be plucked little by little by a weak old man, and the tail of the feeble one to be torn off all at once by a young man of remarkable strength. The order was obeyed. But while the young man's right hand wearied itself with fruitless labour, the hand worn out with age accomplished its task. Then, to the barbarian assembly that was eager to learn to what this matter tended, he suggested that our army was like a horse's tail, of which someone attacking the parts might overwhelm them, while one attempting to lay low the whole would hand over victory more quickly than he could seize it. So the barbarian people, rough and hard to rule, rushing to its own destruction, perceived with its eyes the advantage which it had rejected with its ears.

Come now, how violently did it conduct itself in the breast of the whole Roman people at that time when by its votes the dedication of the temple of Mercury was given to M. Plaetorius, a centurion of the first rank, the consuls being passed over—Appius, because he had obstructed relief being given to his own debt, and Servilius, because he had protected the cause he had undertaken with a languid advocacy. Do you deny that anger is effective, at whose urging a soldier was preferred to the highest command?

One might rightly judge that Quintus Tubero, surnamed Catus, was a pupil of Curius and Fabricius. When he was holding the consulship and the whole nation of the Aetolians had sent to him through envoys silver vessels of great weight and fashioned with exquisite art—the same who at an earlier time, having gone to him to offer congratulations, had reported that they had seen earthenware on his table—he ordered them to depart with their own baggage, warned not to think that his self-control, as though it were poverty, needed to be relieved. How well he had preferred his own household goods to the Aetolian, if a later age had been willing to follow the example of his frugality! Now to what point has it come? It can scarcely be obtained even from slaves that they not disdain the furniture which a consul then did not blush to use.

Using a like severity afterward, the senate, in the consulship of Spurius Postumius Albinus and Quintus Marcius Philippus, charged them to inquire into those women who had used the rites of the Bacchanalia unchastely. When many of them had been condemned by these consuls, their relatives within their houses inflicted punishment upon them all, and the widely extending foulness of the disgrace was amended by the severity of the punishment, because, as much shame as the women had brought upon our state by behaving shamefully, so much praise did they bring, when gravely punished.

Fabius Maximus, moreover, for whom not to fight was to conquer, when he had in his camp a foot-soldier of the people of Nola, a man of outstanding bravery but suspected of doubtful loyalty, and a Lucanian horseman of energetic service who was perishing for love of a harlot, in order that he might rather use both as good soldiers than punish both, dissembled his suspicion in the case of the one, and in the case of the other bent military discipline a little from its straight course: for by praising the former fully before his tribunal and honouring him with every kind of distinction, he compelled his mind to be recalled from the Carthaginians to the Romans, and by allowing the latter to ransom his mistress secretly, he rendered him a most ready skirmisher on our behalf.
