Anger indeed not only trampled commands underfoot, but even wielded them without self-control: for Q. Metellus, when as consul first, then as proconsul, he had subdued almost the whole of both Spains, after he learned that Q. Pompeius the consul, his enemy, was being sent as his successor, dismissed all who only wished their service ended, gave furloughs to those seeking them without the causes being examined or a time appointed, exposed his granaries to plunder by removing their guards, ordered the bows and arrows of the Cretans to be broken and thrown into a river, and forbade fodder to be given to the elephants. By these deeds, as he indulged his desire, so he corrupted the glory of his magnificently accomplished achievements, and, a braver victor over enemies than over his own anger, lost the deserved honour of a triumph.

But when King Perseus had been conquered, Paulus, though with the Macedonian wealth he had so far satisfied the old and hereditary poverty of our city that at that time for the first time the Roman people freed itself from the burden of paying tribute, made his own household goods richer in no part, thinking it gloriously done by him that from that victory others should seize the money, he himself the glory.

But Publicia, who had killed her husband the consul Postumius Albinus with poison, and likewise Licinia, who had killed her husband Claudius Asellus, were strangled by the decree of their kinsmen: for those most severe men did not think that, in so evident a crime, the long time of a public inquiry should be awaited. And so, of women whose defenders they would have been had they been innocent, they proved the prompt avengers, since they were guilty.

I shall come now to those by whom safety was sought through cunning. M. Volusius, plebeian aedile, when he had been proscribed, taking on the dress of a priest of Isis, begging alms along the roads and public highways, did not allow those he met to discern who he really was, and, hidden by this kind of deceit, made his way into the camp of M. Brutus. What is more wretched than that necessity, which bade a magistrate of the Roman people, with the purple-bordered toga of his honour cast off, walk through the city disguised in the insignia of a foreign religion! O men too desirous, these of their own life, those of another's death, who either themselves endured such things or compelled others to suffer them!

What of Sulla, while he complies with this vice—did he not, much foreign blood being poured out, at last pour out his own too? For at Puteoli, burning with indignation because Granius, the leading man of that colony, was too slowly paying the money promised by the decurions for the rebuilding of the Capitol, by too great an agitation of mind and an immoderate impulse of voice, his chest being burst, he vomited up his breath mixed with blood and threats—not now sunk in old age, since he was entering his sixtieth year, but raging with a lack of self-control nourished by the miseries of the state. Therefore it is doubtful whether Sulla or Sulla's anger was extinguished first.

3e.pr. It neither pleases me to seek examples from the unknown, nor is it without shame to reproach the greatest men with their vices. But since the good faith of my undertaking advises me to embrace whatever is most excellent, let my inclination yield to the work, provided that the conscience of one narrating necessary things does not fail to approve gladly the glorious ones.

3e.1. Alexander his own anger all but dragged down from heaven: for what prevented him from rising thither, except that Lysimachus was thrown to a lion, and Clitus run through with a spear, and Callisthenes ordered to die, so that he rendered, as conquered, his three greatest victories by as many unjust slaughters of friends?

3e.2. How vehement, moreover, was Hamilcar's hatred toward the Roman people! For, gazing on his four sons of boyish age, he used to declare that he was rearing as many lion-cubs for the destruction of our empire. Worthy nurslings, which were turned, as it came to pass, to the ruin of their own country.

3e.3. Of these Hannibal so early followed his father's footsteps that, when his father was about to carry his army across into Spain and was on that account sacrificing, the boy of nine years, holding the altars, swore that, as soon as he could by his age, he would be the most keen enemy of the Roman people, and by most persistent prayers wrung out a comradeship in the impending war. The same man, wishing to signify with how great hatred Carthage and Rome were at variance with each other, having struck his foot upon the ground and raised the dust, said that then there would be an end of war between them, when one or the other had been reduced to the condition of that dust.

3e.4. In a boyish breast so great was the force of hatred able to do; but in a woman's too it availed equally much: for Semiramis, queen of the Assyrians, when, busy about the dressing of her head, it was announced to her that Babylon had revolted, with one part of her hair still loose at once ran to storm it, nor did she reduce the comeliness of her hair to order before the city to her power. Wherefore her statue was set up at Babylon in that guise in which she hastened with headlong speed to exact vengeance.

4.pr. ON AVARICE Let avarice too be dragged forth, the tracker of hidden gains, the most greedy whirlpool of manifest plunder, happy neither in the fruit of having nor most wretched in the desire of seeking.

And to this judgement of his spirit subscribed Quintus Fabius Gurges, Numerius Fabius Pictor, and Quintus Ogulnius. These, sent as envoys to King Ptolemy, brought into the treasury the gifts which they had received from him privately, and indeed before they reported their embassy to the senate, judging evidently that from a public service nothing ought to accrue to anyone except the praise of a duty well administered. Now that is a token of the humanity of the senate and of the careful discipline of our ancestors: for what they had laid up in the treasury was given to the envoys, not only by the decree of the conscript fathers, but also by the permission of the people . . . and the quaestors distributed to each what had been bequeathed. Thus in the same matter the liberality of Ptolemy, the abstinence of the envoys, and the equity of the senate and people obtained the due portion of a praiseworthy deed.

By a great crime the severity of these men was roused to exact vengeance; but that of Egnatius Mecenius by a far lesser cause, who, having struck with a cudgel his wife because she had drunk wine, killed her, and that deed lacked not only an accuser but even a censurer, since everyone judged that by an excellent example she had paid the penalty for violated sobriety. And indeed whatever woman immoderately seeks the use of wine closes the door to all virtues and opens it to all faults.

Somewhat more splendid was the help that Sentius Saturninus Vetulo gave himself in the same kind of extreme fortune. He, when he had heard that his name had been posted among the proscribed by the triumvirs, at once seized the insignia of a praetorship, and with men suborned to go before him in the manner of lictors and attendants and public slaves, commandeered vehicles, took over lodgings, cleared those he met from his path, and by so bold a usurpation of office spread, in the broadest daylight, the thickest darkness over the eyes of his enemies. The same man, when he came to Puteoli, just as though he were performing a public service, with the greatest license seized ships and made his way into Sicily, which was then the surest refuge of the proscribed.

That Calpurnius Piso was a rival, in a like kind of praise, of the self-control of the Fabii and Ogulnius, the thing itself is proof. As consul, Sicily having been freed by him from a grievous war of fugitives, he was honouring with gifts, in the manner of a commander, those whose special service he had used. Among them he adorned his own son, who had fought most bravely in several places, with the title of a golden crown of three pounds, prefacing that it was not fitting for a magistrate to disburse from the public money what would return into his own house, and he promised that he would bequeath to the young man by his will so much weight, so that he should receive the honour publicly from a general, the price privately from a father.

Horrid too was the marital sternness of Gaius Sulpicius Gallus: for he dismissed his wife because he had learned that she had gone abroad with her head uncovered—a curt verdict, but yet fortified by some reason: "For the law," he said, "appoints for you only my eyes, by which you may make trial of your beauty. For these prepare the instruments of adornment, for these be beautiful, entrust yourself to the surer knowledge of these. Any further sight of you, summoned by superfluous provocation, must cleave in suspicion and accusation."

With one example of lighter note added to these, I shall return to foreign matters. A certain man, most loving of his son, when he wished to restrain him, inflamed with forbidden and dangerous passions, from his insane desire, tempered his fatherly indulgence with wholesome counsel: for he asked that, before he went to the woman he loved, he should make use of common and permitted love. The young man, complying with his prayers, the impulse of his unhappy spirit being loosened by the satiety of licensed intercourse, and bringing himself slower and more sluggish to what was not permitted, gradually laid the passion aside.

3e.1. When Alexander, king of the Macedonians, warned by lot to order the man who should first meet him as he went out of the gate to be killed, had commanded an ass-driver who happened to come in his way before all others to be hurried off to death, and the man asked why he was condemning him, who deserved nothing and was innocent, to capital punishment, and Alexander to excuse his act referred to the command of the oracle, the ass-driver said, "If it is so, O king, the lot has destined another for this death: for the little ass, which I was driving before me, met you first." Alexander, delighted both at so clever a saying and because he himself had been recalled from his error, snatched at the opportunity of expiating the religious obligation in an animal of considerably less worth. The highest gentleness in this king, in the groom of the other king cunning.

3e.2. When the realm was oppressed by the foul domination of the Magi, Darius, having taken to himself six helpers of the same rank, made a pact with the partners of his glorious work that, mounted on horses, at sunrise they should direct their course to a certain place, and that he should obtain the kingdom whose horse should first neigh there. But while his rivals, men of the greatest reward, awaited the kindness of fortune, he alone obtained the prosperous accomplishment of the wished-for thing by the shrewdness of his groom Oebares, who, having put his hand on the mare's genitals, when they had come to that place, brought it to the nostrils of the horse. Excited by that scent, the horse neighed before all the rest; and on hearing it the remaining six candidates for the supreme power at once slipped from their horses and, as is the custom of the Persians, with their bodies stretched on the ground saluted Darius as king. How great an empire was intercepted by how small a trick!

3e.3. Bias, moreover, whose wisdom is longer-lived among men than his native Priene was—since the latter even now breathes, while of the former only traces survive as of one extinguished—used to say that men ought so to conduct themselves in the practice of friendship that they should remember that it could be turned into the gravest enmities. This precept indeed might at first sight seem perhaps too cunning and hostile to that simplicity in which intimacy especially delights; but if a deeper consideration be brought to bear, it will be found exceedingly useful.

3e.4. The safety of the city of Lampsacus, indeed, rested on the benefit of a single trick: for when Alexander was being carried towards its destruction with the greatest zeal, and had seen his teacher Anaximenes advanced beyond the walls, because it was clear that he would oppose his prayers to his anger, he swore that he would not do what Anaximenes asked. Then Anaximenes said, "I ask that you destroy Lampsacus." This swiftness of shrewdness rescued from the destruction to which it was destined a town renowned for its ancient nobility.

3e.5. By the cunning of Demosthenes too a certain little old woman was wonderfully helped, who had received money on deposit from two strangers on this condition: that she should return it to both of them together. One of them, after some time had passed, as though his comrade were dead, covered with squalor, carried off all the coins of the deceived woman. Then the other came up and began to demand the deposit. The wretched woman was at a loss, and, in the greatest want both of money and of defence alike, was now thinking of a noose and hanging: but opportunely Demosthenes shone upon her as her advocate. When he came into the case, he said, "The woman is prepared to discharge her obligation of the deposit; but unless you bring your partner, she cannot do it, since, as you yourself proclaim, this was the agreement, that the money should not be paid out to one without the other."

3e.6. Nor indeed was that done with little prudence. A certain man at Athens, hateful to the whole people, about to plead his case on a capital charge before them, suddenly began to seek the highest office, not because he hoped he could attain it, but so that men might have somewhere to pour out the onrush of their anger, which is usually most keen. Nor did this so cunning reasoning of his plan deceive him: for, vexed at the elections by hostile shouting and the frequent hisses of the whole assembly, and stung also by the mark of an office denied him, a little later, in a peril of his life, he found the most merciful votes of that same people. But if he had exposed himself to the danger of his head while they still thirsted for vengeance, their ears, barred by hatred, would have admitted no part of his defence.

3e.7. Like this trick was that cunning of . . . Hannibal. Defeated by the consul Duilius in a naval battle, and fearing to pay the penalty for the lost fleet, he wonderfully averted the displeasure by a stratagem: for, before the news of the disaster could reach home, after that unlucky battle he sent a certain one of his friends, prepared and instructed, to Carthage. When this man had entered the senate-house of that city, he said, "Hannibal consults you: since the Roman commander has arrived bringing great maritime forces with him, ought he to engage with him?" The whole senate cried out that there was no doubt that he ought. Then the man said, "He has engaged, and has been defeated." Thus he left them no freedom to condemn the act which they themselves had judged ought to be done.

3e.8. Likewise Hannibal, when Fabius Maximus was mocking the unconquered force of his arms by most wholesome delays of battle, in order to sprinkle him with some suspicion of dragging out the war, while laying waste the fields of all Italy with fire and sword, left his estate alone, immune from this kind of injury. The insidious sketch of so great a benefit would have accomplished something, had not both Fabius's loyalty and Hannibal's crafty character been most well known to the Roman city.

3e.9. To the people of Tusculum too safety was gained by the acuteness of their counsel: for when by their frequent rebellions they had deserved that the Romans should wish to overthrow their city from its foundations, and Furius Camillus, a most distinguished general furnished with a most powerful army, had come to carry this out, they all came to meet him in their togas and most kindly furnished supplies and the other offices of peace. They even allowed him to enter the walls in arms, with neither face nor dress changed. By this steadfastness of tranquillity they penetrated not only to the right of our friendship, but even to the partnership of citizenship—using, by Hercules, a shrewd simplicity, since they had understood that it was more fitting to dissemble fear by services than to protect themselves by arms.

3e.10. But execrable was the counsel of Tullus, leader of the Volsci. He, inflamed with the greatest desire to make war on the Romans, when he observed that the spirits of his men were bruised by several adverse battles and on that account more inclined to peace, drove them where he wished by an insidious device: for when a great multitude of the Volsci had assembled at Rome for the sake of watching the games, he told the consuls that he greatly feared lest they should suddenly set in motion something hostile, and warned them to be more cautious, and immediately himself went out of the city. The consuls reported this matter to the senate. The senate, although no suspicion underlay it, nevertheless, moved by the authority of Tullus, decreed that the Volsci should depart before nightfall. Irritated by this insult, they could easily be impelled to rebel. Thus the lie of the crafty leader, wrapped in a pretence of goodwill, deceived two peoples at once: the Roman, so as to brand the innocent; the Volscian, so as to make them angry at being deceived.

4.pr. STRATAGEMS But there is that outstanding part of cunning, far removed from all reproach, whose works, because by . . . a name they can scarcely be aptly expressed, are called, in Greek pronunciation, "stratagems."

Come, if any illustrious man in this age were to use kidskins for coverlets, and, attended by three slaves, were to govern Spain, and were to make for an overseas province at a cost of five hundred asses, and were content with the same food and the same wine as the sailors, would he not be thought pitiable? And yet the elder Cato endured these things most patiently, because the pleasing habit of frugality kept him in this kind of life with the highest sweetness.

Nor did Quintus Antistius Vetus feel otherwise in repudiating his wife, because he had seen her in public speaking secretly with a certain common freedwoman: for, moved, so to speak, by the cradles and nurslings of fault, not by the fault itself, he furnished a vengeance prior to the offence, so as to guard against the wrong rather than to avenge it.

Far from the ancient self-control, by the space of years, does the later Cato stand, born indeed in a state now rich and rejoicing in luxury. Yet he, when he took part in the civil wars, dragging his son with him, had twelve slaves—more in number than the elder, fewer by reason of the differing manners of the times.

To these is to be joined Publius Sempronius Sophus, who afflicted his wife with the mark of repudiation for nothing other than that she had dared, without his knowledge, to watch the games. Therefore, while women were thus once met, their minds were far from offences.

3e.1. But although the whole world can be instructed by the Roman examples of severity, yet it is not a thing of disgust to know foreign ones too summarily. The Lacedaemonians ordered the books of Archilochus to be exported from their state, because they thought their reading too little modest and chaste: for they were unwilling that the minds of their children should be imbued with them, lest it should harm their characters more than it profited their talents. And so the greatest poet—or certainly the one next to the greatest—because he had torn at a house hateful to him with obscene abuse, they punished with the exile of his poems.

3e.2. The Athenians, moreover, afflicted with capital punishment Timagoras, because, in the course of paying a greeting, he had flattered King Darius after the manner of that nation, taking it grievously that by the humble blandishments of one citizen the dignity of their whole city had been submitted to the Persian domination.

3e.3. Now Cambyses was of unusual severity, who ordered the skin, stripped from the body of a certain bad judge, to be stretched over the chair, and his son to sit on it to give judgment. But, both king and barbarian, by an atrocious and novel penalty for a judge, he provided that no judge afterward could be corrupted.

4.pr. GRAVELY SAID OR DONE A great and good part of praise in famous men is claimed also by those things which either were gravely said by them or done, and which persistent memory has grasped with eternal strength. From their overflowing abundance let us draw, with a hand neither too sparing nor again too greedy, what may rather satisfy desire than abound to satiety.

The mind exults in running over the memory of the greatest men. Scipio Aemilianus, after two famous consulships and as many triumphs of his own special glory, performed the duty of an embassy with seven slaves following. And, I think, he could have procured more from the spoils of Carthage and Numantia, had he not preferred that the praise of his deeds should redound to himself, the spoils to his country. And so, when he made his journey through allies and foreign nations, not his slaves but his victories were counted, nor how much weight of gold and silver, but how much of greatness he bore with him, was reckoned.

But self-control has often been recognized even in the spirits of the whole plebs; yet it will be enough to have related two examples of these, of ages widely distant from one another. Pyrrhus, the terror of his onset broken and his Epirote arms now languishing, desiring to buy the goodwill of the Roman people because he had not been able to weaken its valour, had transferred to our city almost the whole apparatus of his royal wealth. But when gifts both of great price and of various kinds, fitted for the use of men as much as of women, were carried about by his envoys among the houses, no one's door was opened to anyone's gift, and the bold rather than effective defender of Tarentine wantonness was, I know not with how much the greater glory of this city's manners, repulsed. In that storm too, which Gaius Marius and Lucius Cinna had inflicted upon the commonwealth, the wonderful abstinence of the Roman people was beheld: for when they had thrown the household goods of the proscribed to the hands of the crowd to be plundered, no one could be found who would seek booty amid the public mourning: each one held himself back from these just as if from sacred temples. And indeed this so merciful self-control of the plebs was a silent reproach to the cruel victors.

3e.1. And, that we may not begrudge to foreigners the commemoration of the same praise, Pericles, the chief man of the Athenians, when he had as colleague in the praetorship Sophocles, the writer of tragedies, and the latter, while engaged together in the public office, had praised in too lavish words the beauty of a freeborn boy passing by, rebuking his intemperance said that a praetor ought to keep not only his hands free from the gain of money, but also his eyes from a lustful gaze.

3e.2. But Sophocles, now advanced in age, when someone asked him whether he still made use of the pleasures of love, said: 'Heaven forbid! For I have gladly fled from that, as from some raging tyranny.'

3e.3. We have heard that Xenocrates was of an equally abstinent old age. Of which opinion the narrative that follows will be no small proof. At an all-night festival, Phryne, a noble harlot at Athens, lay down beside him, heavy with wine, having laid a wager with some young men whether she could corrupt his temperance. Spurning her neither in touch nor in word, having suffered her to stay in his bosom as long as she had wished, he sent her away baffled in her purpose. A deed abstinent of a soul steeped in wisdom, but the saying of the little harlot too was exceedingly witty: for when the young men mocked her, because she had not been able to entice with her allurements the spirit of a drowsy old man, so beautiful and so elegant as she was, and demanded the agreed price of victory, she answered that she had laid the wager with them about a man, not about a statue. Can this self-control of Xenocrates be more truly and more properly shown by anyone than it was expressed by the little harlot herself? Phryne by her beauty in no part shook his most steadfast abstinence: what then? Could King Alexander shake it with riches? You would think that by him too a statue, and indeed an equally vain one, had been attempted. He had sent envoys to him with several talents. These, led into the Academy, he received with his usual—that is, moderate—equipment and very small means. On the next day, when they asked to whom he wished the money to be counted out, he said: 'What? Did you not understand from yesterday's dinner that I do not need it?' Thus the king wished to buy the friendship of the philosopher, the philosopher was unwilling to sell his own to the king.

3e.4. But Alexander, having gained the surname of Invincible, could not conquer the self-control of Diogenes the Cynic. When he had approached him as he sat in the sun, and was urging him to indicate if there were anything he wished done for him, the man, as he was placed in the bank of the road, of squalid title but of robust eminence, said: 'Presently of other things; in the meantime I should wish you not to stand between me and the sun.' In which words, assuredly, this sentiment was contained: Alexander tries to drive Diogenes from his post with riches more swiftly than Darius with arms. The same man at Syracuse, when, as he was washing his greens, Aristippus said to him, 'If you were willing to flatter Dionysius, you would not be eating these things,' said: 'Nay rather, if you were willing to eat these things, you would not be flattering Dionysius.'

4.pr. ON POVERTY. That children are the greatest ornaments of matrons, we find thus in the book of the collections of Pomponius Rufus . . . : Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi, when a Campanian matron who was a guest with her showed her her own ornaments, the most beautiful of that age, drew her on in conversation until her children should return from school, and said: 'These are my ornaments.' Assuredly he has everything who desires nothing, and indeed more surely than he who possesses all things, because the ownership of things is wont to collapse, but the enjoyment of a good mind admits no assault of sadder fortune. And so to what purpose is it to set either riches in the first part of happiness or poverty in the lowest state of miseries, when both the cheerful face of the former is stuffed within with many bitternesses, and the more rugged aspect of the latter abounds in solid and certain goods? Which will be better represented by persons than by words.

The next step from military institutions must be made to the urban camps, that is, the theatres, since these too have often drawn up spirited battle-lines, and, devised for the sake of the worship of the gods and the delight of men, have, not without some blush upon peace, stained pleasure and religion with civil blood for the sake of scenic monstrosities.

ON THOSE WHO, BORN IN A HUMBLE STATION, CAME FORTH ILLUSTRIOUS. A rustic hut received the cradle of Tullus Hostilius: his youth was occupied in pasturing cattle: his stronger age ruled and doubled the Roman empire: his old age, adorned with the most excellent . . . shone on the highest pinnacle of majesty.

The royal command being ended on account of the excessive pride of Tarquinius, Valerius Publicola, with Junius Brutus, inaugurated the beginning of the consulship, and the same man afterwards held three consulships most acceptable to the Roman people, and by the bordered toga of very many and very great deeds enlarged the title of his own images; while meanwhile that pillar of the calendar departed with a patrimony not even sufficient for the cost of his funeral, and therefore his obsequies were conducted at public expense. It is not to the purpose to scrutinize the poverty of so great a man with further disputation: for it is abundantly clear what he possessed while alive, who, when dead, lacked a funeral couch and a pyre.

ON DUTIFULNESS TOWARD PARENTS AND BROTHERS AND FATHERLAND Coriolanus, a man of the greatest spirit and the deepest counsel, and most excellently deserving of the commonwealth, prostrated by the ruin of a most unjust condemnation, fled to the Volscians, then hostile to the Romans. Everywhere virtue is valued at a great price. And so, in the very place to which he had come seeking a hiding-place, he there in a short time attained the supreme command, and it came to pass that he whom the citizens had been unwilling to have as a salutary commander for themselves they should experience as an almost destructive leader against themselves: for, our armies being frequently routed, he built for the Volscian soldier, by the steps of his victories, an approach right up to the walls of the city. Wherefore that people, fastidious in valuing its own goods, which had not spared the defendant, was compelled to entreat the exile. The envoys sent to plead with him accomplished nothing; the priests then sent with their fillets returned equally without effect. The senate was stupefied, the people trembled, men and women alike lamented the impending destruction. Then Veturia, the mother of Coriolanus, dragging with her his wife Volumnia and his children, sought the camp of the Volscians. As soon as her son beheld her, "You have stormed," he said, "and conquered my anger, fatherland, by the prayers of this woman brought near, to whose womb I grant you, hateful to me though you deservedly are," and at once freed the Roman territory from hostile arms. Therefore his breast, filled with grief at the injury received, with hope of obtaining victory, with shame at refusing his commission, with fear of death, was wholly emptied of all this for itself by dutifulness; and the sight of a single parent changed an atrocious war into a salutary peace.

When our state had been struck by the disaster of Cannae, and the safety of the commonwealth, hanging by a very slender thread, depended on the loyalty of the allies, in order that their minds might be more steadfast in defending the Roman dominion, it pleased the greater part of the senate that the chief men of the Latins should be chosen into their order. But Annius the Campanian asserted that one of the consuls too ought to be created at Capua: so bruised and sick was the spirit of the Roman empire. Then Manlius Torquatus, the son of that man who had routed the Latins in the renowned battle at Veseris, announced, in as clear a voice as he could, that if any of the allies dared to deliver an opinion among the senators, he would kill him at once. These threats of one man both restored their former heat to the languishing minds of the Romans and did not allow Italy to rise up to make its right of citizenship equal with ours: for as it had yielded, broken by the arms of the father, so now by the words of the son. Equal too was the gravity of that Manlius, to whom, when the consulship was offered by the consent of all and he refused it under the excuse of the adverse health of his eyes, when all were pressing him, he said, "Seek another, Quirites, to whom you may transfer this honour: for if you compel me to bear it, neither shall I be able to bear your characters nor you to endure my command." So weighty was the utterance of a private man: how grave would the consul's fasces have proved!

Tullus Hostilius, having attacked Fidenae with all his military forces—which, the cradle of our rising empire, did not allow to grow torpid through their frequent rebellions, and taught his valour, fed by neighbouring trophies and triumphs, to push his hopes further—Mettius Fufetius, leader of the Albans, suddenly disclosed in the very battle line the loyalty of his alliance, always doubtful and suspect: for, deserting the flank of the Roman army, he settled on a nearby hill, to be a watcher of the battle instead of a helper, so that he might either insult the conquered or attack the wearied conquerors. There was no doubt that this matter would weaken the spirits of our soldiers, since at one and the same time they saw the enemy engaging and their auxiliaries failing. And so Tullus provided that this should not happen: for, urging on his horse, he ran through all the knots of fighting men, proclaiming that Mettius had withdrawn by his command, and that, when he himself had given the signal, he would attack the rear of the Fidenates. By this device of a commander's art he changed fear into confidence, and instead of trembling filled the breasts of his men with eagerness.

Alexander, the slave of M. Agrius the banker, was charged with having killed the slave of A. Fannius, and on that account, tortured by his master, most steadfastly maintained that he had committed that crime. And so, handed over to Fannius, he was punished. Then, a very little time intervening, the very man of whose murder it had been believed returned home.

When a certain man had forged a false will for the very wealthy L. Minucius Basilus in Greece, and, to confirm it, had inserted into the tablets as heirs the most powerful men of our state, M. Crassus and Q. Hortensius, to whom Minucius had been unknown, although the fraud was evident, yet each, desirous of money, did not repudiate the gift of another's crime. How great a fault I have related how gently! The lights of the senate-house, the ornaments of the forum, the crime which they ought to have punished, invited by the catch of dishonest gain, covered with their authority.

These [contests] were indeed begun by Messala and Cassius as censors. But on the authority of P. Scipio Nasica it was resolved that the whole apparatus of their work should be sold at auction; and it was even provided by a decree of the senate that no one should wish, in the city or within a mile of it, to have set up benches or, sitting, to watch the games, so that, doubtless, even in the relaxation of their minds . . . the manliness of standing, proper to and characteristic of the Roman nation, might be marked.

But Tullus, though a great example of admirable increase, is nevertheless a domestic one: Tarquinius, on the other hand, Fortune carried into our city to seize the Roman empire—a foreigner, because . . . ; more foreign, because sprung from Corinth; to be scorned, because born of a merchant; to be blushed at, because born of a father who was even an exile. Yet so prosperous an issue of his condition he, by his own industry, rendered glorious instead of odious: for he extended the boundaries, increased the worship of the gods with new priesthoods, enlarged the number of the senate, left the equestrian order richer, and—what is the crown of his praises—by his glorious virtues brought it about that this city did not repent of having borrowed a king from its neighbours rather than chosen one from its own.

Of how great eminence must we judge Menenius Agrippa to have been, whom the senate and the plebs chose as the author of making peace between them? Of how great, indeed, ought the arbiter of the public safety to have been. He, had he not been buried by the people, who contributed sextants per head—so destitute of money did he die—would have lacked the honour of burial. But for this reason did the state, divided by a destructive sedition, wish to be drawn together into one by the hands of Agrippa, because it had perceived them poor indeed, but holy. Of whom, while he lived, there was nothing that could be entered in the census, so, since he died, the harmony of Rome is to this day a most ample patrimony.

The same dutifulness armed with manly strength the elder Africanus, inflamed by his own powers when he had scarcely entered the years of puberty, to bring aid to his father in the battle line: for, when his father, as consul, was fighting under adverse auspices with Hannibal at the river Ticinus, grievously wounded, he saved him by his own intervention; nor could either the weakness of his age, or his rawness in soldiering, or the issue of an unfortunate battle—to be dreaded even by a veteran warrior—interrupt him, so that he should not, conspicuous with a twofold glory, earn the crown by snatching at once his commander and his father from death itself.

No less keen was the gravity of Scipio Aemilianus, whether in the senate-house or in the assembly. He, when he had Mummius as his colleague in the censorship, a man as noble as he was of nerveless life, said before the rostra that he would conduct all things in accordance with the majesty of the commonwealth, whether the citizens had given him a colleague or had not given him one. The same man, when the consuls Servius Sulpicius Galba and Aurelius were contending in the senate which of them should be sent against Viriathus into Spain, and there was great dissension among the senators, all awaiting whither his opinion would incline, said, "Neither of them, in my view, should be sent, because the one has nothing, and to the other nothing is enough"—judging poverty and avarice equally bad mistresses of licentious command. By this saying he obtained that neither was sent into the province.

And, not to depart at once from our kings, Sextus Tarquinius, son of Tarquinius, taking it ill that Gabii could not be stormed by his father's strength, devised a plan stronger than arms, by which he might intercept that town and add it to the Roman empire: for he suddenly betook himself to the Gabini, as though fleeing the cruelty of his parent and the lashes which he had endured of his own will; and little by little, by alluring the goodwill of every individual with feigned and contrived flatteries, when he had obtained the greatest influence among them all, he sent a friend of his to his father to indicate how he held all things in his own hand, and to ask what he wished to be done. To the young man's cunning the old man's craft replied: for Tarquinius, exceedingly delighted with the matter, but trusting too little to the loyalty of the messenger, made no reply, but, leading the man aside into the garden, knocked off with his staff the largest and tallest heads of the poppies. The young man, on learning at once both his father's silence and his deed, perceived the meaning of the one and the proof of the other, and did not fail to grasp that he was being instructed to remove every most eminent man of the Gabini either by exile or by death. Therefore he handed over to him the state, stripped of its good defenders, with its hands all but bound.

On the contrary, Alexander, the slave of P. Atinius, when he had come under suspicion of the murder of C. Flavius, a Roman knight, tortured six times, persistently denied that he had been an accomplice to that crime; but just as though he had confessed, he was condemned by the judges and driven to the cross by L. Calpurnius the commissioner.

But it showed somewhat greater strength in Q. Cassius, who in Spain dismissed Silius and Calpurnius, caught with daggers for the purpose of killing him, having bargained for five million sesterces from the one, six million from the other. Lo, the man of whom you might doubt that, if as much again were given, he would have offered his very throat to them with an even mind.

For five hundred and fifty-eight years the senate, mingled with the people, was present at the spectacle of the games. But this custom Atilius Serranus and L. Scribonius, as aediles, holding the games of the Mother of the gods, following the opinion of the later Africanus, dissolved by separating the places of the senate and the people; and this matter turned away the mind of the multitude and greatly shook the favour toward Scipio.

In Servius Tullius, however, Fortune especially showed her powers, by giving to this city a king born a homebred slave. To him indeed it fell to hold the empire the longest, to establish the census four times, to triumph three times. But from what point he set out and to what he came the inscription of his own statue abundantly attests, with its servile surname and royal title entwined.

But in the houses of Gaius Fabricius and Quintus Aemilius Papus, the chief men of their age, I must confess there was silver: for each had a dish for the gods and a saltcellar, but Fabricius the more elegantly, in that he wished his dish to be supported by a little horn foot. Papus too acted spiritedly enough, who, since he had received these by way of inheritance, did not think they should be alienated for reasons of religion.

With its ears the Roman state received these examples so renowned; the following it saw with its eyes. Pomponius the tribune of the plebs had named a day for Lucius Manlius Torquatus before the people, because, induced by the opportunity of finishing the war well, he had exceeded the lawful term for holding his command, and because he was withdrawing his son, a young man of the best disposition, from public uses, burdening him with rustic labour. After the young Manlius learned of this, he at once sought the city and at first light directed himself to the house of Pomponius. He, thinking that he had come for this, to lay information about the charges against his father, by whom he was treated more harshly than was right, ordered all to leave the bedchamber, that he might more freely carry through the information with the witnesses removed. Having gained an opportunity suited to his purpose, the young man drew the sword which he had brought concealed and, having compelled the tribune by threats and terror, forced him to swear that he would withdraw from the accusation of his father; and by this it was brought about that Torquatus did not plead his cause. Commendable is the dutifulness that is shown to gentle parents; but Manlius, the more grim a father he had, the more praiseworthily did he come to his aid in his peril, because to love him he had been invited, beyond natural affection, by no charm of indulgence.

But Gaius Popilius, sent by the senate as legate to Antiochus, that he should refrain from the war by which he was provoking Ptolemy, when he had come to him, and Antiochus with ready mind and a most friendly countenance had stretched out his right hand to him, was unwilling to stretch out his own in return, but handed over the tablets containing the decree of the senate. When Antiochus had read them, he said that he would confer with his friends. Popilius, indignant that he had interposed some delay, marked with a rod the ground on which Antiochus was standing and said, "Before you step out of this circle, give me an answer which I may report to the senate." You would have believed not that a legate was speaking, but that the very senate-house was set before your eyes: for at once the king affirmed that he would see to it that Ptolemy should complain of him no further, and then at last Popilius grasped his hand as that of an ally. How effective is the curt gravity of spirit and speech! At the same moment it terrified the kingdom of Syria and protected that of Egypt.

That too was provided by our ancestors both prudently in counsel and happily in outcome: for when the city had been taken and the Gauls were besieging the Capitol, and perceived that the only hope of taking it lay in the famine of its defenders, the Romans, using an exceedingly clever kind of counsel, robbed the conquerors of the one incitement to perseverance: for they began to throw down loaves of bread from several places. Astonished at this spectacle, and believing that an unlimited abundance of grain remained over for our men, the Gauls were driven to a compact to abandon the siege. Then truly Jupiter pitied Roman valour, which was borrowing its protection from cunning, when he saw provisions thrown away amid the greatest scarcity of supplies. And so to a crafty and likewise dangerous plan he gave a wholesome outcome.

Likewise, when Fulvius Flaccus was pleading his case, his slave Philippus, on whom the whole inquiry rested, tortured eight times, uttered absolutely no word by which his master could be implicated; and yet the defendant was condemned, although one man tortured eight times offered a surer proof of innocence than eight men tortured once would have offered.

But before all, avarice possessed the heart of L. Septimuleius, who, when he had been an intimate of C. Gracchus, brought himself to cut off his head and carry it about the city fixed on a pike, because the consul Opimius had proclaimed that he would weigh it out in gold. There are those who relate that he filled the hollowed part of the head with molten lead, so that it might be the heavier. Let that man have been seditious, let him have perished as a good example; yet the criminal hunger of a client ought not to have hungered even for these injuries to a man lying low.

4e.1. The avarice of Septimuleius deserved hatred; but that of Ptolemy, king of the Cyprians, is to be accompanied with laughter: for when he had snatched together great wealth by anxious meanness, and saw himself about to perish on account of it, and therefore, all his money placed on ships, had advanced into the deep, so that, the fleet being scuttled, he might perish by his own choice and the enemy might lack the plunder, he could not bring himself to sink the gold and silver, but carried home what was to be the reward of his death. Beyond doubt this man did not possess riches, but was possessed by riches—in title king of the island, in spirit a pitiable slave of money.

Now I shall trace from its origin the cause of the institution of the games. In the consulship of C. Sulpicius Peticus and C. Licinius Stolo, an intolerable force of pestilence that had arisen had afflicted our state, recalled from warlike works, with care for the domestic and internal evil; and now more help seemed to be placed in some choice and new form of religion than in any human counsel. And so, for the sake of placating the heavenly power, having composed songs, it lent willing ears, until then content with the circus spectacle, which Romulus first celebrated under the name of the Consualia, when the Sabine maidens were carried off. But, as it is the manner of men to pursue small beginnings with persistent zeal, the youth, with venerable words toward the gods, added jesting gestures with a rude and disorderly movement of the body; and this matter gave cause for summoning a player from Etruria. His comely agility, in the ancient manner of the Curetes and Lydians, from whom the Etruscans drew their origin, by its welcome novelty charmed the eyes of the Romans; and because a player was called among them "hister," the name of "histrio" was given to the actor. Then little by little the art of acting crept on to the measures of satires, from which Livius, the first poet of all, transferred the minds of the spectators to the plots of plays; and he, the performer of his own work, when, having been too often recalled by the people, he had worn out his voice, with the accompaniment of a boy and a flute-player brought in, performed the gestures in silence. The Atellan plays, moreover, were summoned from the Oscans. This kind of entertainment, tempered by Italic strictness and therefore free from stigma: for neither is the actor moved from his tribe nor repelled from military service.

By a wondrous step Varro too climbed to the consulship from his father's butcher's shop. And indeed Fortune thought it too little to bestow twelve fasces on a man reared by the takings of the basest merchandise, unless she had also given him Lucius Aemilius Paulus as colleague. And so he poured himself into Paulus' bosom that, when at Cannae by his own fault he had drained the strength of the Roman people, he allowed Paulus, who had been unwilling to join battle, to be slain, while he himself returned unhurt into the city. Nay more, he led out before the gates the senate, which was thanking him because he had been willing to return, and forced through the proposal that the dictatorship should be offered to the author of the most grievous disaster.

Were those most wealthy men, who were summoned from the plough to become consuls, turning over the barren and most parching soil of Pupinia for the sake of pleasure, and scattering its vastest clods with much sweat for the sake of delight? Nay rather, those whom the dangers of the commonwealth claimed as generals, the straits of their private estate—why do I delay to render its proper name to truth?—compelled to become ploughmen.

Emulating this dutifulness, Marcus Cotta, on the very day on which he assumed the toga of manhood, immediately, as he came down from the Capitol, indicted Gnaeus Carbo, by whom his father had been condemned, and, having carried the prosecution through, ruined the defendant by the verdict, inaugurating both his talent and his youth by a most illustrious work.

But whether I should rate the words or the deeds of Publius Rutilius more highly I know not: for in both there is equally an admirable strength. When he was resisting the unjust request of a certain friend, and that man had said with the utmost indignation, "What need, then, have I of your friendship, if you do not do what I ask?" he replied, "Nay, what need have I of yours, if on your account I am to do something dishonourable?" Consonant with this utterance is that deed of his, that, having been made a defendant rather by the dissension of the orders than by any fault of his own, he neither put on shabby clothing nor laid aside the insignia of a senator nor stretched out suppliant hands to the knees of the judges nor said anything lower than the splendour of his past years, and brought it about that his peril was not a hindrance to his gravity but a proof of it. And even when the Sullan victory offered him a return to his fatherland, he remained in exile, lest he should do anything against the laws. Wherefore one would more justly assign the surname of "the Fortunate" to the character of a most grave man than to the arms of an uncontrolled one: which surname Sulla seized, Rutilius deserved.

And the same Jupiter afterwards breathed favourably upon the shrewd counsels of our most excellent generals: for when Hannibal was tearing at one side of Italy and Hasdrubal had invaded the other, in order that the joined forces of the two brothers might not press our affairs, already wearied, with an unbearable weight at once, the vigorous counsel of Claudius Nero on the one hand, and the famed foresight of Livius Salinator on the other, brought it to pass: for Nero, having pinned Hannibal down in Lucania, falsely representing his own presence to the enemy, since the strategy of the war so required it, hastened with marvellous speed over a long road to bring help to his colleague. Salinator, about to fight on the next day in Umbria by the river Metaurus, with the greatest dissimulation received Nero into his camp by night: for he ordered tribunes to be taken in by tribunes, centurions by centurions, horsemen by horsemen, foot-soldiers by foot-soldiers, and without any commotion, on ground that could scarcely hold one army, inserted the other. Thereby it came about that Hasdrubal did not know he was going to fight against two consuls until he was laid low by the valour of both. Thus that Punic cunning, infamous throughout the whole world, baffled by Roman prudence, handed over Hannibal to be deceived by Nero, and Hasdrubal by Salinator.

And because, in the case of the other games, it is apparent from their very names whence they are derived, it does not seem absurd to give to the Secular games their own beginning, the knowledge of which is less worn. When the city and fields were being laid waste by a great pestilence, Valesius, a wealthy man of country life, his two sons and a daughter labouring even to the despair of the physicians, seeking warm water for them from the hearth, on bended knees prayed the household Lares to transfer the danger of his children onto his own head. Then a voice arose that he would have them safe, if straightway he should carry them, conveyed down the river Tiber, to Tarentum, and there, with water sought from the altar of Father Dis and Proserpina, restore them. Greatly troubled by this prediction, because both a long and a dangerous voyage was commanded, yet with doubtful hope overcoming his present fear, he immediately carried the boys down to the bank of the Tiber—for he dwelt in his villa near the village Eretum of the Sabine region—and, making for Ostia in a small boat, in the dead of night put in at the Campus Martius; and, desiring to relieve his thirsting sick ones, the fire on the boat failing, he learned from the helmsman that not far off smoke appeared, and, bidden by him to go ashore at Tarentum—that is the name of the place—eagerly seizing a cup, carried, now more joyful, water drawn from the river to the place from which the smoke had arisen, judging that he had found, as it were, certain traces near at hand of the divinely given remedy; and on the ground, which was rather smoking than having any remains of fire, while he more tenaciously grasped at the omen, having gathered light tinder and such fuel as chance offered, by his persistent breath he called forth a flame, and gave the warmed water to the boys to drink. When they had drunk it, lulled in salutary sleep, they were suddenly freed from the long-lasting violence of the disease, and told their father that they had seen in their dreams their bodies wiped over by some one of the gods with a sponge, and that they were bidden that, at the altar of Father Dis and Proserpina, from which the drink had been brought to them, dark victims should be sacrificed, and that couches should be spread and nocturnal games held. He, because he had seen no altar in that place, believing that one was wanted to be set up by himself, went into the city to buy an altar, leaving men to dig the earth down to the solid rock for the sake of laying the foundations. These, executing their master's command, when they had reached, with the earth thrown up, a depth of twenty feet, noticed an altar inscribed to Father Dis and Proserpina. After Valesius had received this from the announcing of his slave, abandoning his plan of buying an altar, he sacrificed black victims, which anciently were called dark, at Tarentum, and held games and couch-spreadings for three nights running, because just so many sons had been freed from danger. His example Valerius Publicola, who was the first consul, following in his zeal to succour the citizens, at the same altar, with vows publicly proclaimed and black oxen slain—males to Dis, females to Proserpina—and with a couch-spreading and games held for three nights, buried the altar with earth, as it had been before.

No small shame to the consulship is Marcus Perpenna, being a consul before he was a citizen; yet in the waging of war a somewhat more useful commander to the commonwealth than Varro: for he captured King Aristonicus and stood forth as the avenger of the Crassian slaughter; while meanwhile, after his life had triumphed, his death was condemned under the Papian law: for they compelled his father, who had grasped the rights of a Roman citizen as in no way belonging to him, to return, on the verdict of a Sabellian, into his former abode. Thus the name of Marcus Perpenna was a shadow, his consulship false, his command like a mist, his triumph a fleeting thing, an alien improperly sojourning in another's city.

But Atilius, those whom the senate had sent to summon him to take up the command of the Roman people, saw scattering seed. But those hands, worn by rustic toil, established the public safety, brought low vast forces of the enemy, and those which had just guided the yoke of ploughing oxen held the reins of a triumphal chariot, nor was it a blush to them, the ivory staff laid aside, to take up again the rustic ploughtail. Atilius can console the poor, but much more can he teach the wealthy how unnecessary to the desire of solid praise is the anxious gathering of riches.

In the case of Gaius Flaminius too a father's authority was equally powerful: for when, as tribune of the plebs, he had promulgated a law on dividing the Gallic land man by man, against the will and resistance of the senate, resisting most fiercely its prayers and threats, and not deterred even by an army enrolled against him should he persevere in the same purpose—after, before the rostra, as he was now bringing forward the law, his father laid a hand on him, broken by a private command he came down from the rostra, not reproached by even the slightest murmur of the deserted assembly.

Marcus Brutus, the parricide of his own virtues before of the parent of his fatherland—for by a single deed he both hurled those virtues into the abyss and suffused all the memory of his name with inexpiable detestation—about to enter his last battle, when some were saying that it ought not to be joined, said, "I go down confidently into the battle line: for today either it shall be well, or I shall care for nothing." He had presumed, of course, that he could neither live without victory nor die without freedom from care.

4e.1. The mention of him suggests to me to relate what was gravely said against Decimus Brutus in Spain: for when almost the whole of Lusitania had surrendered to him, and the single city of that nation, Cinginnia, persistently retained its arms, a ransom being attempted, with almost one mouth it answered the envoys of Brutus that iron had been left to it by its ancestors, with which to protect the city, not gold, with which to buy liberty from an avaricious commander. Better, doubtless, would men of our blood have said that than heard it.

4e.2. But these men nature led into these footprints of gravity; Socrates, however, the most illustrious pillar of Greek learning, when he was pleading his cause at Athens, and Lysias had recited to him a defence, composed by himself, which he might use in the trial, humble and suppliant, accommodated to the impending storm, said, "Take that away, I beg: for I, if I could be induced to deliver it in the furthest wilderness of Scythia, would then grant that I deserved to be punished with death." He scorned his life rather than lack gravity, and Socrates preferred to be extinguished than Lysias to survive.

4e.3. As great in arms as this man in wisdom, Alexander nobly uttered that famous saying: for when Darius, having now tried his valour in one battle and a second, and therefore promising both a part of his kingdom as far as Mount Taurus and his daughter in marriage with ten times a hundred thousand talents, and Parmenion had said that he, if he were Alexander, would use that condition, Alexander answered, "And I would use it, if I were Parmenion"—an utterance answering to two victories and worthy that a third should be assigned to it, as in fact happened.

4e.4. And these utterances, indeed, were both of a magnificent spirit and of a prosperous state; but that one, by which the envoys of the Lacedaemonians attested before his father the wretched condition of their courage, was more glorious than to be wished for: for to him, who was entangling their state in intolerable burdens, they answered that, if he persevered in commanding anything heavier than death, they would prefer death.

4e.5. Nor was the saying of a certain Spartan slight in weight, since, excelling in nobility and holiness but defeated in his candidacy for a magistracy, he declared that it was a matter of the greatest joy to him that his fatherland had some men better than himself. By this speech he made his rejection equal to the honour.

5.pr. ON JUSTICE It is time to approach also the holy inner shrines of justice, in which regard for what is equitable and upright always dwells with religious observance, and where the zeal for modesty yields, where desire yields to reason, and nothing is held useful which can seem too little honourable. And of this our state is the chief and most certain example among all nations.

Memorable too for his counsel was Q. Metellus. He, when as proconsul he was waging war in Spain against the Celtiberians, and could not storm by strength the city of Contrebia, the capital of that people, after turning plans over within his breast much and long, found a way by which he might bring his purpose to fulfilment. He would set out on marches with great impetus, then make for one region after another: he would besiege these mountains, and a little later cross over to those, while meanwhile the cause of his unexpected and sudden vacillation was unknown both to all his own men and to the enemy themselves. Being asked too by a certain man most friendly to him why he was following so scattered and uncertain a kind of warfare, he said, "Cease to ask that: for if I perceive that even the inner tunic of mine is privy to this plan, I shall order it to be burned at once." To what end, then, did that dissimulation break out, or what end did it have? When in truth he had entangled both his own army in ignorance and all Celtiberia in error, having directed his course elsewhere, he suddenly turned back to Contrebia and overwhelmed it, unexpected and stunned. Therefore, unless he had compelled his mind to search out deceptions, he would have had to sit in arms before the walls of Contrebia into his extreme old age.

4e.1. Agathocles, moreover, king of Syracuse, was boldly cunning: for when the Carthaginians had occupied the greater part of his city, he carried his army over into Africa, in order to scatter fear by fear, force by force—and not without effect: for, struck by his sudden arrival, the Carthaginians gladly purchased their own safety by the safety of the enemy, and made a compact that at one and the same time Africa should be freed from Sicilian arms and Sicily from Punic. Come now—if he had persisted in guarding the walls of Syracuse? Sicily would have been pressed by the evils of war, and he would have left the goods of peace to be enjoyed by a secure Carthage. As it was, by inflicting what he was suffering, while he assailed another's resources rather than guarded his own, the more readily he abandoned his kingdom, the more safely he recovered it.

4e.2. What of Hannibal? Did he not, before he came down to fight, bind the Roman battle line at Cannae with several snares of cunning and lead it to so pitiable an end? For above all he provided that it should have both the sun and the dust, which is usually raised there in quantity by the wind, against it. Then he ordered part of his forces, during the very time of the battle, to flee deliberately, and when a Roman legion, cut off from the rest of the army, followed it, he saw to it that it was butchered by those whom he had placed in ambush. Finally he suborned four hundred horsemen, who, with feigned desertion, made for the consul, and being ordered by him to lay down their arms in the manner of deserters and withdraw to the rearmost part of the battle, with the swords which they had hidden between their tunics and breastplates drawn, cut the hamstrings of the fighting Romans. This was Punic bravery, equipped with deceits and ambushes and treachery. And this is now the surest excuse for our circumvented valour, since we were deceived rather than conquered.

5.pr. ON ELECTORAL DEFEATS The condition of the Campus Martius, here set before us, will usefully equip the man entering on the path of ambition to bear more bravely the not very prosperous outcomes of elections; for, with the defeats of the most distinguished men set before their eyes, they will seek honours, just as with no less hope, so with more prudent judgment of mind, and will remember that it is no sacrilege for something to be denied to one man by all, since often individuals have judged it lawful to resist the wishes of all; knowing also that what could not be obtained by favour ought to be sought by patience.

Upon the religion of the games, as wealth grew, sumptuousness followed. At its prompting Q. Catulus, imitating Campanian luxury, was the first to cover the gathering of the spectators with the shade of awnings. Cn. Pompeius, before all, by the running down of water through channels lessened the summer heat. Claudius Pulcher shaded the stage with a variety of colours, having before stretched over it boards bare of painting. The whole of which C. Antonius bordered with silver, Petreius with gold, Q. Catulus with ivory. The Luculli made it revolving; P. Lentulus Spinther adorned it with silvered theatrical fittings. M. Scaurus introduced costly adornment, formerly clad in tunics dyed with Punic dye, in a choice kind of dress. For the gladiatorial show was first given at Rome in the cattle-market, in the consulship of Ap. Claudius and Q. Fulvius. It was given by Marcus and Decimus, the sons of Brutus Pera, honouring the ashes of their father in funeral memory. The contest of athletes was derived from the munificence of M. Scaurus.

But the rise of Marcus Porcius Cato was to be sought with public vows, who made his name, obscure at Tusculum, most noble at Rome: for by him were the monuments of Latin literature adorned, military discipline aided, the majesty of the senate increased, the family prolonged—in which the greatest glory was the later-born Cato.

4e.1. But, to join foreign things to Roman, Socrates, judged the wisest not only by the consent of men but also by the oracle of Apollo, born of his mother Phaenarete, a midwife, and his father Sophroniscus, a stonemason, attained to the brightest light of glory. And not without desert: for, when the talents of the most learned men wandered blindly in disputation and tried to explain the measures of the sun and moon and of the other stars by talkative rather than sure arguments, and even dared to embrace the constitution of the whole world, he was the first to draw his mind away from these unlearned errors and compel it to search out the inmost things of the human condition and the passions stored in the recesses of the breast—the best master of life, if virtue be valued for its own sake.

4e.2. What father Euripides, or what mother Demosthenes had, was unknown even to their own age. But that the mother of the one sold vegetables, and the father of the other little knives, the writings of almost all the learned declare. Yet what is brighter than the tragic power of the one or the oratorical power of the other?

5.pr. ON THOSE WHO DEGENERATED FROM ILLUSTRIOUS PARENTS. There follows the part of my twofold promise to be rendered, the images of illustrious men being veiled, since indeed those must be related who degenerated from their splendour—noble monstrosities steeped in the foulest filth of sloth and worthlessness.

Of the same name and blood was Atilius Regulus, of the First Punic War the greatest glory as he was the greatest disaster, who, when in Africa he was crushing the most insolent power of Carthage by frequent victories, and had learned that his command, on account of his deeds well done, had been prolonged for him into the next year, wrote to the consuls that the bailiff on the little farm of seven iugera which he had in Pupinia was dead, and that the hired man, having found his chance, had departed thence, having carried off the rustic implements, and therefore he asked that a successor be sent to him, lest, the field being deserted, there should be nothing whence his wife and children might be fed. When the senate had received this from the consuls, it ordered both that Atilius' field should at once be let out to be cultivated, and that sustenance be furnished to his wife and children, and that the things he had lost be redeemed at public expense. At so great a price stood to our treasury that example of Atilian virtue, in which every Roman age shall glory.

Great are these works of manly dutifulness, but I know not whether more powerful and more spirited than all of them is the deed of Claudia, a Vestal virgin. When she had noticed her father, as he was triumphing, being dragged from his chariot by the violent hand of a tribune of the plebs, with marvellous swiftness, by interposing herself between the two, she drove off the most ample power kindled with enmity. Therefore the father led one triumph to the Capitol, the daughter another to the temple of Vesta; nor could it be discerned to which more praise should be assigned, the one whom victory accompanied or the one whom dutifulness.

Equally great were the broad estates of Lucius Quintius Cincinnatus: for he possessed seven iugera of land, and of these he lost three, which he had pledged to the treasury on behalf of a friend, by way of a fine. The penalty too on behalf of his son Caeso, because he had not appeared to plead his cause, he paid from the revenue of this little farm. And yet to him, ploughing four iugera, there was constituted not only the dignity of head of a family, but the dictatorship too was conferred. He now thinks himself cramped in his dwelling, whose house spreads out as much as the lands of Cincinnatus spread.

Forgive me, most ancient hearths, and grant pardon, eternal fires, if from your most sacred temple the texture of my work shall have advanced to a part of the city more necessary than splendid: for by no bitterness of fortune, by no squalor does the price of dear dutifulness grow cheap—nay, it has the more certain proof the more wretched it is. A praetor handed over a woman of freeborn blood, condemned at his tribunal on a capital charge, to a triumvir to be put to death in prison. He who was in charge of the custody, having received her, moved by pity, did not strangle her at once: he even gave her daughter access to her, but only after she had been carefully searched, lest she should bring in any food, thinking that the result would be that she would be consumed by starvation. But when several days had now passed, asking himself by what means she was being sustained for so long, having observed the daughter more carefully, he noticed her relieving the hunger of her mother by the help of her own milk, with her breast bared. The novelty of so admirable a spectacle, reported by him himself to the triumvir, by the triumvir to the praetor, by the praetor to the council of judges, obtained a remission of the penalty for the woman. Whither does dutifulness not penetrate, or what does it not devise, which found a new means of saving a mother in prison? For what is so unusual, what so unheard of, as a mother nourished by the breasts of her daughter? One might think this was done against the nature of things, were it not that to love one's parents is the first law of nature.

4e.1. Let the same be deemed proclaimed concerning the dutifulness of Pero, who nourished her father Mycon, afflicted by a like fortune and consigned to a like custody, now in the last stage of old age, brought to her breast as though he were an infant. The eyes of men cling and are amazed when they see the painted image of this deed, and by their wonder at the present spectacle they renew the circumstance of the ancient event, believing that in those mute outlines of the limbs they behold living and breathing bodies. This necessarily happens to the mind also, somewhat more effectively reminded by the painting than by letters to recall old deeds in place of recent ones.

4e.2. Nor shall I wrap you too in silence, Cimon, who did not hesitate to buy your father burial with voluntary chains: for although it afterwards befell you to turn out a great man, both citizen and general, yet you gained somewhat more praise in prison than in the senate-house: for the other virtues deserve much, but only of admiration; dutifulness, however, deserves most also of love.

4e.3. You too, brothers, I shall embrace in remembrance, whose spirit was nobler than your origin, since indeed, born very humble in Spain, by spending your breath for the sustenance of your parents you became famous by the glorious ending of your life: for, having agreed with the Paciaeci that twelve thousand sesterces should be given after your death to your parents, on condition that you should kill Etpastus, the tyrant of their nation, the slayer of their father, you not only dared a notable deed but also closed it with a vigorous and brave ending: for with the same hands you brought forth for the Paciaeci vengeance, for Etpastus punishment, for your parents nourishment, for yourselves a glorious fate. And so even now you live in your tombs, because you judged it better to protect your parents' old age than to await your own.

4e.4. Better known are the pairs of brothers Cleobis and Biton, Amphinomus and Anapias—the former because they drew their mother to perform the rites of Juno, the latter because they carried their father and mother on their shoulders through the midst of the fires—but for neither pair was it the purpose to expire in place of their parents' breath.

4e.5. Nor do I disparage the Argive praise or diminish the glory of Mount Etna, but I bring the light of notice to a dutifulness more obscure on account of unfamiliarity, just as I gladly render to the Scythians the testimony of dutifulness: for, when Darius with all the forces of his kingdom was repeatedly making an onset into their regions, gradually yielding they had now reached the furthest wildernesses. Then, asked by him through envoys what end of flight or what beginning of fighting they would make, they answered that they had neither any cities nor any cultivated fields for which they might contend; but that, when he had come to the monuments of their parents, he would learn how the Scythians were wont to fight. By this one so dutiful a saying an unsociable and barbarous nation redeemed itself from all charge of savagery. The first, therefore, and best teacher of dutifulness is the nature of things, which, needing no service of the voice, no use of letters, pours the love of children into the breasts of parents by its own silent powers. What, then, does instruction accomplish? That natures may become more polished, of course, not better, since indeed solid virtue is born rather than fashioned:

4e.6. for who taught those who wander in wagons and cover their bodies in the hiding-places of forests, and live after the manner of wild beasts on the mangled flesh of cattle, to answer Darius thus? That same nature, surely, which instructed even the son of Croesus, deprived of the use of speech, in the service of his voice to protect the safety of his father: for, when Sardis had been captured by Cyrus, and one of the number of the Persians, ignorant of the man, was being carried with roused impulse to his slaughter, as though forgetting what fortune had denied him at his birth, by crying out that he should not kill King Croesus, he recalled the blade already all but pressed to his throat. Thus he who up to that time had lived mute for himself was made vocal for the safety of his parent.

4e.7. The same love, in the Italian War, armed a young man of Pinna, who was surnamed Pulto, with such strength of spirit and of body that, when he was in charge of the barriers of his besieged city, and the Roman commander had stationed his captive father in his sight and surrounded him with the drawn swords of soldiers, threatening that he would kill him unless he gave passage for his irruption, the youth alone snatched the old man from their hands—memorable for a twofold dutifulness, in that he was both the saviour of his father and not the betrayer of his fatherland.

5.pr. This love the next degree, that of brotherly goodwill, succeeds: for as it is deservedly held the first bond of affection to have received the most and greatest benefits, so it ought to be judged the next to have received them at the same time. For how full of sweetness is that recollection: in the same dwelling I lived before I was born; in the same cradle I passed the seasons of infancy; the same parents I called by name; the same vows watched over me; an equal glory from the images of our ancestors I drew! Dear is a wife, sweet are children, agreeable are friends, welcome are relations by marriage—but, as they are known afterward, no goodwill ought to accrue which would drain away the earlier.

What of the Aelian family, how wealthy! Sixteen Aeli there were at the same time, who had one little house in the same place where now are the monuments of Marius, and one farm in the Veientine territory requiring fewer cultivators than it had owners, and a place for spectacles in the Circus Maximus and the Flaminian. Which places indeed they possessed, given to them publicly on account of their valour.

The same family had not a scruple of silver before Paulus, when Perseus had been conquered, gave to Quintus Aelius Tubero, his son-in-law, five pounds of silver from the booty: for I pass over the fact that the chief man of the state gave his daughter in marriage to him whose money he saw of so meagre a household. He himself too departed so destitute that, unless the farm, the one thing he had left, had been sold, there would have been nothing whence his wife might recover her dowry. The spirits of men and women flourished in the state, and the estimation of dignity was weighed by their goods in all matters. These conciliated commands, these joined alliances, these availed most both in the forum and within private walls: for each one hastened to increase the wealth of his country, not his own, and the poor man preferred to be engaged in command over the rich rather than the rich over the poor. And to this so glorious purpose that reward was rendered, that none of the things owed to virtue could be bought with money, and that the want of illustrious men was relieved at public expense.

And so, when in the Second Punic War Gnaeus Scipio had written to the senate from Spain, asking that a successor be sent to him, because he had a maiden daughter now of grown age, and a dowry could not be provided for her without him, the senate, lest the commonwealth should lack a good leader, took upon itself the parts of a father, and, the dowry having been settled by the counsel of Scipio's wife and kinsmen, disbursed the sum of it from the treasury and gave the girl in marriage. The amount of the dowry was forty thousand asses, from which can be known not only the humanity of the conscript fathers, but also the condition of the old patrimonies: for they were so straitened that Tuccia, daughter of Caeso, was thought to have brought the greatest dowry to her husband, ten thousand asses, and Megullia, because she entered her husband's house with fifty thousand asses, gained the surname of the Dowered. The same senate freed the daughters of Fabricius Luscinus and of Scipio from undowered marriages by its liberality, since to their paternal inheritance there was nothing they could enter as received except a rich glory.

But how small an inheritance Marcus Scaurus received from his father, he relates in the first book of the three which he wrote about his own life: for he says that to him there were left only six slaves and a whole estate of thirty-five thousand sesterces. On this money was nourished the spirit of one who would be the chief man of the senate. These examples, therefore, we ought to regard, in these consolations to find rest, who never allow our scanty fortunes to be free of complaints. We behold no silver, or of very small weight, few slaves, seven iugera of dry land, funerals in want of household expense, daughters destitute of dowries—but distinguished consulships, wonderful dictatorships, innumerable triumphs.
