Why then do we tear at a moderate fortune, as though it were the chief evil of the human race, with reproaches by day and by night, which, with breasts not overflowing but trustworthy, nourished Publicolas, Aemilii, Fabricii, Curii, Scipios, Scauri, and strengths of valour equal to these? Let us rather rise in spirit, and let us refresh, by the memory of the former time, our spirits weakened by the sight of money: for, by the hut of Romulus, and by the humble roofs of the old Capitol, and by the eternal hearths of Vesta, content even now with earthenware vessels, I swear that no riches can be preferred to the poverty of such men.

5.pr. ON SENSE OF SHAME. From which the transition to modesty seems timely: for it has taught the most just men to neglect their private means and to desire that the public ones should be as ample as possible—worthy that temples be raised and altars consecrated to it, as to a heavenly divinity, because it is the parent of every honourable counsel, the guardian of solemn duties, the mistress of innocence, dear to those nearest, acceptable to strangers, bearing before it in every place, at every time, a favourable countenance.

ON OMENS. The observation of omens too is woven by some contact into religion, since they are believed to come about not by chance movement but by divine providence. This it was that brought it to pass that, when the city had been scattered by the Gauls, and the conscript fathers were deliberating whether they should migrate to Veii or restore their own walls, it happened that at that time, as the cohorts on guard duty were returning, a centurion cried out in the assembly-place: "Standard-bearer, plant the standard; here we shall best remain." On hearing this voice the senate answered that it accepted the omen, and at once abandoned the plan of crossing over to Veii. In how few words was the condition of the future seat of the supreme empire confirmed! I believe the gods deemed it unworthy that the Roman name, sprung under the most prosperous auspices, should be changed for the name of the city of Veii, and that the honour of so renowned a victory should be poured out among the ruins of a city just cast down.

A gilded statue no one beheld either in the city or in any part of Italy before one was set up by M'. Acilius Glabrio to his father, of equestrian rank, in the temple of Piety. That temple, moreover, he himself had dedicated in the consulship of P. Cornelius Lentulus and M. Baebius Tamphilus, having become master of his vow when King Antiochus was overcome at Thermopylae.

For what is more like a monster than Scipio, son of the elder Africanus, who, born amid so great domestic glory, endured to be captured from earliest boyhood by the garrison of King Antiochus, when it would have been better for him to be cut off by a voluntary death than, between two most shining surnames, that of his father and that of his uncle—the one won when Africa was already overcome, the other just beginning to rise when Asia was for the greater part recovered—to hand over his hands to be bound by the enemy and by his benefit to obtain a precarious breath of life, concerning which Lucius Scipio was soon to set before the eyes of gods and men a most glorious triumph. The same man, a candidate for the praetorship, brought down into the Campus a white toga so soiled with stains of disgrace that, had he not been helped by the favour of Cicereius, who had been his father's clerk, he would not have seemed likely to obtain the honour from the people. And yet what difference did it make whether he carried home a repulse or a praetorship gained in such a manner? When his kinsmen perceived that this office was being defiled by him, they brought it about that he dared neither set up his chair nor pronounce judgement, and besides drew from his hand the ring on which the head of Africanus was carved. Good gods, what darkness you have suffered to be born from what lightning!

But, that we may come from its praises to deeds, from the foundation of the city down to the consuls Africanus and Tiberius Longus, the place for watching the games was common to senate and people. Yet never did anyone of the plebs endure to watch in the theatre before the conscript fathers: so circumspect was the sense of shame of our state. Which indeed gave the surest proof of itself even on that day on which Lucius Flamininus took his stand in the farthest part of the theatre, because he had been removed from the senate by the censors Marcus Cato and Lucius Flaccus, though he had already discharged the honour of the consulship, and was the brother too of Titus Flamininus, the conqueror of Macedonia and Philip: for all compelled him to pass over into the place due to his dignity.

And I say this with Scipio Africanus as witness, who, although he was joined to Laelius by the closest intimacy, nevertheless as a suppliant begged the senate that the lot of the province should not be taken from his brother and transferred to himself, and promised that he would go as a legate to Lucius Scipio in Asia—both the elder to the younger, and the bravest to the unwarlike, and one excelling in glory to one poor in renown, and—what surpasses all—being already Africanus, to one not yet Asiaticus. And so of the two most illustrious surnames he took one and gave the other; the bordered robe of this man's triumph he took, that man's he handed over—in service somewhat greater than his brother was in command.

When Camillus the consul was besieging Falerii, the schoolmaster led most of the boys, and the most noble, out as if for the sake of a walk, and conducted them into the camp of the Romans. When these had been intercepted, there was no doubt that the Faliscans, laying aside their persistence in waging war, would surrender themselves to our commander. On this account the senate decreed that the boys, beating their bound master with rods, should be sent back into their fatherland. By this justice the minds of those were captured whose walls could not be stormed: for the Faliscans, conquered by a benefit rather than by arms, opened their gates to the Romans. The same state, having several times rebelled and always been crushed by adverse battles, was at last compelled to surrender itself to the consul Quintus Lutatius. The Roman people, desiring to rage against it, after it was taught by Papirius—by whose hand, at the consul's order, the terms of surrender had been written—that the Faliscans had committed themselves not to the power but to the good faith of the Romans, laid aside all its anger with a calm mind, and alike opposed both the forces of hatred, not easily accustomed to be conquered, and the compliance of victory, which most readily supplies license, lest it should be wanting to its own justice. The same people, when Publius Claudius had, under his leadership and auspices, captured the people of Camerinum and sold them under the spear, although it observed that the treasury had been enriched with money, the borders with lands, yet, because that deed seemed to have been done by the commander with too little clear good faith, sought them out with the greatest care, ransomed them, and assigned to them a place on the Aventine for dwelling and restored their estates. It even allotted money for the building of shrines and the performance of sacrifices, and by the most ready maintenance of justice brought it about that they could rejoice in their own destruction, because they had thus been born again. The things which I have related thus far concerning our walls and neighbouring regions . . . ; what follows flowed forth through the whole world. Timochares of Ambracia promised the consul Fabricius that he would kill Pyrrhus by poison, through his own son, who was in charge of his drinks. When this matter had been laid before the senate, having sent envoys, it warned Pyrrhus to conduct himself more cautiously against snares of this kind, mindful that a city founded by the son of Mars ought to wage its wars with arms, not with poisons. But it suppressed the name of Timochares, embracing equity in both ways, because it wished neither to remove an enemy by a bad example nor to betray the man who had been prepared to deserve well.

Q. Aelius Tubero, when Q. Fabius Maximus was giving a feast to the people in the name of his uncle P. Africanus, being asked to spread the dining-couch, covered Punic couches with goat-skins and, instead of silver vessels, set out Samian ware. The unseemliness of this thing so offended men that, though otherwise he was held to be an excellent man, and as a candidate for the praetorship had come down into the Campus relying on his grandfather L. Paulus and his uncle P. Africanus, he went off from there beaten, marked with disgrace: for as in private life they always approved frugality, so in public life the greatest care was taken for splendour. And so the city, believing that not the company of a single banquet, but it itself in its entirety had reclined on those little skins, avenged the shame of the feast with its votes.

ON WITNESSES It follows that I should recall examples relating to witnesses. When Cn. and Q. Servilius Caepio, born of the same parents and advanced through all the grades of honours to the highest eminence, and likewise the brothers Metelli, Quintus and Lucius, both consular and censorian, one also triumphal, were giving testimony most keenly against Q. Pompeius, son of Aulus, a defendant on a charge of extortion, their credit was not annulled by the acquittal of Pompeius, but it was provided that they should not seem to have crushed an enemy by their power.

ON PRIDE AND LACK OF SELF-CONTROL And, that pride too and lack of self-control may be placed in view: M. Fulvius Flaccus, consul, colleague of M. Plautius Hypsaeus, when he was introducing most pernicious laws to the state about giving citizenship to Italy and about appeal to the people for those who should be unwilling to change their citizenship, was with difficulty driven to come into the senate-house: then, to the senate, partly advising, partly begging him to desist from his undertaking, he gave no answer. He would be held a consul of a tyrannical spirit, if he had conducted himself in this way against a single senator, in the way in which Flaccus behaved in despising the majesty of the whole most ample order.

The author of this so splendid work, Camillus, when he had prayed that, if to any of the gods the excessive good fortune of the Roman people should seem too great, that god's envy might be satisfied by some misfortune of his own, suddenly fell by a slip. This was thought to have pertained to the condemnation by which he was afterwards oppressed. Deservedly might the victory and the pious prayer of that most eminent man contend with each other for praise: for it is equally the mark of virtue both to have increased the goods of the fatherland and to have wished its evils transferred to oneself.

The civil law, for many generations hidden among the sacred rites and ceremonies of the immortal gods and known only to the pontiffs, Cn. Flavius, born of a freedman father and a scribe, when, to the great indignation of the nobility, he had been made curule aedile, made public, and posted up the calendar almost in the whole forum. When he came to visit his sick colleague and was not received with a place to sit by the nobles, with whose throng the bedroom was filled, he ordered his curule chair to be brought, and sat down in it, the avenger alike of his honour and of the contempt shown him.

Come, the son of Quintus Fabius Maximus Allobrogicus, a most illustrious citizen and commander, Quintus Fabius Maximus, what a life he led, ruined by luxury! Even if his other disgraces were to be blotted out, yet his character can abundantly be laid bare by that one shame, that Quintus Pompeius, the city praetor, interdicted him from his father's goods, nor in so great a city was anyone found to censure that decree: for men bore it with grief that money, which ought to serve the splendour of the Fabian house, should be squandered upon disgraces. And so him whom his father's excessive indulgence had left as heir, public severity disinherited.

Terentius Varro shattered the commonwealth by his rash entry into the battle of Cannae. The same man, by not enduring to accept the dictatorship offered by the whole senate and people, out of shame redeemed his fault in the greatest disaster, and brought it about that the battle-line should be imputed to the wrath of the gods, his own modesty to his own character. And so it can more gloriously be entered in the inscription of his image that the dictatorship was not accepted than that those of others were held.

But Marcus Fabius the consul, the Etruscans and Veientes having been conquered in a renowned battle, did not endure to lead the triumph offered to him with the highest zeal of senate and people, because in that battle his brother Quintus Fabius, a man of consular rank, fighting most bravely, had fallen. How great a dutifulness of brotherly love may we judge to have dwelt in that breast, on account of which so great a brilliance of the most ample honour could be extinguished?

The highest justice was discerned also in four tribunes of the plebs at the same time: for when, for Lucius Atratinus—under whose leadership they, with the rest of the knights, had restored our line, which had been bent back by the Volscians at Verrugo—their colleague Lucius Hortensius had named a day before the people, they swore before the rostra that they would be in mourning so long as their commander was a defendant: for those outstanding young men could not endure to behold, retaining the insignia of their office and clad in the toga, the extreme peril of him whose danger, armed, they had defended with their wounds and their blood. Moved by this justice, the assembly compelled Hortensius to desist from his prosecution; nor . . . showed itself by the deed which follows.

But P. Scipio Nasica, the most distinguished light of toga-clad power—who as consul declared war on Jugurtha, who received with most holy hands the Idaean Mother as she journeyed from her Phrygian seat to our altars and hearths, who by the strength of his authority suppressed many and pestilent seditions, in whom as their leader the senate gloried for several years—when as a young man he was seeking the curule aedileship and had grasped, in the manner of candidates, somewhat too tightly the hand of a certain man hardened by rustic work, asked him for a joke whether he was accustomed to walk on his hands. This saying, taken up by the bystanders, flowed out to the people and brought Scipio the cause of his defeat: for all the rustic tribes, judging that their poverty had been cast in their teeth by him, unsheathed their anger against his insulting wit. Therefore our state, by recalling the talents of noble young men from insolence, made of them great and useful citizens, and by not allowing honours to be sought from buffoons, added the due weight of authority.

M. Aemilius Scaurus too, the leader of the senate, pursued C. Memmius, a defendant on a charge of extortion, with unsheathed testimony, and likewise tore to pieces C. Flavius, accused under the same law, as a witness; and he tried openly to crush C. Norbanus, subjected to a public inquiry on a charge of treason. Yet neither by his authority, in which he was most powerful, nor by his conscientiousness, of which no one doubted, could he ruin any one of them.

This majesty was outraged with the utmost insult by M. Drusus, tribune of the plebs, too: for he thought it too little to have driven the consul L. Philippus, because he had dared to interrupt him as he was haranguing, headlong into prison with his throat twisted—and indeed not by a constable but by his own client—so violently that much blood was poured from his nostrils; but even, when the senate had sent to him to come into the senate-house, he said, "Why does it not rather itself come into the Hostilian senate-house, near the rostra, that is, to me?" It irks me to add what follows: the tribune despised the command of the senate, the senate obeyed the words of the tribune.

How memorable, too, was that which happened to the consul L. Paulus! When it had fallen to him by lot to wage war against King Perseus, and, on returning home from the senate-house, he had kissed his little daughter, named Tertia, who was then quite small, and noticed that she was sad, he asked her why she had such a look. She replied that Persa had perished. Now a little puppy had died, which the girl had had as a pet, named Persa. Paulus therefore seized upon the omen, and from the chance saying conceived in his mind, as it were, a sure hope of a most glorious triumph.

A trial for poisoning, unknown both to Roman manners and to Roman laws, arose from the crime, laid bare, of several matrons. These, when they were destroying their husbands by secret treachery with poison, dragged forth by the information of a single maidservant, a part being condemned by capital judgement, made up the number of a hundred and seventy.

Clodius Pulcher possessed the favour of the plebs, and the dagger, clinging to the gown of Fulvia, held its military glory subject to a woman's command. Their son Pulcher, besides that he led an enervated and chill youth, was also infamous for a lost love of a most common harlot, and was consumed by a manner of death to be blushed at: for, having greedily devoured . . . , he gave up the spirit of his foul and base intemperance.

But let us pass over to the distinguished work of modesty. With great unpopularity Fortune had led down into the Campus, at the praetorian elections, Gnaeus Scipio, son of the elder Africanus, and the clerk Gaius Cicereius, and, as one too unrestrained, it was carped at in the talk of the crowd, because it had confounded the blood and clientship of so great a man in the contest of an election. But Cicereius turned his fault into his own praise: for, as soon as he saw himself preferred to Scipio in all the centuries, he came down from the place of augury, and, throwing aside his white toga, began to act as a canvasser for his competitor, that he might evidently yield the praetorship the better to the memory of Africanus than claim it for himself. And the price of modesty was not the greatest: Scipio then obtained the honour, but men the rather congratulated Cicereius.

By that example antiquity was adorned, by this one our own age, to which it has fallen to behold the brotherly yoke—the glory first of the Claudian, now also of the Julian clan: for our prince and parent had so great a love implanted in his soul for his brother Drusus that, when, at Ticinum—whither, victor over the enemy, he had come to embrace his parents—he learned that Drusus was tossing in Germany in a grave and dangerous illness, at once, thunderstruck with fear, he burst forth from there. How rapid and headlong his journey was, as though in a single breath, is plain from this, that, having crossed the Alps and the Rhine, by day and night, his horse repeatedly changed, with Namantabagius as his guide, content with him as his only companion, he traversed two hundred miles through a barbarian land but lately conquered. But him, then entangled in the greatest toil and danger and worn out by the throng of mortals, the most sacred divinity of dutifulness, and the gods who favour outstanding virtues, and Jupiter, the most faithful guardian of the Roman empire, accompanied. Drusus too, although he was now nearer to his own fate than to his brother's offices, sinking in the vigour of his spirit and the strength of his body, yet at that very moment by which life and death are distinguished, ordered the legions to come forth with their standards to meet his brother, so that he might be saluted as commander. He even directed that the headquarters be set up on the right-hand side for him, and willed that he should hold both the consular and the imperatorial name; and at the same time he both yielded to his brother's majesty and departed from life. To these men I know indeed that no other model of kindred affection can fittingly be added than that of Castor and Pollux,

When Tiberius Gracchus and Gaius Claudius had exasperated the greater part of the state on account of a censorship conducted too severely, Publius Popilius the tribune of the plebs named a day for them before the people on a charge of treason, kindled, beyond the common consternation, also by private anger, because they had ordered a kinsman of his, Rutilius, to demolish a wall from public ground. In this trial very many centuries of the first class were openly condemning Claudius, while about the acquittal of Gracchus they all seemed to agree. He swore in a clear voice that, if a graver verdict were passed about his colleague, he would, in like deeds, undergo with him the same penalty of exile; and by this justice all that storm was driven away from the fortunes and lives of both: for the people acquitted Claudius, and to Gracchus Popilius remitted the pleading of his cause.

No such error was observed in L. Aemilius Paulus, but nevertheless several times he sought the consulship in vain; and the same man, when he had already wearied the Campus with his defeats, was made consul twice and censor, and obtained also the highest step of dignity. His virtue defeats did not break, but sharpened, since indeed the very mark of disgrace, kindling his desire for the highest honour, brought it more ardent to the elections, so that he conquered by persistence the people whom he had not been able to move by the splendour of his nobility and the goods of his mind.

L. Crassus too, as great among the judges as Aemilius Scaurus among the conscript fathers—for he governed their votes by the most robust and successful campaigns of eloquence, and was as much the leader of the forum as the other of the senate-house—when he had hurled a most vehement thunderbolt of testimony against M. Marcellus, a defendant, appeared grave in his onset, but empty in its outcome.

How insolently, moreover, did Cn. Pompeius act! Who, coming out of the bath, left Hypsaeus, a defendant on a charge of bribery, prostrate before his feet—a noble man and his friend—lying there, trampled upon with an insulting word: for he replied that the man was doing nothing else than delaying his dinner; and conscious of this saying he could dine with an untroubled mind. He even, in the forum, did not blush to demand from the judges, in the place of a favour, his father-in-law P. Scipio, liable under the laws which he himself had carried—and that too in the greatest ruin of illustrious defendants—violating the condition of the state by the blandishments of the marriage bed.

But Caecilia, wife of Metellus, while by ancient custom, in the dead of night, she was seeking a nuptial omen for her sister's daughter, a marriageable maiden, herself produced it: for when she had sat for a good while in a certain little shrine for this purpose, and no voice agreeing with her aim had been heard, the girl, weary with the long standing, asked her aunt to lend her her place for a little while to sit down. To which the other said: "Indeed I gladly yield you my seat." This saying, springing from kindness, came to the issue of a sure omen, since Metellus, not long afterwards, when Caecilia had died, took in marriage the maiden of whom I speak.

The college of flute-players, too, is wont to turn the eyes of the common people upon itself in the forum, when, amid public and private serious transactions, masked and with covered heads and veiled in varied dress, it gives forth its concert. From this a licence was derived. Once forbidden to feast in the temple of Jupiter, which they had been wont to do by ancient custom, in anger they betook themselves to Tibur. The senate, not bearing with even mind the sacred rites deserted by their ministry, sought through legates from the people of Tibur that they would, of their grace, restore them to the Roman temples. These, persisting in their resolve, by the pretence of a festive banquet, lulled with wine and sleep, they took care should be carried back into the city on carts. To them both their former honour was restored and the right of this sport was given. The use of masks has, as its cause, the shame of the drunkenness thus circumvented.

For the grandson of Quintus Hortensius—who, amid the greatest harvest of talented and most eminent citizens, held the highest rank of authority and eloquence—Hortensius Corbio, led a life more abject and more obscene than that of any prostitute, and at the last his tongue prostituted itself among the brothels to the lust of all as much as his grandfather's had kept watch in the forum for the safety of the citizens.

6.pr. I perceive into how dangerous a path I have advanced. And so I shall call myself back, lest, if I persist in pursuing the remaining shipwrecks of the same kind, I be entangled in some unprofitable narrative. I shall therefore draw back my foot and suffer those deformed shadows to lie in the lowest abyss of their turpitude: for it is better to relate what illustrious men, in their dress and other manner of life, indulged themselves in by innovating in some part.

And, that we may not at once depart from the elections, Lucius Crassus, seeking the consulship, when in the manner of all candidates he was compelled to go round the forum as a suppliant to the people, could never be brought to do it in the presence of Quintus Scaevola, a most weighty and most wise man, his father-in-law. And so he begged him to withdraw from him while he attended to that foolish business, paying greater regard to the modesty due to his dignity than to his own white toga.

but it will surely not be ungrateful to the most illustrious commanders of all memory if a soldier's supreme dutifulness toward his brother attaches itself to this part of the volume: for he, performing his service in the camp of Gnaeus Pompeius, when he had killed at close quarters a Sertorian soldier who was pressing him too keenly in the battle line, and as he was stripping him as he lay, recognized him to be his own full brother; having long and much pursued the gods with reproaches for the gift of an impious victory, he carried him near the camp and, having covered him with a precious garment, placed him on the pyre. And then, the torch set beneath, he at once with the same sword with which he had killed him pierced through his own breast, and, prostrate over the body of his brother, gave himself to be cremated in the common flames. It was permitted him, by the benefit of his ignorance, to live an innocent man; but, that he might use his own dutifulness rather than another's pardon, he was not wanting as a companion to his brother's death.

6.pr. To the closest bonds of blood dutifulness has done enough: it remains now that it be shown toward the fatherland. To the majesty of the fatherland even that authority of parents which is equated with the powers of the gods submits its strength, and brotherly affection too yields with an even and willing mind—and indeed with the highest reason, because when a house is overthrown the state of the commonwealth can remain whole, whereas at the ruin of the city the household gods of all are necessarily dragged down with it. But what need is there to embrace these things in words, whose power is so great that some have testified to them at the cost of their own safety?

Great praise that college of tribunes too bore, in that, when one of its number, Lucius Cotta, relying on his sacrosanct power, was unwilling to satisfy his creditors, it decreed that, if he neither paid the money nor furnished someone with whom a wager might be made, it would aid the creditors who appealed to it, holding it unjust that the public majesty should be a screen for private bad faith. And so the tribunician justice dragged Cotta out of the tribunate as out of some sanctuary in which he was lurking.

Q. Caecilius Metellus a few and mournful friends led home, afflicted by the defeat of his consulship, full of sorrow and shame. The same man, triumphing over Pseudophilippus, the whole senate, joyful and eager, escorted to the Capitol. The greater part of the Achaean war too, to which L. Mummius put the finishing touch, was beaten down by this man. Could the people then deny the consulship to one to whom it was soon either going to give or going to owe two most distinguished provinces, Achaea and Macedonia? And indeed by this deed it had the better citizen of him: for he understood how industriously the consulship ought to be conducted by him which he had perceived to be obtained with so great labour.

Come now: Q. Metellus Pius, L. and M. Lucullus, Q. Hortensius, M'. Lepidus—how they not only burdened the safety of C. Cornelius, a defendant on a charge of treason, with their testimony, but even, declaring that with him unharmed the state could not stand, demanded his punishment! These ornaments of the state—it is shameful to relate—were repelled by the judicial buckler.

Foul alike in deed and in word was the banquet of M. Antonius: for when the head of the senator Caesetius Rufus had been brought to him, the triumvir, while the rest turned away from it, ordered it brought nearer and considered it long and carefully. Then, while all awaited what he would say, he said, "This man I have not known." A proud confession about a senator, an uncontrolled one about a slain man.

5e.1. Enough about our own people: let foreign examples now be added. The virtue and good fortune of king Alexander exulted by three most evident steps of insolence: for through disdain of Philip he took to himself Jupiter Ammon as his father, through weariness of Macedonian manners and dress he assumed Persian garb and institutions, and, despising the mortal condition, he emulated the divine, nor was he ashamed to dissemble that he was a son, a citizen, a man.

5e.2. Now Xerxes, in whose name pride and lack of self-control dwell, by his own right so insolently—when, about to declare war on Greece, he had summoned the leading men of Asia—said, "Lest I should seem to have used only my own counsel, I have gathered you together. But remember that you must rather obey me than advise." Arrogant, even if it had befallen him as a victor to seek his palace again: from one so shamefully defeated, you would not know whether it was said more insolently or more imprudently.

5e.3. Hannibal, moreover, elated by the success of the battle of Cannae, neither admitted any of his fellow citizens into his camp nor gave an answer to any except through an interpreter. He spurned even Maharbal, who before his tent affirmed in a clear voice that he had foreseen how within a few days he should dine in the Capitol at Rome. So divided is the companionship of good fortune and moderation.

5e.4. But there was, as it were, a rivalry of insolence between the Carthaginian and the Campanian senate: for the one was bathed in a bath separate from the plebs, the other used a different forum. That this custom was retained at Capua for some time is clear too from the speech of C. Gracchus written against Plautius.

6.pr. ON TREACHERY Let now a hidden and insidious evil, treachery, be dragged from its lurking-places. Its most effective strength is to lie and to deceive; its fruit consists in some crime committed, then sure, when it has surrounded credulity with wicked bonds, bringing as much harm to the human race as good faith affords of safety. Let it have, therefore, no less of reproach than that wins of praise.

For C. Marius, too, the observation of an omen was without doubt his salvation, at the time when, judged a public enemy by the senate, he was led into the house of Fannia at Minturnae to be kept in custody. For he noticed that a little ass, when fodder was thrown to it, neglected it and ran off to water. By this sight, judging that what would follow was set before him by the providence of the gods, being moreover most skilled in interpreting religious signs, he obtained from the multitude, which had flocked together to bring him aid, that he should be led to the sea; and straightway he boarded a little boat, and, conveyed by it to Africa, escaped the victorious arms of Sulla.

There was also that simplicity of the ancients in taking food, a most sure index at once of their humanity and of their self-restraint: for the greatest men felt no shame to lunch and dine in the open. Nor indeed did they have any feasts which they would have blushed to expose to the eyes of the people. They were so attentive to self-restraint that the use of porridge was more frequent among them than of bread, and therefore in the sacrifices the meal that is called "mola" consists of spelt and salt. The entrails are sprinkled with spelt, and to the chickens, by which the auspices are sought, porridge is thrown. For by the firstfruits and libations of their food they appeased the gods the more effectively the more simply they did so.

But Pompey the Great, conquered at the battle of Pharsalus by Caesar, when on the next day he entered Larisa, and the whole people of that town had come out to meet him, said: 'Go and render that office to the victor'—I should say, not worthy to be conquered, had he not been overcome by Caesar; certainly modest in calamity: for, because he could no longer use his own dignity, he used modesty.

To pass to another equally illustrious act of it: Gnaeus Domitius the tribune of the plebs called into the judgment of the people Marcus Scaurus, the chief man of the state, so that, if fortune favoured, he might gain an increase of fame by the ruin, or if not, certainly by the very disparagement of a most ample man. When he was burning with the greatest zeal to crush him, a slave of Scaurus came to him by night, promising that he would furnish his accusation with many and grave charges against his master. There were in the same breast both an enemy and Domitius, weighing the wicked information by a divided estimation. Justice conquered hatred: for at once, both his own ears barred and the informer's mouth closed, he ordered him to be led to Scaurus. An accuser to be, I will not say loved, but certainly praised even by his own defendant! Whom the people, both on account of his other virtues and on this account, more gladly made consul and censor and chief pontiff.

What was so excellent, what so opulent as L. Sulla? He lavished riches and commands, abrogated old laws, brought in new ones. He too, in that Campus of which he afterwards became master, was bruised by the defeat of the praetorship—who would have obtained all the offices he sought, if only some god had set before the Roman people the form and image of his future power.

What of M. Cicero, who by his forensic campaigning attained the highest honours and the most ample place of dignity—was he not, in the very camp of his own eloquence, cast aside as a witness, when he swore that P. Clodius had been at Rome with him, while Clodius defended his sacrilegious outrage by the single argument of his absence? Since indeed the judges preferred to free Clodius from a charge of unchastity rather than Cicero from the infamy of perjury.

Pompey the Great, however, when defeated by Caesar in the battle of Pharsalus, seeking safety in flight, directed his course by fleet to the island of Cyprus, in order to gather some forces there, and, putting in at the town of Paphus, he caught sight on the shore of a handsome building and asked the helmsman what its name was. He answered that it was called "Kakobasileia" ["Evil-kingdom"]. This word lessened his hope, slight as it was, nor did he bear it without showing it: for he turned his eyes away from those roofs and revealed by a groan the grief he had taken from the dire omen.

And the other gods indeed they venerated for doing good, but Fever they worshipped with temples that she might do less harm, of which to this day one stands on the Palatine, another in the area of the Marian monuments, a third on the highest part of the Long Street; and into these were carried the remedies which had been bound to the bodies of the sick. These things were devised, with some reasonable use, for soothing the fevers of the human mind. But for the rest, they guarded their healthfulness by the most sure and faithful protection of industry; and, as it were, a kind of mother of their good health was frugality, hostile to luxurious feasts and a stranger to excessive abundance of wine and averse from immoderate use of love.

That this modesty was special in Gaius Caesar too both often appeared and his last day signified: for, wounded by the daggers of many parricides, even at that very moment in which the divine spirit was being separated from the mortal body, not even by three-and-twenty wounds could he be deterred from obeying modesty, since indeed with both hands he let down his toga, that the lower part of his body, covered, might collapse. In this manner men do not breathe their last, but the immortal gods seek again their own abodes.

5e.1. What follows I shall append to foreign matters, because it was done before the citizenship was given to Etruria. A young man of surpassing beauty in that region, named Spurinna, when by his wonderful appearance he was disturbing the eyes of very many illustrious women, and therefore felt himself to be suspected by their husbands and parents, marred the grace of his face with wounds, and preferred that his deformity should be a proof of his own purity rather than that his beauty should be an incitement to another's lust.

5e.2. At Athens, a certain man of extreme old age, when he had come into the theatre to watch the games, and none of the citizens received him to a seat, came by chance to the envoys of the Lacedaemonians. They, moved by the man's age, venerating his grey hairs and his years by the office of rising, gave him a seat among themselves in a most honoured place. When the people saw this done, with the greatest applause they approved the modesty of a foreign city. They report that then one of the Lacedaemonians said: 'So the Athenians know what is right, but neglect to do it.'

6.pr. ON CONJUGAL LOVE. From a placid and gentle affection I shall proceed to one equally honourable, but somewhat more ardent and more impetuous, and shall set before the eyes of the reader, to be contemplated not without the greatest veneration, certain images, as it were, of lawful love, running over the deeds of fidelity firmly established between spouses, hard to imitate, but useful to be known, because for one observing the most excellent it ought to be a blush not to furnish even moderate ones.

Nor did Lucius Crassus behave otherwise in the same trial of justice. He had laid the charge against Gnaeus Carbo with a hostile mind, as one most inimical to himself; but yet, when Carbo's writing-case had been brought to him by a slave, containing many things by which he could easily be crushed, just as it was sealed he sent it back to him with the slave in chains. By what reasoning, then, may we believe justice to have flourished among friends in those days, when we see it to have held such strength even among accusers and defendants?

But, to relate the greatest crime of the elections, M. Porcius Cato, who was going to add more distinction to the praetorship by his own character than he was going to gain from the splendour of its purple-bordered toga, could not at one time obtain it from the people. Votes next door to madness, which indeed paid heavy enough penalties for their error, since they were forced to give to Vatinius the honour which they had denied to Cato. Therefore, if we wish to estimate truly, it was not the praetorship that was then denied to Cato, but Cato that was denied to the praetorship.

6.pr. ON NECESSITY The most bitter laws and most savage commands of an abominable necessity have forced both our city and also foreign peoples to endure many things grievous not only in the understanding but even in the hearing.

Of so many witnesses set at naught I shall report one, by whose new method of entering the trial his authority was confirmed. P. Servilius, consular, censorian, triumphal, who added to the titles of his ancestors the surname Isauricus, when, passing by the forum, he had seen witnesses being produced against a defendant, took his stand in the place of a witness, and, amid the greatest admiration of both the patrons and the accusers alike, began thus: "This man, judges, who is pleading his case—of what country he is, or what life he has led, or how deservedly or undeservedly he is accused, I do not know: this only I know, that when he met me as I was making a journey on the Laurentine Way, in a very narrow place, he was unwilling to dismount from his horse. Whether this has any bearing on your conscientious duty, you yourselves will judge: I did not think it should be suppressed." The judges, the rest of the witnesses scarcely heard, condemned the defendant: for there prevailed with them both the eminence of the man and his grave indignation at his slighted dignity, and they believed that one who did not know how to revere the leading men would rush into any crime whatsoever.
6.pr. THOSE WHO COMMITTED THEMSELVES WHAT THEY HAD PUNISHED IN OTHERS Let us not allow even those to lie hidden who committed themselves what they had punished in others.

The fitting outcome of M. Brutus, deserving of the parricide he had committed, was marked out by an omen, since after that wicked deed, while celebrating his birthday and wishing to bring out a Greek verse, he set his mind to quote especially that Homeric line: "But baneful fate and the son of Leto slew me"; and that god, given as a watchword by Caesar and Antony at the battle of Philippi, turned his weapons against him.

Now Lucius Sulla wished not so much himself to be safe as Sulpicius Rufus to be ruined, harassed without any end by his tribunician fury. But when he had learned that Sulpicius, proscribed and lurking in a country house, had been betrayed by a slave, he ordered the slave freed—a parricide, that the good faith of his own edict might stand—to be hurled at once from the Tarpeian Rock with that cap of liberty gained by his crime: otherwise an insolent victor, in this command most just.

5e.1. But that we may not seem to have forgotten foreign justice: Pittacus of Mytilene, to whose merits the citizens owed so much, or to whose character they so trusted, that they conferred the tyranny on him by their own votes, held that command only so long as the war over Sigeum had to be waged with the Athenians. But after peace was won by victory, at once, the Mytileneans crying out against it, he laid it down, lest he should remain master of the citizens longer than the necessity of the commonwealth had demanded. And even when half of the recovered land was offered him by the consent of all, he turned his mind away from that gift, judging it base to diminish the glory of his virtue by the magnitude of the booty.

5e.2. Now I must relate the prudence of one man, that the justice of another may be represented. When by a most salutary counsel Themistocles had compelled the Athenians to migrate onto their fleet, and, King Xerxes and his forces having been driven from Greece, he was reshaping the ruins of his fatherland into their former state and nourishing its resources by secret machinations toward seizing the leadership of Greece, he said in the assembly that he had a matter provided for by his own deliberation which, if fortune allowed it to be carried into effect, nothing would be greater or more powerful than the Athenian people, but that it ought not to be made public, and he demanded that someone be given to him, to whom he might secretly set it forth. Aristides was given. After he learned the matter—that Themistocles wished to burn the fleet of the Lacedaemonians, which was wholly drawn up at Gytheum, so that, it being consumed, the dominion of the sea might fall to the Athenians—he went forward to the citizens and reported that Themistocles was revolving in his mind a plan as useful as it was by no means just. On the spot the whole assembly proclaimed that what did not seem equitable was not even expedient, and at once ordered Themistocles to desist from his undertaking.

5e.3. There is nothing braver even than those examples of justice. Zaleucus, having fortified the city of the Locrians with most salutary and most useful laws, when his son, condemned on a charge of adultery, ought, according to the law established by himself, to be deprived of both eyes, and the whole state, in honour of the father, was remitting the necessity of the penalty to the young man, for some time resisted. At last, overcome by the prayers of the people, having had first his own eye plucked out, then his son's, he left the use of seeing to both. Thus he rendered to the law the due measure of punishment, by an admirable tempering of equity dividing himself between a merciful father and a just lawgiver.

5e.4. But somewhat more abrupt and more curt was the justice of Charondas of Thurii. He had pacified the seditious assemblies of the citizens, which went even to violence and bloodshed, by guarding against it with a law that, if anyone entered them with a weapon, he should at once be killed. Then, after an interval of time, returning home from a distant farm girt with a sword, an assembly being suddenly proclaimed, he went into it just as he was; and being warned by one who stood nearest that he had loosed his own law, he said, "I will ratify the same law," and at once, drawing the sword which he had, fell upon it; and although it was permitted to him either to dissemble his fault or to defend it as an error, he yet preferred to enforce the penalty, lest any wrong should be done to justice.

6.pr. ON PUBLIC GOOD FAITH Whose image being set before our eyes, the venerable divinity of Good Faith displays her right hand, the most certain pledge of human safety. That it has always flourished in our state both all nations have felt, and let us recall it by a few examples.

With a consistent throw of the voice fortune tweaked the ear of C. Cassius, whom, when the Rhodians begged that they might not be stripped by him of all the images of their gods, she willed to answer that the Sun was left to them by him; so that she might draw out the insolence of the most rapacious victor by the swelling of his saying, and might compel him, cast down in the battle of Macedonia, to leave behind in very truth, not the image of the Sun, which alone he had yielded to the suppliants, but the Sun itself.

Worthy of note too is that omen under which the consul Petilius fell while waging war in Liguria: for when he was attacking a mountain whose surname was Letum ["Death"], and amid his exhortation of the soldiers had said, "Today I shall by all means take Letum," by fighting too rashly he confirmed the chance throw of his voice by his own death.

5e.1. Two foreign examples of the same kind may not absurdly be added to ours. When the people of Priene were imploring help against the Carians, the Samians, prompted by arrogance, instead of a fleet and an army sent them, by way of mockery, a Sibyl. They, interpreting her as a defence given as if by divine power, gladly received her and had her as their leader to victory, by her true prediction of the fates.

5e.2. Nor did the Apolloniates repent, who, when, hard pressed in the Illyrian war, they had begged the Epidamnians to bring them aid, and the others had said that they were sending a river near their walls, named Aeas, to their assistance, answered, "We accept what is given," and assigned it the first place in the line of battle as if to a commander: for, having unexpectedly overcome the enemy and ascribing their success to the omen, they then sacrificed to Aeas as to a god, and thereafter made it their custom to use him as commander in all their battles.
6.pr. ON PRODIGIES. Of prodigies too, whether they have turned out favourable or adverse, an account is owed to my purpose.

The eyes of his household noted that a flame flashed about the head of Servius Tullius while he was still a little boy, sleeping. This prodigy, marvelled at by Tanaquil, the wife of King Ancus Marcius, caused her to bring up the slave-born child after the manner of a son and raise him to the royal pinnacle.

The same was felt by the Spartan state, nearest to the gravity of our ancestors, which, obeying the most severe laws of Lycurgus, for a long time withdrew the eyes of its citizens from contemplating Asia, lest, captured by its allurements, they should slip into a more delicate kind of life: for they had heard that thence had flowed sumptuousness and immoderate expense and every kind of unnecessary pleasure, and that the Ionians first had discovered, as no small incitements to luxury, the custom of giving perfume and crowns at a banquet and of setting out a second course. And it is by no means a wonder that men who rejoiced in toil and endurance were unwilling that the most enduring sinews of their fatherland should be loosened and blunted by the contagion of foreign delights, since they saw that the passage from virtue to luxury was considerably easier than from luxury to virtue. That they did not fear this in vain their own leader Pausanias made plain, who, after performing the greatest works, as soon as he gave himself over to the manners of Asia, did not blush to soften his courage by its effeminate refinement.

ON THOSE WHO, AMONG ILLUSTRIOUS MEN, INDULGED THEMSELVES IN DRESS OR OTHER ATTIRE MORE FREELY THAN THE CUSTOM OF THEIR FATHERS PERMITTED. Publius Scipio, when in Sicily, while increasing his army and seeking a fitting moment to cross into Africa, was turning over in his mind the ruin of Carthage, amid the counsels and undertakings of so great a matter gave attention to the gymnasium and used a Greek cloak and slippers. Nor for this did he set hands less vigorously upon the Punic armies, but perhaps the more eagerly, because lively and strenuous natures, the more rest they take, the more vehement onsets they put forth. I should even believe that he thought he would gain for himself the fuller favour of the allies, if he approved their manner of life and their solemn exercises. To these, however, he came when he had for a long time . . . wearied his shoulders and other limbs and had compelled himself to prove his strength by military exercise; and his toil consisted in the one, his relaxation from toil in the other.

Tiberius Gracchus, when a male and female snake had been caught in his house, being informed by a soothsayer that, if the male were let go, a swift death threatened his wife, if the female, himself, choosing the part of the augury salutary to his wife rather than to himself, ordered the male to be killed, the female let go, and endured to be himself slain in his own sight by the death of the serpent. And so I should not know whether to call Cornelia the more fortunate, in that she had such a husband, or the more wretched, in that she lost him. O you, Admetus, king of Thessaly, condemned under a great judge for the charge of a cruel and harsh deed, who suffered the fate of your wife to be exchanged for your own, and, when she was consumed by a voluntary death, that you might not be extinguished, were able to look upon the light—and indeed you had first tried the indulgence of your parents!

The consul Brutus, the first to hold that office, clashed on horseback with Arruns, the son of Tarquinius Superbus expelled from his kingdom, in such a way that, their spears thrust at once, each, struck by a deadly wound, was laid low lifeless. Deservedly might I add that liberty cost the Roman people dear.

When King Ptolemy had left the Roman people as guardian to his son, the senate sent Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, chief pontiff, twice consul, to Alexandria to undertake the guardianship of the boy, and willed that the holiness of a most ample and most upright man, engaged in the uses and sacred rites of the commonwealth, should have leisure for a foreign administration, lest the good faith of our state should be thought to have been sought in vain. By his benefit the royal cradle, alike preserved and adorned, left it uncertain to Ptolemy whether he ought to glory more in his father's fortune or in the majesty of his guardians.

For, the Roman military youth being drained by several adverse battles in the second Punic war, the senate, on the proposal of the consul Ti. Gracchus, decreed that slaves should be bought at public expense for the purpose of repelling the enemy; and when, concerning this matter, a bill had been brought before the people by the tribunes of the plebs, three commissioners were created, who procured twenty-four thousand slaves and, having bound them by an oath that they would give energetic and brave service as long as the Carthaginians were in Italy, sent them under arms to the camp. From Apulia too and from the Paedicli, two hundred and seventy were bought to fill up the cavalry. How great is the violence of a bitter mischance! The state which up to that time had disdained to have as soldiers even men of free birth registered among the lowest class—this same state added to its army bodies dragged out of slaves' cells and slaves gathered from shepherds' huts, as though they were its chief support. Sometimes, then, a noble spirit yields to expediency and succumbs to the strength of fortune, where, unless you choose the safer counsels, you must perish following the showy ones. The disaster of Cannae, moreover, so vehemently confounded our city that, while M. Junius Pera as dictator administered the state, the spoils of the enemy fastened to the temples of the gods, consecrated to their divine power, were torn down to serve as instruments of war, boys still wearing the purple-bordered toga put on arms, and even six thousand of those bound over for debt and condemned on capital charges were enrolled. These measures, if they be regarded in themselves, may carry some shame; but if they be weighed with the strength of necessity brought to bear, they may seem protections suited to the savagery of the time. On account of the same disaster, when Otacilius, who held Sicily, and Cornelius Mammula, who held Sardinia, as propraetors, complained that the allies were furnishing neither pay nor grain for their fleets and armies, affirming even that they had not the means whence to furnish it, the senate wrote back that the treasury was not sufficient for distant expenses: accordingly, they should themselves see by what means so great a want should be relieved. By this letter what else did the senate do but cast from its own hands the helm of its empire, and dismiss in a few words Sicily and Sardinia—the most generous nurses of our city, the steps and supports of its wars, reduced into its power with so much sweat and blood—at your bidding, Necessity, of course?

C. Licinius, surnamed Hoplomachus, demanded of the praetor that his father be interdicted from his goods on the ground that he was squandering them; and indeed he obtained what he had sought, but a little later, the old man being dead, he hastily consumed the ample money left by him. He went free from the reciprocal penalty, since he preferred to use up the inheritance rather than to do away with the heir.

In the reign of Romulus, Spurius Tarpeius was in command of the citadel. His maiden daughter, having gone out beyond the walls to fetch water for the rites, Tatius corrupted, that she might receive the armed Sabines with her into the citadel, she having bargained as a wage for what they wore on their left hands: now on these were armlets and rings of great weight of gold. The column of Sabines, having gained the place, killed the girl who was demanding her reward, overwhelmed with their arms, just as though they had discharged the promise, because they had carried that too on their left hands. Let reproach be absent, because the impious betrayal was avenged with a swift punishment.

Of an equally happy outcome was that flame which shone forth from the head of L. Marcius, the commander of the two armies which the destruction of Publius and Gnaeus Scipio in Spain had crippled, while he was haranguing the troops: for the soldiers, still terrified, were admonished by the sight of it to recover their former courage, and, with eight-and-thirty thousand of the enemy slain and a great number reduced to their power, they captured two camps filled with Punic wealth.

The armies of the same state were not wont to go down to fight before they had drawn the warmth of exhortation into their spirits by the concert of the flute and the measure of the anapaestic foot, admonished by the lively and frequent sound of the beat to assail the enemy vigorously. The same men, to dissemble and conceal the blood of their wounds, used in battle Punic-dyed tunics, not lest the sight of them should bring terror to themselves, but lest it should bring any confidence to the enemy.
But the statue of Lucius Scipio we behold on the Capitol clad in a chlamys and slippers. In which dress, evidently because he had once used it, he wished his likeness to be fashioned and set up.

A cheaper victim than Gracchus to unjust fortune, although a man of senatorial rank, was Gaius Plautius Numida, but in a like love an equal example: for, hearing of the death of his wife, unable to restrain his grief, he struck his breast with a sword. Then, prevented by the intervention of his household from carrying out what he had begun, and bound, as soon as the chance was given, his bandages torn and his wound rent open, with steadfast right hand he drained out from his very heart and entrails the spirit mingled with the bitterness of grief, attesting by so violent a death how much of the marital flame he had held shut within that breast.

When, moreover, in the middle part of the forum the earth sank down in a vast and sudden chasm, and the answer was given that it could be filled only by that in which the Roman people was strongest, Curtius, a young man of the noblest spirit and of the noblest birth, interpreting that our city excels especially in valour and arms, adorned with military insignia, mounted his horse and, the spurs vehemently applied, drove it headlong into that abyss; upon him all the citizens, for the sake of honour, vying with one another threw fruits, and at once the earth recovered its former state. Great glories afterward shone in the Roman forum, yet none even today hovers before us more illustrious than the dutifulness of Curtius toward his fatherland. To this man, holding the chief place of glory, I shall append a like deed.

Splendid too was that Roman good faith. When a huge fleet of the Carthaginians had been conquered around Sicily, its commanders, with broken spirits, were debating plans of seeking peace. Of these, Hamilcar said that he did not dare go to the consuls, lest chains should be cast upon him in the same manner in which they had been cast by them upon the consul Cornelius Asina. But Hanno, a surer estimator of the Roman temper, judging that nothing of the kind was to be feared, made his way with the greatest confidence to a conference with them. When he was treating with them about the end of the war, and a military tribune had said to him that what had befallen Cornelius could deservedly happen to him, both consuls, having ordered the tribune to be silent, said, "From that fear, Hanno, the good faith of our state frees you." It had made them famous to have been able to bind so great a commander of the enemy, but it made them far more famous to have been unwilling to.

The same Necessity made the men of Casilinum, shut up by the siege of Hannibal and failing in the supply of provisions, willing to chew thongs drawn off for the necessary uses of bindings, and hides stripped from their shields and softened in boiling water. What was more wretched than they, if you regard the bitterness of their lot; what more loyal, if you look to their steadfastness? They who, lest they should revolt from the Romans, endured such a kind of food, while they gazed upon their own richest fields and most fertile plains lying beneath their walls. And so Casilinum, situated nearby—famed for the valour of . . . —struck with the pledge of its persevering friendship the impious eyes of the Campanian city, which in its greed had fostered Punic ferocity with its delights.

C. Marius, moreover, when he had played the part of a great and salutary citizen of the state in crushing L. Saturninus—by whom, in the manner of a flag, a cap had been displayed to slavery for the taking up of arms—when L. Sulla was bursting into the city with his army, fled to the aid of the slaves by raising the cap. And so, while he imitated the crime which he had punished, he found another Marius, by whom he should be cast down.

Ser. Galba too was of the utmost treachery: for, the people of three states of Lusitania being summoned together as though he were going to treat of their advantage, he chose and disarmed eight thousand, in whom the flower of the youth consisted, and partly butchered, partly sold them. By which crime he surpassed the greatest disaster of the barbarians by the greatness of his guilt.

Likewise, when in a fierce and protracted war the Veientines, driven within their walls by the Romans, could not be captured, and that delay seemed no less intolerable to the besiegers than to the besieged, the immortal gods opened the way to the longed-for victory by a marvellous prodigy: for suddenly the Alban lake, neither swollen by rains from heaven nor aided by the flooding of any river, exceeded its usual level of standing water. To investigate this, envoys were sent to the Delphic oracle, and they reported that the lots prescribed that the water of that lake should be let out and spread over the fields: for thus the Veientines would come into the power of the Roman people. And before the envoys reported this, a soothsayer of the Veientines, seized by one of our soldiers, because native interpreters were lacking, and carried into the camp, had foretold the future. The senate, therefore, warned by the double prediction, at almost the same time both obeyed religion and became master of the enemy's city.

The outstanding spirits of warlike valour of the Lacedaemonians the Athenians, most prudent in the manners of peace, follow close behind, among whom idleness, growing slack with languor in its hiding-places, is dragged into the forum just as some offence, and becomes the defendant of a fault not criminal indeed, yet to be blushed at.
Lucius Sulla too, when he was commander, did not think it disgraceful to walk about at Naples in a chlamys and slippers.

Of the same name, and likewise of the same love, was Marcus Plautius: for when by command of the senate he was leading back into Asia the fleet of the allies, sixty ships, and had put in at Tarentum, and there his wife Orestilla, who had accompanied him thither, was overcome by sickness and died, after she was buried and placed upon the pyre, amid the office of anointing and kissing he fell upon a drawn sword. His friends joined him, just as he was, in toga and shoes, to the body of his wife, and then, applying torches, burned them both together. There their tomb was made—at Tarentum it is to this day seen—which is called 'the tomb of the two lovers.' Nor do I doubt that, if there be any sense at all in the dead, Plautius and Orestilla, rejoicing in the partnership of their fate, bore glad countenances into the darkness. And assuredly, where the same love is both greatest and most honourable, it is somewhat better to be joined by death than parted by life.

As the praetor Genucius Cipus, in his general's cloak, was going out of the gate, a portent of a new and unheard-of kind befell him: for on his head horns suddenly crept up as it were, and the answer was given that he would be king if he returned to the city. That this might not happen, he proclaimed for himself a voluntary and perpetual exile—a dutifulness worthy, so far as it concerns solid glory, to be preferred to seven kings. As witness to it, a bronze likeness of his head was set into the gate by which he had departed and was called the Raudusculan: for of old bronze pieces were called raudera.

Against these same enemies the senators displayed an equal good faith in protecting the law of embassy: for in the consulship of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Lucius Flaminius they took care that Lucius Minucius and Lucius Manlius should be surrendered, through the fetials, by Marcus Claudius the praetor, to the envoys of the Carthaginians, because they had laid hands upon them. The senate then regarded itself, not those to whom this was rendered.

In that siege, while three hundred men of Praeneste persisted in their loyalty, it came to pass that one of them preferred to sell a captured mouse for two hundred denarii rather than to consume it himself for the soothing of his hunger. But, I believe, the providence of the gods assigned to both seller and buyer the end that each of them deserved: for the greedy man, consumed by famine, was not allowed to enjoy the gains of his meanness, while the man of even temper lived on the food procured dearly indeed, but out of necessity, for a wholesome outlay.

C. Licinius Stolo, moreover, by whose benefit power was given to the plebs of seeking the consulship, when he had sanctioned by law that no one should possess more than five hundred jugera of land, himself acquired a thousand, and, to disguise the crime, emancipated half to his son. On which account, accused by M. Popilius Laenas, he was the first to fall by his own law, and taught that nothing ought to be enjoined except what each man has first commanded for himself.

Cn. Domitius, moreover, a man of the highest birth and great spirit, too great a desire of glory forced to become treacherous: for, angry at Bituitus, king of the Arverni, because he had urged his own people and that of the Allobroges, while Domitius was still tarrying in the province, to flee to the right hand of Q. Fabius, his successor, he, summoned under the pretence of a conference and received in hospitality, bound him and had him carried to Rome by ship. His deed the senate could neither approve nor rescind, lest Bituitus, sent back to his country, should renew the war. Therefore it relegated him to Alba for the sake of custody.

Nor was the success that follows any less prosperous. The consul L. Sulla, in the Social War, when he was sacrificing before the headquarters in the territory of Nola, suddenly caught sight of a snake gliding out from the lowest part of the altar. At this sight, on the urging of the soothsayer Postumius, he immediately led the army out on campaign and captured the most strongly defended camp of the Samnites. This victory became the first step and foundation of his future most ample power.

The most holy council of the same city, the Areopagus, used most diligently to inquire what each of the Athenians did and by what gainful occupation he supported himself, so that men, mindful that an account of their manner of life must be rendered, should follow honour.

And Gaius Duellius, who first carried back a naval triumph over the Carthaginians, as often as he had feasted in public, was accustomed to return home from dinner by the light of a wax torch, with a flute-player and a lyre-player going before, attesting by a nightly celebration his notable success in war.

A like affection was noted in Julia, daughter of Gaius Caesar. She, when at the aedilician elections she had seen the garment of her husband Pompey the Great, sprinkled with blood, carried back home from the Campus, terrified with fear lest some violence had been done him, fell down lifeless, and was forced by the sudden consternation of her spirit and the grievous pain of her body to cast forth the child she had conceived in her womb—and indeed with great loss to the whole world, whose tranquillity would not have been disturbed by the most savage frenzy of so many civil wars, had the concord of Caesar and Pompey, bound by the tie of common blood, remained.

Genucius hands over the succession of this praise, than which one can scarcely be conceived greater, to the praetor Aelius. When, as he was administering justice, a woodpecker had settled on his head, and the soothsayers had affirmed that, if it were preserved, the state of his house would be most happy, that of the commonwealth most wretched, but, if it were killed, each would turn out the contrary, he with his own bite killed the woodpecker on the spot, in the sight of the senate. The Aelian family then lost seventeen men of outstanding bravery in the battle of Cannae; the commonwealth, as time went on, rose to the highest summit of empire. These examples, doubtless, Sulla and Marius and Cinna laughed at as foolish.

Following his example, the elder Africanus, when he had reduced into his power a ship laden with many and illustrious men of the Carthaginians, dismissed it inviolate, because they said that they were envoys sent to him, although it was manifest that they, for the sake of avoiding the present danger, were embracing the false name of an embassy, so that the good faith of the Roman commander should be judged rather deceived than implored in vain.

But when C. Marius and Cn. Carbo were consuls, at variance in civil war with L. Sulla—at which time not victory for the state was being sought, but the state itself was the prize of victory—by a decree of the senate the golden and silver ornaments of the temples were melted down, lest pay should be lacking to the soldiers: for it was a worthy cause indeed—whether this side or that should glut its cruelty by the proscription of citizens—that the immortal gods should be despoiled! Not, then, the will of the conscript fathers, but the savage hand of a most foul necessity pressed its pen upon that decree.

Q. Varius, moreover, surnamed Hybrida on account of his doubtful right of citizenship, as tribune of the plebs carried through, against the veto of his colleagues, a law which ordered an inquiry into those by whose malicious deceit the allies had been forced to take up arms—with great disaster to the state: for first he stirred up the war with the allies, then the civil war. But while he played the part of a pestilent tribune of the plebs before that of a sound citizen, his own law, binding him in domestic snares, destroyed him.

7.pr. ON ZEAL AND INDUSTRY Why do I delay to recall the strength of industry, by whose lively spirit the campaigns of military service are strengthened, forensic glory is kindled, all studies received into its faithful bosom are nourished, and whatever is admirable in mind, in hand, in tongue, is brought to the summit of praise? And since it is the most perfect virtue, it is confirmed by the hardening of itself.

The murder of Viriathus too admits a double accusation of treachery—in his friends, because he was killed by their hands, and in the consul Q. Servilius Caepio, because he was the instigator of this crime by promising impunity, and did not earn the victory but bought it.

6e.1. But, to contemplate the very fountain of treachery: the Carthaginians, simulating that they were carrying him home, drowned in the deep Xanthippus the Lacedaemonian, whose excellent service they had used in the first Punic war, and by whose help they had captured Atilius Regulus—seeking what by so great a crime? Was it that no partner of their victory should survive? He survives nevertheless, and indeed with reproach, whom without any loss of glory they might have left unharmed.

6e.2. Hannibal, furthermore—when the men of Nuceria had gone out at his urging, with two garments each, from their city girt with impregnable walls, did he not strangle them with the heat and smoke of the baths, and the senate of the Acerrani, called out beyond the walls in the same way, throw into the depth of wells; and did he not wage a war against good faith itself more keenly than against the Roman people and Italy, rejoicing in lies and deceit as though in glorious arts? By which it came about that, though otherwise about to leave a notable memory of his name, he set it in doubt whether he ought to be held a greater or a worse man.

Of especial wonder, too, were those prodigies which occurred in our city in the consulship of C. Volumnius and Ser. Sulpicius, amid the beginnings and disturbances of wars: for an ox, with its lowing turned into human speech, terrified the minds of the hearers by the novelty of the portent. Pieces of flesh too, scattered like rain, fell down, the greater number of which the birds of prey snatched away, while the rest lay on the ground for several days, changed neither by foul smell nor by deformed appearance. Portents of the same kind were believed in another disturbance: that a six-month-old infant boy in the cattle-market cried "Triumph"; that another was born with the head of an elephant; that in Picenum it rained stones; that in Gaul a wolf drew the sword from the scabbard of a sentinel; that in Sardinia two shields sweated blood; that at Antium bloody ears of corn fell into the basket of the reapers; that the waters at Caere flowed mingled with blood. In the second Punic war too it was established that the ox of Cn. Domitius said, "Beware for yourself, Rome."

The same city first introduced the custom of decorating good citizens with a crown, encircling the famous head of Pericles with two olive twigs joined together, a praiseworthy institution, whether you wish to consider the thing or the person: for honour is the most fruitful nourishment of virtue, and Pericles was worthy that the power of giving such a gift should take its beginning especially from him.

For Papirius Masso, indeed, when, having served the commonwealth well, he had not obtained a triumph from the senate, made on the Alban Mount the beginning of triumphing for himself, and afterwards furnished an example to others; and instead of a laurel crown, when he was present at some spectacle, he used one of myrtle.

Your most chaste fires too, Porcia, daughter of Marcus Cato, all ages shall pursue with due admiration. You, when you learned that your husband Brutus had been conquered and slain at Philippi, because steel was not given you, did not hesitate to swallow burning coals with your mouth, imitating with a woman's spirit the manly end of your father. But I know not whether this be the braver, that he was consumed by a usual, you by a new kind of death.

6e.1. There are foreign loves too, lawful, not overwhelmed by the obscurity of ignorance, of which it will be enough to have touched a few. How greatly Artemisia, queen of the nation of Caria, longed for her husband Mausolus, taken away by fate, it is a slight thing to argue from the magnificence of honours of every kind sought out, and of a monument advanced even to the seven wonders: for what should one either collect those things or speak of that famous mound, when she herself desired to become the living and breathing sepulchre of Mausolus, on the testimony of those who relate that she drank the bones of the dead man sprinkled in a drink?

6e.2. Queen Hypsicratea too loved her husband Mithridates with the reins of affection let loose, on whose account she counted it for a pleasure to change the special grace of her beauty into a manly guise: for, her hair cut, she accustomed herself to horse and arms, that she might the more easily share in his toils and dangers. Nay more, when he was conquered by Gnaeus Pompey and was fleeing through savage nations, she followed him with spirit and body alike untiring. Her so great fidelity, in harsh and difficult circumstances, was to Mithridates the greatest comfort and the most pleasant solace: for he believed himself to be wandering with home and household gods, his wife being in exile along with him.

6e.3. But why do I search Asia, why the immense solitudes of barbarian lands, why the lurking-places of the Pontic gulf, when Lacedaemon, the most splendid glory of all Greece, all but displays before our very eyes a special specimen of wifely fidelity, to be compared, by the admiration of the deed, with the very many and very great praises of its country? The Minyae, whose origin, conceived from the famous number of Jason's allies on the island of the Lemnians, had through the changes of several ages remained in a fixed abode, driven out by the Pelasgian . . . , in need of another's help, occupied the lofty ridges of the Taygetus mountains as suppliants. These the Spartan state, out of regard for the sons of Tyndareus—for in that ship of noble fame the pair of brothers, destined for the stars, had shone forth—led down thence and admitted to its laws and privileges. But this so great benefit they turned into an injury to the well-deserving city by aspiring to the kingship. Therefore, shut up in the public prison, they were kept for capital punishment. And when, by the old custom of the Lacedaemonians, they were to suffer it by night, their wives, of illustrious blood there, as though to speak with their husbands who were about to perish, having obtained access from the guards, entered the prison, and, their clothing exchanged under the pretence of grief, their heads veiled, suffered them to depart. In this place what else should I add than that they were worthy that the Minyae should wed them?

7.pr. ON FRIENDSHIP. Let us now contemplate the bond of friendship, powerful and most strong and in no part inferior to the strength of blood—even surer and more proven than it, in that the latter is contracted by the lot of birth, a work of chance, the former by a will begun upon each man's own solid judgement. And so you would more swiftly, without reproach, turn away a kinsman than a friend, because the one severance is not necessarily subject to the charge of injustice, the other necessarily to that of fickleness: for, since the future life of a man encircled by the protection of no friendship is destined to be desolate, so necessary an aid ought not to be rashly taken up, but, once rightly grasped, it is not fitting that it be spurned. But friends of sincere fidelity are recognized chiefly in adversity, in which whatever is rendered proceeds wholly from steadfast goodwill. The cultivation of prosperity is for the greater part paid out from flattery rather than affection, and certainly is suspect, as one always seeking more than it spends. To this is added that men of broken fortune the more desire the zeal of friends, whether for protection or for solace: for joyful and prosperous affairs, since they are cherished by divine support, less need human aid. The memory of posterity, therefore, more tenaciously lays hold of the names of those who did not desert the adverse chances of their friends than of those who accompanied the prosperous course of life. No one speaks of the intimates of Sardanapalus; Orestes is almost better known by his friend Pylades than by his father Agamemnon, since indeed the friendship of those wasted away in the partnership of delights and luxury, while the comradeship of these, of a hard and harsh condition, shone forth by the very trial of their miseries. But why do I touch foreign matters, when domestic ones may first be used?
