Publius Decius Mus, who first brought the consulship into his family, when in the Latin War he saw the Roman line wavering and now almost prostrate, devoted his own life for the safety of the commonwealth and at once, his horse spurred on, burst into the midst of the enemy's column, seeking safety for his fatherland, death for himself, and, having made an immense slaughter, overwhelmed by very many weapons, fell upon them. From his wounds and his blood an unhoped-for victory emerged.

Let us represent also that work of the senate by no means to be passed over. When envoys had been sent from the city of Apollonia to Rome, Quintus Fabius and Gnaeus Apronius, men of aedilician rank, a quarrel having arisen, assaulted them. When the senate learned this, it at once, through the fetials, surrendered them to the envoys, and ordered a quaestor to go with them to Brundisium, lest they should receive any injury on the way from the kinsmen of those surrendered. Who would call that senate-house a council of mortals and not a temple of Good Faith? As our state always showed it kindly, so it recognized it as steadfast also in the minds of its allies.

6e.1. After the pitiable slaughter of the two Scipios in Spain and of as many armies of Roman blood, the Saguntines, driven by the victorious arms of Hannibal within the walls of their own city, when they could no longer ward off the Punic force, having gathered into the forum what was dearest to each, and surrounded it on all sides with kindling and set fire to it, lest they should desert our alliance, threw themselves upon the public and common pyre. I could believe that then Good Faith herself, surveying human affairs, wore a sad countenance, beholding her most persistent worship condemned, by the verdict of unjust fortune, to so bitter an end.

6e.2. By doing the same the people of Petelia earned the same honour of praise. Besieged by Hannibal, because they had been unwilling to revolt from our friendship, they sent envoys to the senate imploring aid. Help could not be brought to them, on account of the recent disaster of Cannae. But they were allowed to do what should seem most useful for their own safety. It was therefore free for them to embrace the favour of the Carthaginians. They, nevertheless, having cast out of the city the women and all the unwarlike age, that, armed, they might the longer drag out their hunger, most persistently stood upon the walls, and their whole state expired before it laid aside in any part its regard for the Roman alliance. And so it befell Hannibal to capture not Petelia, but the faithful sepulchre of Petelia.

The army of the deified Julius, that is, the unconquered right hand of an unconquered leader, when it had shut up Munda by arms and material was lacking for building a rampart, raised to the height it required a heap of enemy corpses, and palisaded it, since oaken stakes were lacking, with light javelins and pikes, using necessity as the instructress of a new kind of contrivance.

C. Flaminius, moreover, made consul without auspices, when, being about to engage Hannibal at Lake Trasimene, he had ordered the standards to be plucked up, his horse slipping, was thrown to the ground over its head; and, in no way checked by that prodigy, when the standard-bearers said the standards could not be moved from their place, he threatened them with chastisement unless they straightway dug them out. But would that he had paid the penalty of this rashness with his own great disaster only, and not also with that of the Roman people! For in that battle fifteen thousand Romans were slain, six thousand captured, ten thousand put to flight. The body of the slaughtered consul was sought by Hannibal for burial, by him who, so far as in him lay, had buried the Roman empire.

Come, how memorable is that institution of Athens, that an ungrateful freedman, convicted by his patron, is stripped of the right of freedom! "I forbear," he says, "to have you as a citizen, an impious appraiser of so great a gift, nor can I be brought to believe that he is useful to the city whom I see wicked to my house. Go therefore and be a slave, since you knew not how to be free."

Then there is the almost insolent deed of Gaius Marius: for after his Jugurthine and Cimbric and Teutonic triumph he always drank from a tankard, because Father Liber, when leading his triumph over the Indians from Asia, was reported to have used this kind of cup, so that amid the very drinking of the wine he might compare his own victories with Liber's victory.

He would be the sole model of such a commander, had he not begotten a son answering to his own spirit: for he, in his fourth consulship, following his father's example, by a like devotion, in an equally vigorous fight, with a consonant end, restored the tottering and lost strength of our city. And so it is hard to discern whether the Roman state had the Decii more usefully as leaders or lost them, since their life stood in the way that it should not be conquered, while their death made it conquer.

And, to join a mention of the divine son to the heavenly remembrance of the father: when Phraates, king of the Parthians, seemed about to pour himself into our provinces, and the regions neighbouring his empire were shaken by the proclamation of a suddenly declared alarm, so great a scarcity of provisions came upon the region of the Bosporus that for six thousand denarii single vessels of oil and the same number of pecks of grain were exchanged for an equal number of slaves. But the care of Augustus, then at leisure for the guardianship of the lands, dispelled this most bitter tempest.

6e.1. To the Cretans no such protection shone forth, who, driven by the siege of Metellus to the utmost want, tortured—I should more justly say than sustained—their thirst with the urine of themselves and their beasts of burden, because, while they feared to be conquered, they suffered that which not even a conqueror would have forced them to suffer.

6e.2. The Numantines, moreover, surrounded by Scipio with palisade and rampart, when they had consumed all that could prolong their hunger, in the end made use of the banquets of human bodies. Wherefore, when the city had now been taken, several were found carrying in their bosoms limbs and members of butchered bodies. There is no excuse of necessity in these men: for those to whom it was permitted to die had no need to live thus.

6e.3. This savage obstinacy of theirs in a like crime the execrable impiety of the men of Calagurris surpassed. They, in order that, the more persistently, they might keep faith with the ashes of the slain Sertorius by frustrating the siege of Cn. Pompeius—because no other living creature now remained in their city—turned their wives and children to the use of a wicked banquet; and that their armed youth might the longer nourish their own vitals with their own vitals, they did not hesitate to salt the unhappy remains of the corpses. Behold the kind of men one might exhort in the battle line to fight bravely for the safety of their wives and children! From this enemy, surely, punishment was to be sought by so great a leader rather than victory, because to have avenged them could bring more glory than to have conquered them, since they surpassed every kind of serpent and wild beast in comparison with themselves in the title of ferocity: for those pledges of life which to such creatures are dearer than their own breath became to the men of Calagurris their luncheons and dinners.

7.pr. ON WILLS THAT WERE ANNULLED Let us now be at leisure for a business which belongs to a man's affairs of especial care and of his last hour, and let us consider which wills, though lawfully made, were rescinded, or which, though they could deservedly be rescinded, remained valid, or which transferred the honour of an inheritance to others than those who expected it; and let me set these forth in the order in which I have proposed them.

The headlong audacity of Flaminius is followed by the mad persistence of C. Hostilius Mancinus. To this consul, as he was about to go to Spain, these prodigies occurred: when he wished to make a sacrifice at Lavinium, the sacred chickens, released from the coop, fled into the nearest wood, and, sought with the utmost diligence, could not be found. When he was embarking from the harbour of Hercules, to which he had come on foot, a voice of this kind, without any author, came to his ears: "Mancinus, stay." Terrified by this, when, having changed his journey, he had made for Genua and there had entered a small boat, a snake of remarkable size, seen, vanished from sight. Thus he equalled the number of prodigies with the number of calamities: by an unlucky battle, a shameful treaty, and a disastrous surrender.

The same custom the Massilians too practise to this time, conspicuous especially for the gravity of their discipline, their observance of ancient custom, and their affection for the Roman people. They permit three manumissions of the same man to be rescinded, if they learn that the master has been deceived three times by him. The fourth error they think ought not to be relieved, because he has already received the injury by his own fault, who exposed himself to it so often. The same state is a most keen guardian of strictness, giving no entrance to the stage to mimes, whose plots for the greater part contain acts of debauchery, lest the custom of watching such things should take also the licence of imitating them. To all, moreover, who under any pretence of religion seek nourishment for their idleness, it has its gates closed, judging that lying and counterfeit superstition must be removed. Moreover, from the founding of the city there is there a sword by which the guilty are slain, eaten away indeed with rust and scarcely sufficient for its service, but an index of men who preserve, even in the smallest matters, all the monuments of ancient custom. Two chests too lie before their gates, the one in which the bodies of the free, the other in which those of slaves, are conveyed to the place of burial on a cart, without lamentation, without beating of the breast. The mourning for a funeral is ended on the same day by a domestic sacrifice and a banquet of relations brought in: for what does it profit either to indulge human grief or to make envy against the divine power, because it has been unwilling to share its immortality with us? Poison tempered with hemlock is kept at public expense in that state, which is given to him who has shown to the Six Hundred—for that is the name of their senate—the reasons on account of which death ought to be sought by him, the inquiry tempered by a manly benevolence, which neither suffers anyone to depart from life rashly, and offers a swift path of death to him who wisely desires to depart, so that, whether to those who have used adverse or prosperous fortune too much—for either gives a reason for ending the breath, the one that it may not persist, the other that it may not fail—it may be terminated by an approved end.
But Marcus Cato as praetor conducted the trials of Marcus Scaurus and of the other defendants clad in no tunic, but covered only by his bordered toga.

7.pr. But these and things like these are tokens of a virtue claiming for itself some liberty in innovating upon custom: but in those things which I shall next subjoin, it will be known how great a confidence in itself virtue is wont to have.

The elder Scipio Africanus was not extinguished for the commonwealth, but by admirable virtue provided that the commonwealth should not be extinguished: since indeed, when, our city stricken by the disaster of Cannae, it seemed nothing other than the prey of the victor, and therefore the remnants of the routed army, on the proposal of Quintus Metellus, were debating the plan of deserting Italy, the military tribune, still a very young man, with sword drawn, threatening death to each man, compelled all to swear that they would never abandon the fatherland, and not only displayed the fullest dutifulness himself but even recalled it as it was departing from the breasts of others.

The sad death of Ti. Gracchus, a most weighty citizen, announced by a prodigy and not avoided by counsel, makes the rashness of Mancinus, a man of too little judgement, seem less to be wondered at: for when as consul he was sacrificing among the Lucanians, two snakes, having slipped out from a hiding-place, suddenly devoured the liver of the victim he had immolated and withdrew into the same lairs. On account of this, then, when the sacrifice had been renewed, the same prodigy occurred. When a third victim too had been slain and the entrails more diligently watched, the gliding of the serpents could neither be kept off nor their flight hindered. Although the soothsayers said that this pertained to the safety of the commander, Gracchus nevertheless did not take care to avoid being led, by the treachery of his treacherous host Flavius, into the place where the Carthaginian general Mago lay hidden with an armed band, and being there slain unarmed.

This custom of the Massilians I judge to have arisen not in Gaul but to have been transferred thither from Greece, because I noticed that it was preserved also on the island of Ceos, at the time when, making for Asia with Sex. Pompeius, I entered the town of Iulis: for it chanced that then a woman of the highest dignity there, but already of extreme old age, having rendered a reason to her fellow-citizens why she ought to depart from life, had resolved to make away with herself by poison, and esteemed it highly that her death should be made more illustrious by the presence of Pompey. Nor did that man, as he was furnished with all virtues, so also most fully with the praise of humanity, bear to spurn her prayers. He came therefore to her, and with most eloquent speech, which flowed from his mouth as if from some blessed fountain of eloquence, having long tried in vain to recall her from her undertaken resolve, at last suffered her to carry out her purpose. She, having passed her ninetieth year, with the greatest soundness both of mind and of body, reclining on a couch spread, as far as could be discerned, more elaborately than in daily custom, and leaning on her elbow, said: "To you indeed, Sex. Pompeius, may the gods—rather those whom I leave than those whom I seek—render thanks, because you have disdained neither to be an exhorter of my life nor a beholder of my death. But for myself, having always experienced the cheerful countenance of fortune, lest, through greed of light, I be compelled to gaze upon a sad one, I exchange the remains of my breath, by a prosperous end, leaving behind me two daughters and a flock of grandchildren as survivors." Then, having exhorted her own people to concord, and having distributed her patrimony among them, and handed over her household worship and domestic rites to her elder daughter, she seized with steadfast right hand the cup in which the poison had been tempered. Then, having poured out libations to Mercury and invoked his divine power, that he might lead her by a peaceful journey to the better part of the infernal abode, with eager draught she drew the deadly potion, and signifying by speech what parts of her body the chill was successively seizing, when she had declared that it was now drawing near to her vitals and her heart, she summoned the hands of her daughters to the last office of pressing shut her eyes. But our people, although they were stupefied by the strange spectacle, yet she dismissed suffused with tears.

Come now, that I may pass from individuals to all together: with how great and how equal a love of the fatherland did the whole state burn! For when, in the Second Punic War, the treasury was so exhausted that it did not suffice even for the worship of the gods, the tax-farmers of their own accord approached the censors and urged them to let out all the contracts just as if the commonwealth abounded in money, and promised that they would furnish everything and would seek not a single as until the war was finished. The masters too of those slaves whom Sempronius Gracchus had set free for a notable battle at Beneventum forbore to exact the prices from the commander. In the camp also neither knight nor centurion desired pay to be given to him. Men and women contributed whatever of gold or silver they had, the children likewise the insignia of their freeborn status, to support the difficulty of the time. And not even of the senate's benefit—which had freed those who performed these services from the burden of tribute—did anyone wish to avail himself, but moreover all rendered it with the most ready minds: for they were not unaware that, when Veii was captured, since the gold owed under the name of the tithe which Camillus had vowed had to be sent to Delphic Apollo, and there was no means of buying it, the matrons had brought their ornaments into the treasury; and likewise they had heard that a thousand pounds of gold, which was owed to the Gauls for the abandoned siege of the Capitol, had been made up out of their adornment. And so, admonished both by their own disposition and by the example of antiquity, they judged that they should be slack in no matter.

6e.1. There are external examples also of the same purpose. Codrus, king of the Athenians, when the Attic region, weakened by an immense army of the enemy, was being laid waste with iron and fire, in distrust of human aid took refuge in the oracle of Delphic Apollo and through envoys inquired by what means that so grievous war might be dispelled. The god answered that there would be an end of it for him thus, if he himself fell by a hostile hand. This indeed spread abroad not only throughout all Athens but even in the opposing camp, and so it came about that it was proclaimed that no one should wound the body of Codrus. After he learned this, having laid aside the insignia of command, he put on the dress of a servant and cast himself into a band of foraging enemies, and, by striking one of them with his sickle, drove him to his own slaying. By his death it was brought about that Athens should not perish.

6e.2. From the same fountain of dutifulness flowed the spirit of Thrasybulus also. He, when he desired to free the city of the Athenians from the most foul domination of the Thirty Tyrants and was attacking the mass of a most mighty enterprise with a small band, and when one of his confederates had said, "What great thanks, pray, will the Athenians owe to you for the liberty gained through you?" answered, "May the gods grant that I may seem to have repaid as much as I myself owe to them." By this disposition he crowned with praise the renowned work of the tyranny destroyed.

6e.3. Themistocles, moreover, whom his own virtue had made a conqueror, and the injury of his fatherland had made commander of the Persians, that he might refrain from assailing it, having set up a sacrifice, received and drank in a bowl the blood of a bull, and before the very altar fell, like a certain illustrious victim of dutifulness. By this so memorable a departure of his it was brought about that Greece should not have need of a second Themistocles.

6e.4. There follows an example of the same kind. When between Carthage and Cyrene there was a most obstinate contention about the measure of territory, at last it was agreed that young men should be sent from each side at the same time and that the place at which these should meet should be held the boundary for both peoples. But this agreement two brothers of the Carthaginians, by name the Philaeni, anticipated by treachery, hastening their pace before the appointed hour and pushing the boundaries forward into the distance. When the young men of the Cyrenians had perceived this, having long complained of their deceit, at last by the harshness of a condition they tried to break up the wrong: for they said that the boundary would be ratified thus, if the Philaeni suffered themselves to be buried alive there. But the outcome did not answer to the design: for they, with no delay interposed, handed over their bodies to be covered by the earth there. They, since they preferred the boundaries of their fatherland to be longer than those of their own life, lie well, with the Punic empire widened by their hands and their bones. Where are the lofty walls of proud Carthage? Where the maritime glory of its renowned harbour? Where its fleet terrible to all shores? Where so many armies? Where so great a cavalry? Where its spirit not content with the immense space of Africa? All these things fortune has divided between two Scipios: but the memory of the noble deed of the Philaeni not even the destruction of their fatherland extinguished. There is nothing, therefore, except virtue, which by a mortal mind and hand can be sought as immortal.

6e.5. This dutifulness is full of youthful ardour. But Aristotle, scarcely guarding the last remnants of his life in his aged and wrinkled limbs in the highest leisure of letters, so vigorously watched over the safety of his fatherland that, lying on his sickbed at Athens, he raised it up again when it had been levelled to the ground by hostile arms—and indeed by the hands of the Macedonians, by whom it had been cast down. Thus the work known is not so much the city overthrown and ruined by Alexander as restored by Aristotle. It is plain, therefore, how kindly and how lavish a dutifulness toward the fatherland men of all orders, of every age, have displayed; and to the most sacred laws of nature the abundance of marvellous examples too has subscribed its testimony, illustrious to the world.

7.pr. ON PARENTS' LOVE AND INDULGENCE TOWARD THEIR CHILDREN Let now the indulgence of the dutiful and gentle affection of parents toward their children spread its sails, and, borne forward by a salutary breeze, bring with it the pleasing endowment of sweetness.

The partnership of consulship, the fellowship of error, and the like kind of death draw me from Ti. Gracchus to the memory of M. Marcellus. He, inflamed by the glory of the capture of Syracuse and of Hannibal being for the first time compelled by him to flee before the walls of Nola, when he was striving with the greatest zeal either to lay low the Carthaginian army in Italy or to drive it from Italy, and was inquiring into the will of the gods by a solemn sacrifice, the first victim that fell before the hearth had its liver found without a head, the next had a double head to its liver. When these had been examined, the soothsayer with a sad countenance answered that the entrails did not please him, because, after the mutilated one, the favourable had appeared. Thus warned not to attempt anything rashly, M. Marcellus, having dared on the following night to go out with a few men for the sake of reconnoitring, was surrounded by a multitude of the enemy among the Bruttii, and by his death brought equally great grief and loss to his country.

But that I may return to the state of the Massilians, from which I digressed into this byway, it is permitted to no one to enter their town with a weapon, and there is at hand one who, having received it for safekeeping, gives it back to him as he leaves, so that their hospitality, as it is humane to those arriving, so may be safe for themselves too.

For the consul Octavius feared the dire omen, yet could not avoid it: for from a statue of Apollo, whose head had broken off of itself and so fixed itself in the ground that it could not be torn away, Cinna, who was at variance in arms with his colleague, conceived in his mind that his own destruction was thereby signified, and fell, in the augury for his own fears, by a sad end of life; and only then could the immovable head of the god be loosed from the earth.

As one leaves their walls, that ancient custom of the Gauls meets us, who, it is handed down by memory, used to give money on loan to be repaid to them in the lower world, because they held it persuaded that the souls of men are immortal. I would call them fools, if these trousered men had not felt the same thing which the cloaked Pythagoras believed.

M. Crassus, to be numbered among the gravest losses of the Roman empire, does not permit us to keep silence about himself in this place, struck before so great a ruin by very many and most evident blows of portents. He was about to lead his army from Carrhae against the Parthians. A dark-coloured general's cloak was handed to him, when white or purple is usually given to those going out to battle. Sad and silent the soldiers gathered at the headquarters, who, by ancient custom, ought to have come running with a lively shout. One of the eagles could scarcely be plucked up by the chief centurion; the other, drawn out with the greatest difficulty, turned itself in the direction opposite to that in which it was being carried. Great were these prodigies, but those disasters were considerably greater: the destruction of so many most beautiful legions, so many standards intercepted by the enemy's hands, so great a glory of Roman soldiery crushed by the cavalry of the barbarians, the eyes of the father bespattered with the blood of a son of the best disposition, the body of the general cast amid the promiscuous heaps of corpses for the rending of birds and beasts. I could wish indeed to relate it more gently, but what is told is true. Thus the warnings of the gods, when despised, blaze up; thus human counsels are chastised, when they set themselves before the heavenly.

Avaricious and given to usury was the philosophy of the Gauls; eager and brave that of the Cimbri and Celtiberians, who in the battle-line exulted with joy, as though about to depart from life gloriously and happily, but lamented in sickness, as though about to perish basely and pitiably. The Celtiberians too thought it impious to survive a battle when he had fallen for whose safety they had devoted their breath. The presence of mind of both is to be praised, because they judged that both the safety of the fatherland must be bravely, and the fidelity of friendship steadfastly, maintained.

Almighty Jupiter, too, had abundantly warned Cn. Pompey not to strive to make trial of the last fortune of war against C. Caesar, hurling lightning against his column as it left Dyrrachium, obscuring the standards with swarms of bees, entangling the minds of the soldiers with sudden gloom, terrifying the whole army with nocturnal alarms, and causing the flight of the victims from the very altars. But the unconquered laws of necessity did not allow a breast otherwise far removed from madness to weigh those prodigies with just estimation. And so, while he made light of them, he shattered in the space of a single day his most ample authority, his power loftier than any private station, and all those distinctions which from his earliest youth he had gathered even to the point of envy. After which it is established that in the shrines of the gods the statues turned of their own accord; that the shout of soldiers and the din of arms was heard so loud at Antioch and Ptolemais that men ran to the walls; that the sound of drums issued from the hidden parts of the shrine at Pergamum; that at Tralles, in the temple of Victory, beneath the statue of Caesar, a green palm of fair size sprang up among the joints of the stones. From which it is clear that the divine power of the gods both favoured the glory of Caesar and wished to restrain the error of Pompey.

But that nation of Thrace might deservedly claim for itself the praise of wisdom, which, celebrating the births of men with weeping, and funerals with cheerfulness, without any precepts of the learned, saw through the true condition of our state. Let, therefore, the natural sweetness of life, common to all living beings, be set aside, which compels us to do and to suffer many base things, if a somewhat happier and more blessed end than its beginning will be found.

Revering your altars and your most holy temples, divine Julius, I pray that with your propitious and favouring divine power you may suffer the misfortunes of such great men to lie hidden under the protection and tutelage of your example: for we have received it that, on that day on which, clad in a purple robe, you sat down on a golden chair, lest you should seem to have scorned an honour sought out with the greatest zeal of the senate and bestowed on you, before you offered the sight of yourself, longed for, to the eyes of the citizens, you devoted yourself to the worship of religion, into which you were soon to pass; and that, when a fat ox had been sacrificed, no heart was found among the entrails; and that you were answered by the soothsayer Spurinna that this sign pertained to your life and your counsel, because both of these are contained in the heart. Then there broke out the parricide of those who, while they wished to remove you from the number of men, added you to the council of the gods.

6e.1. Let the domestic account of such portents be closed with this example, lest, if I take up more of the Roman, I should seem to have transferred from the heavenly temple to private houses uses not befitting. I shall therefore touch upon foreign instances, which, as they have less authority for being inserted into Latin literature, so they may bring some agreeable variety. In the army of Xerxes, which he had assembled against the province of Greece, it is established that a hare was brought forth by the birth of a mare. By this kind of portent the outcome of so great a preparation was signified: for he who [had covered] the sea with fleets, the land with infantry, . . . even a timorous animal, was compelled by a fearful retreat to seek again his own kingdom. To the same Xerxes, who had with difficulty at last crossed Mount Athos, before he destroyed Athens, while he was contemplating the plan of invading Sparta, a remarkable prodigy occurred during dinner: for the wine poured into his bowl was turned into blood, and that not once but a second and a third time. Consulted about this, the magi warned that he should abstain from his undertaken plan: and if there had been any trace of sense in his foolish breast, . . . he had been abundantly warned beforehand concerning Leonidas and the Spartans.

6e.2. To Midas, indeed, under whose rule Phrygia was subject, ants heaped grains of wheat into his mouth as he slept, when a boy. When his parents thereafter inquired whither the prodigy tended, the augurs answered that he would be the richest of all mortals. Nor did the prediction prove vain: for Midas surpassed the wealth of almost all kings in the abundance of his money, and made up for the cradle of his infancy, endowed with the cheap gift of the gods, by treasures laden with gold and silver.

6e.3. To the ants of Midas I should by right and merit prefer the bees of Plato: for those were indices of a fleeting and frail felicity, these of a solid and eternal one, inserting honey on the lips of the little child as he slept in his cradle. When this was heard, the interpreters of prodigies said that a singular sweetness of speech would flow from his mouth. And to me, indeed, those bees seem to have fed, at the instigation of the goddesses, not on Mount Hymettus fragrant with the flower of thyme, but on the Heliconian hills of the Muses, green with every kind of learning, and to have instilled into a most great genius the sweetest nourishment of the highest eloquence.
Wherefore rightly the Lycians, when mourning befalls them, put on women's clothing, so that, moved by the unseemliness of the dress, they may be willing the sooner to cast off foolish grief.

But why should I praise the bravest men in this kind of prudence? Let the women of the Indians be looked upon, who, when by ancestral custom several are wont to be married to the same man, on the death of the husband come into contest and judgement, which of them he most loved. The victress, exulting with joy, and led by her relations bearing a glad countenance before them, casts herself upon the flames of her husband and is burned with him as the happiest of women; the vanquished remain in life with sadness and grief. Bring forth into the midst Cimbric audacity, add Celtiberian fidelity, join the spirited [wisdom] of Thrace, annex the cunningly sought method of the Lycians in casting off grief: yet to the Indian pyre you will prefer none of these, which wifely devotion, secure of approaching death, mounts in the manner of a marriage-bed.

To which glory of women I shall append, that from comparison it may appear the more base, a disgrace of Punic women: for at Sicca there is a temple of Venus, into which the matrons used to betake themselves, and going forth thence to gain, by the injury of their bodies they collected their dowries, doubtless about to join honourable marriages by so dishonourable a bond.

For the institution of the Persians was quite praiseworthy, that they did not look upon their children before they had completed their seventh year, in order that they might bear the loss of little ones with more even mind.

Not even the kings of Numidia are to be blamed, who, by the custom of their nation, gave a kiss to no mortal: for whatever is placed on a lofty height ought to be free of lowly and worn usage, that it may be the more venerable.

7.pr. ON MILITARY DISCIPLINE. I come now to the chief glory and the support of the Roman empire, by salutary perseverance preserved sound and unimpaired to this time, the most tenacious bond of military discipline, in whose bosom and protection the serene and tranquil condition of blessed peace finds repose.

ON DREAMS. But since I have touched on the rich dream of Midas and the eloquent dream of Plato, I shall relate by how sure images the slumber of many has been foreshadowed. And from what point should I rather begin this subject than from the most sacred memory of the divine Augustus? When his physician Artorius was taking sleep on the night which the day followed on which the Roman armies clashed against each other in the plains of Philippi, an apparition of Minerva arose and bade him warn Augustus, who was entangled in a grave illness, not to absent himself from the next battle on account of his bad health. When Caesar had heard this, he ordered himself to be carried into the line on a litter. And while there, beyond the strength of his body, he kept watch for the winning of the victory, his camp was captured by Brutus. What else, then, are we to think but that it was brought about by divine power that the head already destined for immortality should not feel the violence of a fortune unworthy of its heavenly spirit?

P. Cornelius Scipio, to whom the destruction of Carthage gave the surname of his grandfather, sent as consul into Spain to crush the most insolent spirits of the city of Numantia, fostered by the fault of former commanders, at the same moment of time at which he entered the camp, decreed that all things which had been procured for the sake of pleasure should be removed and carried away: for it is established that there then departed thence the greatest number of hucksters and sutlers, together with two thousand harlots. Emptied of this base and shameful bilge, our army, which a little before, through fear of death, had stained itself with the shameful striking of a treaty, with its courage raised and renewed, made level with the ground that fierce and spirited Numantia, burned with fires and laid low in ruins. And so the wretched surrender of Mancinus was a token of military discipline neglected, the most glorious triumph of Scipio the reward of it preserved.

ON SELF-CONFIDENCE. When Publius and Gnaeus Scipio with the greater part of their army had been overwhelmed by the Punic battle-line in Spain, and all the nations of that province had followed the friendship of the Carthaginians, and none of our commanders dared to set out thither to set the matter right, Publius Scipio, in his twenty-fourth year, promised that he would go. And by this confidence indeed he gave to the Roman people hope of safety and of victory.

7.1a. And he used the same confidence in Spain itself: for when he was besieging the town of Badia, he ordered those who approached his tribunal to enter into bonds, for the next day, in the temple which was within the enemy's walls; and at once, having taken the city, at the time and place which he had foretold, his chair being set, he pronounced judgement upon them. Nothing is nobler than this confidence, nothing truer than this prediction, nothing more effective than this swiftness, nothing even more worthy than this dignity.

7.1b. No less spirited or less prosperous was that crossing of his into Africa, into which he led his army from Sicily against the senate's prohibition; because, had he not in this matter trusted his own counsel more than that of the conscript fathers, the end of the Second Punic War would not have been found.

7.1c. Equal to this deed is that confidence, that, after he had reached Africa, the spies of Hannibal who had been caught in his camp and brought to him he neither punished nor questioned about the counsels and forces of the Carthaginians, but took care that they should be led most carefully around all the companies, and, having asked them whether they had sufficiently observed what they had been ordered to spy out, he gave them a meal and dismissed them unharmed, themselves and their beasts. By so confident a spirit he crushed the enemy's courage before their arms.

7.1d. But, to come to the deeds of his extraordinary confidence at home: when, by Lucius Scipio, an account of four million sesterces out of the money of Antiochus was demanded back in the senate-house, the book which had been produced by him, in which the sums received and expended were contained, and by which the accusation of his enemies could be refuted, he tore to pieces, indignant that doubt should be raised concerning a matter that had been administered under himself as lieutenant. Nay more, he spoke in this manner: 'I do not render to your treasury, conscript fathers, the account of four million sesterces, I who, as the minister of another's command, made it richer by two hundred million sesterces under my own leadership and auspices: for I do not think it has come to such a pitch of malignity that inquiry should be made into my innocence: for, when I subjected all Africa to your power, I carried back nothing from it that I might call my own, save the surname. Neither, then, did the Punic treasures make me, nor the Asiatic treasures make my brother, greedy; but each of us is richer in envy than in money.' This so steadfast defence the whole senate approved, as it did that deed of his, that, when there was need to draw money from the treasury for a necessary use of the commonwealth, and the quaestors, because the law seemed to stand in the way, did not dare to open it, he as a private citizen demanded the keys, and, the treasury opened, forced the law to yield to expediency. And this confidence was given him by that consciousness whereby he remembered that all the laws had been kept by himself.

7.1e. I shall not be wearied of relating again and again the deeds of the same man, since not even he was wearied of producing his virtues in a like kind. A day before the people had been appointed for him by Marcus Naevius, tribune of the plebs, or, as some record, by the two Petillii. Led down into the forum by a vast throng, he ascended the Rostra, and, placing on his head a triumphal crown, said: 'On this day, Quirites, I compelled Carthage, breathing great things, to accept our laws: it is therefore just that you should go with me to the Capitol to offer thanksgiving.' Then his most glorious utterance was followed by an equally glorious issue: since, making for the couches of Jupiter Best and Greatest, he had as his companion the whole senate, the entire equestrian order, and all the plebs. It remained for the tribune to plead before the people without a people, and, deserted in the forum, to linger alone, to the great mockery of his own false charge. To avoid which shame he went up to the Capitol and, from an accuser of Scipio, became one of his worshippers.

Tiberius Gracchus was thought to have been an enemy of his country, and not without desert, because he had preferred his own power to its safety. Yet how steadfast a friend, even in this so depraved purpose, he had in Gaius Blossius of Cumae, is worth knowing. Judged a public enemy, visited with the utmost punishment, despoiled of the honour of burial, he yet did not lack his goodwill: for when the senate had charged the consuls Rupilius and Laenas to punish, according to the custom of the ancestors, those who had agreed with Gracchus, and Blossius had come to Laelius—by whose counsel the consuls chiefly used—to entreat on his own behalf, and was using the excuse of his friendship, and Laelius had said: 'What? If Gracchus had ordered you to set fire to the temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest, would you, on account of that friendship which you boast, have obeyed his will?' he said: 'Gracchus would never have ordered that.' Enough, nay even too much: for he dared to defend the character of one condemned by the agreement of the whole senate. But what follows is much bolder and much more perilous: for, pressed by the persistent questioning of Laelius, he stood in the same grade of steadfastness, and answered that he would do even this, if only Gracchus had assented. Who would have thought him to have been wicked, had he kept silent? Who would not have thought him even wise, had he spoken according to the necessity of the time? But Blossius would protect his safety neither by an honourable silence nor by a prudent speech, lest in any part he should desert the memory of an unfortunate friendship.

Fabius Rullianus, after five consulships had been carried through with the highest glory and after all the campaigns both of valour and of life had been served out, did not refuse to go as a legate to his son Fabius Gurges, to bring to completion a difficult and dangerous war—about to serve, almost with his spirit alone, so to speak, without his body, inasmuch as, on account of his extreme old age, he was fitter for the leisure of his couch than for the toil of battles. The same man counted it among his greatest pleasures to follow on horseback, as he triumphed, the son whom he himself, when a little child, had carried in his own triumphs, and he was beheld not as an addition to that glorious procession, but as its author.

ON THE FAITHFULNESS OF WIVES TOWARD THEIR HUSBANDS And, that we may touch also upon wifely faithfulness, Tertia Aemilia, the wife of the elder Africanus, the mother of Cornelia the mother of the Gracchi, was of such courtesy and patience that, when she knew that a little maidservant of her own was pleasing to her husband, she dissembled it, lest she, a woman, should make Africanus, the tamer of the world, a great man, a defendant on a charge of impatience; and so far was her mind from vengeance that, after the death of Africanus, she freed the maidservant and gave her in marriage to her own freedman.

The father of a certain soldier, having received from the camp a false report of his son's death, died after appointing other heirs. Then, his service completed, the young man made for home: by his father's error and the shamelessness of strangers he found it closed against him. For what could be more shameless than they? He had spent the flower of his youth for the state, had endured the greatest labours and very many dangers, showed the scars received on the front of his body—and they demanded to possess his ancestral household gods, themselves idle burdens to the city! And so, laying aside his arms, he was forced to enter in the Forum a toga-clad campaign: a bitter one—for with most wicked heirs he contended before the Hundred Men over his father's goods; and he came off superior not only in all their counsels but even in their votes.

Cato, in his eighty-sixth year, while with a youthful spirit he persisted in protecting the state, accused by his enemies on a capital charge, pleaded his own cause; and no one observed either his memory the slower, or the firmness of his lungs shaken in any part, or his mouth hampered by hesitation, because he kept all these in their condition by an even and continuous industry. Nay, even at the very end of a life lived to its utmost length, he set his own defence against the accusation of the most eloquent orator Galba, on behalf of Spain. The same man longed to be instructed in Greek letters: how late, let us judge from this, that he learned Latin letters too almost in old age; and when he had won great glory by his eloquence, he took pains that he should also be most skilled in the civil law.

ON VIOLENCE AND SEDITION But, that deeds of violence and sedition both toga-clad and even armed may be related: L. Equitius, who pretended that he was the son of Ti. Gracchus and was seeking the tribunate against the laws together with L. Saturninus, when he had been led into the public prison by C. Marius, who was holding his fifth consulship, the people, having burst the bars of the prison, snatched him out and carried him on their shoulders with the utmost eagerness of spirit.

Augustus, indeed, beyond the natural vigour of his mind in perceiving all things keenly, was admonished also by a recent and domestic example to obey the dream of Artorius: for he had heard that Calpurnia, the wife of the divine Julius his father, on the night which he last passed on earth, had seen in her sleep him lying in her lap pierced with many wounds, and, violently terrified by the dreadfulness of the dream, had not ceased to beg that on the next day he abstain from the senate-house. But he, lest he should be thought to have done it moved by a woman's dream, insisted on holding the senate, in which the hands of the parricides were laid upon him. It is not [fitting] to make a comparison between father and son in any matter, especially when joined by the height of divinity; but the one had already by his works built himself an approach to heaven, while for the other a long round of earthly virtues still remained. Wherefore the immortal gods willed that by the one only the impending change of his condition should be recognized, while by the other it should even be postponed, so that one glory might be given to heaven and another promised.

Following his school, Metellus, when as consul he had received in Africa, in the Jugurthine war, an army corrupted by the excessive indulgence of Spurius Albinus, strove with all the sinews of his command to recall it to the discipline of former military service: nor did he take hold of single parts, but straightway brought the whole back into its proper state. For at once he removed the sutlers from the camp and forbade cooked food to be set out for sale; on the march he suffered no soldier to use the service of slaves and pack-animals, so that they themselves should carry their own arms and provisions; from time to time he changed the place of the camp; and each one he girded most aptly, as if Jugurtha were always present, with rampart and ditch. What, then, did restored self-restraint, what did renewed industry accomplish? It brought forth, namely, frequent victories and many trophies from that enemy whose back the Roman soldier, under an ambitious commander, had not had the fortune to see.

An excellent successor to his grandfather's spirit was Scipio Aemilianus, who, when he was besieging a very strong city, and some advised him to scatter iron caltrops around its walls and to strew all the fords with leaden plates having the points of nails, lest by a sudden sally the enemy might make an attack upon our garrisons, answered that it did not belong to the same man both to wish to capture some of them and to fear them.

In the same house arise equally robust examples of steadfast friendship: for when the counsels and affairs of Gaius Gracchus were now laid low and ruined, and his whole conspiracy was being sought far and wide, only two friends, Pomponius and Laetorius, sheltered him, deserted of all help, by the opposition of their own bodies to the hostile weapons rushing from every side. Of these Pomponius, that he might the more easily escape, checked for some while the roused column of pursuers at the Trigeminal Gate in a most fierce fight, nor could be driven back alive, but, finished by many wounds, gave them passage over his own corpse—unwilling, I believe, even after death. But Laetorius took his stand on the Sublician bridge and fenced it with the ardour of his spirit until Gracchus crossed, and, now overwhelmed by the force of the multitude, turning his sword upon himself, with a swift leap sought the depth of the Tiber, and the affection which Horatius Cocles had displayed on that bridge towards his whole country, he rendered, with voluntary death added, to a single friendship. How good soldiers Gracchus could have had, had they been willing to enter upon the way of life either of his father or of his maternal grandfather! For with what onset, with what perseverance of spirit Blossius and Pomponius and Laetorius would have aided their trophies and triumphs—the comrades, so strenuous, of frenzied attempts, having followed, with sinister auspices indeed, the condition of friendship, but the more wretched, the surer examples of friendship faithfully cultivated.

Less splendid was the lot of Caesetius, a Roman knight, in respect of his fatherland, but his indulgence was equal. When he was ordered by Caesar—now victor over all enemies both foreign and domestic—to disown his son, because that son, as tribune of the plebs with his colleague Marullus, had raised odium against Caesar as one aiming at kingship, he ventured to answer in this manner: "More quickly will you, Caesar, snatch from me all my sons than I will drive out one of them by my mark of disgrace." Now he had besides two sons of the best disposition, to whom Caesar was promising that he would kindly give increases of dignity. Although the supreme clemency of the divine prince kept this father safe, yet who would not think that he had ventured something greater than human disposition could compass, in that he did not yield to one to whom the whole world had succumbed?

Quintus Lucretius, proscribed by the triumvirs, his wife Turia kept safe from impending destruction, hidden between the vaulting and the roof of his bedchamber, with a single little maidservant aware of it, not without great danger to herself, and accomplished it by singular faithfulness, so that, while the rest of the proscribed scarcely escaped in foreign and hostile regions through the utmost torments of body and mind, he kept his safety in his bedchamber and in the bosom of his wife.

Likewise the son of M. Anneius of Carseoli, a most distinguished Roman knight, adopted by his uncle Sufenas, rescinded before the Hundred Men the will of his natural father, in which he had been passed over, although in it Tullianus, a friend of Pompey the Great, had been written as heir, with Pompey himself indeed as one of the witnesses. And so in the trial he had more business with the favour of a most excellent man than with the ashes of his parent. But although both these things strove against him, nevertheless he obtained his father's goods: for L. Sextilius and P. Popilius, whom M. Anneius, joined to himself by blood, had made heirs in the same portion as Tullianus, did not dare to contend at law with the young man, although by the eminent strength of Magnus at that time they might have been invited to defend the tablets of the will; and it helped the heirs somewhat that M. Anneius had passed over into the family and sacred rites of Sufenas. But the closest bond of procreation among men overcame at once the father's will and the authority of the foremost man of the state.

His wonderful descendant Cato, nearer to our age, so burned with a desire for learning that not even in the senate-house, while the senate was being convened, did he refrain from reading Greek books. By this industry indeed he showed that some men lack time, and others lack the will to use their time.

And the same people tried to lay low with stones the censor Q. Metellus, because he was unwilling to receive the census from Equitius as the son of Gracchus, when Metellus affirmed that Ti. Gracchus had had only three sons, of whom one, serving campaigns in Sardinia, another, an infant, at Praeneste, and a third, born after his father's death, at Rome, had died, and that the unknown baseness ought not to be inserted into a most distinguished family; while meanwhile the improvident rashness of the excited multitude—O for the shamelessness and audacity!—aimed at the consulship and the censorship and harassed its own leading men with every kind of insolence.

That dream too is of great wonder and of a clear outcome which on the same night the two consuls P. Decius Mus and T. Manlius Torquatus saw, when their camp was pitched in the Latin War, grave and dangerous, not far from the foot of Mount Vesuvius: for to each of them a certain apparition foretold in his sleep that from one army the commander, from the other the army, was owed to the gods of the dead and to Mother Earth; and that, whichever commander had devoted to death the forces of the enemy and himself above them, his side would depart victorious. This, on the next dawn, agreed with the entrails of the victims, which the consuls were about either to expiate, if it could be averted, or to carry out, if it should be deemed certain even by the warning of the gods; and it was agreed between them that, whichever of them should first begin to be hard pressed on his wing, he should atone for the fates of the fatherland with his own life. Of this neither shrank, and the fates demanded Decius.

Well too did those serve military discipline who, the bonds of kinship broken, did not hesitate to exact vengeance and punishment, with disgrace to their own houses, for discipline harmed: for the consul P. Rupilius, in that war which he waged in Sicily against the runaways, ordered Q. Fabius, his own son-in-law, because by negligence he had lost the citadel of Tauromenium, to depart from the province.

To whatever part of memorable examples I turn, willing or unwilling, I must needs cling to the surname of the Scipios: for who, indeed, could in this place pass over Nasica, that most illustrious author of a saying of confident spirit? When the dearness of provisions was increasing, Gaius Curiatius, tribune of the plebs, having brought the consuls forward into the assembly, was urging them to lay before the senate the matter of buying corn and of sending envoys to settle that business. To interrupt this most unprofitable measure, Nasica began to set on foot a contrary action. Then, the plebs clamouring against him, he said: 'Be silent, I beg, Quirites: for I understand better than you what is expedient for the commonwealth.' On hearing this voice, all, in silence full of veneration, paid more regard to his authority than to their own sustenance.

But Lucius Reginus, if he be examined for the sincerity due to a public office, is to be torn by the reproach of posterity; if he be appraised by the faithful pledge of friendship, is to be left in the best harbour of a praiseworthy conscience: for as tribune of the plebs he freed from public custody Caepio, who had been cast into prison because by his fault our army was thought to have been destroyed by the Cimbri and Teutones, mindful of an old and close friendship; nor, content to have acted thus as a friend, he became too the companion of his flight. O great and unconquerable divinity, friendship! When on the one side the commonwealth laid its hand upon him, on the other your right hand drew him, and it demanded that he should be willing to be sacrosanct, while you proclaimed exile—so winning is the command you use—he preferred punishment to honour.

But I know not whether Octavius Balbus was of a more impetuous and more ardent goodwill toward his son. Proscribed by the triumvirs, when he had secretly gone out of his house by the back door and now had a ready beginning of flight, after he had received, by a false outcry of the neighbourhood, the report that his son was being slaughtered within, he offered himself to that death which he had escaped and handed himself over to the soldiers to be killed, valuing, doubtless, that moment in which it had befallen him to see his son safe beyond his hope more than his own safety. Wretched the eyes of the young man, with which he was compelled to behold his father, most loving of him, thus expiring by his own doing!

7e.1. But, to come to things more pleasant to learn of: Antiochus, son of King Seleucus, seized by a boundless love for his stepmother Stratonice, mindful with what wicked flames he was burning, covered the impious wound of his breast with dutiful dissimulation. And so contrary affections, enclosed in the same flesh and marrow—the highest desire and the greatest modesty—reduced his body to the last wasting away. He himself lay on his couch, like one dying; his kinsmen lamented; his father, prostrate with grief, thought of the death of his only son and of his own most wretched bereavement; the countenance of the whole house was funereal rather than royal. But this cloud of sadness the foresight of Leptines the astrologer—or, as some relate, of Erasistratus the physician—dispelled: for, sitting beside Antiochus, when he noticed that at the entrance of Stratonice he was suffused with a blush and his breath quickened, and that as she went out he grew pale and presently recovered a more agitated panting, by a more careful observation he penetrated to the very truth: for, when Stratonice entered and again departed, by dissemblingly grasping the young man's arm, he discovered, by the now more lively, now more languid beating of the veins, of what disease the patient was sick, and at once disclosed it to Seleucus. He did not hesitate to yield to his son the wife most dear to himself, attributing to fortune the fact that he had fallen into love, but to his own modesty the fact that he had been prepared to conceal it even unto death. Let an old man, a king, a lover be set before our minds: now it will be plain how many and how difficult things the indulgence of a father's affection overcame.

7e.2. And Seleucus, indeed, yielded a wife; but Ariobarzanes yielded to his son the kingdom of Cappadocia, in the sight of Gnaeus Pompeius. When he had mounted Pompeius's tribunal and, invited by him, had sat in the curule chair, after he beheld his son holding, on the corner among the scribes, a place lower than his fortune, he could not endure to look upon him placed below himself, but at once descended from the chair and transferred the diadem to his head and began to exhort him to pass over to the place from which he himself had risen. Tears fell from the young man, his body shuddered, the diadem slipped down, nor could he advance whither he had been bidden; and—what almost exceeds the credit of truth—he who was laying down a kingdom was joyful, he to whom it was given was sad. Nor would so distinguished a contest have had any end, had not the authority of Pompeius supported the will of the father: for he both called the son king and ordered him to take the diadem and compelled him to sit in the curule chair.
8.pr. These fathers were of comic mildness, those of tragic harshness.

But Sulpicia, when she was being most diligently watched by her mother Julia, lest she should follow her husband Lentulus Cruscellio, proscribed by the triumvirs, into Sicily, nevertheless, having put on servile dress, with two maidservants and as many slaves, came to him by clandestine flight, and did not refuse to proscribe herself, that her faithfulness to her proscribed husband might be established.
8.pr. ON THE FAITHFULNESS OF SLAVES It remains that we relate also the faithfulness of slaves toward their masters—the less expected, the more praiseworthy.

C. Tettius, moreover, disinherited by his father in infancy, born of his mother Petronia, whom Tettius had kept in marriage as long as he lived, the deified Augustus, using the spirit of a father of his country, ordered by his decree to enter upon his father's goods, since Tettius, with the greatest injustice, had revoked the name of father from a son begotten in his own home.

Terentius Varro, moreover, having completed the span of human life not in the years by which he equalled the time of a century, was more long-lived with his pen than with his breath: for on the same couch both his breath and the course of his excellent works were extinguished.

The former sedition was only frenzied; this other was even bloody: for the people, when nine tribunes had already been created and there remained two candidates for one place, first by violence drove Nunnius, the competitor of Saturninus, into a private house, then, having dragged him out, slew him, so that by the slaughter of a most blameless citizen the means of obtaining power might be given to a most foul man.

There follows a dream equally pertaining to public religion. When at certain plebeian games a head of a household, before the procession was brought in, had driven through the Flaminian circus his slave, beaten with stripes, under a yoke to punishment, Jupiter in his sleep bade T. Latinius, a man of the people, tell the consuls that the leading dancer at the next circus games had not pleased him: and that, unless this matter were expiated by a careful repetition of the games, no slight danger to the city would follow. He, fearing lest he should entangle the supreme authority in some inconvenience to himself by a religious scruple, kept silence, and at once his son, seized by a sudden violence of disease, perished. He himself too, asked in his sleep by the same god whether he had paid a sufficiently great penalty for neglecting his command, persisting in his resolve, was loosed in the strength of his body; and only then, by the counsel of his friends, carried on a little litter to the tribunal of the consuls and thence to the senate, having set forth in order the whole of his misfortune, to the great wonder of all recovered the firmness of his limbs and returned home on foot.

The consul C. Cotta compelled P. Aurelius Pecuniola, joined to him by blood, whom, being about to cross to Messana to renew the auspices, he had set over the siege of Lipara, having been beaten with rods, to discharge military service among the infantry, because by his fault the siege-mound had been burned and the camp had almost been taken.

The spirit of Livius Salinator too is to be handed down to everlasting memory. He, when he had destroyed Hasdrubal and the army of the Carthaginians in Umbria, and it was said to him that the Gauls and Ligures, scattered and straggling without leaders and standards from the battle-line, could be crushed with a small force, answered that in this they ought to be spared, lest the enemy should lack home-bred messengers of so great a disaster.

Admirable is this work of yours, but what follows is somewhat more praiseworthy: for recognize to what point you carried the steadfast affection of Volumnius towards his friend, without any injury to the commonwealth. He, of equestrian birth, when he had familiarly cultivated Marcus Lucullus, and Marcus Antonius had killed him because he had followed the party of Brutus and Cassius, amid great license to flee clung to his lifeless friend, poured out so far in tears and groans that by his excessive devotion he brought upon himself the cause of death: for on account of his special and persevering lamentation he was dragged to Antonius. After he stood in his sight, he said: 'Order me, commander, to be led straightway to the body of Lucullus and slain: for I ought not to survive him, now that he is consumed, since I was the author to him of his unfortunate service.' What is more faithful than this goodwill? He lightened the death of his friend by the hatred of an enemy, bound his own life by the charge of his counsel, and, that he might render the other more pitiable, made himself more hated. Nor did he find the ears of Antonius difficult, and, led whither he had wished, having eagerly kissed the right hand of Lucullus, he took up the head, which lay severed, and pressed it to his breast, and then offered his bent neck to the sword of the victor. Let Greece say that Theseus, abetting the wicked loves of Pirithous, committed himself to the realms of Father Dis: that is the telling of a vain man, the believing of a fool. To see the mingled blood of friends, and wounds interwoven with wounds, and death clinging to death—these are the true tokens of Roman friendship; those are lies, like to a portent, of a nation ready to invent.

Septicia too, the mother of the Trachali of Ariminum, angry at her sons, in order to insult them, when she could now no longer bear children, married a very old man, Publicius, passing over both her sons also in her will. Approached by them, the deified Augustus disapproved both the woman's marriage and her last dispositions: for he ordered the sons to have their mother's inheritance, but forbade the husband to keep the dowry, because the union had not been entered upon for the sake of begetting children. If Equity herself were to take cognizance of this matter, could she have pronounced more justly or more weightily? You scorn those whom you bore; you marry, worn out; with violent spirit you confound the order of your will, nor do you blush to make over your whole patrimony to one beneath whose laid-out corpse you have spread your withered old age. Therefore, while you so conduct yourself, you have been blasted by a heavenly thunderbolt even down to the shades below.

Of like perseverance was Livius Drusus, who, failed by the strength of his years and the sharpness of his eyes, interpreted the civil law most kindly to the people, and composed most useful records for those desiring to learn it: for as nature could make him old and fortune blind, so neither could prevent his mind from both seeing and being vigorous.

The consternation of creditors too blazed up in an intolerable manner against the life of Sempronius Asellio, the city praetor. Him, because he had undertaken the cause of debtors, the creditors, stirred up by L. Cassius, tribune of the plebs, while he was making a sacrifice before the temple of Concord, forced to flee from the very altars beyond the forum, and, as he hid in a little shop, tore to pieces, still in his praetextate toga.

7M.1. The condition of the forum is to be detested; but if you look to the camp, an equally great indignation will arise. When the province of Asia had been decreed to C. Marius, as a private citizen, by the Sulpician law, that he might wage war against Mithridates, the soldiers butchered Gratidius, the legate sent by him to the consul L. Sulla for the purpose of receiving the legions—indignant beyond doubt because they were being forced to pass over from the highest command to one who was in no office. But who could endure a soldier correcting the decrees of the plebs by the death of a legate?

7M.2. That was an army so violent against a proconsul; this other was against a consul: for Q. Pompeius, Sulla's colleague, who by the order of the senate had dared to make for the army of Cn. Pompeius, which he had for some time held against the will of the state, the soldiers, corrupted by the enticements of the ambitious leader, attacked as he was beginning to sacrifice and slew like a victim; and so great a crime, the senate-house confessing that it yielded to the camp, went unavenged.

7M.3. That army too was wickedly violent which deprived of life C. Carbo, the brother of Carbo three times consul, because, on account of the civil wars, he had tried to bind more strictly and rigidly a military discipline that had been relaxed, and thought it better to be defiled by the greatest crime than to change depraved and foul morals.

8.pr. ON RASHNESS The impulses of rashness too are sudden and vehement, by whose blows the minds of men, shaken, are able neither to discern their own perils nor to follow the deeds of others with a just estimation.

Nor is this either to be wrapped in silence. M. Cicero, driven from the city by the conspiracy of his enemies, when he was staying in a certain villa of the field of Atina, his mind sunk in sleep, while he wandered through deserted places and pathless regions, thought that C. Marius, adorned with the insignia of the consulship, met him and asked him why he was being carried with so sad a countenance on an uncertain journey. Then, having heard the misfortune with which he was struggling, he seized his right hand and handed him over to the nearest lictor to be led to his own monument, saying that there was laid up for him there the hope of a happier state. Nor did it turn out otherwise: for in the temple of Marian Jupiter the decree of the senate concerning his return was made.

Q. Fulvius Flaccus too, as censor, removed from the senate his brother Fulvius, his colleague, because he had dared, without the consul's order, to dismiss home a legion in which he was a military tribune. These examples would not be related so briefly, were I not pressed by greater ones: for what is so difficult to do as to pronounce upon a partner united by the fellowship of birth and ancestral images a dishonourable return to the fatherland, or to apply the insulting blows of rods to one cohering, by the series of an old kinship, in the community of name and family, or to unbend the censorial brow against brotherly affection? Let these singly be granted to states however illustrious, yet they will be seen abundantly furnished with the glory of military discipline:

This excellence of spirit was in war; that which Publius Furius Philus the consul displayed in the senate was of the toga, but no less praiseworthy: for Quintus Metellus and Quintus Pompeius, men of consular rank, his bitter enemies, who again and again reproached him with his eager setting-out for the province of Spain, which he had drawn by lot, he compelled to go thither with him as his lieutenants: a confidence not only brave but almost rash, which dared to gird its own sides with two most bitter hatreds, and endured to seek the use of a service scarcely safe among friends from the bosom of enemies!

Lucius Petronius too rightly claims a share of this praise: for to one who has dared a deed equal in the cultivation of friendship an equal portion of glory is to be assigned. Born in a very humble station, he had come, by the benefit of Publius Caelius, to the equestrian order and the pay of a splendid service. To him he showed a grateful spirit, with much fidelity, in that which fortune willed to be unhappy, because it had not befallen him to show it in a joyful matter. Caelius had been set in charge of Placentia under the consul Octavius. When it was captured by Cinna's army, and he, now elderly and afflicted with grave ill health, that he might not come into the power of the enemy, fled for help to the right hand of Petronius. He, having vainly tried to draw him from his begun resolve, killed him as he persevered in the same entreaties, and joined his own death to his slaying, lest, with him dead through whom he had obtained all the increase of his dignity, he should survive him. Thus the modesty of the one, the devotion of the other, furnished the cause.

Distinguished too was the ruling of C. Calpurnius Piso, praetor of the city: for when Terentius laid before him a complaint that, out of eight sons whom he had brought up to manhood, by one given in adoption he had been disinherited, he gave him possession of the young man's goods and did not allow the heirs to proceed at law. Surely the majesty of fatherhood moved Piso, the gift of life, the benefit of upbringing; but it also bent him somewhat that the number of children standing around—because he saw the seven brothers impiously disinherited together with their father.

Publilius the senator and Lupus Pontius, a Roman knight, famous pleaders of cases in their own times, having lost their sight, carried out their forensic campaigns with the same industry. And so they were even heard more frequently, some flocking to them because they were delighted by their talent, others because they admired their steadfastness: for those who, struck by such a misfortune, seek retirement, double their darkness by adding the voluntary to the accidental.

To C. Gracchus, moreover, the dreadfulness of the impending misfortune was announced openly and plainly in his sleep: for, oppressed by slumber, he saw the image of his brother Tiberius saying to him that by no means could he avoid perishing by that same fate by which he himself had fallen. Many heard this from Gracchus before he entered upon the tribunate, in which he met his brother's end. Caelius too, a reliable authority on Roman history, writes that the report of this matter reached his own ears while Gracchus was yet alive.

but our city, which has filled the whole circle of the world with every kind of wonderful examples, received from the camp, at public cost splendid, in private grievous, the axes dripping with the very blood of the commanders' sons—lest, with the order of military service disturbed, vengeance should be wanting—with a double countenance, uncertain whether first to discharge the office of congratulating or of consoling. Therefore I too, with hesitating mind, embrace you in memory and narrative, most severe guardians of warlike affairs, Postumius Tubertus and Manlius Torquatus, because I perceive that, overwhelmed by the weight of the praise which you have deserved, I shall rather lay bare the feebleness of my talent than represent, as is fitting, your virtue. For you, Postumius, as dictator, ordered A. Postumius—whom you had begotten for propagating the succession of your race and of the sacred rites of your house, whose infancy you had cherished with caresses in your bosom and with kisses, whom as a boy you had instructed in letters, as a youth in arms, holy, brave, loving you alike and your country, because, not by your order but of his own accord, he had advanced from his post and routed the enemy—being victor, to be struck with the axe, and to carry out this command you had strength enough by the service of a father's voice: for I am sure that your eyes, in the clearest light overspread with darkness, could not behold the mighty work of your spirit. You likewise, Torquatus, as consul in the Latin war, ordered your son—because, challenged by Geminus Maecius, leader of the Tusculans, he had gone down to fight without your knowledge—as he was bringing back a glorious victory and splendid spoils, to be hurried off by the lictor and to be slaughtered after the manner of a victim, judging it better that a father should lack a brave son than that the fatherland should lack military discipline.

If this deed pleases anyone, the resolve of Lucius Crassus too, who among our ancestors was most illustrious for eloquence, must needs not displease him: for when, after his consulship, he held the province of Gaul, and Gaius Carbo, whose father he had condemned, came into it to spy out his acts, he not only did not remove him thence, but besides assigned him a place upon his tribunal, nor took cognizance of any matter unless Carbo were admitted to his counsel. And so the keen and vehement Carbo gained nothing else by his Gallic journey than to perceive that his guilty father had been sent into exile by a man of the utmost integrity.

To Petronius is to be joined Servius Terentius, although it did not befall him, as he had wished, to perish on behalf of his friend: for he ought to be appraised by his distinguished undertaking, not by the unsuccessful outcome, because, as far as lay in him, both he himself was slain and Decimus Brutus escaped the danger of death. Brutus, fleeing from Mutina, when he learned that horsemen sent by Antonius to kill him had arrived, was trying in a certain place to steal away from the darkness the breath owed to just punishment, and, an irruption having already been made there, Terentius, by a faithful falsehood, the very obscurity aiding him, pretended that he was Brutus, and offered his own body to the horsemen to be slaughtered. But, recognized by Furius, to whom the office of Brutus' avenging had been entrusted, by his own death he could not avert his friend's punishment. Thus, against his will, fortune compelling, he lived.

What of the weighty decree of Mamercus Aemilius Lepidus, the consul! A certain Genucius, a Gallus of the Great Mother, had obtained from Cn. Orestes, praetor of the city, that he should be ordered restored to the goods of Naevius Anius, possession of which he had received from him according to the tablets of the will. Mamercus, appealed to by Surdinus, whose freedman had made Genucius his heir, annulled the praetorian jurisdiction, because he said that Genucius, having of his own accord cut off the genital parts of his own body, ought to be reckoned in the number neither of men nor of women. A decree fitting for Mamercus, fitting for the foremost man of the senate, by which it was provided that the tribunals of the magistrates should not be polluted by the obscene presence and defiled voice of Genucius under the pretext of a right claimed.

Then P. Crassus, when as consul he had come to Asia to make an end of the war against king Aristonicus, grasped with such care the knowledge of the Greek tongue in his mind that he thoroughly knew it, divided into five kinds, through all its parts and measures. This thing won him the greatest love of the allies, since to each who had made a petition before his tribunal in his own tongue, he gave back his decrees in that same tongue.

The dream which follows surpasses the dire aspect of this one. At Actium, when the resources of M. Antonius had been broken, Cassius of Parma, who had followed his party, fled to Athens. There, while in the dead of night he lay on his little bed, his mind lulled by anxieties and cares, he thought there came to him a man of huge size, of black colour, with a squalid beard and unkempt hair, and that, being asked who he was, he answered, "An evil spirit." Then, terrified by the foul sight and the dreadful name, he called out to his slaves and asked whether they had seen anyone of such appearance either entering or leaving the bedroom. When they affirmed that no one had come there, he gave himself again to rest and sleep, and the same apparition presented itself to his mind. And so, sleep being put to flight, he ordered a light to be brought in and forbade the boys to leave him. Between this night and the capital punishment with which Caesar afflicted him, a very little time intervened.

Come, with how great a spirit do we suppose L. Quintius Cincinnatus the dictator to have acted at that time when, the Aequiculi having been conquered and sent under the yoke, he compelled L. Minucius to lay down the consulship, because the same enemy had besieged his camp? For he believed unworthy of the highest command one whom not his own valour, but a ditch and rampart, had rendered safe, and to whom it had been no shame to keep the Roman arms shut up, trembling with fear, behind closed gates.
