Therefore the most imperious twelve fasces, in whose power was the highest honour of the senate and the equestrian order and the whole plebs, and by whose nod Latium and the forces of all Italy were governed, bruised and broken, prostrated themselves to the dictatorial chastisement; and, lest the injured military glory should be unavenged, the consul, the avenger of every offence, was himself punished. By these expiations, so to speak, Mars, father of our empire, wherever in some part there had been a degeneracy from your auspices, was propitiated as to your divine power, by the disgrace of kinsmen and relations and brothers, by the slaughter of sons, by the shameful abdication of consuls.

The elder Cato, often summoned by his enemies to plead his cause, and never convicted of any crime, at the last reposed so much confidence in his own innocence that, when brought to public trial by them, he demanded as his judge Tiberius Gracchus, from whom in the administration of the commonwealth he greatly differed, even to much hatred. And by this very excellence of spirit he checked the obstinacy of those who pursued him.

From this rough and sad face of obstinate friendship let us pass over to the glad and serene one, and, calling it forth thence, where all had been filled with tears, groaning, and slaughter, let us place it in that dwelling of happiness of which it is the more worthy, shining with favour, honour, and most abundant wealth. Arise therefore from that seat which is believed to be dedicated to the shades of the holy—on this side you, Decimus Laelius, on that, Marcus Agrippa, the one of men, the other of gods, having drawn by sure judgement and prosperous omens the greatest friend—and the whole flock of the blessed throng, which under your leadership accomplished the venerable service of sincere fidelity, laden with praises and rewards, draw forth with you into the light: for your steadfast spirits, your strenuous services, your unconquerable silence, and, on behalf of the dignity and safety of friends, your perpetual watch and station of goodwill, and again the most plentiful fruits of these things, a later age, beholding, will the more gladly and the more religiously labour in the cultivation of the right of friendship.

7e.1. The mind clings to domestic matters, but the candour of the Roman city urges us to relate the good deeds of foreigners too. Damon and Phintias, initiated in the mysteries of Pythagorean wisdom, had joined between themselves so faithful a friendship that, when Dionysius of Syracuse wished to kill one of them, and he had obtained from him time, that before he perished he might go home and set his affairs in order, the other did not hesitate to give himself as surety to the tyrant for his return. He was freed from the peril of death who but lately had had his neck set beneath the sword: to the same had bared his own head one to whom it was permitted to live secure. Therefore all, and chiefly Dionysius, watched for the outcome of the new and doubtful affair. Then, the appointed day drawing near, and the man not returning, each one condemned for folly so rash a sponsor. But he kept declaring that he feared nothing concerning the steadfastness of his friend. At that same moment and hour appointed by Dionysius, the man who had accepted came up. The tyrant, marvelling at the spirit of both, remitted the punishment of fidelity, and besides asked them to receive him into the partnership of their friendship as a third grade of the comradeship, to be cherished with mutual goodwill. Such are the powers of friendship: they could engender contempt of death, extinguish the sweetness of life, soften cruelty, turn hatred into love, and requite punishment with a benefit. To which almost as much veneration is owed as to the rites of the immortal gods: for in those is contained the public safety, in these the private, and as the temples of those are sacred dwellings, so the faithful breasts of these men are, as it were, certain shrines filled with a holy spirit.

7e.2. That it is so, King Alexander felt. Having gained the camp of Darius, in which were all his kinsfolk, with Hephaestion, his most dear, guarding his side, he came to address them. At his arrival the mother of Darius, restored, raised her head, prostrate on the ground, and, paying homage to Hephaestion, because he excelled both in stature and in beauty, after the manner of the Persians saluted him as Alexander. Then, warned of her error, in the utmost trepidation she sought words of excuse. To her Alexander said: 'There is no reason why you should be confounded at this name: for this man too is Alexander.' Whom should we first congratulate? Him who was willing to say this, or him to whom it befell to hear it? For a king of the greatest spirit, who now embraced the whole world either by his victories or by his hope, shared himself with his companion in so few words. O gift of a famous voice, glorious alike to the giver and to the receiver! Which privately too I deservedly venerate, having experienced the most ready goodwill towards me of a most illustrious and most eloquent man. Nor do I fear that it ill suits me that my Pompey should be the equal of Alexander, when to him his Hephaestion was a second Alexander. But I should indeed be liable to a most grave charge, had I passed over the examples of steadfast and kind friendship without any mention of him, in whose spirit, as in the breast of most loving parents, the gladder state of my life flourished, the sadder found rest; from whom I received the increases of all advantages, freely offered; through whom I stood the safer against misfortunes; who rendered our studies, by his leadership and auspices, more bright and more eager. And so I fed the envy of certain men by the loss of the best of friends, evidently because I had tormented—not, indeed, by my own desert—their . . . , having shared my favour, however great it was, with those who wished to use it. But no happiness is so modest that it can escape the teeth of malice. And into what retreat would you flee from certain men, or with what fillets of pity would you soften them, that they should not rejoice and exult at others' evils as at their own goods? They are rich by others' losses, wealthy by calamities, immortal by funerals. But to what extent they may, themselves as yet without experience of their own misfortunes, insult at others' troubles, let the best avenger of insolence, the variety of the human condition, see to it.

Q. Metellus played the part of a city praetor much sterner than Orestes had played. He did not give to the pimp Vecillus, seeking the possession of the goods of Vibienus according to the tablets of the will, because, a most noble and most weighty man, he judged that the condition of the Forum and of the brothel must be kept separate, and was unwilling either to approve the act of the one, who had cast his fortunes into a contaminated stable, or to render to the other, as to a citizen of unimpaired standing, his rights, since he had cut himself off from every honourable kind of life.

8.pr. WILLS THAT REMAINED VALID THOUGH THEY HAD CAUSES WHY THEY COULD BE RESCINDED Content with these examples of rescinded wills, let us touch on those which remained valid, though they had causes on account of which they could be rescinded.

Let not even Roscius be withdrawn, a most notable example of stage industry, who never dared to bring out, before a watching people, any gesture which he had not rehearsed at home. Wherefore it was not the player's art that commended Roscius, but Roscius the player's art; nor did he embrace only the favour of the crowd, but even the intimacies of the leading men. These are the rewards of an attentive and anxious study that never ceases, on account of which the person of an actor inserted itself, not shamelessly, among the praises of such great men.

7e.1. Greek industry too, since it has profited ours much, let it receive from the Latin tongue the fruit it deserves. Demosthenes, at the mention of whose name the consummation of the greatest eloquence rises before the hearer's mind, when in the beginning of his youth he could not pronounce the first letter of the art he aimed at, overcame the defect of his mouth with such zeal that no one rendered that letter more distinctly than he. Then, on account of its excessive thinness, harsh to the ear, he brought his voice by continual exercise to a mature sound pleasing to the ears. Failed also by the firmness of his lungs, the strength which his bodily constitution had denied him he borrowed from toil: for he would embrace many verses in a single breath, and pronounce them as he climbed steep places at a rapid pace, and, standing on shoaling shores, deliver declamations against the roaring of the waves, so that, his ears hardened by endurance, he might use them against the clamour of excited assemblies. He is said too to have been accustomed to speak much and long with pebbles inserted in his mouth, that, free of them, it might be the readier and more loosened. He fought with the nature of things, and indeed went off the victor, overcoming its malice by the most persistent strength of his mind. And so his mother brought forth one Demosthenes, industry another.

7e.2. And, to pass to a more ancient example of industry, Pythagoras, having entered upon the most perfect work of wisdom from his youth, and likewise with a desire of perceiving all that was honourable—for nothing which is to reach its furthest end fails to begin both early and eagerly—made for Egypt, where, accustomed to the letters of that people, scrutinizing the commentaries of the priests of past ages, he came to know the observations of countless centuries. Thence, setting out for the Persians, he handed himself over to be moulded by the most exact prudence of the Magi, from whom he drank in with a docile mind the motions of the heavenly bodies and the courses of the stars, and the force, property, and effect of each one, most kindly demonstrated. Then he sailed to Crete and Lacedaemon, and, having inspected their laws and customs, came down to the Olympic contest; and when, amid the greatest admiration of all Greece, he had given a specimen of his manifold knowledge, being asked by what surname he should be reckoned, he declared himself not a wise man—for the seven outstanding men had already taken that—but a lover of wisdom, that is, in Greek, "philosopher." He proceeded also into that part of Italy which was then called Magna Graecia, in which by his very many and most opulent cities he approved the results of his studies. His burning pyre the town of Metapontum gazed upon with eyes full of veneration, a monument nobler and more famous of Pythagoras than of its own ashes.

7e.3. Plato, moreover, having obtained Athens as his country and Socrates as his teacher—both a place and a man most fruitful in learning—equipped also with a divine abundance of talent, when he was now held the wisest of all mortals, even to such a degree that, if Jupiter himself had come down from heaven, he would not seem likely to use either more elegant or more blessed eloquence, traversed Egypt, while he learned from the priests of that people the manifold numbers of geometry and the method of the celestial observations. And at the very time when Athens was being sought by zealous young men eagerly looking for Plato as their teacher, he himself, the disciple of Egyptian old men, was surveying the inextricable banks of the river Nile and its vast plains, the spreading barbarian land and the winding circuits of the canals. The less do I wonder that he crossed into Italy, to receive from Archytas at Tarentum, and from Timaeus and Arion and Echecrates at Locri, the precepts and institutions of Pythagoras: for so great was the force, so great the abundance of letters to be gathered from every side, that they could be scattered and spread abroad in turn throughout the whole world. Even in his eighty-first year, dying, he is said to have had the mimes of Sophron under his head. Thus not even his last hour was free from the activity of study.

7e.4. But Democritus, when he could have been rated by his riches—which were so great that his father could easily give a feast to the army of Xerxes—in order that with a more unencumbered mind he might be occupied in the studies of letters, keeping only a very small sum, gave his patrimony to his country. Having stayed at Athens for several years, devoting all the moments of his time to perceiving and exercising learning, he lived unknown to that city, as he himself testifies in a certain volume. The mind is amazed in admiration of so great industry, and now passes to another.

7e.5. Carneades, a laborious and long-serving soldier of wisdom—since indeed, ninety years being completed, the same was the end for him both of living and of philosophizing—had so wonderfully devoted himself to the works of learning that, when he had reclined for the sake of taking food, clinging to his thoughts, he would forget to stretch out his hand to the table. But Melissa, whom he kept in place of a wife, with a tempered care of not interrupting his studies and of relieving his fasting, fitted his right hand to its necessary uses. Therefore he enjoyed life only in his mind, but was surrounded by his body as by something alien and superfluous. The same man, about to dispute with Chrysippus, used first to purge himself with hellebore, to bring forth his own talent more attentively and to refute that of the other more keenly. What draughts industry has made to be sought after by those desirous of solid praise!

7e.6. With what zeal, moreover, do we believe Anaxagoras to have burned? Who, when he had sought his country again after a long sojourn abroad and had seen his possessions deserted, said, "I should not be safe, unless these had perished." A voice possessed of the wisdom it sought! For if he had had leisure for the cultivation of his estates rather than of his talent, the master of his property would have remained within his household gods, and no such great Anaxagoras would have returned to them.

7e.7. I should call the industry of Archimedes too fruitful, had not the same both given him life and taken it away: for when Syracuse was taken, Marcellus, although he felt that his victory had been long and much hindered by his contrivances, nevertheless, delighted by the man's outstanding prudence, proclaimed that his life should be spared, placing almost as much glory in Archimedes saved as in Syracuse crushed. But he, while with mind and eyes fixed on the earth he was drawing his figures, to the soldier who had burst into his house for the sake of plunder and, with sword drawn over his head, was asking who he was, on account of his too great desire of investigating what he was seeking, could not declare his own name, but, protecting the dust with his hands, said, "Do not, I beg, disturb that," and, just as though heedless of the conqueror's command, was cut down and confounded with his own blood the outlines of his art. So it came about that on account of the same study he was now granted his life, now robbed of it.

7e.8. It is agreed too that Socrates, advanced in age, began to give his effort to the handling of the lyre, judging it better to learn the use of that art late than never. And how small an addition to his knowledge would that have been to Socrates? But the man's persistent industry wished that even the cheapest element of musical theory should be added to the so great riches of his learning. Therefore, while he always believed himself poor for learning, he made himself most wealthy for teaching.

7e.9. And, to gather, as it were into one heap, examples of long and fortunate industry, Isocrates composed his most noble book, which is entitled Panathenaicus, in his ninety-fourth year, as he himself indicates—a work full of an ardent spirit. From which it appears that, the limbs growing old, the minds of the learned within retain, by the benefit of industry, the flower of youth. Nor did he close the limits of his life with this pen: for he reaped the fruit of admiration for it for five years.

7e.10. The vivacity of Chrysippus turned the bounds of a nearer age, but of no small span nevertheless: for in his eightieth year he left a thirty-ninth volume of his Logical works, begun, of the most exact subtlety. His zeal in handing down the monuments of his talent undertook so much trouble and labour that to come to know thoroughly the things he wrote, a long life is needed.

7e.11. You too, Cleanthes, drinking in wisdom so laboriously and handing it down so persistently, the very deity of industry looked up to with admiration, when it saw you as a young man sustaining your poverty by the trade of drawing water in the night time, while by day you had leisure for taking in the precepts of Chrysippus, and the same man instructing your hearers with attentive care to your ninety-ninth year: for by a double labour you filled the span of a single century, leaving it uncertain whether you were the more praiseworthy as a pupil or as a teacher.

7e.12. Sophocles too had a glorious contest with the nature of things, displaying to it his wonderful works as generously as it bestowed on him liberally the time for those works: for he reached almost his hundredth year, having, at the very passage to death, written his Oedipus at Colonus, by which one play alone he was able to snatch away the glory of all the poets of the same pursuit. And his son Iophon did not wish this to be unknown to posterity, inscribing on his father's tomb what I have related.

7e.13. Simonides the poet, moreover, in his eightieth year boasts that he both taught songs and entered them in a contest. Nor was it unjust that he should long reap pleasure from his talent, since he was to hand it down to be enjoyed in every age.

7e.14. For with how great industry Solon burned, he both embraced in verses, by which he signifies that he grows old learning something every day, and confirmed on the last day of his life; for, when friends were sitting by and discussing some matter among themselves, with his head now pressed down by the fates, he raised it and, being asked why he had done this, replied, "That, when I have learned that, whatever it is, which you are discussing, I may die." Sloth would surely have departed from among men, if they entered life with the spirit with which Solon left it.

7e.15. How industrious, moreover, was Themistocles, who, occupied as he was with the care of the greatest matters, nevertheless grasped in his memory the names of all his fellow citizens; and, driven from his country by the greatest injustice and forced to flee to Xerxes, whom a little before he had conquered, before he came into his sight accustomed himself to the Persian speech, so that he might bring to the royal ears, by a recommendation procured by toil, a sound of voice familiar and accustomed.

7e.16. The praise of both these kinds of industry two kings divided between them, Cyrus by learning the names of all his soldiers, Mithridates the languages of the twenty-two peoples that were under his rule, the one that he might salute his army without a prompter, the other that he might address those over whom he ruled without an interpreter.

8.pr. ON LEISURE Leisure, which seems most contrary to industry and study, ought especially to be appended—not that by which virtue fades, but that by which it is refreshed: for the one must be avoided even by the inert, the other must sometimes be sought even by the energetic, by those lest they pass their life unarmed in idleness, by these that by a timely intermission of labour they may become more vigorous for labouring.

Yet on closer lines, so to speak, the dream of Haterius Rufus, a Roman knight, was brought to a sure outcome. He, when a gladiatorial show was being given at Syracuse, in his sleep saw himself stabbed by the hand of a net-fighter, and the next day told it to those sitting beside him at the spectacle. It then happened that, at the place next to the knight, a net-fighter was brought in together with a swordsman. When he had seen his face, he said to the same men that he thought he was being slaughtered by that net-fighter, and at once wished to leave from there. They, having dispelled his fear by their talk, brought the cause of destruction upon the wretched man: for the net-fighter, having driven the swordsman into that very place and cast him down, while trying to strike him as he lay, ran Haterius through with his sword and killed him.

7e.1. Hannibal too had a dream, as detestable to Roman blood as it was of sure prediction, whose not only waking hours but even sleep itself was hostile to our empire: for he drank in an image agreeing with his purpose and his wishes, and thought that there was sent to him from Jupiter a young man, in mortal shape but loftier than mortal, as a guide for the invasion of Italy. At his bidding he followed at first with his eyes turned to no side, but soon, by the forward inclination of human nature to scrutinize forbidden things, looking back behind him, he noticed a serpent of immense size, sweeping away with violent onset everything whatever lay in its path, and behind it, with a great crash of the sky, bursting clouds and a light wrapped in murky darkness. Then, astonished, he asked what that monster might be and what it portended. "You see," said the guide, "the devastation of Italy: therefore be silent, and leave the rest to the fates in silence."

7e.2. How well had Alexander, king of Macedon, been forewarned by an image seen in his sleep to be a more diligent guardian of his life, if fortune had been willing to furnish him also with the counsel of guarding against the danger: for he knew the deadly right hand of Cassander from a dream before he felt it in the event; for he thought that he was being slain by him, although he had never seen him. Then, after an interval of time, when Cassander came into his sight, and the image of his nocturnal fear was revealed, when he recognized him to be the son of Antipater, adding a Greek verse which makes light of the credit of dreams, he drove from his mind the suspicion of the poison already prepared against his life, by which he is believed to have perished at the hand of Cassander.

7e.3. Far more indulgent were the gods toward the poet Simonides, whose salutary admonition in his sleep they strengthened by the firmness of his resolve: for when he had put his ship in to shore and had committed to burial a body lying unburied, and was warned by it not to sail on the next day, he remained on land. Those who had set out from there were overwhelmed by waves and storms in his sight: he himself rejoiced that he had preferred to entrust his life to a dream rather than to a ship. And, mindful of the benefit, he consecrated [the man] to eternity in a most elegant poem, setting up for him a better and more lasting sepulchre in the minds of men than he had built in the deserted and unknown sands.

7e.4. Effective too was that image of sleep which afflicted the mind of King Croesus first with the greatest fear, then also with grief: for he thought that Atys, the more excellent of his two sons in agility of mind and gifts of body, and destined for the succession to the kingdom, had been snatched from him by the sword. And so whatever pertained to avoiding the bitterness of the announced disaster, his fatherly care did not in any part cease to attend to. The young man had been accustomed to be sent to wage wars; he was kept at home. He had an armoury filled with an abundance of weapons of every kind; this too he ordered to be removed. He used to have companions girded with swords; they were forbidden to come near. Yet necessity gave an entrance for grief: for when a boar of huge size was laying waste, with frequent slaughter of the country folk, the cultivated lands of Mount Olympus, and royal aid was implored against the unwonted evil, the son wrung from his father that he should be sent to crush it, the more easily indeed because it was not the savagery of a tusk but of iron that was held in dread. But while all were intent with eager zeal upon killing the beast, persistent chance, by the violence of the impending peril, turned aside upon him a lance hurled for the sake of attacking the wild creature; and it willed that that right hand above all should be sprinkled with the crime of a wicked slaughter, to which the protection of the son had been entrusted by the father, and which Croesus, defiled by the blood of an unintended homicide, fearing the gods of hospitality, had expiated as a suppliant by sacrifice.

7e.5. Nor is Cyrus a lesser proof of the unconquered necessity of the fates. His maternal grandfather Astyages, when Cyrus's birth pointed toward the empire of all Asia, vainly tried to dispel two heralds of a dream, by giving his daughter Mandane in marriage—because in his sleep he had seen her urine flood all the nations of Asia—not to the most excellent of the Medes, lest the honour of the kingdom be transferred into his family, but to a man of Persia of moderate fortune; and by ordering the newborn Cyrus to be exposed, because in like manner, in his hours of sleep, he had thought that a vine, sprung from the genital part of Mandane, had grown so far as to overshadow all the regions of his dominion: for he frustrated himself, by trying with human counsels to hinder the felicity of his grandson, destined by the judgement of the gods.

7e.6. While Dionysius of Syracuse was still keeping himself within a private station, a certain woman of Himera, of no obscure family, in her sleep, as it seemed to her, ascended to heaven, and there, having surveyed the seats of all the gods, noticed a powerful man, of fair colour, with a freckled face, bound with iron chains, set beneath the throne and feet of Jupiter; and when she asked the young man whom she had used as a guide in viewing heaven who he was, she heard that he was the dire fate of Sicily and Italy, and that, loosed from his bonds, he would be the destruction of many cities. This dream she made public the next day in conversation. When afterwards a fortune hostile to the liberty of Syracuse and dangerous to the lives of the innocent had cast Dionysius, from heavenly custody, like a thunderbolt, upon their ease and tranquillity, as she saw him entering the walls of Himera amid the crowd that had poured out to do him homage and to gaze upon him, she cried out that this was the man she had seen in her sleep. This, made known to the tyrant, gave him cause to remove the woman.

7e.7. Of a safer dream was the mother of the same Dionysius. She, when she carried him conceived in her womb, seemed to give birth to a little Satyr, and, on consulting an interpreter of prodigies, learned, with a sure outcome, that he would be the most illustrious and most powerful of Greek blood.

7e.8. But Hamilcar, the general of the Carthaginians, when he was besieging Syracuse, believed that in his sleep he heard a voice announcing that on the next day he would dine in that city. Joyful therefore, as if victory had been promised him by divine power, he was preparing his army for battle. In which, a quarrel having arisen between the Sicilians and the Carthaginians, his camp was overwhelmed by a sudden onset of the Syracusans, and they dragged him in chains within their own walls. Thus, deceived more by hope than by the dream, he dined at Syracuse a captive, not, as he had presumed in his mind, a victor.

7e.9. Alcibiades too foresaw his wretched end by a not deceptive nocturnal image: for with whatever cloak of his mistress he had seen himself covered while sleeping, with that, slain and lying unburied, he was covered.

7e.10. The next dream, although it is a little longer, yet, on account of its excessive clearness, prevails not to be omitted. Two intimate friends, Arcadians, making a journey together, came to Megara, of whom the one betook himself to a guest-friend, the other turned aside to an inn for hire. He who was in his friend's lodging saw in his sleep his companion begging him to come to his aid, since he had been entrapped by the treachery of the innkeeper: for he could be snatched from the impending peril by his speedy approach. Roused by this vision, he leaped up and tried to make for the inn in which the other was lodging. Then, by a baleful fate, he condemned his most humane purpose as superfluous and went back to bed and sleep. Then the same man, wounded, presented himself to him and begged that, since he had neglected to bring help to his life, he would at least not deny vengeance for his death: for his body, slaughtered by the innkeeper, was at that very moment being carried to the gate in a cart, covered over with dung. Compelled by the so persistent prayers of his friend, he ran at once to the gate, and seized the cart which had been pointed out to him in his sleep, and brought the innkeeper to capital punishment.

8.pr. ON MARVELS. Many things too have happened by day and to those awake, just as if wrapped in the cloud of darkness and sleep. These, because it is hard to discern whence they have flowed or by what reason they have come to be, may deservedly be called marvels. Of these, out of a great heap, this one occurs first.

Of the same order is what follows. Papirius the dictator, when against his command Q. Fabius Rullianus, the master of the horse, had led the army out into the line, although, the Samnites having been routed, he had returned into the camp, yet, moved neither by his valour nor by his success nor by his nobility, ordered the rods to be made ready and him to be stripped. O wondrous spectacle! Both Rullianus, both the master of the horse, both the victor, with his garment torn and his body despoiled, offered himself to be torn by the lashings of the lictors, so that, by the knotty blows, the blood of the wounds received in the battle being renewed, he might bespatter the titles of the victories which he had just most splendidly won. Then by its prayers the army gave Fabius the occasion of fleeing into the city, where in vain he implored the aid of the senate: for none the less did Papirius persevere in exacting the penalty. And so his father was compelled, after his dictatorship and third consulship, to call the matter before the people, and as a suppliant to seek the aid of the tribunes of the plebs on behalf of his son. Nor by this could the severity of Papirius be checked. But, when he was entreated by all the citizens and by the very tribunes of the plebs, he testified that he was remitting that penalty not to Fabius but to the people and to the tribunician power.

The same was the fortune of Marcus Scaurus, equally long and robust old age, the same spirit. When he was accused before the Rostra of having received money from King Mithridates for betraying the commonwealth, he pleaded his cause thus: 'It is unfair, Quirites, that, having lived among some, I should render account of my life before others; but yet I shall dare to ask you, the greater part of whom could not be present at my honours and acts: Varius Severus of Sucro says that Aemilius Scaurus, corrupted by a royal bribe, betrayed the empire of the Roman people; Aemilius Scaurus denies that he is involved in this guilt: which of the two do you believe?' The people, moved by admiration of him, drove Varius from that most senseless prosecution with persistent clamour.

L. Calpurnius Piso too, the consul, when in Sicily he was waging war against the runaways and C. Titius, a prefect of cavalry, surrounded by a multitude of the enemy, had surrendered his arms to them, afflicted the prefect with these kinds of disgrace: he ordered him, clad in a toga with its borders cut off and girt with a loosened tunic, with bare feet, to be present at the headquarters from morning until night for the whole time of his military service. He also forbade him the company of men and the use of the baths; and the squadrons of cavalry which he had commanded, their horses taken away, he transferred into the wings of the slingers. A great disgrace, indeed, of the fatherland was avenged by an equal disgrace of the guilty, since Piso brought it about that those who, led by greed of life, had granted to runaways most worthy of the cross the setting up of trophies over them, and had not blushed that a shameful yoke should be set by a servile hand upon their liberty, should experience a bitter use of the light, and manfully desire the death which they had effeminately feared.

On the other hand, that eloquent Marcus Antonius—for it was not by rejecting but by embracing the pleading of his cause that he attested how innocent he was—as quaestor setting out for Asia, had already reached Brundisium, where, informed by letter that he had been charged with incest before the praetor Lucius Cassius, whose tribunal, on account of its excessive severity, was called the reef of defendants—though he might avoid it by the benefit of the Memmian law, which forbade the names of those who were absent on the commonwealth's business to be received—nevertheless hurried back into the city. By this counsel, so full of good confidence, he obtained both a swift acquittal and a more honourable departure.

No less keenly than Piso did Q. Metellus act. He, when an action was being carried on at Contrebia, ordered five cohorts, which he had placed in a certain post and which had been driven from it by the forces of the enemy, to make for the same post on the instant, not because he hoped that the lost place could be recovered by them, but that he might punish the fault of the past battle by the manifest danger of the following struggle. He decreed also that, if any one of these, fleeing, should make for the camp, he should be slain as an enemy. Compelled by this severity, the soldiers, though their bodies were wearied and their minds entangled in despair of life, yet overcame the unfavourableness of the place and the multitude of the enemy. Necessity, therefore, is the most effective hardener of human weakness.

There are also those glorious examples of public confidence: for when, in that war which was being waged against Pyrrhus, the Carthaginians had of their own accord sent a fleet of a hundred and thirty ships to Ostia in aid of the Romans, it pleased the senate that envoys should go to their commander to say that the Roman people was accustomed to undertake wars which it could wage with its own soldiers: therefore let them lead the fleet back to Carthage. The same people, some years later, when the strength of the Roman empire had been drained by the disaster of Cannae, dared to send a force into Spain as a reinforcement for the army, and so brought it about that the site of the enemy's camp—at the very moment when Hannibal was beating upon the Capene Gate with his arms—should not be sold for less than if the Carthaginians did not hold it. So to bear oneself in adversity—what else is it than to turn raging Fortune, conquered by shame, into an aid to oneself?

In the same province Q. Fabius Maximus, desiring to crush and weaken the spirits of a most fierce nation, having for the time laid aside his most gentle disposition, compelled himself to use severity: for of all those who had deserted from the Roman garrisons to the enemy and had been captured, he cut off the hands, so that, bearing their maimed arms before them, they might strike fear of revolt into the rest. And so their rebellious hands, torn from their bodies and scattered on the bloodied ground, were a warning to the others not to dare to commit the same.

By a great space the transition is divided from the senate to the poet Accius. But, that we may pass from him more becomingly to foreign matters, let him be brought forward into the midst. He never rose to his feet for Julius Caesar, a most eminent and most flourishing man, when he came into the college of poets—not unmindful of his majesty, but because he was confident that in the comparison of common studies he was somewhat the superior. Wherefore he was free from the charge of insolence, because there were practised contests of volumes, not of images.

7e.1. Nor did Euripides at Athens seem arrogant when, the people demanding that he should remove a certain sentiment from a tragedy, he came forward onto the stage and said that he was accustomed to compose plays to teach the people, not to learn from them. Confidence is indeed to be praised, which weighs the estimate of itself with a sure weight, claiming for itself just so much as is enough to stand apart from contempt and from insolence. And so that too which he answered to the tragic poet Alcestis is to be approved. When, with him, he complained that in three days he could not, with the greatest labour expended, bring out more than three verses, and the other boasted that he had very easily written a hundred, Euripides said: 'But there is this difference, that yours will suffice only for three days, mine for all time': for the writings of the one, with his fertile course, fell to ruin within the first bounds of memory, while the work of the other, laboured out with a hesitating pen, will be borne through all the ages with the full sails of glory.

7e.2. I shall add an example from the same stage. Antigenidas, the flute-player, to a pupil of his who had made great progress but with too little success was winning the people's approval, said in the hearing of all: 'Play for me and for the Muses,' since indeed a perfected art, deserted by the allurements of fortune, is not stripped of its just confidence, and the praise which it knows it deserves, if it does not obtain it from others, it nevertheless carries away as received from its own judgement.

7e.3. Zeuxis, moreover, when he had painted Helen, did not think he should wait to hear what men would feel about that work, but at once added these verses: 'No blame that Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans should for so long a time suffer woes for such a woman.' Did the painter arrogate so much to his own right hand that he believed he had grasped in it as much of beauty as either Leda could bring forth by a heavenly birth or Homer could express by his divine genius?

7e.4. Phidias too played upon Homer's verses with an excellent saying: for, when the statue of Olympian Jupiter was finished, than which no work of human craftsmanship is more eminent or more admirable, being asked by a friend whither directing his mind he had embraced in lines of ivory the countenance of Jupiter, all but fetched from heaven itself, he answered that he had used those verses as his master: 'He spoke, and with his dark brows the son of Cronos nodded; and the ambrosial locks of the lord flowed streaming from his immortal head; and he made great Olympus tremble.'

7e.5. The bravest commanders do not allow me to dwell any longer upon slighter examples. For Epaminondas, when his fellow-citizens, in anger, entrusted to him, by way of insult, the care of paving the streets in the town—for that service was among them the basest—accepted it without any hesitation and declared that he would take pains that in a short time it should be made most splendid. Then by his wondrous management he made the most abject business, instead of a most ample ornament, a thing to be sought after at Thebes.

7e.6. Hannibal, indeed, when he was in exile with King Prusias and was the author to him of joining battle, and the king said that the entrails did not portend the same to him, said: 'Do you really prefer to trust a little piece of calf's flesh rather than an old commander?' If you count the words, briefly and tersely; if you weigh the sense, copiously and forcibly: for he poured out before the man's feet the Spains snatched from the Roman people, and the strength of the Gauls and of Liguria reduced into his own power, and the ridges of the Alps laid open by a new passage, and Lake Trasimene branded with dire memory, and Cannae, the most glorious monument of a Punic victory, and Capua possessed, and Italy mangled; and he could not endure with a calm spirit that his own glory, attested by long experience, should be set after the liver of a single victim. And indeed, as far as concerned the exploring of the arts of war and the appraising of military leadership, the breast of Hannibal would have outweighed all the braziers and all the altars of Bithynia, with Mars himself as judge.

7e.7. That saying too of King Cotys was capable of a generous spirit: for when he learned that the citizenship had been given him by the Athenians, he said: 'And I will give them the right of my nation.' He made Thrace equal to Athens, lest, by judging himself unequal to the return of such a benefit, he should be thought to feel too humbly of his own origin.

7e.8. Nobly too spoke each of two Spartans: both he who, rebuked by someone for going down lame into battle, answered that his purpose was to fight, not to flee; and he who, when someone related that the sun was wont to be darkened by the arrows of the Persians, said: 'You bring good news: for we shall fight in the shade.' A man of the same city and spirit said to his guest, who was showing him the high and broad walls of his country: 'If you have made these for women, well; if for men, shamefully.'

8.pr. ON STEADFASTNESS. The open and spirited breast of good confidence being measured out, there remains, as a debt owed, the representation of steadfastness: for it is so ordained by nature that whosoever is confident that he has grasped something in due order and with a right mind, either defends it keenly, if it is already done and is assailed, or, if it is not yet brought forth and is interrupted, carries it through to its accomplishment without any hesitation.

Nothing was gentler than the elder Africanus. He, however, for the sake of strengthening military discipline, thought that something of bitterness must be borrowed from a cruelty most alien to himself: for, Carthage being conquered, when he had reduced into his power all who from our armies had gone over to the Carthaginians, he punished the Roman deserters more gravely than the Latin: for these he affixed to crosses as fugitives from their fatherland, those he struck with the axe as faithless allies. I shall not pursue this deed further, both because it is Scipio's and because it is not fitting to insult with a servile punishment Roman blood, however deservedly it suffered, especially when it is permitted to pass over to those things which can be related as done without a domestic wound.
For the later Africanus, the Punic empire being overthrown, cast deserters of foreign nations to wild beasts in the spectacles given to the people;

and L. Paulus, King Perseus being overcome, laid prostrate men of the same kind and fault to be trampled by elephants, by a most useful example indeed, if nevertheless it is permitted to estimate humbly the deeds of the most excellent men without the reproach of insolence: for military discipline needs a harsh and abrupt kind of chastisement, because strength rests in arms, which, when they depart from the right course, are about to oppress, unless they be oppressed.

But it is time that mention be made also of those things which now not by individuals but by the whole senate were administered for maintaining and defending the military custom. L. Marcius, a military tribune, when by wonderful valour he had gathered the scattered remnants of the two armies of Publius and Gnaeus Scipio, which the Punic arms had consumed in Spain, and by their votes had been created their leader, writing to the senate concerning his deeds, began in this manner: "L. Marcius, propraetor." The conscript fathers were not pleased that he should use the assumption of this honour, because leaders were wont to be created by the people, not by the soldiers. At which time, so unjust, so grievous on account of the immense loss to the state, even a military tribune was to be flattered, since indeed he alone had sufficed to set right the condition of the whole state. But no disaster, no merit was more powerful than military discipline. For it came into their minds with how spirited a severity their ancestors had used in the Tarentine war, in which, with the forces of the state shaken and worn, when they had received a great number of their own captured citizens sent back unbidden by King Pyrrhus, they decreed that of those who had served on horseback should serve in the number of the infantry, and those who had been infantry should be transferred into the auxiliaries of the slingers; and that none of them should pitch his tent within the camp, nor gird with rampart or ditch a place outside the assigned one, nor have a tent of skins. They proposed, moreover, a return for these to the former order of military service, if anyone should have carried off two sets of spoils from the enemy. Crushed by these punishments, out of the disgraceful little gifts of Pyrrhus they came forth most keen enemies. An equal anger the senate unsheathed against those who at Cannae had deserted the state: for when by the gravity of its decree it had banished them beyond the condition of the dead, having received a letter from M. Marcellus, that it might be permitted him to use their service for the storming of Syracuse, it wrote back that they were unworthy to be received into the camp; but that it permitted him to do what he should judge expedient for the state, provided that none of them should be free from duty, or be presented with a military gift, or come into Italy so long as the enemy were in it. Thus is virtue wont to hate nerveless spirits. Come, how grievously the senate took it that they had suffered the consul Q. Petilius, fighting most bravely against the Ligurians, to be slain! It willed that to the legion neither the pay of the year should accrue nor the wage be given, because for the safety of the commander they had not offered themselves to the weapons of the enemy. And that decree of the most ample order stood forth as a splendid and eternal monument of Petilius, beneath which rest his ashes, illustrious by death in the battle-line, by vengeance in the senate-house. With a like spirit, when Hannibal had made him the offer of ransoming six thousand Romans whom he held captured in his camp, the senate spurned the condition, remembering that so great a multitude of armed young men, if they had been willing to die honourably, could not have been basely captured. Of whom I know not whether the disgrace was greater—that their fatherland set no hope, or that their enemy set no fear, in them—the one making light of them as fighting for it, the other as fighting against it. But although the senate kept watch on several occasions severely for military discipline, I know not whether especially then, when it shut up in prison the soldiers who had seized Regium in an unjust war and, their leader Iubellius being dead, had of their own accord chosen as commander M. Caesius, his scribe; and although M. Fulvius Flaccus, tribune of the plebs, gave notice that it should not, contrary to the custom of its ancestors, take vengeance upon Roman citizens, none the less it carried out its resolve. But that this might be accomplished with the less odium, it ordered fifty to be beaten with rods on each single day and struck with the axe, and forbade their bodies to be committed to burial and their death to be mourned.

7e.1. This the conscript fathers did gently, if we are willing to consider the violence of the Carthaginian senate in conducting the business of military service, by which leaders who waged wars with bad counsel, even if prosperous fortune had followed, were yet affixed to the cross, imputing what they had done well to the aid of the immortal gods, what they had done ill to their own fault.

7e.2. But Clearchus, the leader of the Lacedaemonians, used to maintain the discipline of military service by an excellent saying, dinning again and again into the ears of his army that the commander rather than the enemy ought to be feared by the soldiers. By which he openly gave notice that it would come to pass that they should pay with their life the penalty for the battle which they had hesitated to give. And they did not wonder that this was enjoined by their leader, mindful of their mothers' caresses, by which, as they went out to fight, they were admonished that they should either come alive into their sight with their arms, or be brought back dead in their arms. Having received this watchword within their household walls, the Spartan lines fought. But it is enough merely to have looked at foreign instances, since it is permitted to boast of our own much richer and happier examples.

8.pr. Military discipline, keenly maintained, brought forth for the Roman empire the chieftainship of Italy, bestowed the governance of many cities, great kings, and most powerful nations, opened the jaws of the Pontic gulf, handed over the torn-asunder barriers of the Alps and of Mount Taurus, and made the origin from the little hut of Romulus the pinnacle of the whole circle of the world. And since from her bosom all triumphs have flowed, it follows that I should begin to speak of the right of triumphing.

When at Lake Regillus the dictator A. Postumius and Mamilius Octavius, leader of the Tusculans, were clashing with each other with great forces, and neither line for some time gave ground, Castor and Pollux, champions of the Roman side, appearing, utterly routed the enemy's forces. Likewise, in the Macedonian War, P. Vatinius, a man of the prefecture of Reate, making for the city by night, thought that two young men of surpassing beauty, riding on white horses, met him and announced that on the day that had just passed King Perseus had been captured by Paulus. When he had reported this to the senate, as a despiser of its majesty and greatness by an idle tale, he was cast into prison; but afterwards, when by Paulus's letter it appeared that Perseus had been captured on that day, he was both freed from custody and, besides, presented with land and exemption from service. That Castor and Pollux, even at that time, kept watch on behalf of the empire of the Roman people, was made known by the fact that they were seen washing off their own sweat and that of their horses at the lake of Juturna, and the temple of theirs joined to the spring stood open, unbarred by the hand of any man.

ON THE RIGHT OF TRIUMPHING. For trifling battles certain commanders desired triumphs to be decreed to themselves. That this might be met, it was provided by law that no one should triumph unless he had slain five thousand of the enemy in a single battle: for our ancestors judged that the honour of our city would be the more lofty not by the number but by the glory of its triumphs. But lest so excellent a law should be obliterated by the desire for the laurel, it was supported by the aid of another law, which L. Marcius and M. Cato, tribunes of the plebs, brought: for it threatens a penalty to commanders who should have dared to report to the senate in writing a false number either of enemy slain in battle or of citizens lost, and orders them, as soon as they have entered the city, to swear before the city quaestors that they have truly written to the senate concerning both numbers.

But while I pursue examples of the proposed subject, as I look more widely about me, before all the steadfastness of Fulvius Flaccus presents itself. He had taken Capua by arms, which had been persuaded by the deceitful promises of Hannibal, by a wicked defection, to bargain for the sovereignty of Italy. Then, as just an appraiser of the enemy's guilt as he was a glorious victor, he resolved to destroy utterly the Campanian senate, the author of the impious decree. And so, loaded with chains, he divided it between two prisons, Teanum and Cales, intending to execute his plan when he had finished those things whose administration seemed of nearer necessity. But, a rumour having arisen of a milder sentence of the senate, lest the guilty should escape their due punishment, by night, putting his horse to the gallop, he hastened to Teanum, and, having killed those who were kept there, immediately crossed over to Cales to carry out the work of his perseverance; and, the enemy being already bound to the stake, he received a letter from the conscript fathers, in vain bringing safety to the Campanians: for he put it in his left hand, just as it had been handed to him, and, having ordered the lictor to proceed according to law, he then at last opened it, after it was no longer possible to obey it. By this steadfastness he surpassed even the glory of victory, because, if you appraise him, the praise being divided within itself, you would find him greater for having punished Capua than for having captured it.

ON GENEROSITY. Let our work, carried by a dutiful digression to a grief of my own, be recalled to its own order, and let us be free for the commemoration of generosity. Of which there are two especially approved springs, true judgement and honourable goodwill: for when it arises from these, then at last is its reckoning sound. But to a gift itself its very magnitude indeed wins favour, yet opportunity wins it somewhat more effectively: for to the price of the thing the moment of occasion adds an inestimable weight. Which made a small sum of money disbursed by Fabius Maximus, so many ages ago, praiseworthy down to this very time. He had received captives from Hannibal, a bargain of money having been struck. When these were not furnished by the senate, having sent his son into the city, he sold the farm, the only one he possessed, and at once paid out its price to Hannibal—small, if it be reckoned upon the counters, since indeed it came to seven iugera, and these too pledged in Pupinia; but, if it be reckoned by the spirit of one giving freely, greater than all money: for he preferred that he himself should be destitute of patrimony rather than his country of good faith, and indeed with the greater commendation, because it is a surer token of ready zeal to strive beyond one's powers than to use one's powers with ease: for the one furnishes what he can, the other even more than he can.

ON THE SEVERITY OF FATHERS TOWARD THEIR CHILDREN Lucius Brutus, equal in glory to Romulus—because the one founded the city, the other Roman liberty—holding the supreme command, ordered his own sons, who were bringing back the domination of Tarquinius that had been expelled by him, to be seized, and, before the tribunal, beaten with rods and bound to the stake, to be struck with the axe. He put off the father, that he might play the consul, and chose to live bereaved rather than to fail in public vengeance.

Marcus Antonius, in the time of our grandfathers a most illustrious orator, was prosecuted as a defendant for incest. In his trial the accusers most persistently demanded a slave for examination under torture, because they contended that, when they went to commit the debauchery, a lantern had been carried before them by him. Now this slave was even then beardless and was standing in the crowd, and he saw that the matter pertained to his own torments; nor yet did he flee them. Indeed, when they had returned home, he of his own accord exhorted Antonius—more vehemently troubled and anxious on this account—to hand him over to the judges to be tortured, affirming that no word would issue from his mouth by which his master's cause might be harmed; and he kept the good faith of his promise with marvellous endurance: for, torn by very many lashes and placed on the rack, burned too with glowing plates, he overturned all the force of the accusation, the safety of the defendant being guarded. Fortune may deservedly be reproached, in that it shut up so dutiful and so brave a spirit under the name of a slave.

How certain, how even notorious was the madness of Tuditanus! Inasmuch as he scattered coins among the people, and was seen, to the great laughter of men, trailing his toga in the Forum like a tragic garment, and did many things consistent with these. By his will he appointed . . . as heir, which Ti. Longus, his nearest in blood, tried in vain to overthrow by the judgment of the spear-court: for the Hundred Men thought it must be considered rather what was written in the tablets than who had written them.

The pair of true friendship most distinguished were Scipio and Laelius, joined to each other by the bond of love and also by the partnership of all the virtues; and as they followed the path of an active life with an equal step, so too in the relaxations of the mind they rested in common: for it is agreed that they, wandering on the shores of Caieta and Laurentum, used to gather little shells and sea-snails; and P. Crassus often declared that he had heard this from his father-in-law Scaevola, who was the son-in-law of Laelius.

How rashly did the elder Africanus cross from Spain to Syphax with two quinqueremes, about to deposit his own safety and that of his country alike in the faithless heart of a single Numidian! And so by a slight moment the chance of the greatest matter wavered, whether Syphax should become the slayer or the captor of Scipio.

But that we may pursue the favourable divine power of the other gods too toward this city: when our state had been afflicted by pestilence for three years on end, and saw that an end to so great and so long-lasting an evil could be imposed neither by divine mercy nor by human aid, by the care of the priests, on consulting the Sibylline books, it perceived that the former health could not be recovered otherwise than if Aesculapius were summoned from Epidaurus. And so, having sent envoys thither, it believed that, by its own authority, which was already in the world most ample, it would obtain the sole help of the fated remedy. Nor did its opinion deceive it: for with equal zeal the protection was sought and promised, and straightway the Romans' envoys were led into the temple of Aesculapius, which is five miles distant from their city, of Epidaurus, and most kindly invited to take, as of their own right, whatever they thought they would carry as health-giving to their country. The divine power of the god himself followed their so prompt indulgence and confirmed the words of mortals with heavenly compliance: for that serpent, which the Epidaurians had venerated, rarely seen but never without great benefit to themselves, in the likeness of Aesculapius, began to glide through the most frequented parts of the city with gentle eyes and a soft motion, and, beheld for three days amid the religious wonder of all, plainly bearing on its face the eagerness of one seeking a more illustrious seat, made its way to the Roman trireme; and, while the sailors were frightened by the unaccustomed sight, it climbed aboard to where the tent of the envoy Q. Ogulnius was, and coiled itself in a manifold circle into deepest quiet. Then the envoys, as if having attained the object of their wishes, when their thanksgiving was completed and the worship of the serpent had been received from those skilled in it, joyfully set sail thence; and, having accomplished a prosperous voyage, after they had put in at Antium, the serpent, which had remained everywhere on the vessel, gliding out, wound itself around a palm of lofty height overhanging in the forecourt of the temple of Aesculapius a myrtle spread with thick branches; and for three days, with the food on which it was wont to feed set out, not without great fear on the part of the envoys lest it should be unwilling to return thence to the trireme, having made use of the hospitality of the temple at Antium, it gave itself back to be conveyed to our city; and when the envoys had gone out onto the bank of the Tiber, it swam across to the island where the temple is dedicated, and by its arrival dispelled the pestilence, as a remedy for which it had been sought.

After these laws a timely mention of that judgement is to be introduced, in which, concerning the right of triumphing, between most illustrious persons the matter was both pleaded and thoroughly sifted. The consul C. Lutatius and the praetor Q. Valerius had destroyed off Sicily a notable fleet of the Carthaginians. On which account the senate decreed a triumph to the consul Lutatius. But when Valerius desired that it should be decreed to him also, Lutatius denied that this ought to be done, lest in the honour of the triumph the lesser power should be made equal to the greater; and the dispute having gone forward rather obstinately, Valerius challenged Lutatius by a wager, that the Punic fleet had not been crushed under his leadership, and Lutatius did not hesitate to make the counter-stake. And so Atilius Calatinus was agreed upon as judge between them, before whom Valerius pleaded in this manner: that the consul in that battle had lain lame in a litter, but that he himself had discharged all the duties of a commander. Then Calatinus, before Lutatius began his cause, said: "I ask you, Valerius, if you had differed in contrary opinions as to whether or not battle should be given, whether what the consul or what the praetor had commanded would have had the greater weight." Valerius answered that he made no controversy but that the consul's part would have been the prior. "Come then," said Calatinus, "if you had received differing auspices, by whose auspice would the matter rather have stood?" "Likewise," answered Valerius, "the consul's." "Now, by Hercules," said he, "since I have undertaken the dispute between you concerning command and auspice, and you confess that in both your adversary was the superior, there is nothing for me to doubt further. And so, Lutatius, although you have hitherto been silent, I give the suit in your favour." Wonderful judge, in that he did not suffer time to be wasted in a manifest business; more praiseworthy Lutatius, in that he steadfastly defended the right of the most ample honour; but not even Valerius dishonourably, because he sought, for a brave and prosperous battle, a reward, though not lawful, yet . . .

And that steadfastness indeed was of severity; but admirable was that of piety which Quintus Fabius Maximus rendered untiring to his country. He had paid out money to Hannibal for the captives; being defrauded of it by the state, he kept silence: the senate had made Minucius, the master of the horse, equal to him, the dictator, in the authority of command; he held his peace: provoked besides by many injuries, he remained in the same disposition of spirit, nor ever allowed himself to be angry with the commonwealth for his own sake. So persevering was he in his love of the citizens. And what? In the waging of war was not his steadfastness equal? The Roman empire, almost destroyed by the battle of Cannae, seemed scarcely able to suffice for the raising of armies. And so, judging it better to baffle and elude the onsets of the Carthaginians than to join hands with them in full battle-line, though provoked by very many threats of Hannibal, and often even with the show of a successful action offered him, he never receded from the wholesomeness of his counsel, not even for the hazard of a small engagement; and—what is most difficult—he everywhere appeared superior to anger and to hope. Therefore, as Scipio by fighting, so this man by not fighting, seemed most of all to have succoured our city: for the one by his swiftness crushed Carthage, the other by his delay brought it about that Rome could not be crushed.

And so a woman of the same time, Busa by name, the richest of the Apulian region, may indeed deservedly receive testimony of generosity, but would not compare her surpassing wealth with the straits of the Fabian estate: for although she most kindly sustained with food, within the walls of Canusium, about ten thousand of our citizens, the remnants of the battle of Cannae, yet, the condition of her fortunes being safe, she showed herself munificent to the Roman people; Fabius, in honour of his country, changed poverty into destitution.

Emulating his example, Cassius condemned at home his son Spurius Cassius—who, as tribune of the plebs, had first carried an agrarian law and, by many other measures conducted in a popular manner, held the minds of men bound to himself by love of him—after he had laid down that office, having summoned the council of his kinsmen and friends, on the charge of aiming at kingship, and, after he had been scourged, ordered him to be put to death, and consecrated his property to Ceres.

But the consul Gaius Marius, who had been allotted the wretched end of the siege of Praeneste, when he had vainly tried to escape through the hiding-places of a tunnel and had been grazed by a light wound from Telesinus, with whom he had resolved to die together, his own slave, that he might make him exempt from Sullan cruelty, ran through with a sword and killed, though he saw that great rewards were set before him if he should hand him over to the victors. The so timely service of his right hand yields in nothing to the dutifulness of those by whom the safety of their masters was protected, because at that time for Marius not life but death lay in the benefit.

The life of Tuditanus was mad; but the tablets of the will of Aebutia, who had been the wife of L. Menenius Agrippa, were full of frenzy: for, though she had two daughters of equally similar uprightness, Pletonia and Afronia, carried away rather by the inclination of her own mind than moved by any injuries or services of the other, she appointed Pletonia alone as heir; to the sons of Afronia too she left, out of a very ample patrimony, twenty pieces of money. Afronia nevertheless was unwilling to contend at law with her sister, and judged it better to honour her mother's will by submission than to overturn it by a lawsuit, showing herself the more undeserving of the injury the more even-temperedly she bore it.

Scaevola, moreover, the surest witness of their rest and relaxation, is reported to have played ball excellently, because, of course, he used to transfer to this diversion his mind wearied by forensic services. He is said too to have had leisure sometimes for the board and the dice, when he had well and long ordered the laws of the citizens and the ceremonies of the gods: for as in serious matters he acted Scaevola, so in his games he acted the man whom the nature of things does not allow to be capable of continuous labour.

8e.1. And this Socrates saw, to whom no part of wisdom was obscure; and therefore he did not blush when, with a reed put between his legs, playing with his little children, he was laughed at by Alcibiades.

8e.2. Homer too, the prophet of a heavenly genius, felt nothing different when he fitted melodious strings to the most vehement hands of Achilles, so that their martial strength might be relaxed by the gentle pursuit of peace.

9.pr. HOW GREAT IS THE POWER OF ELOQUENCE The power of eloquence, although we observe it to avail very greatly, it is yet fitting to review under its proper examples, so that, of course, its strength may become better attested.

For the doubtful attempt of C. Caesar, although it was protected by the care of the heavenly powers, can yet scarcely be related without a shudder of the mind: since indeed, impatient of the too slow crossing of his legions from Brundisium to Apollonia, having gone out from a banquet under the pretence of ill health, his majesty concealed in a slave's garment, he boarded a little boat and made from the river Aoüs for the jaws of the Adriatic sea in a savage storm, and at once, the ship being ordered to be steered into the deep, much and long tossed by contrary waves, at last yielded to necessity.

No less voluntary was the passage of Juno into our city. When Veii had been captured by Furius Camillus, the soldiers, by order of their general, about to transfer into the city the image of Juno Moneta, which there was worshipped with especial religion, were trying to move it from its place. When the goddess was asked in jest by one of them whether she wished to migrate to Rome, she answered that she did. On hearing this voice, the jest turned to wonder, and now believing that they were carrying not the image but Juno herself, sought from heaven, they joyfully set her up on that part of the Aventine mount where now we behold her temple.

What would you do with Cn. Fulvius Flaccus, who spurned and rejected the honour of a triumph, so to be sought by others, decreed to him by the senate for affairs well conducted—doubtless not plucking beforehand more than befell him?—for as he entered the city, straightway afflicted by a public inquiry he was punished with exile—so that, if by his insolence he had committed any offence against religion, he might expiate it by punishment.

That Gaius Piso too bore himself wonderfully and steadfastly as consul in a turbulent state of the commonwealth will appear from the following narrative. The favour of the people, snatched away by the pestilent flatteries of Marcus Palicanus, a most seditious man, was attempting at the consular elections to commit the greatest disgrace, desiring to confer the most ample command upon a man to whose foulest deeds an exquisite punishment rather than any honour was owed. Nor was there lacking to the distracted multitude a furious tribunician torch, to accompany his rashness as it rushed on and to inflame it with its own actions when it flagged. In this state of the city, at once pitiable and to be blushed at, Piso, placed before the Rostra all but by the hands of the tribunes, when they had canvassed him on this side and on that, and he was asked whether he would declare Palicanus elected consul by the votes of the people, at first answered that he did not think the commonwealth was overspread with such darkness that it should come to this pitch of unworthiness. Then, when they persistently pressed him and said, 'Come, what if it does come to that?' he said: 'I will not declare him.' By this so decisive answer he snatched the consulship from Palicanus before he could obtain it. Many and terrible things Piso despised, while he would not have the glorious rigour of his mind bent.

In Quintus Considius too generosity of the most wholesome example, and not without no small fruit to himself, has been noted. He, when the commonwealth had been so thrown into confusion by the frenzy of Catiline that not even by the wealthy could the moneys owed be paid to creditors, on account of the tumult, the prices of possessions being diminished, when he had a sum of fifteen million sesterces out at interest, suffered none of his debtors to be dunned by his agents either for the principal or for the interest, and, as far as lay in himself, mitigated the bitterness of the public confusion by his private tranquillity, attesting opportunely and wonderfully that he was a lender of his own money, not of the citizens' blood: for those who now especially delight in money-dealing, when they have brought home bloody money, will learn with what wicked joy they exult, if they do not disdain to read diligently the senatorial decree by which thanks were given to Considius.

But Titus Manlius Torquatus, on account of his many outstanding qualities of rare dignity most skilled also in the civil law and in the pontifical rites, in a like deed did not believe that he had need even of the counsel of his kinsmen: for, when Macedonia had laid complaints before the senate through envoys about his son Decimus Silanus, who had held that province, he asked of the senators that they should determine nothing about the matter before he himself had examined the cause of the Macedonians and of his son. Then, with the highest consent both of that most ample order and even of those who had come to complain, having undertaken the inquiry, he sat at home and alone gave his leisure to each side for two whole days, and on the third day, after the witnesses had been heard most fully and most diligently, he thus pronounced: "Since it has been proved to me that my son Silanus accepted moneys from the allies, I judge him unworthy both of the commonwealth and of my house, and I order him at once to depart from my sight." Stricken by so grim a sentence of his father, Silanus could not endure to look upon the light any longer and made away with himself by hanging the next night. Torquatus had now performed the parts of a severe and scrupulous judge; satisfaction had been made to the commonwealth; Macedonia had its revenge; the father's rigour could have been bent by so modest a death of his son: but he neither attended the obsequies of the young man and, when his funeral was being conducted at its very height, lent attentive ears to those wishing to consult him: for he saw that he was sitting in that hall in which the image of that imperious Torquatus, conspicuous for his severity, had been placed, and it occurred to a most prudent man that the likenesses of ancestors with their inscriptions are wont to be set in the front part of houses for this reason, that posterity should not only read of their virtues but also imitate them.

Equally illustrious is what follows. Gaius Gracchus, that he might not come into the power of his enemies, offered his neck to his slave Philocrates to be cut. When he had cut it off with a swift stroke, he drove the sword, dripping with his master's blood, through his own vitals. Some think this man was called Euporus: I dispute nothing about the name; I only admire the strength of servile faithfulness. If the noble young man had imitated his presence of mind, he would have avoided the impending punishments by his own benefit, not his slave's: as it is, he brought it about that the corpse of Philocrates lay more splendidly than that of Gracchus.

Less to be wondered at was the womanish error which Q. Metellus committed: for though very many and most famous men of the same name were flourishing in our city, and the family of the Claudii too, with which he was connected by the closest bond of blood, was in its prime, he left Carrinas as his sole heir; nor on this account did anyone attack his will.

Come now, how execrable was that rashness of soldiers! For it brought it about that A. Albinus, an outstanding citizen in nobility, character, and the completion of all honours, was overwhelmed with stones in the camp by the army on account of false and empty suspicions; and—what admits of no addition of indignation—when the leader begged and beseeched, the power of pleading his cause was denied him by the soldiers.

8e.1. And so I wonder the less that with the savage and cruel mind of Hannibal there was no place for the defence of an innocent helmsman, whom, as he sought Africa again from Petilia with his fleet and was driven by the current into the strait, while he did not believe Italy and Sicily to be divided from each other by so small a space, he killed as though a treacherous director of his course, and afterwards, the truth being more carefully examined, then acquitted, when nothing further than the honour of a tomb could be given to his innocence. Therefore a statue on a high mound, watching over the narrow and surging sea, was set up as a token both of the memory of Pelorus and of Punic rashness to the eyes of those sailing this way and that.

8e.2. Now the city of the Athenians was rash even to the point of madness, which condemned to death by a capital judgment ten of its commanders all together—and indeed coming from a most beautiful victory—because they had not been able to commit to burial the bodies of the soldiers, the savagery of the sea preventing them, punishing necessity when it ought to have honoured virtue.

9.pr. ON ERROR Nearest to rashness is error, as equal to it in causing harm, so one that anyone would more easily pardon, because not of its own accord, but excited by empty appearances, it involves itself in fault. How widely it wanders in the breasts of men, if I should try to embrace, I should be liable to the very vice of which I speak. We shall therefore report a few of its slips.

The image of Womanly Fortune too, which is on the Latin way at the fourth milestone, consecrated at that time with its temple when the prayers of his mother turned Coriolanus back from the destruction of his native city, it is established spoke, not once but twice, formerly with these words: "Duly, matrons, have you given me, and duly have you dedicated me."

Wiser, therefore, were Q. Fulvius, who, Capua being captured, and L. Opimius, who, the Fregellans being compelled to surrender, sought from the senate the power of triumphing, each magnificent for the works he had performed, but neither master of the thing sought—not indeed through any envy of the conscript fathers, to which they never wished an entrance into the senate-house, but through the utmost diligence in observing the law, by which it was provided that a triumph should be decreed for empire enlarged, not for the recovery of what had belonged to the Roman people: for there is as much difference whether you add something or restore what has been taken away, as there is distance between the beginning of a benefit and the end of an injury.

But Metellus Numidicus, on account of a like kind of perseverance, also met with a storm unworthy of his majesty and character: for when he perceived whither the deadly attempts of Saturninus, tribune of the plebs, were tending, and into how great an evil for the commonwealth they would burst forth, if they were not met, he chose to go into exile rather than into his law. Can anyone be called more steadfast than this man, who, that he might not be driven from his opinion, endured to be deprived of his country, in which he held the highest grade of dignity?

The Roman people now seems to me to have long been complaining that, while I pursue the munificence of individuals, I keep silent about its own: for it pertains to its highest praise that there be recognized what spirit it showed towards kings and cities and nations, because every glory of a distinguished deed grows green again in itself by frequent memory. Asia, taken in war, it handed over to King Attalus to be possessed by way of a gift, believing that the empire would be the more lofty and the more glorious for our city if it had preferred to lay up the richest and most pleasant part of the world among its benefits rather than its profits. The victory itself was a more fortunate gift, because to have seized much could have had envy, to have bestowed so much could not lack glory.

But Marcus Scaurus, the light and ornament of his fatherland, when at the river Athesis the Roman knights, routed by the onset of the Cimbri, having deserted the consul Catulus, were fearfully making for the city, sent to his own son, a partaker in their consternation, one who should tell him that he would more gladly meet the bones of him slain in the battle line than see him guilty of so disgraceful a flight: and so, if any remnant of shame at least survived in his breast, he would avoid the sight of his degenerate father: for by the recollection of his own youth he was reminded what kind of son ought either to be kept by Marcus Scaurus or spurned. On receiving this message the young man was compelled to use his sword more bravely against himself than he had used it against the enemy.

Another nobility, another madness, but a like example of faithfulness.
