Pindarus, lately freed by him, by his own order dispatched Gaius Cassius, defeated in the battle of Philippi, and snatched him from the insulting of the enemy, and took himself out of the sight of men by a voluntary death, so that not even the body of him thus made away with was found. Which of the gods, the avenger of the most grievous crime, bound with so great a torpor that right hand which had blazed forth to the slaying of the parent of his fatherland, that, trembling, it submitted itself to the knees of Pindarus, lest it should pay, by the arbitration of a dutiful victory, the penalties which it deserved for public parricide? You, indeed, then, deified Julius, exacted from your heavenly wounds the due vengeance, by compelling the head treacherous toward you to become the suppliant of sordid help, driven by such a tempest of mind that it neither wished to keep its life nor dared to end it by its own hand.

Likewise Pompeius Reginus, a man of the transalpine region, when he had been passed over in his brother's will, and, to convict it of injustice, had recited in the assembly-place, before a very great gathering of both orders, two tablets of his own wills inscribed in marble, in which the brother had for the most part been written as heir, and there was bequeathed to him by way of legacy fifteen million sesterces, after complaining much and long among friends who agreed with his indignation, as far as concerned the judgment of the spear-court, allowed his brother's ashes to rest in peace. And there had been appointed by him as heirs men neither equal to Reginus in blood nor near to him, but strangers and lowly, so that not only the disgraceful silence but even the insulting preference might seem visible.

But under the consul Valerius Publicola, who, after the kings had been driven out, waged war with the Veientines and Etruscans—while the latter desired to restore to Tarquinius his former power, and the Romans to retain the liberty newly won—when the Etruscans and Tarquinius had got the upper hand in the battle on the right wing, so great a terror suddenly came upon them that not only did the victors themselves flee, but they even dragged with them the Veientines, partners of their panic. As a proof of this matter a marvel is added: a sudden mighty voice from the neighbouring wood of Arsia, which is reported to have been sent forth by the mouth of Silvanus almost in this manner: "By one more shall the Tuscans fall; the Roman army shall depart victorious." The corpses, counted by number, showed the wonderful truth of the saying.

Indeed the right of which I speak was so guarded that to P. Scipio for Spain recovered, to M. Marcellus for Syracuse captured, a triumph was not decreed, because for managing those affairs they had been sent without any magistracy. Let those now be approved, greedy of any glory whatever, who from deserted mountains and from the piratical beaks of pirate cutters, poor in praise, with hurrying hand plucked the little twigs of the laurel: Spain, torn from the empire of Carthage, and the head of Sicily cut off, Syracuse, could not be joined to triumphal chariots. And by what men? By Scipio and Marcellus, whose very names are the equivalent of an eternal triumph. But, although the senate desired to behold crowned those most illustrious authors of solid and true valour, bearing on their shoulders the safety of their fatherland, yet it thought they should be reserved for a juster laurel.

But, while I should set no one before him, yet I should rightly compare with him Quintus Scaevola the augur. The factions of his enemies being scattered and laid low, Sulla, having seized the city, had assembled the senate under arms and was carried with the utmost eagerness to have Gaius Marius declared a public enemy as quickly as possible. When no one dared to go against his will, Scaevola alone, being asked his opinion on this matter, refused to give it. Nay more, to Sulla, who was pressing him more savagely, he said: 'Though you display the columns of soldiers with which you have surrounded the senate-house, though you threaten death again and again, yet you will never bring it about that, for the sake of my scanty and aged blood, I should judge Marius, by whom the city and Italy were saved, a public enemy.'

But the heavenly spirit of that Roman generosity no writings will pursue with sufficiently worthy praises: for, Philip, king of Macedonia, having been overcome, when all Greece had assembled at the Isthmian spectacle, Titus Quintius Flamininus, silence having been made at the signal of the trumpet, ordered these words to be recited by a herald: 'The Senate and People of Rome, and Titus Quintius Flamininus the commander, order that all the cities of Greece which were under the sway of King Philip be free and exempt from tribute.' When these things were heard, men, struck with the greatest and most unexpected joy, at first kept silent, believing as it were that they had not heard what they had heard. Then, at the repeated proclamation of the herald, they filled the heavens with so great an eagerness of shouting that it is certainly agreed that the birds which were flying overhead, astonished and terrified, fell down. It would have been the deed of a great spirit to have stripped servitude from the persons of as many captives as the Roman people then bestowed liberty upon noblest and most opulent cities. And it pertains to its majesty that there be commemorated not only what it kindly bestowed, but also what it felt when another bestowed: for as there is the commendation of deserved praise, so here of praise repaid.

8e.1. Hiero, king of Syracuse, hearing of the disaster by which the Romans had been afflicted at Lake Trasimene, sent as a gift to our city three hundred thousand pecks of wheat and two hundred thousand of barley and two hundred and forty pounds of gold. And, not ignorant of the modesty of our ancestors, lest they should be unwilling to accept the gold, he fashioned it into the shape of Victory, that, moved by religion, he might compel them to use his munificence—liberal first in the willingness of sending, again in the foresight of providing against its being sent back.

8e.2. I shall append to this man Gillias of Acragas, who, it is agreed, possessed almost the very heart of generosity itself. He was eminent in wealth, but much richer in spirit even than in riches, and always occupied in disbursing rather than in gathering money, so much so that his house was believed to be, as it were, a certain workshop of munificence: for from there were built monuments fitted for public uses, from there spectacles pleasing to the eyes of the people were exhibited, from there magnificent provisions of banquets and aids for the failing grain-supply arose. And when these things were disbursed to all in common, privately there were disbursed sustenance to those labouring under want, dowries to maidens pressed by poverty, aids to those shattered by the onset of losses. Guests too, whether in his city dwelling or in his rustic roofs, were most kindly received and, adorned with various gifts, sent away. At one time indeed he fed and clothed five hundred horsemen of the Geloans, driven by the force of a storm into his possessions. Why say more? You would call it not some mortal, but the kindly bosom of propitious Fortune. Therefore what Gillias possessed was, as it were, the common patrimony of all. For whose safety and increase both the Acragantine state and the neighbouring regions watched in their prayers. Set on the contrary side chests barred with inexorable locks: would you not think that expenditure somewhat more eminent than this hoarding?

1.pr. ON HUMANITY AND CLEMENCY What more fitting companions could I have given to generosity than humanity and clemency, since they seek the same kind of praise? Of these the first is bestowed in answer to poverty, the second in answer to pressing distress, the third in answer to the doubtful turns of fortune; and although you may not know which to approve most highly, yet the recommendation of that one seems to take precedence whose name has been derived from divinity itself.

1.1a. But before all else I shall set forth the most humane and clement acts of the senate. When envoys of the Carthaginians had come to the city to ransom captives, the senate at once, without accepting any money, gave back to them their young men, who made up a number of two thousand seven hundred and forty-three . . . so great an army of the enemy released, so great a sum of money scorned, pardon granted for so many Punic wrongs. I imagine that the envoys themselves were dumbfounded and said to one another: "O the munificence of the Roman race, to be matched with the kindness of the gods! O our embassy, fortunate beyond our prayers! For the favour we should never have granted, we have received."

1.1b. This too is no small mark of the senate's humanity: it decreed that Syphax, once the wealthiest king of Numidia, who had died a captive in custody at Tibur, should be carried out with a public funeral, so that it might add to the gift of his life the honour of burial.

1.1c. And it used a like clemency in the case of Perseus: for when he had died at Alba, to which he had been relegated for the sake of custody, it sent a quaestor to carry him out with a public funeral, so as not to allow the remains of a king to lie unhonoured.

1.1d. These offices were rendered to enemies, to the wretched, and to those whose fate was accomplished; the following were bestowed upon friends, the fortunate, and the living. When the Macedonian war was finished, Misagenes, the son of Masinissa, having been sent back by the commander Paulus to his father along with the cavalry whom he had brought up in support of the Romans, was carried, sick, to Brundisium when his fleet was scattered by a storm. As soon as the senate learned of this, it at once ordered a quaestor to go there, by whose care both lodging should be arranged for the young man and everything that his health required should be supplied, and expenses liberally furnished both to himself and to his whole retinue, and ships also looked to, in which he might cross over to Africa well and safely with his men. It ordered that each of the cavalry be given a pound of silver apiece and five hundred sesterces. So prompt and so refined a humanity of the senators could bring it about that, even if the young man had expired, his father would have borne his loss with a more even mind.

1.1e. The same senate, when it heard that Prusias, king of Bithynia, was coming to congratulate it on the defeat of Perseus, sent Publius Cornelius Scipio, a quaestor, to meet him at Capua, and decreed that the best possible house should be rented for him at Rome, and that provisions should be furnished at public expense not only to himself but also to his companions; and in receiving him the whole city wore the face of a single loving friend. And so he who had come most devoted to us returned to his own kingdom with his goodwill toward us doubled.

1.1f. Not even Egypt was without a share of Roman humanity. Its king Ptolemy, stripped of his kingdom by his younger brother, had come to Rome with very few slaves, covered in filth, in order to seek aid, and had taken himself to the lodging of an Alexandrian painter. After this was reported to the senate, it summoned the young man and offered as careful an apology as it could because it had neither sent a quaestor to meet him after the custom of the ancestors nor received him with public hospitality, and it said that this had happened not through its own negligence but through his own sudden and secret arrival; and it led him straight from the senate-house to the public residence and urged him, having laid aside his squalor, to ask for a day on which to approach the senate itself. It even took care that gifts should be given to him daily through the quaestor. By these steps of attentions it raised him, prostrate as he was, to the height of royalty, and brought it about that he placed more hope in the aid of the Roman people than fear in his own fortune.

Nor with less spirit did Aulus Fulvius, a man of senatorial order, draw back his son as he was going into the battle line than Scaurus rebuked his as he was fleeing from the battle: for, when the youth, distinguished among his peers both in talent and in letters and in beauty, by perverse counsel had followed the friendship of Catiline and was rushing with rash impulse into his camp, he had him taken in mid-journey and afflicted him with the punishment of death, declaring beforehand that he had not begotten him for Catiline against his fatherland, but for his fatherland against Catiline. It was permitted, until the madness of the civil war should pass by, to keep him shut up and restrained: but that would be told as the work of a cautious father; this is recorded as the work of a severe one.
9.pr. But that the milder characters of fathers, now to be related, may temper this vehement and harsh severity by an admixture of their clemency, let pardon granted be joined to punishment exacted.

To these disasters Gaius Plotius Plancus joined himself, the brother of Munatius Plancus the consular and censorian. He, when, proscribed by the triumvirs, he was lurking in the region of Salernum, by a too delicate manner of life and by the scent of perfume betrayed the hidden guardianship of his safety: for by these traces a keen care, brought to bear by those who were pursuing the wretched, scented out the hidden lair of his flight. The slaves of the man in hiding, having been seized and much and long tortured by them, denied that they knew where their master was. Then Plancus could not endure that slaves so faithful and of so good an example should be tortured any longer, but came forward into the midst and offered his throat to the swords of the soldiers. Which contest of mutual goodwill makes it hard to discern whether the master was the worthier, in experiencing so steadfast a faithfulness of his slaves, or the slaves, in being freed by so just a pity of their master from the savagery of the examination.

WILLS WHICH HAD HEIRS CONTRARY TO MEN'S EXPECTATIONS Of equally fortunate impunity, but, I do not know whether, of a fouler offence, are these wills. Q. Caecilius, who by the most ready zeal and greatest generosity of L. Lucullus had attained both an honourable step of dignity and a most ample patrimony, when he had always carried it openly before him that that one man alone was his heir, and dying had even handed him his rings, adopted Pomponius Atticus by his will and left him heir of all his goods. But the corpse of the deceitful and treacherous man the Roman people, a rope thrown around its neck, dragged through the streets. And so the wicked fellow had indeed the son and heir he wished, but the funeral and obsequies he deserved.

What? Is not the aid of Mars, by which he helped the victory of the Romans, to be celebrated in memory? When the Bruttii and Lucani, roused by most furious hatred and with the greatest forces, were seeking the destruction of the city of Thurii, and the consul C. Fabricius Luscinus with especial zeal was protecting its safety, and the matter, with doubtful outcome, was being carried on with the forces of both sides brought together into one place, when the Romans did not dare to enter battle, a young man of remarkable size first began to exhort them to take up courage. Then, when he noticed that they were rather slow, having snatched up ladders, he passed through the midst of the enemy's line to the opposing camp, and, applying them, mounted the rampart. Thence, crying out with a mighty voice that the step toward victory had been made, he drew both our men to the capturing of the enemy's camp and the Lucanians and Bruttii to the defence of their own, where, crowded together, they were being worn down in a doubtful struggle. But the same man, by the impulse of his own arms, handed over the prostrate enemy to the Romans to be slaughtered and captured: for twenty thousand were slain, five thousand together with Statius Statilius, the leader of both nations, and three-and-twenty military standards were taken. On the next day, when the consul, among those to be honoured, whose strenuous service he had used, said that he was reserving a rampart-crown for the man by whom the camp had been stormed, and no one could be found who claimed that reward, it was alike recognized and believed that Mars the father had then been present to his own people. Among the other manifest signs of this matter, a helmet distinguished by two plumes, with which the heavenly head had been covered, furnished proof. And so by the edict of Fabricius a thanksgiving was held to Mars, and by the laureled soldiers, with great gladness of heart, testimony was rendered to him of the aid offered.

To this I shall append the following: it is the custom that the consuls be invited to dinner by the commander who is about to lead a triumph, and then be asked to forbear to come, lest anyone on that day on which he triumphs should be, in the same banquet, of greater authority.

What has a woman to do with a public assembly? If the custom of our fathers be kept, nothing: but where domestic quiet is tossed by the waves of seditions, the authority of ancient usage is shaken, and that which violence compels avails more than what modesty advises and enjoins. And so you, Sempronia, sister of Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, wife of Scipio Aemilianus, I shall pursue with honoured memory—not that I should comprehend you in a malicious narrative as one absurdly thrusting yourself in among the gravest works of men, but because, brought before the people by a tribune of the plebs in the greatest confusion, you in nothing degenerated from the greatness of your kindred. You were compelled to take your stand in that place where the brows of the chief men of the state were wont to be troubled; a most ample power, pouring forth threats with grim countenance, pressed upon you; the whole forum, ringing with the clamour of an unskilled multitude, strove with the keenest zeal that you should give a kiss to Equitius—for whom a false right to the Sempronian family was being sought—as to a son of your brother Tiberius. You, nevertheless, repulsed that monster, dragged forth I know not from what darkness, who with execrable boldness was stretching out to usurp another's kinship.

What of the slave of Urbinus Panapio, of how admirable faithfulness! When he had learned that soldiers, made aware by the information of the household, had come to the villa at Reate to kill his proscribed master, having exchanged clothing with him, and exchanged his ring too, he secretly sent him out by the back door, but withdrew himself into the bedchamber and the bed and suffered himself to be killed as if he were Panapio. The narration of this deed is brief, but no small matter for praise: for if anyone wishes to set before his eyes the sudden onrush of the soldiers, the wrenched bars of the door, the menacing voice, the fierce faces, the gleaming arms, he will follow the matter with a true estimation, and will not think that, as quickly as it is told that someone wished to die for another, so easily too the thing could be done. Panapio confessed how much he owed to his slave, by making him an ample monument and by rendering the testimony of his devotion in a grateful inscription.

Nor was T. Marius of Urbinum worthy of others, who, raised from the lowest rank of military service by the benefits of the deified emperor Augustus to the highest honours of the camp, and made wealthy by their most abundant profits, not only at all other times of his life proclaimed that he would leave his fortunes to him from whom he had received them, but even on the day before he died said this very thing to Augustus himself, while meanwhile he did not even add his name to the tablets of his will.

I shall now relate what, recognized in its own age, has flowed down to posterity: that Aeneas, having conveyed the household gods from Troy, placed them at Lavinium; that thence, transferred by his son Ascanius to Alba, which he himself had founded, they sought again their former shrine; and that, because this could be thought to have been done by human hand, when brought back to Alba they signified their will by a second passage. Nor does it escape me in how uncertain an opinion the estimate is held concerning the motion and voice of the immortal gods perceived by human eyes and ears; but because no new things are said, but things handed down are repeated, let the authorities vouch for their credit: it is for us not to have shrunk from things consecrated by the renowned monuments of letters, as if true.

But although anyone might have done splendid deeds, and most useful to the state, in civil war, yet he was not on that account called "imperator," nor were any thanksgivings decreed, nor did he triumph either in ovation or in a chariot, because, as those victories were necessary, so they were always esteemed mournful, inasmuch as they were won not by foreign but by domestic blood. And so both Nasica slaughtered Ti. Gracchus, and G. Metellus the factions of Opimius, in grief. Q. Catulus, when, with his colleague M. Lepidus together with all the forces of the sedition extinguished, returned into the city bearing before him a moderate joy. C. Antonius too, the victor over Catiline, brought back his swords wiped clean into the camp. L. Cinna and C. Marius had indeed greedily drunk civil blood, but they did not straightway make for the temples and altars of the gods. Now L. Sulla, who completed very many civil wars, whose successes were most cruel and most insolent, when, his power consummated and built up, he led a triumph, conveyed in it many cities of Greece and Asia, but no town of Roman citizens. It is irksome and wearisome to go further through the wounds of the state. The laurel neither did the senate give to anyone, nor did anyone desire it to be given to himself, while a part of the state wept. But to the oak ready hands are stretched forth, where for citizens saved a crown is to be given, with which the doorposts of the house of Augustus triumph in everlasting glory.

9.pr. ON THE CENSORIAL MARK. The most tenacious bond of camp discipline and the diligent observance of military method admonish me to pass over to the censorship, the mistress and guardian of peace: for as the resources of the Roman people surpassed in greatness, by the virtues of its commanders, so probity and self-restraint, examined under the censorial brow, are a work equal in effect to warlike praises: for what does it profit to be vigorous abroad if at home one lives badly? Let cities be stormed, nations be seized, hands be laid upon kingdoms—unless duty and its modesty stand firm in forum and senate-house, the heap of acquired things, made level with heaven, will have no stable seat. It pertains to the matter, therefore, to know, and indeed to recall, the acts of the censorial power.

The lights of our city will not be indignant if, amid their surpassing splendour, the valour of centurions too has offered itself to be regarded: for, as humility ought to venerate eminence, so by the nobility the newness of good disposition is rather to be cherished than spurned. Or ought Titius to be driven from the connection of these examples? Who, keeping watch for the party of Caesar, intercepted by the garrison of Scipio, when safety was to be given him by him on one condition only, if he affirmed that he would be a soldier of Gnaeus Pompey, Scipio's own father-in-law, did not hesitate to answer thus: 'To you indeed, Scipio, I give thanks; but I have no need to use that condition of life.' A noble spirit, without any images of ancestors!

I should be content with the examples of this kind, did not admiration of the deed compel me to add one. Antius Restio, proscribed by the triumvirs, when he saw all his household occupied around plunder and booty, having dissembled his flight as much as he could, withdrew himself from his household gods in the dead of night. His furtive departure a slave of his—one who had been restrained by him with the penalty of chains and branded, with the utmost insult to his face, with the inexpiable mark of letters—observed with watchful eyes, and, following his footsteps as they wandered hither and thither with benevolent zeal, crept up as a voluntary companion to his side. By that so refined and so risky a service he had filled up the most perfect heap of unexpected devotion: for, while those whose station in the house had been more fortunate were intent on gain, he himself—nothing but the shadow and image of his punishments—judged the safety of him by whom he had been so grievously punished to be his greatest profit, and, when it would have been abundant to remit his anger, he added even affection. Nor did his goodwill proceed thus far only, but in preserving him he used marvellous skill too: for when he perceived soldiers, greedy for blood, coming upon them, having removed his master, he built a pyre and threw upon it an old man, in want, seized and killed by him. Then, when the soldiers asked where Antius was, stretching his hand toward the pyre he answered that he was being burned there, having paid him the due expiations of his cruelty. Because he spoke things like the truth, his voice was believed. Whence it came about that Antius obtained a safe occasion of seeking his preservation.

9.pr. ON THE CHANGE OF CHARACTER OR FORTUNE The change of character and of fortune, recognized in famous men, can add much both of confidence to the minds of men and take away much of anxiety, whether we contemplate our own states or those of our neighbours: for since, by looking at the fortunes of others, we see that fame has emerged from a station abject and despised, what will be wanting to prevent us too from always thinking better things of ourselves, mindful that it is foolish to condemn oneself in advance to perpetual unhappiness, and at times to turn into certain despair a hope which, even when uncertain, is rightly cherished?

L. Valerius, moreover, whose surname was Heptachordus, having found Cornelius Balbus a toga-clad enemy—inasmuch as he had been harassed by his work and counsel in several private suits and at last, with an accuser suborned, accused on a capital charge—passing over his advocates and patrons, left Balbus alone as heir. Doubtless a certain bewilderment turned his mind awry: for he loved his own squalor and cherished his dangers and sought condemnation in his prayers, pursuing the author of these things with goodwill, and those who would ward them off with hatred.

Mention having been made of the city from which our state drew its origins, the divine Julius, the fortunate offspring of it, offers himself to us. Him C. Cassius, never to be named without a preface of public parricide, when at the battle of Philippi he was standing firm with most ardent spirit, saw, more august than human in appearance, clad in a purple cloak, with menacing countenance and on a galloping horse making an attack upon him. Terrified by this sight, he turned his back to the enemy, having first uttered these words: "For what more can I do, if to have slain him is not enough?" You had not indeed slain Caesar, Cassius, for no divinity can be extinguished; but by violating him while he still used a mortal body you deserved to have so hostile a god.

Maevius, a centurion of the divine Augustus, following the same resolve of steadfastness, when in the Antonian war he had again and again fought outstanding battles, surrounded by an unforeseen ambush of the enemy and brought to Antony at Alexandria, and asked what should be decided concerning him, said: 'Order me to be slain, since I can be induced neither by the benefit of safety nor by the punishment of death either to cease to be Caesar's soldier or to begin to be yours.' But the more steadfastly he despised his life, the more easily he obtained it: for Antony granted him his safety in tribute to his valour.

8e.1. Many Roman examples of this stamp survive, but excess is now to be avoided. And so I shall permit my pen to glide down now to foreign matters. Of these let Blassius hold the first place, than whose steadfastness nothing is more persistent: for, desiring to restore to the Romans his country Salapia, occupied by a Punic garrison, he dared to attempt—with greater desire than sure hope—to bring over to the same work Dasius, who differed from him with the keenest zeal in the administration of public affairs and was otherwise wholly given to the friendship of Hannibal, and without whom the planned design could not be carried out. Dasius at once reported his conversation to Hannibal, adding what seemed likely both to make himself more commended and his enemy more hated. By Hannibal they were ordered to attend, that the one might prove his charge and the other defend himself. But, while the matter was being conducted before the tribunal and all eyes were intent upon that inquiry, while by chance some other business of nearer concern was being handled, Blassius, with dissembling countenance and lowered voice, began to advise Dasius to favour the part of the Romans rather than of the Carthaginians. Thereupon indeed Dasius cried out that he was being solicited against Hannibal in the very sight of the commander. But, because it was thought incredible, and had penetrated to but one pair of ears, and was alleged by an enemy, it lacked the credit of truth. Yet not long after, the wondrous steadfastness of Blassius drew Dasius over to him, and he handed over to Marcellus both Salapia and the five hundred Numidians who were there for its guard.

8e.2. Phocion, indeed, when the Athenians had managed a matter prosperously otherwise than he had advised, stood forth so persevering a defender of his own opinion that in the assembly he said that he rejoiced indeed at their success, but that his own counsel had nevertheless been somewhat better: for he did not condemn what he had rightly seen, because what another had ill counselled had turned out well, judging the latter the more fortunate, the former the wiser. And indeed chance makes the mind fond of rashness, when it propitiously breathes upon a depraved counsel, and the more vehemently it harms, the more unexpectedly it profits. Placid and merciful and liberal, and tempered with every sweetness, were the manners of Phocion, which assuredly the agreement of all judged most fitly to be adorned with the surname of Goodness. And so the steadfastness, which by nature seems the more rigid, flowed gentle from his mild breast: but the spirit of Socrates, fortified by the strength of manliness, gave forth a somewhat harsher example of perseverance.

8e.3. The whole state of the Athenians, stirred up by a most unjust and savage frenzy, had passed a grim sentence concerning the lives of the ten praetors who at Arginusae had destroyed the Lacedaemonian fleet. By chance Socrates then held that office by whose decision the resolutions of the plebs were arranged; and, judging it unworthy that so many and so well-deserving men should be carried off by an unworthy cause through an onset of envy, he set his own steadfastness against the rashness of the multitude, and by the greatest uproar of the assembly and by the most furious threats was not compelled to enroll himself as the author of the public madness. And it, forbidden by his opposition to rage by the lawful path, persevered in defiling its hands with the unjust blood of the praetors. Nor did Socrates fear lest the eleventh frenzy of his distracted country should be his own death.

8e.4. The next example, though not of the same splendour, can yet be held an equally sure proof of steadfastness. At Athens, Ephialtes, a man of effective service in the forum and of no hidden good faith, was ordered to prosecute publicly, and was compelled to lay an information, among others, against the name of Demostratus, whose son was Demochares, a boy of surpassing beauty, clinging to him in a most ardent love of his spirit. And so, by the lot of his common duty a grim accuser, by the condition of his private affection a pitiable defendant, he could neither repel the boy, who came to entreat him to press the less hard upon his father's accusations, nor look upon him as a suppliant fallen at his knees, but, with covered head, weeping and groaning, suffered him to pour out his prayers, and nonetheless, with sincere good faith, condemned the accused Demostratus. A victory won with I know not whether the greater praise or the greater torment, since, before he crushed the guilty, Ephialtes conquered himself.

8e.5. Him the Syracusan Dio outweighs by the severity of his example. When some warned him to be more cautious against Heraclides and Callippus, in whose faith he placed the greatest trust, as men weaving snares for him, he answered that he preferred to depart from life rather than, through fear of a violent death, to set friends on a level with enemies.

8e.6. What follows is illustrious both by the wonder of the thing itself and by the renown of its author. Alexander, king of the Macedonians, the surpassing wealth of Darius having been already crushed in a famous battle, heated by the burning of the season and of his march, plunged his body in Cilicia into the Cydnus, which, conspicuous for the clearness of its water, flows through Tarsus. Then suddenly, from the excessive draught of cold, his sinews being stupefied and his limbs benumbed by torpor, with the utmost dismay of the whole army he was carried into a town near the camp. There he lay sick at Tarsus, and amid his adverse health the hope of impending victory wavered. And so the physicians, called together, were considering with most careful counsel the remedies of his safety. When they had directed their opinions to a single draught, and Philip the physician—who was indeed his friend and companion—had handed it, tempered by his own hands, to Alexander, there came a letter sent by Parmenio, warning the king to beware the treachery of Philip, as one corrupted by money from Darius. When he had read it, without any hesitation he drank the medicine and then handed the letter to Philip to read. For so steadfast a judgement towards his friend he received a most worthy reward from the immortal gods, who would not have the safeguard of his safety interrupted by a false information.

1.pr. ON MODERATION. I shall pass over to the most wholesome part of the soul, moderation, which does not allow our minds to be carried astray by the onset of unrestraint and rashness. Whence it comes that it is free from the bite of censure and most richly endowed with the gaining of praise. Let it therefore recognize its own effects in illustrious men.

T. Barrus handed his rings, as though to a sole heir, on his death-bed to Lentulus Spinther, whose most loving spirit and most generous friendship he had felt, though he was in no part leaving him heir. How great a punishment did conscience, in that moment of time—if only it possesses the strength it is believed to have—exact from a most foul man! For amid the very thought of his deceitful and ungrateful fault he gave up the breath, as though some torturer were racking his mind within, because he perceived that his passage from life to death would be both hateful to the gods above and detestable to those below.

Now as for the fact that L. Lentulus, sailing past the shore on which the body of Cn. Pompey the Great, slain by the treachery of King Ptolemy, was being burned on the wood of a shattered boat, ignorant of his misfortune, when he had seen a pyre at which Fortune herself ought to have blushed, said to his comrades, "How do we know but that by this flame Cn. Pompey is being cremated?"—it is the marvel of a divinely sent voice.

M. Popilius, moreover, of senatorial rank, on his death looked back with kindly countenance, in accordance with the ancient law of friendship, upon Oppius Gallus, most intimate with him from his earliest years, and addressed him with words bearing before them a great affection, and even, of the many who sat by, judged him alone worthy of a last embrace and kiss, and besides handed him his rings too—that, of course, he might lose nothing of that inheritance which he was not going to enter upon. These rings Oppius, a careful man, but recognizing them as the mockery, full of insult, of a dying friend, placed in a little casket and, after they had been sealed by those present, most carefully restored to his heirs, himself disinherited. What is more dishonourable than this jest, or what more untimely? A senator of the Roman people, gone forth from the senate-house, a man about presently to lack the enjoyments of life, with his eyes pressed shut in death and his breath giving up its last gasps, chose for himself, by a buffoon's sport, things that should bring him reproach.

1.pr. NOTORIOUS DEFENDANTS, AND THE GROUNDS ON WHICH THEY WERE ACQUITTED OR CONDEMNED Now, in order that the doubtful turns of trials may be borne with a more even mind, let us recall, in the case of those labouring under prejudice, on what grounds they were either acquitted or condemned.

1a.1. M. Horatius, condemned by king Tullus on the charge of having killed his sister, was acquitted when the judgment was referred to the people on appeal. The one verdict the atrocity of the killing moved, the other the cause bent, because it judged the untimely love of the maiden to have been punished severely rather than impiously. And so his brother's right hand, freed by a brave punishment, was able to draw as much glory from a kinsman's blood as from an enemy's.

1a.2. The Roman people showed itself then a keen guardian of chastity, afterwards a judge milder than was just. When Ser. Galba was being vehemently rebuked before the rostra by Libo, tribune of the plebs, because as praetor in Spain he had destroyed a great band of Lusitanians after pledging his faith, and M. Cato, in the extreme of old age, was supporting the tribune's prosecution with his speech, which he included in his Origins, the defendant, now refusing nothing on his own behalf, began weeping to commend his little children and a son joined to him by the blood of a Gaul; and by this deed the assembly was softened, and one who by the consensus of all had been about to perish had almost no hostile vote. Pity, then, governed that inquiry, not equity, since the acquittal which could not be granted to his innocence was given in consideration of the children.

1a.3. In keeping is what follows. A. Gabinius, in the greatest blaze of his ill repute, exposed to the votes of the people with C. Memmius as accuser, seemed to be of broken hope, since both the accusation displayed its part fully, and the defences of his case rested on weak faith, and those who judged, stirred by anger, eagerly sought the man's punishment. Therefore the constable and the prison hovered before his eyes, when meanwhile all this was scattered by the intervention of favourable fortune: for Sisenna, the son of Gabinius, driven on by his consternation, threw himself a suppliant at the feet of Memmius, seeking some assuaging of the storm from the very quarter whence the whole onset of the tempest had burst forth. The insolent victor, repelling him with grim countenance and shaking the ring from his hand, allowed it to lie on the ground for some time. This spectacle brought it about that Laelius, tribune of the plebs, with the approval of all, ordered Gabinius to be released, and a lesson was given that one ought neither to abuse insolently the windfall of prosperity nor to be crushed prematurely by adversity; and this is equally clear from the next example.

1a.4. App. Claudius—I do not know whether his injury to religion or to his country was the greater, since indeed he neglected the most ancient custom of the one and lost the most beautiful fleet of the other—exposed to a hostile people, when it was believed that he could in no way escape his due punishment, was kept safe from condemnation by the benefit of a suddenly arisen shower: for, the inquiry being broken off, it did not seem good to begin another afresh, as though the gods were interposing. Thus to him to whom a storm at sea had brought the pleading of his cause, a storm from heaven brought safety.

1a.5. By the same kind of aid the chastity of the Vestal virgin Tuccia, accused of the crime of unchastity, emerged though darkened by the cloud of ill repute. She, certain in the consciousness of her own integrity, dared to seek the hope of safety by a doubtful proof: for, seizing a sieve, she said, "Vesta, if I have always brought chaste hands to your rites, bring it about that with this I may draw water from the Tiber and carry it to your temple." Nature herself yielded to the rashly and boldly cast vows of the priestess.

1a.6. Likewise L. Piso, accused by L. Claudius Pulcher of having inflicted grave and intolerable injuries on the allies, avoided the fear of undoubted ruin by a chance aid: for at that very time when grim sentences were being passed upon him, a sudden violence of cloudburst fell, and when he, prostrate on the ground, kissed the feet of the judges, he filled his mouth with mud. The sight of this transferred the whole inquiry from severity to clemency and gentleness, because they thought that he had already given the allies penalties grave enough, reduced to such necessity that he was forced to throw himself down so suppliantly and lift himself up so unsightly.

1a.7. I shall append two acquitted by the fault of their own accusers. Q. Flavius, brought to trial before the people by C. Valerius the aedile, when he had been condemned by the votes of fourteen tribes, cried out that he, an innocent man, was being crushed. To him Valerius, in an equally loud voice, replied that it made no difference to him whether a guilty or an innocent man perished, provided that he perished. By the violence of this saying he gave the remaining tribes to his adversary. He had cast down his enemy; the same man, while he believed him assuredly ruined, raised him up again, and lost his victory in the very moment of victory.

1a.8. C. Cosconius too, a defendant under the Servilian law, beyond all doubt guilty on account of his very many and most evident crimes, was raised up by a poem of his accuser Valerius Valentinus, recited at the trial, in which by a poetic jest he had indicated that a boy of free birth in the purple-bordered toga and a freeborn maiden had been corrupted by him; since indeed the judges thought it unjust to dismiss as victor one who deserved not to carry off the palm from another, but to grant it concerning himself. Valerius, indeed, was condemned in the acquittal of Cosconius more than Cosconius was freed in his own case.

1a.9. I shall touch too on those whose safety, overwhelmed by their own crimes, was granted to the distinction of their kinsmen. A. Atilius Calatinus, a defendant most notorious on a charge of betraying the town of Sora, was rescued from the peril of imminent condemnation by a few words of his father-in-law Q. Maximus, by which he affirmed that, if he had himself found him guilty of that charge, he would have broken off the connection: for at once the people yielded to the judgment of one man their own almost already settled opinion, thinking it unworthy not to trust the testimony of a man to whom in the most difficult times of the state it remembered that it had well trusted its armies.

1a.10. M. Aemilius Scaurus too, a defendant on a charge of extortion, brought into court a defence so desperate and lamented that, when the accuser said that by the law it was allowed him to summon a hundred and twenty men to testify, and that he would not refuse Scaurus's acquittal if he should name as many men from whom he had taken nothing in his province, Scaurus could not avail himself of so good a condition. Nevertheless, on account of his most ancient nobility and the recent memory of his father, he was acquitted.

1a.11. But just as the splendour of the most eminent men availed very much in protecting defendants, so in crushing them it availed not really much; nay, even when men were evidently guilty, by attacking them too keenly it did them good. P. Scipio Aemilianus accused Cotta before the people. His case, though pierced by the gravest charges, was adjourned seven times, and at last in the eighth trial was acquitted, because men feared lest his condemnation should be thought to have been granted to the outstanding eminence of his accuser. I should believe that they said this among themselves: "We do not wish a man seeking the life of another to carry into court triumphs and trophies and spoils and the beaks of conquered ships: let him be terrible by these against the enemy, but let him not pursue the safety of a citizen propped up by so great a clamour of glory."

1a.12. The judges were as vehement against a most distinguished accuser as they were mild toward a defendant of far inferior fortune. Calidius of Bononia, caught at night in the bedroom of a married man, when on that account he pleaded a charge of adultery, emerged from among the greatest and gravest waves of disgrace, embracing, like a plank of shipwreck, a very flimsy kind of defence: for he affirmed that he had been led there by love of a boy slave. Suspect was the place, suspect the time, suspect the person of the matron, suspect too his own youth; but a confession of intemperance freed him from the charge of unchastity.

1a.13. This is an example of milder material, that following of somewhat graver. When the brothers Caelii were pleading a charge of parricide—men born in a distinguished place at Tarracina, whose father T. Caelius, resting in his bedroom, with his sons lying one on either bed, had been killed, and neither any slave nor free man could be found to whom the suspicion of the murder applied—they were acquitted on this one ground, because it was made plain to the judges that they had been found asleep with the door open. Sleep, the surest token of guiltless tranquillity, brought help to the wretched men: for it was judged that the nature of things did not admit that, their father being slain, they could take rest above his wounds and his blood.

1d.1. We shall now run through those whom in the pleading of their case the things outside the inquiry harmed more than their own innocence helped. L. Scipio, after a most splendid triumph led over king Antiochus, was condemned just as though he had received money from him. Not, I think, because he had been corrupted by a bribe to remove beyond Mount Taurus that man, lord of all Asia and already laying victorious hands on Europe. But a man otherwise of the most sincere life and far removed from this suspicion, he could not resist the prejudice which then dwelt in the famous surnames of the two brothers.

1d.2. And to Scipio indeed the greatest brilliance of fortune brought ruin; but to C. Decianus, a man of approved integrity, his own voice brought destruction: for when he was accusing P. Furius, a man of most defiled life, before the rostra, because in a certain part of his pleading he had dared to lament the death of L. Saturninus, he both failed to condemn the defendant and besides paid the penalties assigned to him.

1d.3. A like mischance laid Sex. Titius low too. He was innocent, he was popular with the people for the agrarian law he had carried; nevertheless, because he had kept an image of Saturninus at home, the whole assembly crushed him with their votes.

1d.4. Let there be added to these Claudia, whom, innocent of the charge of which she was accused, an impious vow overturned, because, when on her way home from the games she was being crushed by the crowd, she had wished that her brother—the chief loss of our naval power—might come back to life and, made consul more often, might by his unlucky leadership diminish the too-great crowding of the city.

1d.5. We can pass also by a brief detour to those whom the onset of condemnation snatched away for trivial causes. M. Mulvius, Cn. Lollius, and L. Sextilius, the three commissioners, because they had come too slowly to put out a fire that had broken out in the Sacred Way, were condemned before the people by the tribunes of the plebs on the appointed day.
1d.6. Likewise P. Villius, the night-commissioner, accused by P. Aquilius, tribune of the plebs, fell by the people's judgment, because he had made his round of the watches too negligently.

1d.7. Of a very severe stamp too was that judgment of the people, when it afflicted with a heavy fine M. Aemilius Porcina, accused by L. Cassius on the charge of a villa built too lofty in the Alsian territory.

1d.8. Nor must the condemnation of that man be suppressed, who, seized by too great a love of his little boy, being asked by him in the country that he should order tripe to be made for dinner, since there was no means of buying beef nearby, killed a tamed ox and so satisfied his desire, and on that account was crushed by a public inquiry—innocent, had he not been born in so old-fashioned an age.

1A.1. And, that we may report also those who, brought into peril of their life, were neither condemned nor acquitted: before M. Popilius Laenas the praetor a certain woman pleaded her case, because she had killed her mother by a blow with a club. Concerning her sentences were passed in neither direction, because it was abundantly clear that she, moved by grief for her children poisoned to death—whom the grandmother, hostile to her daughter, had made away with—had avenged the parricide by a parricide. Of these acts the one was judged not worthy of vengeance, the other not worthy of acquittal.

1A.2. By the same hesitation the mind of Publius Dolabella too, holding Asia with proconsular command, wavered. A matron of Smyrna killed her husband and her son, when she had learned that by them a young man of the best disposition, whom she had borne by a former husband, had been slain. This matter, brought to him, Dolabella referred to Athens for the cognizance of the Areopagus, because he himself could neither acquit a woman contaminated by two murders nor punish one driven on by so just a grief. Thoughtful and gentle was this magistrate of the Roman people; but the Areopagites too no less wisely, who, after inspecting the case, ordered both accuser and accused to return to them after a hundred years, moved by the same feeling as Dolabella. But he by transferring the inquiry, they by deferring it, avoided the inextricable hesitation of condemning and acquitting.
2.pr. ON NOTABLE PRIVATE TRIALS To public trials I shall add private ones, in which the equity of the inquiries can please the reader rather than an immoderate multitude offend him.

And this indeed was a matter of a man and of chance, while that other was uttered well-nigh by the very mouth of Apollo, by which the truth-telling fidelity of the Pythian prophecy ran ahead of the death of Appius. In the civil war, in which Cn. Pompey had broken himself away from concord with Caesar by a counsel ruinous to himself and useless to the state, Appius, desiring to explore the outcome of that gravest of disturbances, by the strength of his command—for he was in charge of Achaea—compelled the priestess of the Delphic cauldron to descend into the inmost part of the sacred cavern, whence, as sure lots are sought by those consulting, so the too great draught of the divine breath proves baleful to those who render them. Therefore, by the impulse of the divine power that seized her, the inspired maiden, with the dread sound of her voice, sang the fates to Appius amid obscure ambiguities of words: "This war," she said, "is nothing to you, Roman: you shall obtain the Hollows of Euboea." But he, thinking that he was being warned by the counsels of Apollo not to be present at that crisis, withdrew into that region which, lying between Rhamnus, a noble part of the Attic soil, and Carystus, near to the Chalcidic strait, holds the name of the Hollows of Euboea, where, before the battle of Pharsalus, consumed by disease, he took possession by burial of the place foretold by the god.

There are also those things that hold the place of marvels: that, when the chapel of the Salii was burned down, nothing was found whole in it except the lituus of Romulus; that the statue of Servius Tullius, when the temple of Fortune was consumed by fire, remained inviolate; that the statue of Quinta Claudia, set in the forecourt of the temple of the Mother of the gods, when that temple was twice consumed by fire—first in the consulship of P. Nasica Scipio and L. Bestia, again in that of M. Servilius and L. Lamia—stood untouched by the flames upon its base.

Some wonder the pyre of Acilius Aviola too brought to our state, who, believed dead both by the physicians and by his household, when he had lain for some time at home, was carried out; and after the fire had seized his body, he cried out that he was alive and called upon the help of his tutor—for he alone had remained there—but, already surrounded by the flames, he could not be withdrawn from his fate. It is established that L. Lamia too, a man of praetorian rank, likewise had a voice upon the pyre.

8e.1. Less marvellous than these is the case of Er the Pamphylian, whom Plato writes lay for ten days among those who had fallen in battle, and, two days after he had been taken up thence and placed on the pyre, came back to life, and told of certain wondrous things seen at the time of his death.

8e.2. And since we have crossed over to foreign matters: a certain very learned man at Athens, when he had received the blow of a stone on his head, retaining everything else with the most tenacious memory, forgot only letters, to which he had especially devoted himself. The dire and malignant wound erupted into his mind, as if of set purpose, after the senses had been searched out, upon that very thing above all in which he most rejoiced, with the bitterness of harming, bearing the man's singular learning out to its grave with a funeral full of envy. If it was not permitted him to enjoy such studies, it had at some time been more useful never to have obtained access to them than, having once tasted their sweetness, to have been deprived of it.

8e.3. Yet more pitiable is the account of the following case: for the wife of Nausimenes the Athenian, when she had come upon the incest of her son and daughter, struck by the sight of the unexpected monstrosity, was struck dumb, both for the present time to express indignation and for the future to speak. They paid for the wicked coupling by a voluntary death.

8e.4. In this manner fortune, raging, took away a voice; in that other, propitious, she gave one. Echecles of Samos, an athlete, dumb, when the title and prize of the victory he had won were being snatched from him, kindled with indignation, came forth vocal.

8e.5. Of Gorgias of Epirus too, a brave and famous man, the origin was marvellous, in that, at the funeral of his mother, having slipped from her womb, by his unexpected wailing he forced those carrying the bier to halt, and offered his country a strange spectacle, having all but obtained light and a cradle from the very pyre of his mother: for at the same moment of time the one, already dead, gave birth, and the other was carried out before he was born.

8e.6. A wound of divine fortune inflicted on Jason of Pherae . . . one desirous of his destruction inflicted: for when amid an ambush he had struck him with a sword, he so burst an abscess, which had been able to be healed by none of the physicians, that he freed the man from his deadly malady.

8e.7. Equally acceptable to the immortal gods was Simonides, whose safety, preserved from an impending [duty], was also withdrawn from ruin: for as he was dining at the house of Scopas at Crannon, which is a town in Thessaly, it was announced that two young men had come to the door, earnestly begging that he would come out to them at once. Going out to them, he found no one there. But at that moment of time the dining-room, in which Scopas was feasting, collapsed and crushed both him and all the guests. What is richer than this good fortune, which neither sea nor land raging availed to extinguish!

8e.8. Not unwillingly I append to this man Daphnitas, lest anyone be ignorant how much it has mattered to have sung the praises of the gods and to have disparaged the divine power. He, since he was of that pursuit whose professors are called sophists, of a foolish and biting cast of opinion, consulted Apollo at Delphi, by way of mockery, whether he could find a horse, although he had none at all. From the oracle a voice was rendered to him: that he would find a horse, but that, driven off by it, he would perish. Whence, as he was returning in jesting mood, as though the credit of the sacred lots had been deluded, he fell in with King Attalus, often provoked by him with insulting words in his absence; and by his order he was thrown headlong from a rock whose name was Horse, and so paid the just penalties of his mad spirit, even to the mocking of the gods.

8e.9. By the same oracle Philip, king of the Macedonians, was warned to guard his safety from the violence of a four-horse chariot, and ordered chariots throughout his whole kingdom to be unyoked, and always avoided that place in Boeotia which is called Quadriga. Yet he did not escape the kind of danger announced: for Pausanias had a four-horse chariot engraved on the hilt of the sword with which he slew him.

8e.10. This same so persistent necessity appeared alike in the father and in the son Alexander: since Callanus the Indian, about to cast himself of his own will upon a blazing pyre, when interrupted by Alexander, who asked whether he wished to charge him with anything or to say anything, said, "Soon I shall see you": nor that without cause, since his voluntary departure from life was followed by the swift death of Alexander.

8e.11. The case of a rower equals royal deaths in the greatness of the marvel; for when, on a Tyrian hexere, he was baling out the bilge-water, and a wave had cast him from the ship, an opposing wave, rebounding from the other side, carried him back into the ship. And so to the lamentation of one at once wretched and fortunate was mingled congratulation.

8e.12. What? Are not those mockeries of nature in human bodies to be believed to have existed—tolerable indeed, because they lacked savagery, but yet themselves to be reckoned among marvels? For the son of Prusias, king of Bithynia, by the same name as his father, had, in place of the upper row of teeth, one bone extended evenly, neither in appearance unsightly nor in any way inconvenient for use.
8e.13. But Drypetina, the daughter of King Mithridates, born of Queen Laodice, exceedingly deformed by a double row of teeth, was a companion of her father's flight when he was conquered by Pompey.

8e.14. Nor of small wonder either are the eyes of Strabo, who, it is established, used so sure a keenness of sight that from Lilybaeum he could behold the fleets going out of the harbour of the Carthaginians.

8e.15. More marvellous than his eyes was the heart of Aristomenes of Messene, which the Athenians, on account of his extraordinary cunning, cut out and found stuffed with hairs, when, having several times taken him captive and seen him slip away by craft, they had captured him.

8e.16. And the poet Antipater of Sidon was every year, on one day only, that on which he had been born, seized with a fever; and when he had reached extreme old age, on his birthday, by that fixed recurrence of the malady, he was consumed.

8e.17. In this place are aptly mentioned Polystratus and Hippoclides, philosophers, born on the same day, followers of the sect of the same teacher Epicurus, joined also by community in possessing a patrimony and keeping a school, and extinguished at the same moment of time in extreme old age. So great and so equal a fellowship of fortune alike and of friendship, who would not think to have been born, nurtured, and ended in the very bosom of heavenly Concord herself?

8e.18. Wherefore these things especially—whether in the children of most powerful kings, or in a most illustrious king, or in a poet of flourishing genius, or in most learned men, or in a man of unknown lot . . . —not even she herself, the fruitful artificer of all good and bad material, would render a reason for: no more than why she so greatly loved the wild she-goats born in Crete, which, when pierced through with arrows, she leads, all but with her own hands, to the saving help of the herb dittany, and brings it about that, when it has been eaten, they straightway spew forth from their wounds both the darts and the force of the poison; or why, on the island of Cephalania, although all flocks everywhere are daily refreshed by drinking water, she established that goats, for the greater part of the year, with open mouth, receiving the winds from on high, should slake their thirst; or wherefore at Croton, in the temple of Juno Lacinia, she has endowed an altar with ash that is unmoved by all the winds; or above all why she has willed that one water in Macedonia, and another in the territory of Cales, should possess the property of wine, by which men become intoxicated. These things we ought to follow up not with wonder but with mere record, since we know that licence is rightly claimed in the greatest measure by her in whose power rests the boundless labour of begetting all things.

8e.19. And because we have touched on things exceeding the usual order of reason, let mention be made also of the serpent related by T. Livy at once carefully and eloquently: for he says that in Africa, by the river Bagrada, . . . there was one of so great a size that it kept the army of Atilius Regulus from the use of the river, and, when many soldiers had been seized in its huge mouth and several crushed by the coils of its tail, since it could not be pierced by the casting of weapons, at last, attacked on all sides by the engines of ballistae, it sank down beneath the frequent and heavy blows of flints, and seemed to all the cohorts and legions more terrible than Carthage itself; and moreover, when the eddies had been steeped with its gore and the neighbouring region polluted by the deadly exhalation of its lying body, it drove the Roman camp away from there. He adds that the skin of the beast, a hundred and twenty feet long, was sent to the city.

pr.1. Having explored the rich and powerful kingdom of Nature, I shall set my pen to the ancient and memorable institutions both of our city and of foreign nations: for it is worthwhile to learn what the elements were of this life, which we live happily under the best of princes, so that the regard for them too may bring some profit to our present manners.

The censors Camillus and Postumius ordered those who had come to old age unmarried to pay money, by way of a fine, into the treasury, deserving to be punished a second time if in any way they dared to complain of so just an ordinance, when they were rebuked in this manner: "Nature prescribes to you a law of begetting as of being born, and your parents, by rearing you, have bound you, if there is any shame, to the duty of nurturing grandchildren. To this is added that fortune has even granted you a long postponement of discharging this duty, while meanwhile your years have been consumed, empty of the name of husband and father. Go therefore and pay the not-odious contribution, useful to a numerous posterity."

ON THE MODERATION OF PARENTS TOWARD SONS UNDER SUSPICION Lucius Gellius, having discharged all the offices up to the censorship, when he held all but proven the most grievous charges against his son—of debauchery committed with his stepmother and of parricide contemplated—did not nevertheless rush at once to vengeance, but, having admitted almost the whole senate to his council, after he had set forth his suspicions, gave the young man the power of defending himself, and, the cause having been most diligently examined, acquitted him both by the verdict of the council and even by his own sentence. But if, carried away by the impulse of anger, he had hastened to rage, he would have committed a crime rather than avenged one.

Manlius Torquatus, in the beginnings of his youth thought of so dull and blunted a wit that by his father Lucius Manlius, a most ample man, because he seemed useless both for domestic and for public services, he was relegated to the country and wearied with rustic toil, afterwards freed his father, a defendant, from judicial peril, struck with the axe his son, a victor, because against his command he had joined hands with the enemy, and restored his fatherland, weary with the Latin tumult, by a most splendid triumph—in this cloud, I believe, of the contempt of his adolescence steeped, that the glory of his old age might shine forth more brightly.

When the kings had been driven out, the plebs, at variance with the senators, encamped in arms by the bank of the river Anio on the hill which is called Sacred; and the condition of the state was not only deformed but most wretched, since the rest of the body was divided from its head by a pestilent sedition. And had not the eloquence of Valerius come to the rescue, the hope of so great an empire would have collapsed almost at its very birth: for he, recalling by a speech the people that was rashly rejoicing in a new and unaccustomed liberty to better and saner counsels, subjected it to the senate—that is, he joined the city to the city. To eloquent words, then, anger, consternation, and arms gave way.

C. Helvius Cinna, tribune of the plebs, making for his home from the funeral of C. Caesar, was torn to pieces by the hands of the people in place of Cornelius Cinna, against whom they thought they were raging, angry with him because, although he was a kinsman of Caesar, he had delivered before the rostra an impious speech against him when he was wickedly murdered; and they were driven on by that error so that they carried the head of Helvius, just as though it were Cornelius's, on a javelin around the pyre of Caesar—a pitiable expiation, of his own duty, of another's error!

Their severity M. Valerius Maximus and C. Iunius Brutus Bubulcus, as censors, imitated by a like kind of chastisement: for they removed from the senate L. Annius, because he had repudiated her whom he had taken in marriage as a maiden, without the counsel of any of his friends. But this crime is, I know not whether, greater than the former: for in that the conjugal rites were only spurned, in this they were even injuriously handled. By the best judgement, therefore, the censors deemed him unworthy of entrance to the senate-house;

But of Quintus Hortensius, who in his time was the ornament of Roman eloquence, there was an admirable forbearance in the case of his son: for, although he held his impiety so suspect and his worthlessness so hateful that, intending to make Messala, his sister's son, his heir, while defending a man accused of bribery, he said to the judges that, if they condemned him, there would remain to him nothing but the kisses of his grandchildren, in whom he might find rest—by this sentiment, of course, which he even inserted into the published oration, placing his son among the torments of his soul rather than among his pleasures—yet, that he might not confound the order of nature, he left not his grandchildren but his son as heir, using his affections with moderation, because both while alive he rendered a true testimony to his character and when dead he rendered the due honour to his blood.

But the elder Scipio Africanus, whom the immortal gods willed to be born so that there should be one in whom virtue might effectively show itself to men through all its measures, is said to have passed the first years of his adolescence in a rather loose life—removed indeed from the charge of luxury, but yet more tender than the Punic trophies and the yoke imposed on the necks of conquered Carthage.

These restrained even the Marian and Cinnan swords raging with desire to pour out civil blood: for soldiers sent by the most savage leaders to slay M. Antonius, stunned by his speech, returned their already drawn and brandished swords, empty of blood, to their scabbards. When they had departed, P. Annius—for he alone had stood at the entrance untouched by Antonius's eloquence—carried out the cruel command by a savage service. How eloquent, then, may we think him to have been, whom not even any of his enemies could bear to kill, who had only been willing to admit his voice to his ears?

For error forced C. Cassius to exact penalties from himself: for, amid that varied and, to the leaders themselves, unknown outcome of the battle of four armies at Philippi, the centurion Titinius, sent by him at night-time to spy out in what state the affairs of M. Brutus were, while he sought frequent departures from the road—because the obscurity of the darkness did not allow him to distinguish whether enemies or comrades met him—returned too slowly to Cassius. Cassius, thinking that he had been captured by the enemy and that all had fallen into their power, hastened to end his life, though both the enemy's camp had in turn been taken and the forces of Brutus were for the most part safe. But the virtue of Titinius is not to be blotted out by silence: he stuck for a little while with his eyes, stunned by the unexpected spectacle of his leader lying low; then, dissolved in tears, "Although unwittingly, commander," he said, "I was the cause of your death, yet, lest that very thing go unpunished, receive me as the companion of your fate"; and over his lifeless body he plunged his sword up to the hilt into his own throat, and, the blood of both mingled, a double victim lay—this of devotion, that of error.

just as Porcius Cato deemed L. Flamininus, whom he removed from the number of the senators, because in his province he had struck with the axe a certain condemned man, the time of the punishment having been chosen at the will and for the spectacle of a little woman by whose love he was held. And he could have been restrained by regard for the consulship, which he had held, and by the authority of his brother Titus Flamininus. But, being both censor and Cato, a double example of severity, he resolved that he was the more to be marked, because he had defiled the majesty of the most ample honour by so foul a deed, and had not held it of any account that to the same ancestral images should be ascribed both the eyes of a harlot delighted with human blood and the suppliant hands of King Philip.

The same thing was done by Quintus Fulvius, a man of illustrious family and great dignity, but in a son somewhat more foul: for, when he had implored the aid of the senate, that, being suspected of parricide and on that account in hiding, he should be sought out by a triumvir, and the son had been seized by order of the senators, he not only did not brand him but even, when dying, wished him to be master of all his goods, appointing as his heir the one whom he had begotten, not the one whom he had found him to be by experience.

Gaius Valerius Flaccus too, in the times of the Second Punic War, began an adolescence ruined by luxury. But made a flamen by Publius Licinius the chief pontiff, that he might the more easily withdraw from his vices, his mind turned to the care of the sacred rites and ceremonies, using the religion of frugality as his guide, he proved afterward as great a model of self-restraint and holiness as he had before been an example of luxury.

The deified Julius too, the most perfect summit as much of heavenly power as of human genius, expressed properly the force of eloquence by saying, in his accusation of Cn. Dolabella, whom he prosecuted, that a most excellent cause was being wrested from him by the advocacy of L. Cotta—since indeed the greatest eloquence of that time then complained of the force of eloquence. Mention of his having been made, since I could add no greater domestic example, we must go abroad.

9e.1. Pisistratus is reported to have prevailed so much by speaking that the Athenians, captivated by his oration, permitted him royal power, although on the opposing side the most patriotic Solon strove. But the harangues of the one were more wholesome, those of the other more eloquent. So it came about that a state otherwise most prudent preferred slavery to liberty.

9e.2. Pericles, moreover, equipped with the most fortunate gifts of nature, polished with the greatest zeal under the teacher Anaxagoras, imposed the yoke of slavery on the free necks of Athens: for he drove and turned that city at his own pleasure, and when he spoke against the will of the people, his voice was none the less pleasant and popular. And so the abusive tongue of the old comedy, though it desired to censure the man's power, nevertheless confessed that a charm sweeter than honey dwelt on the man's lips, and declared that there were left, as it were, certain stings in the minds of those who had heard him. It is reported that a certain man, when, very old, he was present at the first harangue of the youthful Pericles, and as a young man had heard Pisistratus, now decrepit, haranguing, could not restrain himself from crying out that one ought to beware of that citizen, because his oration was very like the oration of Pisistratus. Nor did either the estimate of his eloquence or the augury of his character deceive the man. For what was there between Pisistratus and Pericles, except that the one bore tyranny in arms, the other without arms?

9e.3. How greatly do we judge eloquence to have availed Hegesias the Cyrenaic philosopher? Who so represented the evils of life that, by inserting a pitiable image of them in the breasts of his hearers, he engendered in many a desire of meeting a voluntary death; and therefore he was forbidden by king Ptolemy to discourse further on this matter.

10.pr. HOW GREAT IMPORTANCE THERE IS IN DELIVERY AND FITTING MOVEMENT OF THE BODY The ornaments of eloquence consist in a delivery apt and suitable and in movement of the body. Equipped with these, it assails men in three ways, by invading their minds itself, and by giving to one its ears, to the other its eyes, to be charmed.

But a false opinion brought, I do not know whether, the chief injury upon the household gods of Lars Tolumnius, king of the Veientines: for when in a lucky throw of the dice he had said in jest to his fellow player "Kill," and Roman envoys had by chance come in, his attendants, driven on by the error of the word, by killing the envoys transferred the game into a command.

10.pr. ON VENGEANCE The stings of vengeance, moreover, are as just as they are keen, which, when provoked, are roused, desiring to repay the grief received with grief; to embrace these more widely is not to the purpose.

What shall I say of the censorship of Fabricius Luscinus? Every age has told and hereafter will tell that by him Cornelius Rufinus, who had most splendidly discharged two consulships and a dictatorship, was, because he had procured silver vessels of ten pounds' weight, not retained in the senatorial order, as luxurious by a bad example. By Hercules, the very letters of our age seem to me to be stupefied, when they are compelled to lend their service to recording so great a severity, and to fear lest they be thought to commemorate the deeds not of our city: for it is scarcely credible that within the same pomerium ten pounds of silver should have been both a hateful census and that poverty should be held most contemptible.

To the clement acts of great men I shall add the plan of an obscure father, of a new and unusual method. When he had learned that snares were being plaited for him by his son and could not bring himself to believe that his true blood had advanced to such a degree of crime, he took his wife aside and humbly begged her not to conceal it from him any further, whether she had substituted that young man or had conceived him by another. Then, persuaded by her assertion and her oath that he should suspect nothing of the kind, having led his son to a deserted place, he handed him the sword which he had brought hidden with him and offered his throat to be struck, affirming that he had need of neither poison nor brigand to accomplish the parricide. By this deed not gradually but with great force a right way of thinking took possession of the young man's breast, and at once, casting away the sword, he said: "Nay, you, father, live, and—if you so compliant will permit your son to make this prayer too—surpass me in this too. But only this I ask, that my love toward you be not the cheaper to you for this, that it springs from repentance." O solitude better than blood, and woods more peaceful than household gods, and iron sweeter than nourishment, and the benefit of death offered happier than of life given!
10.pr. Having commemorated fathers who bore the injuries of their children patiently, let us relate those who tolerated their deaths with an even mind.

Nothing did our state hold, in that age, more infamous than Quintus Fabius Maximus—who by his Gallic victory won the surname Allobrogicus for himself and his posterity—as a young man; nothing more honoured or more splendid than the same man as an old man.

M. Antonius, moreover, and L. Flaccus, as censors, removed Duronius from the senate, because, as tribune of the plebs, he had abrogated a law passed for restraining the expenses of banquets. A wonderful cause of the mark: for how shamelessly Duronius mounted the rostra to say these things: "A bridle has been put upon you, Quirites, by no means to be endured. You are bound and constricted by the bitter chain of slavery: for a law has been passed which bids you be frugal. Let us therefore abrogate that command, overgrown with the rust of rough antiquity: for what need is there of liberty, if to those who wish it it is not permitted to perish by luxury?"

Who is ignorant that the authority of Quintus Catulus held a lofty step in the greatest crop of most illustrious men? If his earlier age be reviewed, many sports, many indulgences would be found. These indeed were no hindrance to him from becoming the chief man of his fatherland, and from his name shining on the Capitoline summit, and from his virtue burying, with immense upheaval, a civil war as it was arising.

Come, let me bring forth a pair joined by an equal yoke of virtue and a fellowship of honours, but disagreeing in mind by the impulse of rivalry. Claudius Nero and Livius Salinator, in the times of the second Punic war the firmest flanks of the state, how rigorous a censorship they conducted together! For when they were reviewing the centuries of knights, and were themselves still, by the vigour of their age, of their number, when it came to the Pollian tribe, the herald, the name of Salinator being read out, hesitated whether or not he was to be cited by him. When Nero perceived this, he ordered both his colleague to be cited and his horse to be sold, because he had been condemned by the judgement of the people. Salinator too pursued Nero with the same chastisement, adding as a cause that he had not returned into favour with him in sincere faith.
