To which men, if any of the heavenly powers had signified that it would come to pass that their blood, drawn down through a series of illustrious images, would flow together into the rise of our salutary prince, having laid aside their enmities they would have joined themselves by the closest treaty of friendship, about to leave the fatherland, saved by themselves, to be saved by a common stock. But Salinator did not hesitate to enrol four-and-thirty tribes among the aerarii, because, when they had condemned him, they had afterwards made him consul and censor; and he gave as a pretext the cause that it was necessary that they be held, by one or the other deed, guilty of the charge of rashness or of perjury. One tribe only, the Maecian, he left free of the mark, which by its votes had judged him worthy neither of condemnation nor yet of honour. How steadfast and how very strong a character should we think that man to have been, who could neither be compelled by the sad issue of judgements nor be induced by the greatness of honours to bear himself more flatteringly in the administration of the state?

But Lucius Sulla led, up to the elections of his own quaestorship, a life stained with lust, wine, and the love of the theatrical art. Wherefore the consul Gaius Marius is said to have taken it grievously that to him, waging a most harsh war in Africa, so delicate a quaestor had fallen by lot. The virtue of the same man, as if having burst through and scattered the barriers of the worthlessness by which it was besieged, cast chains upon the hands of Jugurtha, checked Mithridates, repressed the floods of the Social War, broke the domination of Cinna, and compelled him who had disdained him as a quaestor in Africa to seek that very province, proscribed and an exile. If anyone should wish to weigh in his mind, by a more attentive comparison, things so diverse and so contrary to one another, he would believe that there were two Sullas in one man—a base youth and a man whom I should call brave, had he not himself preferred to be called fortunate.

A good and great part of the equestrian order too, four hundred young men, bore the censorial mark with patient mind, whom M'. Valerius and P. Sempronius, because, having been ordered to go in Sicily to carry out the work of fortifications, they had neglected to do it, stripped of their public horses and enrolled in the number of the aerarii.

And, that we may weave in, after the nobility, men who—admonished of their own selves by the benefit of repentance—dared to look back, and to hope for things higher than their station: Titus Aufidius, when he had held a very small share of the Asian revenue-contract, afterwards held all Asia with proconsular command. Nor were his allies indignant to obey the fasces of one whom they had seen flattering at the tribunals of others. He even conducted himself most uprightly and most splendidly. By which means indeed he demonstrated that his former gain ought to be imputed to fortune, but his present increase of dignity to his own character.

The censors exacted a penalty with the utmost severity even for base fear: for M. Atilius Regulus and L. Furius Philus took care that M. Metellus the quaestor and several Roman knights, who after the unhappily begun battle of Cannae had sworn that they would depart from Italy with him, should, their public horses taken away, be enrolled among the aerarii. They also affected with a grievous mark those who, when they had come into the power of Hannibal, sent by him as legates to the senate concerning the exchange of captives, and not having obtained what they sought, remained in the city; because it was both fitting to keep faith with Roman blood, and the censor M. Atilius Regulus marked perfidy, whose father had judged it better to expire amid the greatest torments than to deceive the Carthaginians. Now this censorship passed from the forum into the camp, which willed that the enemy should neither be feared nor deceived.

But Publius Rupilius did not act as a tax-farmer in Sicily, but gave his services to the tax-farmers. The same man supported his utter poverty by hiring out his labour to the contractors. From him afterwards, as consul, all the Sicilians received their laws and were freed from a most bitter war of brigands and runaways. The very harbours, if indeed there is any feeling in dumb things, admired, I think, so great a variety of state in the same man: for him whom they had observed exacting the daily catches, the same they saw giving laws and ruling fleets and armies.

There follow two examples of the same kind, and it will be enough to have added these. C. Geta, when he had been removed from the senate by the censors L. Metellus and Cn. Domitius, was afterwards made censor. Likewise M. Valerius Messala, grazed by the censorial mark, afterwards obtained the censorial power. Their disgrace sharpened their virtue: for, roused by the blush of it, they laboured with all their strength to seem worthy citizens, to whom the censorship ought rather to be given than offered as a reproach.

10.pr. ON MAJESTY. There is also that, as it were, private censorship—the majesty of famous men, powerful in maintaining its own dignity without the loftiness of tribunals, without the service of attendants: for by a pleasing and agreeable entrance it glides into the minds of men, veiled under the pretext of admiration. Rightly might one call it a long and blessed honour without office.

To this so great an increase I shall add a greater. When Asculum was captured, Gnaeus Pompeius, the father of Magnus, brought Publius Ventidius, a boy not yet of age, before the eyes of the people in his triumph. This is that Ventidius who afterwards led a triumph at Rome over the Parthians, and through the Parthians for the shades of Crassus, lying pitiably on hostile soil. Thus he who as a captive had shuddered at prison, as a victor thronged the Capitol with good fortune. In him too was that remarkable thing, that in the same year he was made praetor and consul.

Let us now contemplate the variety of chances. Lucius Lentulus, a consular, overwhelmed under the Caecilian law on a charge of extortion, was created censor with Lucius Censorinus. Him indeed fortune turned about, by alternate vicissitude, between ornaments and disgraces, by setting condemnation after his consulship, and the censorship after his condemnation, and by suffering him neither to enjoy perpetual goods nor to groan under eternal evils.

It wished to use the same force in the case of Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina. He, as consul captured by the Carthaginians at Lipara, when by the law of war he had lost everything, presently aided by its more cheerful countenance recovered all and was even created consul a second time. Who would have believed that he would pass from twelve axes to the chains of the Carthaginians? Who again would have thought that he would pass from Punic chains to the insignia of the highest command? But nevertheless from a consul he was made a captive, and from a captive a consul.

What, did not the magnitude of his money give Crassus the name of "the Rich"? But on the same man afterwards poverty branded the disgraceful appellation of a bankrupt, since indeed his goods were sold by his creditors, because he could not pay in full. And so he who did not lack the bitter sneer, when he walked about needy, was saluted "Dives" by those who met him.

Crassus, Quintus Caepio outran in bitterness of misfortune: for he, having attained by the splendour of his praetorship, the renown of his triumph, the dignity of his consulship, the priesthood of the chief pontificate, to be called the patron of the senate, laid down his breath in the public prison, and his body, mangled by the deadly hands of the executioner, was beheld lying on the Gemonian Stairs, with great horror of the whole Roman forum.

Now there is Gaius Marius, with the struggle of the greatest fortune: for all its onsets he sustained most bravely, by the strength now of body, now of mind. Judged inferior in the honours of Arpinum, he dared to seek the quaestorship at Rome. Then, by his endurance of rejections, he burst into the senate-house rather than entered it. In his candidacy for the tribunate too and the aedileship having experienced a like mark of the Campus, as a candidate for the praetorship he clung to the last place, which yet he obtained not without peril: for, accused of bribery, he scarcely and with difficulty obtained acquittal from the judges. Out of that Marius, so humble at Arpinum, so ignoble at Rome, so contemptible a candidate, emerged that Marius who subdued Africa, who drove King Jugurtha before his chariot, who destroyed the armies of the Teutons and the Cimbri, whose two trophies are beheld in the city, whose seven consulships are read in the calendars, to whom it fell, after exile, to be created consul, and, proscribed, to make a proscription. What is more inconstant or more changeable than his condition? Whom, if you place him among the wretched, you will find most wretched; if among the fortunate, most fortunate.

But Gaius Caesar, whose virtues built him an approach to heaven, in the beginnings of his first youth, a private man, seeking Asia, was taken by the pirates of the sea around the island of Pharmacusa and ransomed himself for fifty talents. For a small sum, therefore, fortune willed the most illustrious star of the world to be weighed out in a piratical skiff. What is there, then, that we should complain of it any further, if it spares not even the partners of its own divinity? But the heavenly power avenged itself of the wrong: for at once Caesar, having captured the pirates, affixed them to crosses.

9e.1. With attentive zeal we have commemorated our own affairs: now with a more relaxed mind let foreign ones be narrated. Polemo, a young man of ruined luxury at Athens, rejoicing not only in its allurements but even in its very infamy, when he had risen from a banquet not after the setting but after the rising of the sun, and, returning home, had seen the open door of Xenocrates the philosopher, heavy with wine, anointed with perfumes, his head wreathed with garlands, clad in a translucent robe, entered his school, crowded with a throng of learned men. And not content with so unseemly an entrance, he even sat down, that he might cheapen the most illustrious eloquence and the most prudent precepts by the wantonness of his drunkenness. Then, the indignation of all arising, as was fitting, Xenocrates kept his countenance in the same state and, leaving the subject he was discussing, began to speak about modesty and temperance. By the gravity of his discourse Polemo, compelled to come to his senses, first cast off the garland torn from his head, a little after drew his arm within his cloak, as time went on laid aside the convivial cheerfulness of his face, at last put off all his luxury, and, cured by the most salutary medicine of a single speech, out of an infamous reveller turned out a very great philosopher. His mind travelled abroad in worthlessness; it did not dwell there.

9e.2. It irks me to touch upon the adolescence of Themistocles, whether I look at his father imposing on him the mark of disinheritance, or at his mother compelled to end her life by hanging on account of her son's disgrace—when he afterwards proved the most illustrious of all the men of Greek blood and was the pledge, between Europe and Asia, of either hope or despair: for the one had him as the patron of its safety, the other took him as the surety of victory.

9e.3. The cradle of Cimon, indeed, was filled with the reputation of foolishness; but his salutary commands, when grown, the Athenians felt. And so he compelled them to condemn themselves of stupidity, who had believed him stolid.

9e.4. For Alcibiades two fortunes, as it were, divided between them—the one, which assigned to him outstanding nobility, abundant riches, a most excellent form, the propense favour of the citizens, the highest commands, the chief forces of power, a most blazing talent; the other, which inflicted condemnation, exile, the sale of his goods, want, the hatred of his fatherland, a violent death—and neither these nor those together, but variously interwoven, like a strait and a tide.

9e.5. The brilliance of the life of Polycrates, tyrant of the Samians, conspicuous for most abundant goods, advanced even to envy, and not without cause: for all his attempts were received on a calm course, his hopes grasped the sure fruit of the thing desired, his vows were vowed and at the same time fulfilled, to will and to be able were placed on an equality. Only once did he change his countenance, shaken by a very brief jolt of sadness, then when he deliberately threw into the deep a ring most pleasing to him, that he might not be free of all inconvenience. Yet he at once recovered it, a fish being caught which had devoured it. But this man, whose good fortune always held a prosperous course with full sails, Orontes, the prefect of King Darius, affixed to a cross on the loftiest peak of Mount Mycale—from which his rotting joints and his limbs dripping with corrupt gore, and that left hand to which Neptune had restored the ring by the hand of a fisherman, shrivelled with decay, Samos, for some time oppressed by bitter slavery, beheld with free and joyful eyes.

9e.6. But Dionysius, when he had received the tyranny of the Syracusans, and almost of all Sicily, by way of inheritance from his father—master of the greatest resources, leader of armies, ruler of fleets, powerful in cavalry—on account of poverty taught letters to little boys at Corinth, and at the same time, by so great a change, warned his elders, made a schoolmaster out of a tyrant, that no one should trust too much in fortune.

9e.7. This man King Syphax follows, who experienced a like iniquity of fortune—he whom, sought of their own accord on this side by Rome through Scipio, on that by Carthage through Hasdrubal as a friend, both had come to his household gods. But, raised to such renown that he proved almost the arbiter of victory between most powerful peoples, after the lapse of a little time he was dragged in chains by Laelius the legate to Scipio the commander, and at the knees of him whose right hand, sitting on a royal throne, he had touched with an arrogant hand, he fell down a suppliant. Frail indeed and fragile, and consonant with childish rattles, are those things which are called human powers and resources. They flow in suddenly, they slip away suddenly; in no place, in no person do they stand fixed on stable roots, but, driven hither and thither by the most uncertain breath of fortune, those whom they have raised on high, abandoned by a sudden recoil, they pitiably plunge into the deep of disasters. And so they ought neither to be deemed nor called goods which, that they may double the longing for themselves by the bitterness of inflicted evils, . . .

1.pr. ON GOOD FORTUNE We have related a good many examples of fortune in its changeable course; of fortune consistently favourable very few can be told. From this it is clear that fortune deals out adversity with a greedy spirit, and prosperity with a sparing hand. Yet this same fortune, when it has bidden itself forget its malice, heaps up not only the greatest and most numerous blessings, but enduring ones as well.

For what more could be granted to a consul than was given to Metellus when on trial? When he was pleading his cause for extortion, and his account-books, demanded by the accuser, were carried around among the judges for the inspection of his name, the whole court turned its eyes away from the contemplation of them, lest it should seem to have doubted concerning anything which was entered in them. The judges believed that the proofs of a province sincerely administered must be read by them not in the account-books but in the life of Q. Metellus, deeming it unworthy that the integrity of so great a man should be weighed by a little wax and a few letters.

ON PARENTS WHO BORE THE DEATH OF THEIR CHILDREN WITH A BRAVE SPIRIT Horatius Pulvillus, when on the Capitol, as pontifex, he was dedicating a temple to Jupiter Best and Greatest, and amid the pronouncement of the solemn words, holding the doorpost, had heard that his son was dead, neither removed his hand from the doorpost, lest he should interrupt the dedication of so great a temple, nor turned his countenance from public religion to private grief, lest he should seem to have played the part of a father rather than of a pontifex. A famous example, and yet no less illustrious is the one which follows.

But, that the trustworthiness of the proposition may be displayed in illustrious persons, C. Gracchus, a young man of more fortunate eloquence than purpose—since, with a most ardent genius, when he could best protect the state, he impiously preferred to throw it into confusion—as often as he harangued before the people, kept behind him a slave skilled in the art of music, who secretly with an ivory pipe shaped the modulations of his delivery, either by exciting it when too languid or by recalling it when more excited than was right, because the heat and impulse of the pleading did not allow him to be an attentive judge of this tempering.

The tribune of the plebs M. Flavius brought before the people a motion concerning the Tusculans, because he said that by their counsel the people of Velitrae and Privernum were going to rebel. When they had come to Rome as suppliants, with their wives and children, covered with squalor, it happened that, the rest of the tribes following the salutary opinion, the Pollian tribe alone judged that they ought to be publicly scourged and beheaded, and the unwarlike multitude sold under the crown. On which account the Papirian tribe, in which afterwards the Tusculans, received into citizenship, had very great influence, never made any candidate of the Pollian tribe a magistrate, lest any honour should reach by its votes that tribe which had taken away from them, as far as in it lay, their life and liberty.

But what wonder if due honour was paid by his fellow-citizens to Metellus, when even an enemy did not hesitate to render it to the elder Africanus? For King Antiochus, in the war which he was waging with the Romans, received most honourably his son, intercepted by his soldiers, and, having presented him with royal gifts, sent him back to his father of his own accord and speedily, although he was then especially being driven by him from the bounds of his empire. But the king, and one provoked, preferred to venerate the majesty of a most excellent man rather than to avenge his own grief. To the same Africanus, while he was keeping himself in his villa at Liternum, several leaders of brigands chanced to flock together at the same time to see him. When he supposed that they had come to do violence, he stationed a guard of his household within the house, and was occupied both in spirit and in preparation for repelling them. When the brigands perceived this, having dismissed their men and cast away their arms, they approached the door and announced in a clear voice that they had come to Scipio not as enemies of his life but as admirers of his virtue, seeking the sight and meeting of so great a man as if some heavenly benefit: therefore he need not be troubled to offer himself, secure, to be beheld by them. After his household had reported this to Scipio, he ordered the doors to be unbarred and them to be admitted. They, having venerated the doorposts of the door as if some most holy altar and sacred temple, eagerly grasped the right hand of Scipio, and, having long kissed it, having laid before the vestibule gifts such as are wont to be consecrated to the divine power of the immortal gods, joyful that it had fallen to their lot to have seen Scipio, returned to their homes. What is more lofty than this fruit of majesty, what indeed more agreeable? He appeased the anger of an enemy by the admiration of himself; he saw the longing eyes of brigands at the spectacle of his presence. If the stars, fallen from heaven, should offer themselves to men, they would receive no greater veneration.

Aemilius Paulus, the most illustrious representation now of a most fortunate, now of a most wretched father, of his four sons of remarkable beauty and outstanding disposition denied two to himself by the right of adoption, having transferred them into the Cornelian and Fabian clans; two fortune took from him. Of these, the one went before his father's triumph by his own death four days before it, the other, beheld in the triumphal chariot, expired three days after. And so he who had abounded even to the point of giving away his children was suddenly left destitute in bereavement. With what strength of spirit he bore this misfortune he left ambiguous to no one by adding this conclusion to the speech which he delivered before the people about the things done by him: "When, amid the greatest abundance of our good fortune, Quirites, I feared lest fortune should be contriving some evil, I prayed Jupiter Best and Greatest and Juno the Queen and Minerva that, if any adversity threatened the Roman people, it might be turned wholly upon my house. Wherefore it is well: for by granting my prayers they have so brought it about that you should grieve at my misfortune rather than that I should groan at yours."

Q. Hortensius, moreover, believing that much was placed in the graceful movement of the body, expended almost more zeal in elaborating it than in cultivating eloquence itself. And so you would not know whether men flocked more eagerly to hear him or to watch him: so much did the orator's appearance serve his words, and again his words serve his appearance. It is agreed that Aesopus and Roscius, most skilled in the player's art, often stood by in the ring while he was pleading cases, so that they might carry to the stage the gestures sought in the forum.

That vengeance, indeed, both the senate and the consensus of all approved: for when Adrianus had harassed with a sordid command the Roman citizens who dwelt at Utica, and on that account had been burned alive by them, neither was any inquiry held in this city about the matter nor any complaint stirred.

10e.1. Famous in vengeance was each queen, both Tomyris, who ordered the severed head of Cyrus to be plunged into a skin filled with human blood, reproaching him with his insatiable thirst for gore and at the same time exacting the penalties for her son slain by him, and Berenice, who, bearing heavily the interception of her son by the treachery of Laodice, mounted her chariot armed, and, having pursued the royal attendant, the minister of the cruel work, named Caeneus, whom she had vainly aimed at with her spear, laid him low struck with a stone, and, her horses driven over his body, made her way through the hostile columns of the opposing party to the house in which she supposed the body of the slain boy to be hidden.

10e.2. Whether a sufficiently just vengeance carried off Jason the Thessalian, who was preparing to make war on the king of the Persians, is of ambiguous estimation: for when Taxillus the gymnasiarch had complained that he had been struck by certain young men, he permitted that he should either exact thirty drachmas from them or inflict ten blows on each. The men who had been beaten, when he used the latter penalty, killed Jason, estimating the measure of the punishment by the grief of the mind, not of the body. But by a small incitement of free-born shame the expectation of the greatest matter was undermined, since in the opinion of Greece as much was placed in the hope of Jason as in the achievement of Alexander.

11.pr. WICKED SAYINGS OR CRIMINAL DEEDS Now, inasmuch as we pursue both the good and also the bad of human life by setting in place the images of examples, let wicked sayings and criminal deeds be reported.

And these things indeed befell Scipio living; but the following befell Aemilius Paulus dead: for when his obsequies were being celebrated, and by chance the chief men of Macedonia were then staying at Rome in the name of an embassy, they of their own accord put themselves beneath the funeral bier. Which will seem somewhat greater, if anyone learns that the front of that bier had been adorned with Macedonian triumphs: for how much they paid to Paulus, on whose account they did not shudder to carry the tokens of the disasters of their nation before the faces of the crowd! Which spectacle added to the funeral the appearance of a second triumph: for twice, Paulus, did Macedonia show you illustrious to our city—unharmed by her spoils, and in death by her shoulders.

With one more domestic example added even now, I shall permit my discourse to wander among the griefs of others. Quintus Marcius Rex, the colleague of the elder Cato in the consulship, lost a son of the highest dutifulness and great promise, and—what was no small addition to his calamity—an only son; and when he saw himself undermined and overthrown by his death, he so curbed his grief by the depth of his counsel that from the young man's pyre he at once sought the senate-house and convened the senate, which on that day he was obliged by law to hold. Had he not known how to bear his mourning bravely, he could not have divided the light of a single day between a calamitous father and a vigorous consul, with no part of his duty neglected on either side.

10e.1. Pericles, the chief of the Athenians, within the space of four days bereft of two marvellous young sons, in those very days both with his countenance retaining its former state and with his oratory in no part more broken delivered a public address. He even endured to wear his head crowned in the wonted manner, that he might detract nothing from the old rite on account of his domestic wound. Not without cause, then, did a spirit of so great strength rise to the surname of Olympian Jupiter.

10e.2. Xenophon, moreover, as far as concerns the Socratic school the nearest after Plato in the rank of happy and blessed eloquence, when he was performing a solemn sacrifice, learned that of his two sons the elder by birth, named Gryllus, had fallen in battle at Mantinea: nor on that account did he think the worship of the gods that he had begun should be omitted, but was content only to lay aside his garland. And having inquired about that very garland in what manner he had fallen, when he heard that he had perished fighting most bravely, he set it back upon his head, calling to witness the divinities to whom he was sacrificing that he felt greater pleasure from his son's valour than bitterness from his death. Another would have removed the victim, would have cast away the altar, would have scattered the incense bedewed with tears: the body of Xenophon stood unmoved in its religious office, and his mind remained steadfast in the counsel of prudence, and he judged it more grievous to succumb to grief than to the very disaster which had been announced.

10e.3. Nor should Anaxagoras be suppressed: for, on hearing of the death of his son, he said, "You announce to me nothing unexpected or new: for I knew that he, born from me, was mortal." Such utterances, imbued with the most useful precepts, virtue sends forth. And if anyone shall receive them effectively into his ears, he will not be ignorant that children are to be begotten in such a way that he remember that to them, by the nature of things, the law of both receiving breath and rendering it is appointed at one and the same moment of time; and that, as no one is wont to die who has not lived, so neither can anyone live who is not destined to die.

1.pr. ON CHASTITY From what source shall I invoke you, Chastity, the chief stay of men and women alike? For you dwell on the hearths of Vesta, consecrated by the ancient religion; you recline upon the cushions of Capitoline Juno; you frequent, with unbroken watch, the pillar of the Palatine, its august household gods and the most sacred marriage couch of Julia; by your protection the insignia of boyhood are made safe; by regard for your divinity the pure flower of youth endures; under your guardianship the matron's gown is held in honour. Be present, then, and recognize the things which you yourself willed to come to pass.

M. Cicero, moreover, in his speech which he delivered for Gallius, indicated how great importance there is in each of the things of which we speak, by reproaching M. Calidius the accuser, because, when he affirmed that he would prove by witnesses, written documents, and interrogations under torture that poison had been prepared for him by the defendant, he had used a relaxed countenance, a languid voice, and a loose kind of oratory; and at once he both uncovered the orator's fault and added a proof for the imperilled defendant, by thus closing this whole passage: "Would you, M. Calidius, plead that thus, unless you were inventing it?"

10e.1. In keeping with this is the judgment of Demosthenes, who, when he was asked what was most effective in speaking, replied, "Delivery." Then, interrupted again a second and a third time, he said the same, confessing that he owed almost all to it. Rightly, therefore, did Aeschines, when on account of a judicial disgrace he had left Athens and made for Rhodes, and there, at the request of the city, had recited first his own speech against Ctesiphon, then that of Demosthenes for the same man, in a most clear and most pleasant voice—when all were admiring the eloquence of both volumes, but somewhat more that of Demosthenes—say, "What, if you had heard the man himself?" So great an orator, and a little before so hostile an adversary, so looked up to the force and ardour of his enemy's speaking that he declared himself too inadequate a reader of his writings, having experienced the keenest vigour of his eyes, the terrible weight of his countenance, the sound of voice fitted to single words, the most effective movements of his body. Therefore, although nothing can be added to his work, yet in Demosthenes a great part of Demosthenes is absent, because he is read rather than heard.

11.pr. HOW GREAT THE EFFECTS OF THE ARTS ARE The effects of the arts too, to review them, can bring some pleasure; and forthwith it will be clear both how usefully they were devised, and matters worthy of mention will be placed in a clear light, and the labour in setting them forth will not lack its own fruit.

Nor was too little honour paid to the majesty even of your son Scipio Aemilianus, whom by giving in adoption you willed to be the ornament of two families, when the Carthaginians and King Masinissa had him, while quite a young man, sent from Spain into Africa by the consul Lucullus for the sake of seeking aid, as an arbiter of peace, like a consul and a commander. Carthage indeed was ignorant of its own fates: for that glory of rising youth, by the indulgence of gods and men, was being nourished for her destruction, so as to give to the Cornelian clan the former surname Africanus when she was captured, the latter when she was overthrown.

What is more wretched than condemnation, what than exile? And yet P. Rutilius, struck down by the conspiracy of the publicans, they could not avail to deprive of his authority. To him, as he made for Asia, all the cities of that province sent legates to meet him, awaiting his retirement. One might more justly say that someone was triumphing in this place than going into exile.

C. Marius too, cast into the depths of the utmost miseries, emerged from the very crisis of his life by the benefit of majesty: for a public slave, by nation a Cimbrian, sent to slay him as he lay shut up in a private house at Minturnae, did not bring himself to attack an old man, unarmed and covered with squalor, though he held a drawn sword, and, blinded by the renown of the man, casting away the steel, fled thence astonished and trembling. The Cimbric calamity, no doubt, dazzled the eyes of the man, and the destruction of his conquered nation shattered his courage—the immortal gods too deeming it unworthy that Marius should be slain by one of that nation which he had wholly destroyed. The people of Minturnae, moreover, captivated by his majesty, preserved unharmed him whom they had already seized and bound, freeing him from the dread necessity of fate. Nor was the most harsh victory of Sulla a terror to them, especially when Marius himself could have deterred them from preserving Marius.

M. Porcius Cato too the admiration of his brave and sincere life made so venerable to the senate that, when against the will of C. Caesar the consul he was drawing out the day by speaking in the senate-house against the publicans, and on that account by his order was being led by a lictor to prison, the whole senate did not hesitate to follow him. This thing bent the perseverance of that divine spirit.

While the same man was watching the Floral games, which Messius the aedile was holding, the people blushed to demand that the mime-actresses should be stripped. When he had learned this from Favonius, his closest friend, sitting beside him, he departed from the theatre, lest by his presence he should hinder the custom of the spectacle. As he was going away, the people followed him with mighty applause, and recalled the ancient manner of jests to the stage, confessing that they paid more majesty to him alone than they claimed for their whole selves. By what resources, by what commands, by what triumphs was this granted? The man's patrimony was small, his manners bound by self-restraint, his clients modest, his house closed to ambition, of his paternal line a single image, his brow least flattering—but his virtue perfect in all its numbers. Which indeed brought it about that whoever wishes to signify a holy and excellent citizen defines him under the name of Cato.

10e.1. Some place must be given also to foreign examples, so that, sprinkled upon the domestic, they may delight by their very variety. The bronze statues of Harmodius and Aristogiton, who tried to free Athens from tyranny, Xerxes, when he had conquered that city, transferred into his own kingdom. Then, after a long interval of time, Seleucus took care that they should be carried back to their former seat. The Rhodians too, when they had been brought to their city, since they had invited them at public expense to hospitality, even placed them on sacred couches. Nothing is happier than this memory, which possesses so much veneration in so very little bronze.

10e.2. How great an honour, moreover, was paid at Athens to Xenocrates, illustrious alike for wisdom and for holiness! When, compelled to give testimony, he had approached the altar, in order to swear, after the custom of that city, that he had reported everything truly, all the judges rose up and proclaimed that he should not take the oath, and what they were afterwards not going to remit to themselves, in giving their own sentence, they thought ought to be conceded to his sincerity.

pr.1. I shall touch, as it were, upon certain cradles and first elements of virtue, and shall set down the foretastes given, with sure proof of natural disposition, of a spirit destined in the course of time to attain the highest summit of glory.

The very great zeal of Sulpicius Gallus in perceiving every kind of learning profited the state very much: for when he was the legate of L. Paulus, who was waging war against king Perses, and on a clear night the moon was suddenly eclipsed, and our army, terrified by it as by some dire portent, had lost the confidence to engage with the enemy, by disputing most skilfully about the nature of the heavens and the character of the stars, he sent it eager into the battle line. And so the liberal arts of Gallus gave access to that famous Paulian victory, because, unless he had conquered the fear of our soldiers, the commander could not have conquered the enemy.

From whom, moreover, should I rather begin than from Tullia, because in time it is a most ancient, in conscience a wicked, in report a monster-like example? When she was being carried in a carriage and he who drove the team, the reins jerked, had halted, she demanded the cause of the sudden delay; and when she learned that the body of her slain father Servius Tullius lay there, she ordered the vehicle to be driven over it, so that she might come the more quickly into the embrace of his slayer Tarquinius. By so impious and so shameful a haste she defiled not only herself with eternal infamy, but even the very street with the surname of crime.

Of Spurinna too the knowledge in conjecturing the warnings of the gods appeared more effective than the city of Rome would have wished. He had foretold to C. Caesar that he should beware the next thirty days as though they were fatal, of which the last was the Ides of March. When on that day both happened to meet in the morning at the house of Calvinus Domitius to pay their respects, Caesar said to Spurinna, "Do you know at all that the Ides of March have now come?" But he said, "Do you know at all that they have not yet passed?" The one had cast off fear as though the suspected time were spent, the other thought that not even its last part was free from peril. Would that security had deceived the soothsayer about his augury rather than the father of his country!

11e.1. But, to scrutinize a foreign example, when, the sun being suddenly darkened, Athens, bathed in unaccustomed shadows, was tormented with anxiety, believing that destruction was being portended to it by a heavenly announcement, Pericles came forth into their midst and discoursed on what he had received from his teacher Anaxagoras concerning the course of the sun and moon, and did not allow his fellow citizens to tremble further with vain fear.
11e.2. How great dignity, moreover, do we suppose was assigned to art by king Alexander, who wished to be painted by Apelles alone and modelled by Lysippus only?

11e.3. The Vulcan fashioned by the hands of Alcamenes holds those who view it at Athens: for besides the other tokens of the most perfect art running through it, men admire also this, that it stands, lightly representing under its garment the trace of a dissembled lameness, so that it is shown gracefully, not as a fault reproached, but as a sure and proper mark of the god.

11e.4. His consort Praxiteles placed in marble, as though breathing, in the temple of the Cnidians, too little safe, on account of the beauty of the work, from the lustful embrace of a certain man. The more excusable, therefore, is the error of the horse which, on seeing the picture of a mare, was forced to neigh, and the barking of dogs roused by the sight of a painted dog, and the bull at Syracuse driven to love and union with a bronze cow by the incitement of too great a likeness: for why should we wonder that creatures void of reason were deceived by art, when we see that the sacrilegious desire of a man was excited by the outlines of mute stone?

11e.5. THAT CERTAIN THINGS CAN BE ACHIEVED BY NO ART But nature, just as it often suffers art to be the rival of its powers, so sometimes dismisses it baffled with weary labour. This the hands of the supreme artist Euphranor felt: for when he was painting at Athens the twelve gods, he embraced the image of Neptune in the most excellent colours of majesty he could, intending to represent that of Jupiter as somewhat more august. But, all the impulse of his thought being spent on the former work, his later attempts could not rise to where they aimed.

11e.6. What of that other equally noble painter, representing the mournful sacrifice of Iphigenia, when he had set Calchas sad, Ulysses grieving, Menelaus lamenting around the altar—did he not, by veiling the head of Agamemnon, confess that the bitterness of the deepest grief could not be expressed by art? And so his picture is wet with the tears of the soothsayer, the friend, and the brother, but he left the father's weeping to be estimated by the feeling of the beholder.

11e.7. And, to add an example of the same pursuit, a painter of outstanding art had captured, by the labour of his industry, a horse coming all but alive from its exercise. Desiring to add foam to its nostrils, so great an artist was much and long worn out in vain over so tiny a matter. Then, kindled with indignation, he seized a sponge soaked in all the colours, which happened to be placed beside him, and dashed it against the panel as though about to spoil his own work. Fortune, directing it to the very nostrils of the horse, forced it to fulfil the painter's desire. And so what art could not sketch, chance imitated.
12.pr. THAT EACH MAN IS THE BEST AUTHORITY AND DISPUTANT OF HIS OWN ART That each man is the best authority and disputant of his own art, lest we doubt it, let us be reminded by a few examples.

Less atrocious was the deed and saying of C. Fimbria; but if each be estimated in itself, both were most audacious. He had brought it about that Scaevola should be slain at the funeral of C. Marius. After he learned that he had recovered from his wound, he set about to accuse him before the people. Being asked then what he was going to say against a man to whom, for the holiness of his character, no worthy enough praise could be rendered, he replied that he would reproach him because he had received the weapon too sparingly into his body. A licence of frenzy to be accompanied with the groan of an ailing state!

L. Catiline, moreover, when in the senate M. Cicero said that a conflagration had been stirred up by him, said, "I perceive it, and indeed, if I cannot quench it with water, I will quench it with ruin." What else should we think of him than that, driven by the goads of conscience, he carried himself through as the defendant of a parricide he had begun?

The breast of the Magian Chilo too was distracted by madness, who with his own hand took away the life given to M. Marcellus by Caesar—an old friend and companion of Pompeian service, indignant that some of his friends were preferred to him by Marcellus: for, as Marcellus was making again for the city from Mytilene, whither he had betaken himself, he stabbed him with a dagger in the harbour of the Athenians, and at once made for the things that incited his frenzy, to butcher them—an enemy of friendship, an interceptor of a divine benefit, a bitter blot upon the public religion, as far as it concerned the recovery of the safety of a most distinguished citizen.

This cruelty, to which nothing seems able to be added, C. Toranius surpassed by the atrocity of a parricide: for, having followed the party of the triumvirs, he disclosed to the centurions who pursued him the hiding-place, the age, and the bodily marks by which he could be recognized, of his proscribed father, a praetorian and distinguished man. The old man, anxious rather about the life and advancement of his son than about his own remaining breath, began to ask them whether he was safe and whether he satisfied the commanders. One of them said, "By that man whom you so greatly love, pointed out, you will be killed by our service, on your son's information"; and at once he ran his sword through his breast. And so the unhappy man collapsed, more wretched in the author of his murder than in the murder itself.

The bitterness of this fate L. Villius Annalis drew by lot, who, going down into the Campus to the quaestorian elections of his son, when he learned that he had been proscribed, fled to his client. But that he might not be safe by his loyalty was effected by the crime of the wicked youth, since indeed, leading the soldiers along the very footsteps of his father, he set him before them to be killed in his own sight—twice a parricide, first by counsel, again by spectacle.

Not even Vettius Salassus, when proscribed, had too little a bitter end. Him, hidden, did his wife hand over to be killed—what shall I say, or did she slay him herself? For how much lighter is a crime from which only the hand is absent?

11e.1. But that deed, because it is foreign, will be related with a more tranquil feeling. When Scipio Africanus was celebrating the memory of his father and uncle with a gladiatorial show at New Carthage, two sons of a king, whose father had recently died, came forth into the arena and promised that they would there fight it out about the kingdom, so that they might make that spectacle more illustrious by their combat. When Scipio had advised them to prefer to decide by words rather than by the sword which of them ought to reign, and the elder was now obeying his counsel, the younger, relying on the strength of his body, persisted in his madness, and, the contest joined, the more obstinate impiety was punished with death by the judgment of fortune.

11e.2. Mithridates, moreover, was much more criminal, who waged war about dominion not with his brother over the paternal kingdom, but with his very father. He who in it either found any men as helpers or dared to invoke the gods is held in especial wonder.

11e.3. Although why should we wonder at this as something unusual to those peoples, when Sariaster against his father Tigranes, king of Armenia, so agreed with his friends that they all let blood from their right hands and drank it in turn? I should scarcely endure a man making a covenant by so bloody a conspiracy for the safety of a parent.

11e.4. But why do I pursue these things or why do I dwell on them, when I see all crimes surpassed by the mere thought of a single parricide? With every impulse of mind, therefore, with all the strength of indignation, I am carried, by a feeling more pious than strong, to tear it to pieces: for who, when the loyalty of friendship was extinguished, could drive with words sufficiently effective into the depth of deserved execration one who tried to bury the human race in bloody darkness? You, of course, more savage than the monstrousness of maddened barbarism, were able to seize the reins of the Roman empire, which our prince and parent holds with his salutary right hand? Or, with you master of your frenzy, would the world have remained in its condition? The city captured by the Gauls, and the river Cremera defiled by the slaughter of three hundred men of a famous family, and the day of the Allia, and the Scipios crushed in Spain, and the lake Trasimene, and Cannae, and the frenzies of the civil wars dripping with domestic blood, you wished to bring back by the mad designs of your frenzy, and to surpass. But the eyes of the gods kept watch, the stars retained their vigour, the altars, the sacred couches, the temples were walled about by a present divine power, and nothing which ought to have kept watch over the august head and the country permitted itself torpor; and above all, the author and guardian of our safety, lest his most excellent deserts should collapse in the ruin of the whole world, provided by divine counsel. And so peace stands, the laws are strong, the sincere course of private and public duty is preserved. But he who, the bonds of friendship being violated, tried to overthrow these things, crushed with all his stock by the might of the Roman people, pays even among the shades below—if indeed he was received there—the punishments he deserves.

12.pr. ON DEATHS NOT COMMON The condition of human life, moreover, is contained chiefly in its first and last day, because it makes the greatest difference under what auspices it is begun and with what end it is closed; and therefore we judge that man only to have been happy to whom it fell both to receive the light prosperously and to render it back peacefully. The course of the middle time, as fortune has guided the helm, is passed through now with a harsh, now with a tranquil motion, always less than our hope, while it is both eagerly stretched out by our prayers and generally consumed without reason. For even if you wish to use it well, you will make even a small life most ample, by surpassing the number of years by the multitude of your works: otherwise, what is the point of rejoicing in an inert delay, if you spin out life rather than approve it? But, not to wander further, I shall make mention of those who were carried off by a kind of death not common.

Q. Scaevola, the most famous and most reliable prophet of the laws, as often as he was consulted about the law concerning surety for the state's property, would refer his consultors to Furius and Cascellius, because they were devoted to this knowledge. By this deed indeed he commended his own moderation rather than diminished his authority, confessing that that business could be more aptly explained by those who were expert in it by daily practice. The wisest professors of their art, therefore, are those by whom both their own studies are modestly and the studies of others shrewdly appraised.

12e.1. The most erudite breast of Plato too this thought touched, who ordered the contractors of a sacred altar, who had tried to confer with him about its size and form, to go to Euclid the geometer, yielding to his knowledge—nay, to his profession.

12e.2. Athens glories in its arsenal, and not without cause: for that work is to be viewed both for its expense and its elegance. Its architect Philo, it is agreed, gave the account of his construction in the theatre so eloquently that the most eloquent people awarded no less praise to his eloquence than to his art.

12e.3. Wonderfully too did that artist, who, having allowed himself to be corrected in his work by a shoemaker about the sandal and its little straps, when the man began to dispute also about the leg, forbade him to climb above the sole.

13.pr. ON OLD AGE Old age too, advanced to its furthest limit, has been observed in this same work among the examples of industry in several famous men. Let it nevertheless have a separate and proper heading, lest he to whom the especial indulgence of the immortal gods was present should be thought to have lacked our honoured mention; and at the same time, that there may be given, as it were, certain supports for the hope of a longer life, leaning on which one may make oneself more eager by regard for ancient happiness, and from time to time may confirm by trust the tranquillity of our age, than which none was ever more blessed, by prolonging the safety of our salutary prince to the longest limits of the human condition.

Tullus Hostilius, struck by a thunderbolt, was burned up with his whole house. A singular lot of fate, by which it happened that the pillar of the city, snatched away in the very city, could not be honoured by his fellow citizens even with the last honour of a funeral, reduced by a heavenly flame to this condition, that he had the same household gods for both palace and pyre and tomb.

It is scarcely like the truth that in snatching away the breath joy could have the same power as a thunderbolt; and yet the same had power. For, the disaster which had befallen at the lake Trasimene being announced, one mother, made to meet her safe son at the very gate, expired in his embrace; another, when she sat at home in mourning at a false report of her son's death, was struck lifeless at the first sight of his return. An unusual kind of mischance! Those whom grief had not extinguished, joy consumed. But I wonder the less, because they were women.

M'. Iuventius Thalna, consul, colleague of Ti. Gracchus consul for the second time, when in Corsica, which he had recently subdued, he was sacrificing, having received a letter announcing that supplications had been decreed to him by the senate, reading it with intent mind, a mist arising, collapsed before the little altar and lay dead on the ground. What else should we think than that he was killed by too great joy? Lo, to whom Numantia or Carthage might be handed over to be destroyed!

Of somewhat greater spirit was the leader Q. Catulus, given by the senate as a sharer in the Cimbrian triumph to C. Marius, but of a more violent end: for, ordered to die afterwards by this same Marius on account of civil dissensions, he killed himself shut up in a chamber smeared with fresh lime and heated thoroughly by much fire. His . . . so dire a necessity became the greatest blush of Marian glory.

At which storm of the state L. Cornelius Merula too, consular and flamen Dialis, lest he should be a mockery to most insolent conquerors, in the sanctuary of Jupiter, his veins cut, escaped the announcement of an insulting death, and the most ancient hearth was wet with the blood of its own priest.

Keen too and spirited was the departure from life of Herennius the Sicilian, whom C. Gracchus had used both as a soothsayer and as a friend: for when on that account he was being led to prison, dashing his head against its doorpost, he fell at the very entrance of disgrace and gave up his breath, by one step nearer than public punishment and the hand of the executioner.

By a like impulse of death, C. Licinius Macer, a praetorian man, the father of Calvus, a defendant on a charge of extortion, while the votes were being counted, climbed up to a balcony. Since indeed, when he had seen M. Cicero, who was convening that court, laying down his praetextate toga, he sent to him to say that he had perished not as a condemned man but as a defendant, and that his goods could not be subjected to the spear; and at once, with the handkerchief which he happened to have in his hand stuffed into his mouth and throat, his breath shut in, he forestalled his punishment by death. On learning this, Cicero pronounced nothing about him. Therefore an orator of illustrious genius was rescued both from the poverty of his property and from the charge of a domestic condemnation by an unusual kind of his father's fate.

The death of this man was brave; those of the following were most ridiculous: for Cornelius Gallus, a praetorian, and T. Etereius, a Roman knight, were carried off during the use of love. Although, to what end is it to scoff at the fates of those whom not their own lust but the principle of human frailty carried off? For, the end of our life being exposed to various and hidden causes, sometimes things that are undeserving occupy the title of the supreme fate, since they rather coincide with the time of death than themselves summon death.

12e.1. There are also foreign deaths worthy of note. Such, before all, was that of Comas, who, they say, was the brother of Cleon, the greatest leader of the brigands: for, led before the consul P. Rupilius after Henna, which the robbers had held, had been reduced into our power, when he was being questioned about the strength and attempts of the fugitives, taking time to collect himself, he covered his head, and, leaning on his knees, with his breath compressed, amid the very hands of his guards and in the sight of the highest command, rested in the security he had longed for. Let the wretched torment themselves for whom to be extinguished is more useful than to survive, in trembling and anxious counsel seeking by what means they may go forth from life: let them sharpen the sword, temper poisons, grasp nooses, look around at vast heights, as though great apparatus or an exquisite contrivance were needed for the partnership of body and mind, cohering by a weak bond, to be sundered. None of these did Comas use, but his soul, shut up within his breast, found its own end: for, in truth, that good is not to be retained with too great zeal, whose perishable possession could be so easily shaken loose and slip away by so light a breath of violence.

12e.2. But the departure of the poet Aeschylus, as it was not voluntary, so on account of the novelty of the mischance is to be related. In Sicily, having gone out beyond the walls of the city in which he was staying, he sat down in a sunny place. Over him an eagle bearing a tortoise, deceived by the brightness of his head—for it was bare of hair—dashed it against him as though against a stone, so that, the shell broken, it might feed on the flesh; and by that blow the source and origin of the stronger tragedy was extinguished.

12e.3. The cause of Homer's death too is reported to have been not common, who in the island of Ios, because he could not solve a question put by fishermen, is believed to have been consumed by grief.

12e.4. But Euripides was ended somewhat more atrociously: for, making his way home from a dinner of king Archelaus in Macedonia to his host's house, he died torn by the bites of dogs—a cruelty of fate not owed to so great a genius.

12e.5. Just as those departures of illustrious poets were most unworthy both of their characters and of their works, so was Sophocles, now in extreme old age, when he had submitted a tragedy to the contest, long anxious at the doubtful outcome of the votes, yet at last victor by a single vote, had joy as the cause of his death.

12e.6. Philemon, moreover, the force of immoderate laughter carried off. Figs prepared for him and placed in his sight, an ass began to consume; he called out to a boy to drive it away. When the boy came up after all had now been eaten, "Since," he said, "you were so slow, give the ass now some unmixed wine"; and at once, accompanying the wit of his saying with frequent gasps of guffaws, he burdened his aged throat with the joltings of his breath.

12e.7. But Pindar, when in the gymnasium, his head placed upon the lap of a boy in whom he uniquely delighted, he had given himself to rest, was not known to have died before, when the gymnasiarch wished to close that place, he was in vain roused. To him indeed I should believe were granted, by the same kindness of the gods, both so great poetic eloquence and so peaceful an end of life.

12e.8. As to Anacreon too, whom, having passed the usual measure of human life, while he was nourishing the slender and feeble remains of his strength with the juice of dried grapes, a too obstinate delay of a single seed in his parched throat carried off.

12e.9. I shall join those whom both their purpose and their end made alike. Milo of Croton, when, making a journey, he had seen an oak split in a field by wedges driven in, relying on his strength approached it, and, inserting his hands, tried to tear it apart. The tree, the wedges being shaken out and it recalled to its own nature, compressed them, and offered him, with so many gymnastic palms, to be torn to pieces by wild beasts.

12e.10. Likewise the athlete Polydamas, forced by a storm to enter a cave, when, by the too great and sudden rush of water, it was shaken and falling, while his other companions went out in flight from the peril, alone remained, as though about to sustain on his own shoulders the mass of the whole ruin; but, overpowered by a weight more powerful than any human body, he had as the sepulchre of his senseless deed the hiding-place he had sought from the rain. These men can furnish a lesson that by too great strength of limbs the vigour of the mind is dulled, as though, nature refusing the bestowal of both goods, it were above mortal felicity for the same man to be both most strong and most wise.

13.pr. ON THE DESIRE OF LIFE But because we have touched in our discourse on departures from life both chance and manly, and some even rash, let us now subject to our estimation the nerveless and effeminate, so that by the very comparison it may be clear how much braver, and even wiser, the desire of death sometimes is than that of life.

M. Valerius Corvinus completed his hundredth year. Between his first and sixth consulships forty-six years intervened; and he was sufficient, with the strength of his body unimpaired, not only for the most splendid public services, but also for the most exact cultivation of his own fields—a model to be desired both as a citizen and as a head of a household.

M'. Aquilius, when he could have been extinguished gloriously, preferred to serve Mithridates basely. Whom would not someone deservedly call more worthy of a Pontic punishment than of a Roman command, since he brought it about that a private disgrace became a public blush?

The span of his life Metellus equalled, and in the fourth year after his consular commands, when very old, being created pontifex maximus, he carried the guardianship of the ceremonies for twenty-two years, neither with his mouth hesitating in pronouncing the vows nor with a trembling hand in performing the sacrifices.

Cn. Carbo too is of great shame to the Latin annals. In his third consulship, led to punishment in Sicily by order of Pompey, he begged of the soldiers humbly and tearfully that he might be allowed to relieve his bowels before he expired, so that he might enjoy the use of the most wretched light a little longer, drawing out his delay so far that his head was cut off while he sat in a filthy place. The very words of one relating so great a disgrace struggle with themselves, neither friendly to silence, because it does not deserve to be hidden, nor familiar to relation, because they are loathsome to tell.

Q. Fabius Maximus, moreover, held the priesthood of the augurate for sixty-two years, having attained it at an already robust age. And these two periods, if they be brought together into one, would easily fill out the measure of a century.

What of D. Brutus—with how great dishonour did he buy a scanty and unhappy moment of life! Who, caught by Furius, whom Antonius had sent to kill him, not only withdrew his neck from the sword, but even, being advised to offer it more steadfastly, swore in these very words, "So may I live, I will offer it." O wretched delaying of fate! O stupid faith in swearing! But you, immoderate sweetness of retaining the breath, suggest these frenzies, overcoming the measure of sound reason, which has taught us to love life, not to fear death.

13e.1. The same sweetness forced king Xerxes to pour out tears for the armed youth of all Asia, because within a hundred years it would die. He seems to me to have bewailed in appearance another's condition, in truth his own—happier in the greatness of his wealth than in any deeper feeling of mind: for who of moderate prudence would have wept that he was born mortal?

13e.2. I shall now report those who, holding some men suspected, sought a more exquisite guard of themselves: nor shall I begin from the most wretched, but from him who is believed to have been among the few most happy. King Masinissa, placing little trust in the breasts of men, walled his safety about with a guard of dogs. To what purpose so widely-extending an empire? To what so great a number of children? To what, finally, the friendship of Rome bound by so close a goodwill, if for guarding this he thought nothing stronger than the bark and bite of a dog?

13e.3. Than this king more unhappy was Alexander, whose heart on this side love, on that fear, tormented: for when he was held by an infinite ardour for his wife Thebe, coming to her from his feasts into the bedroom, he ordered a barbarian pricked with Thracian marks, with drawn sword, to go before him, nor did he commit himself to the same bed before he had been carefully searched by his guards. A punishment composed by an angry divine power, to be able to command neither lust nor fear. Of which fear the same was both the cause and the end: for Thebe, her anger roused by his concubinage, killed Alexander.

13e.4. Come now, Dionysius, tyrant of the Syracusans—how long a tale is there of this torment! Who carried through a domination of thirty-eight years in this manner. His friends removed, in their place he substituted men of the most ferocious nations, and most strong slaves chosen from the households of the wealthy, to whom he might commit his sides. Through fear of barbers too he taught his daughters to shave him. And of these very women, after they approached an adult age, not daring to entrust the steel to their hands, he established that they should singe his beard and hair with the glowing shells of walnuts. Nor did he act a less safe husband than father: for, bound at the same time by marriages to two women, Aristomache of Syracuse and Doris of Locri, he never sought the embrace of either except after she had been searched, and even surrounded his bedroom couch, just as a camp, with a broad ditch, into which he received himself by a wooden bridge, when he had himself carefully bolted with an inner bar the door of the bedroom, closed on the outside by the guards.

14.pr. ON RESEMBLANCE OF FORM About the resemblance of the face and of the whole body men endowed with deeper learning dispute more subtly, and some of them are of this opinion, that they think it corresponds to origin and to the connection of blood, and they draw no small argument from the other animals, which are generally born like their begetters. Others deny that this is a fixed law of nature, but that the appearances of mortals are assigned as the chance lot of conception offered them, and that therefore for the most part from handsome parents deformed and from robust ones weak offspring are produced. Therefore, since this question is in doubt, we shall report a few examples of resemblance observed among strangers.

Now what shall I say of M. Perpenna? Who survived all those whom he had as consul summoned into the senate, and saw remaining among the conscript fathers only the seven whom, as censor, with L. Philippus as colleague, he had chosen—more long-lived than the whole most ample order.

The age of Appius indeed I should measure by his calamity, because he passed an infinite number of years deprived of his sight, had he not, burdened by this misfortune, most bravely governed four sons, five daughters, very many dependents, and finally the state. Nay, even when now weary of living, he ordered himself to be carried in a litter into the senate-house, to prevent a disgraceful peace from being made with Pyrrhus. Let someone call this man blind, by whom his country, itself too little discerning of what was honourable, was forced to perceive it through him!

The span of women's lives too appeared no less long in several, of whom it will be enough for me to have related a few briefly: for both Livia, wife of Rutilius, completed her ninety-seventh year, and Terentia, wife of Cicero, her hundred and third, and Clodia, wife of Aufilius, having lost fifteen sons before, her hundred and fifteenth.

13e.1. I shall join to these two kings, whose long life was most useful to the Roman people. Hiero, ruler of Sicily, reached his ninetieth year. Masinissa, king of Numidia, exceeded this measure, having traversed a reign of sixty years, and admirable beyond all men for the strength of his old age. It is agreed that he—as Cicero relates in the book which he wrote On Old Age—could never be induced, by any rain or any cold, to cover his head with a garment. They report too that he was wont to stand for several hours in the same spot, not moving his foot before he had wearied young men with a like exertion; and if anything had to be done by him seated, he would often, the whole day through, hold out in his chair without turning his body in any direction. He even, mounted on his horse, would lead his armies, joining night to day for the most part, and omitted absolutely nothing of those toils which he had been accustomed as a young man to bear, that he might pass his old age more softly. He flourished also so always in the use of love that after his eighty-sixth year he begot a son, whose name was Methymnus. The land too, which he had received vast and deserted, he left fruitful by perpetual zeal of cultivation.

13e.2. Gorgias of Leontini too, the teacher of Isocrates and of very many men of great genius, was in his own opinion most happy: for when he was in his hundred and seventh year, being asked why he wished to remain so long in life, he said, "Because I have nothing of which to accuse my old age." What is either longer or more blessed than that stretch of years? Having now entered upon a second century, he neither found in this any complaint nor left any in the other.

13e.3. Two years younger was Xenophilus of Chalcis, a Pythagorean, but not inferior in good fortune, since indeed, as Aristoxenus the musician says, free of every human misfortune, he was extinguished in the highest splendour of the most perfect learning.

13e.4. Arganthonius of Gades, moreover, reigned as long as it would have been abundantly enough even to have lived to satiety: for he ruled his country for eighty years, having come to the throne forty years old. Of this matter there are sure authorities. Asinius Pollio too, no slight part of the Roman pen, in the third book of his Histories records that he completed a hundred and thirty years—himself no small example of a sinewy vivacity.

13e.5. The completion of this king's years the Ethiopians make less wonderful, whom Herodotus writes to pass the hundred and twentieth year, and the Indians, of whom Ctesias relates the same, and Epimenides of Cnossos, whom Theopompus says lived a hundred and fifty-seven years.

13e.6. Hellanicus, moreover, says that certain men of the people of the Epii, which is a part of Aetolia, complete two hundred years each, and Damastes subscribes to him, affirming this further, that a certain Litorius of these, of the greatest strength and outstanding stature, heaped up his three-hundredth year.

13e.7. Alexander, indeed, in that volume which he composed about the Illyrian region, affirms that a certain Dando advanced to his five-hundredth year, in no part growing old. But much more generously does Xenophon, whose Periplus is read: for he bestowed eight hundred years of life on the king of the island of the Latmii. And, lest his father should seem too little generously received, he assigned to him too six hundred years.

14.pr. ON THE DESIRE OF GLORY But whence glory arises, or what is its character, or by what means it ought to be acquired, and whether it is better neglected by virtue as not necessary—let those see who wear away their care in contemplating such things, and to whom it has fallen to express eloquently what they have prudently observed. I, content in this work to render their deeds to authors and their deeds to the authors, shall try to demonstrate by their proper examples how great the desire of it is wont to be.

The elder Africanus wished an image of the poet Ennius to be placed among the monuments of the Cornelian house, because he judged that his own deeds had been made illustrious by the man's genius—not, indeed, ignorant that, as long as the Roman empire flourished and Africa lay subjected at the feet of Italy and the Capitoline citadel held the highest summit of the whole world, the memory of them could not be extinguished, but esteeming it of great worth that to them the light of letters too should be added—a man worthier of a Homeric than of a rude and unpolished herald.

To Pompey the Great, Vibius, of free-born stock, and Publicius, a freedman, were so similar that, their condition exchanged, both Pompey could be saluted in them and they in Pompey. Certainly, wherever either Vibius or Publicius had come, they turned the faces of men toward themselves, each man noting the appearance of a most eminent citizen in persons of middling rank.

Similarly honoured was the mind toward the poet Accius of D. Brutus, a leader famous in his own times, who, delighted by his familiar attentions and ready praise, adorned with verses the entrances of the temples which he had consecrated from his spoils.

This chance mockery indeed penetrated to him as though hereditary: for his father too seemed so similar to Menogenes his cook that a man both most powerful in arms and fierce in spirit could not avail to repel from himself that sordid name.

Not even Pompey the Great was averse from this passion for glory, who presented Theophanes of Mitylene, the writer of his deeds, with citizenship in an assembly of his soldiers, accompanying the benefit, ample in itself, with a careful and attested speech as well. By which it was effected that no one should doubt that he was repaying gratitude rather than beginning it.

But Cornelius Scipio, a young man of outstanding nobility, when he abounded in very many and most distinguished surnames of his family, was branded in the common talk with the servile appellation of Serapio, because he was exceedingly like a victimarius of this name. Nor did either the uprightness of his character or the regard for so many ancestral images help him not to be spattered with this insult.

L. Sulla, moreover, although he directed his attention to no writer, nevertheless claimed for himself so eagerly the whole credit of Jugurtha being handed over by king Bocchus to Marius, that he had that surrender engraved on the signet ring which he used. And how great he afterwards became, who despised not even the least trace of glory!

A most well-born college of the consulship was that of Lentulus and Metellus. Both were on the stage all but gazed at on account of their resemblance to actors. But the one drew the surname Spinther from a certain player of second parts; the other, had he not received that of Nepos from his character, would have had that of Pamphilus, a player of third parts, to whom he was reported to be most similar.

And, to append to commanders the glory-loving spirit of a soldier: when Scipio was distributing military gifts to those who had displayed energetic service, T. Labienus advised him to bestow golden armlets on a brave horseman, and when Scipio denied that he would do this, lest a camp honour should be profaned in one who a little before had been a slave, Labienus himself bestowed on the horseman gold from the Gallic plunder. Nor did Scipio take this in silence: for to the horseman he said, "You will have the gift of a rich man." And when the man received it, throwing the gold before the feet of Labienus, he cast down his face. The same man, when he heard Scipio saying, "The commander presents you with silver armlets," went off eager with joy. There is, then, no humility so great that it is not touched by the sweetness of glory.

But M. Messala, consular and censorian, was forced to receive the name of Menogenes, and Curio, abounding in all honours, that of Burbuleius—the former on account of the look of his face, the latter on account of a like movement of his body—both the name of a stage-player. Let these things about our own people be enough, since they are both of distinguished persons and are made famous by no obscure renown.

14e.1. To king Antiochus one of his peers, himself too of royal stock, named Artemo, is reported to have been exceedingly similar. Him Laodice, the wife of Antiochus, when she had killed her husband, for the sake of disguising her crime laid on a couch just as though it were the sick king himself, and, the whole people being admitted, deceived them by his speech and his very similar countenance; and men believed that by the dying Antiochus Laodice and her sons were being commended to them.

14e.2. But Hybreas of Mylasa, an orator of copious and excited eloquence, the eyes of all Asia all but assigned as a brother-german to the slave of a man of Cyme who collected the scrapings of the gymnasium: so matched were they in the outlines of the face and of all the limbs.

14e.3. But that man, who in Sicily is agreed to have been exceedingly like the governor of the province, was of a saucy spirit: for, when the proconsul said that he wondered why he was so like himself, since his father had never gone to that province, "But mine," he said, "went to Rome": for, the chastity of his own mother having been provoked in jest, he avenged it by throwing back the suspicion in turn upon the proconsul's mother, more boldly than was fitting for one subject to the rods and axes.

15.pr. ON THOSE WHO, BORN IN THE LOWEST PLACE, TRIED BY A LIE TO INSERT THEMSELVES INTO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED FAMILIES But this rashness is tolerable and perilous to one man only. The kind of shamelessness that follows is neither to be endured in any way and is widely perilous both privately and also publicly.

But this was sometimes sought even by famous men from the most humble matters: for what did C. Fabius, a most noble citizen, mean, who, when he had painted the walls in the temple of Salus, which C. Junius Bubulcus had dedicated, inscribed on them his own name? For this alone was wanting to the ornament of a family most renowned for consulships and priesthoods and triumphs. But a mind given over to a sordid pursuit was unwilling that that labour of his, whatever it was, should be blotted out in silence—following, of course, the example of Phidias, who enclosed his own likeness in the shield of Minerva, in such a way that, if it were torn out, the whole binding-together of the work would be loosened.

14e.1. But somewhat better, if he was captivated by imitation of another, would he have emulated the ardour of Themistocles, who, they say, driven on by the goads of virtue, and on that account passing restless nights, replied to those who asked why he was abroad at that hour, "Because the trophies of Miltiades rouse me from sleep." Marathon, surely, was urging on his mind by silent torches to make illustrious Artemisium and Salamis, names fertile in naval glory. The same man, going to the theatre, when he was asked whose voice would be most pleasant to him to hear, said, "His by whom my deeds shall be best sung." The sweetness of glory—I almost added, glorious!

14e.2. For the breast of Alexander was insatiable of praise, who, when his companion Anaxarchus, on the authority of his teacher Democritus, related that there were innumerable worlds, said, "Alas, wretched me, that I have not yet made myself master even of one!" A narrow possession for the man, which is sufficient for the dwelling of all the gods.

14e.3. To the most ardent desire of the king and young man I shall append the like thirst of Aristotle in grasping at praise: for he had presented to his pupil Theodectes the books of the oratorical art to publish as his own, and afterwards, taking it ill that their title had thus passed to another, in a volume of his own, dwelling on certain matters, he added that these had been treated more plainly by himself in the books of Theodectes. Did not the modesty of so great and so widely extending a knowledge restrain me, I should say that he was a philosopher worthy that the establishing of his morals should be handed over to a philosopher of loftier mind. But glory is neglected not even by those who try to introduce contempt of it, since indeed they diligently add their own names to their very volumes, so that what they belittle by their profession they may attain by the usurpation of memory. But the dissimulation of these, of whatever sort, is far more tolerable than the purpose of those who, in order to attain eternal memory, did not hesitate to become notorious even by crimes.

14e.4. Of whose number I do not know whether Pausanias should not be reported among the first: for when he had inquired of Hermocles how he could suddenly become famous, and he had replied that, if he killed some illustrious man, it would come about that his glory would overflow to him, he at once slew Philip, and indeed attained what he had sought: for he made himself as known to posterity by his murder as Philip by his virtue.

14e.5. But that desire of glory was sacrilegious: for there was found one who wished to burn the temple of Diana at Ephesus, so that, the most beautiful work being consumed, his name might be spread throughout the whole world; which madness of mind he disclosed when placed on the rack.
