And the Ephesians had well consulted by a decree abolishing the memory of the most foul man, had not the genius of Theopompus of great eloquence embraced him in his histories.

15.pr. THE MAGNIFICENT THINGS THAT BEFELL EACH MAN To candid minds, moreover, the magnificent things which deservedly befell each man, placed in view, will afford pleasure, because the contemplation of the rewards of virtue is as pleasant as that of its works, nature herself supplying us with eagerness, when we see honour industriously sought and gratefully discharged. But although the mind in this place is borne at once with all its impulse to the Augustan house, that most beneficent and most honoured temple, it will better be restrained, since to him for whom the ascent into heaven lies open, the things that are bestowed on earth, however great, are yet less than is due.

To the elder Africanus the consulship was given before the lawful time, because the army admonished the senate by letter that it ought to be done. So you would not know whether the authority of the conscript fathers or the counsel of the soldiers added the more distinction to him: for the toga created Scipio leader against the Carthaginians, but arms demanded it. The chief things assigned to him in his life it would be both long to relate, because they are many, and not necessary, because they have for the most part already been related. And so I shall add what even today receives outstanding honour. He has an image placed in the chamber of Jupiter Best and Greatest, which, as often as any funeral of the Cornelian house is to be celebrated, is sought from there; and to him alone the Capitol serves as an entrance-hall:

For, to pass over Equitius, a monster coming from Firmum in Picenum, already related in the earlier part of this book, whose evident lie in embracing Ti. Gracchus as his father was, by the turbulent error of the crowd, walled about with the most ample power of the tribunate—Herophilus, an eye doctor, by claiming C. Marius, seven times consul, as his grandfather, brought it about that several colonies of veterans and splendid municipalities and almost all the guilds adopted him as their patron. Nay, even when C. Caesar had admitted the people into his gardens, the young Cn. Pompeius having been crushed in Spain, Herophilus, in the next intercolumniation, was saluted with an almost equal zeal of crowding. And unless the divine strength of Caesar had withstood this blush-worthy storm, the state would have received a similar wound to that which it had received in Equitius. But, relegated beyond Italy by Caesar's decree, after he was received into heaven, he returned to the city and brought himself to form a plan of killing the senate. On which charge, slain by order of the fathers, he paid in prison the late penalties of a spirit ready for the contriving of every crime.

as much, by Hercules, as the senate-house does as the entrance-hall of the image of the elder Cato, which is brought out for the services of his kind. A grateful order, which wished to have a senator most useful to the state all but always dwelling with it—rich in every measure of virtue, and great rather by his own desert than by the benefit of fortune, by whose counsel rather than by Scipio's command Carthage was destroyed.

Not even the most excellent divine power of the deified Augustus, even now ruling the earth, was untried by this kind of injury. There arose one who dared to feign that he was born from the womb of his most distinguished and most holy sister Octavia, and, on account of the great weakness of his body, was retained by the man to whom he had been given as if his own son, with the man's own son substituted in his place—saying this, of course, so that at the same time the most holy household gods should be robbed of the memory of their true blood and stained by the sordid contagion of the false. But while with sails full of shamelessness he was borne to the highest step of audacity, by the command of Augustus he was fastened to the oar of a public trireme.

A rare specimen of honour arises in Scipio Nasica too: for the senate wished the goddess summoned from Pessinus at the warning of Pythian Apollo to be received by his hands and household gods, while he was not yet even a quaestor, because by the same oracle it had been enjoined that these services should be rendered to the Mother of the gods by the most blameless man. Unroll the whole calendar, set up all the triumphal chariots, yet you will find nothing more splendid than a primacy of character.
There was found too one who said that he was the son of Q. Sertorius, whom his wife could be compelled by no force to acknowledge.

From time to time the Scipios furnish us with their distinctions to be recorded: for the people made Aemilianus consul out of a candidate for the aedileship. The same man, when at the quaestorian elections he had come down into the Campus as a supporter of Q. Fabius Maximus, his brother's son, it brought back as consul a second time. To him the senate twice gave a province without the lot, first Africa, then Spain—and these things neither to an ambitious citizen . . . a senator, as not only the most severe course of his life but even his death, brought by secret treachery, declared.

What of Trebellius Calca—how assertively did he carry himself as Clodius! And indeed, while he contended about his goods, he came down into the court of the Hundred Men so favourably that consternation of the people scarcely left any place for just and fair verdicts. Nevertheless in that inquiry the conscientiousness of the judges yielded neither to the calumny of the claimant nor to the violence of the plebs.

M. Valerius too the gods and his fellow citizens alike rendered conspicuous by two notable things, the gods by sending a raven as his champion when he was fighting hand to hand with a certain Gaul, the citizens by granting him the consulship when he had entered his twenty-third year. The one of these distinctions a family of ancient origin, of best name, has embraced and assumes, taking the surname Corvinus; the other it joins to its highest ornament, glorying as much in the speed as in the beginning of the consulship.

Much bolder was that man who, when Cornelius Sulla was master of affairs, burst into the house of Cn. Asinius Dio and drove his son from the paternal household gods, vociferating that not he, but himself, had been begotten by Dio. But after Caesarian equity restored the state from Sullan violence, the helm of the Roman empire being held by a juster prince, he gave up his breath in public custody.

15e.1. Under the same guardian of the state, in a like lie, a woman's rashness was suppressed at Milan. Since indeed, when a certain woman, as though it had been falsely believed that Rubria had perished in a fire, tried to insert herself into goods in no way pertaining to her, and there were not wanting to her either the splendid witnesses of that region or the favour of the Augustan cohort, on account of the unconquerable steadfastness of Caesar she went off frustrated of her wicked design.

15e.2. The same guardian of the state forced a certain barbarian aiming at the kingdom of Cappadocia on account of his outstanding resemblance, as though he were Ariarathes—whom it was clearer than daylight had been killed by M. Antonius—although his head, propped up by the credulous support of almost all the cities and peoples of the East, madly threatened the empire, to undergo a just punishment.

Nor indeed is the glory of Q. Scaevola, whom L. Crassus had as colleague in the consulship, too little illustrious, who held Asia so uprightly and so bravely that the senate afterwards set forth Scaevola by its decree as the model and norm of duty to magistrates going to that province.

To a single saying of the younger Africanus there cling the seven consulships of C. Marius and his two most ample triumphs: for to his very pyre he exulted with joy that, when at Numantia he was serving cavalry campaigns under Scipio as leader, and by chance at dinner a certain man had asked Scipio, if anything happened to him, what equally great commander the state would have, Scipio, looking back at him reclining above himself, said, "This man here." Whether by this augury the most perfect virtue saw more surely or kindled more effectively the greatest rising virtue can scarcely be weighed: that military dinner, surely, omened the most splendid dinners that were to be Marius's throughout the whole city: for after the news that the Cimbri had been destroyed by him came at the beginning of the night, there was no one who did not pour a libation to him, as to the immortal gods, at the sacred rites of his own table.

Now the things both ample and new that were heaped upon Cn. Pompeius resound in the monuments of letters, here with the assent of favour, there with the murmur of envy. A Roman knight, he was sent as proconsul into Spain against Sertorius with an equal command alongside Pius Metellus, the leading man of the state. Having as yet taken the auspices of no curule honour, he triumphed twice. He took the beginnings of his magistracies from the highest command. His third consulship, by decree of the senate, he held alone. Over Mithridates and Tigranes, over many kings besides and very many states and peoples and pirates, he led a single triumph.

Q. Catulus too the Roman people exalted by its own voice almost to the very stars: for when he asked by them before the rostra whether, if he had persisted in placing everything in the one Pompey the Great, in whom he would have hope should the onset of a sudden mischance carry him off, with the highest consensus they cried out, "In you." A power of honoured judgment to be admired! Since indeed it equalled to Catulus Pompey the Great, with all the ornaments which I have related, enclosed within the space of two syllables.

The landing of M. Cato too, returning from Cyprus with the royal money, at the bank of the city may seem memorable, to whom, as he disembarked from his ship, the consuls and the other magistrates and the whole senate and the Roman people were present for the sake of paying respect—rejoicing not that he brought a great weight of gold and silver, but that that fleet had brought M. Cato safe.

But I do not know whether L. Marcius is not the chief example of unusual distinction, whom, a Roman knight, two armies, torn by the death of P. and Cn. Scipio and the victory of Hannibal, chose as their leader, at a time when their safety, reduced to the utmost straits, left no place for ambition.

Deservedly to the commemoration of these men is added Sulpicia, daughter of Servius Paterculus, wife of Q. Fulvius Flaccus, who, when the senate, the Sibylline books having been inspected by the decemvirs, had decreed that an image of Venus Verticordia should be consecrated, so that the mind of maidens and women might more easily be turned from lust to chastity, and that out of all the matrons a hundred, and out of the hundred ten chosen by lot, should make judgment about the most blameless woman—was preferred to all in chastity.

15e.1. But since, without any diminution of Roman majesty, foreign distinctions too can be regarded, we shall pass over to them. To Pythagoras so great veneration was granted by his hearers that they thought it sacrilege to bring into dispute what they had received from him. Nay, even when challenged to render a reason, they answered only this, that he himself had said it. A great honour, but only within the school: that other was granted by the votes of cities. With earnest zeal the people of Croton begged of him that he should suffer their senate, which consisted of a thousand men, to use his counsels; and that most opulent state, having venerated his so well-frequented house, made it after his death a shrine of Ceres; and as long as that city flourished, both the goddess was worshipped in the memory of the man and the man in the religion of the goddess.

15e.2. To Gorgias of Leontini, indeed, surpassing all the men of his age in the studies of letters—so much so that he was the first to dare in an assembly to ask about what matter each man wished to hear—all Greece set up in the temple of Delphic Apollo a statue of solid gold, whereas up to that time it had placed gilded ones of others.

15e.3. The same people with the highest consensus bent itself to honouring Amphiaraus, reducing the place where he was buried to the form and condition of a temple, and there establishing the receiving of oracles. His ashes possess the same honour that is given to the Pythian tripod, to the bronze of Dodona, to the fountain of Hammon.

15e.4. Of Berenice too the honour was not common, to whom alone of all women it was permitted to be present at a gymnastic spectacle, when she had brought her son Eucles to enter the contest at Olympia—herself born of an Olympic victor as father, and with brothers who had attained the same palm girding her sides.

1.pr. ON LUXURY AND LUST Luxury too, an alluring evil, which it is somewhat easier to accuse than to avoid, let it be inserted into our work—not, indeed, that it may receive any honour, but so that, recognizing itself, it may be driven to repentance. Let lust be joined with it, since it arises from the same beginnings of vices; nor let them be separated either from reproach or from correction, bound together as they are by a twin error of the mind.
